book: How to write a good resume
summary: A ByteByteGo guide for software developers on how hiring works and how to write, structure, tailor and lay out a resume, with examples and templates.

unitSummaries.Introduction and Chapter 1: The goal of a resume, what separates good from great, and why LinkedIn and even a resume alone are not enough.
unitSummaries.Chapter 2: How recruiters, hiring managers and applicant tracking systems process applications, and where the resume sits in that process.
unitSummaries.Chapter 3: The first glance a resume gets, ground rules, simplicity and consistency, and leaving out personal details and photos.
unitSummaries.Chapter 4: How to structure a resume for new graduates, working developers and senior people, including languages, technologies and the summary.
unitSummaries.Chapter 5: Writing results and impact, not being humble, tailoring to each job and company, and using keywords without stuffing.
unitSummaries.Chapter 6: Poor format, forgetting the audience, unnecessary details and badly handled links, with the fix for each.
unitSummaries.Chapter 7: How to adapt a resume for students, bootcamp graduates, career changers, career breaks, senior engineers, tech leads and engineering managers.
unitSummaries.Chapters 8 and 9: Exercises to polish a resume, then LinkedIn, GitHub, blogs, social sites and cover letters as the rest of the application.
unitSummaries.Chapter 10: Top-down and two-column layouts, how recruiters and hiring managers scan a resume, and what a good template achieves.
unitSummaries.Chapter 11: Resume generators versus templates, the recommended developer template, reviews of templates and other options.
unitSummaries.Chapter 12: Real anonymised resumes of different levels, with the improvements made and the reasons for them.
unitSummaries.Chapter 13: Why screening is often broken and how hiring managers can treat recruitment as a partner function, write good job descriptions and keep a feedback loop.
unitSummaries.Reading the book as a whole: Connects the hiring pipeline, resume rules and templates into one approach to a strong application.

concepts.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
concepts.title: What the author's experience backs up
concepts.question: What is the author's claim about resumes based on, and how strong does the book say it is?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you weigh a tip in this book, separate the claim, the evidence the author gives for it and the strength he says that evidence has.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Decide how much weight each piece of advice deserves before you rebuild your resume around it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The advice comes from the author's own work as a hiring manager, not from a controlled study. The book itself calls its content opinion that might not apply in every country, industry or company.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author, who writes a newsletter for engineering managers and senior engineers, says most developer resumes he saw hid the person behind them. In a hurry, he would have passed on many otherwise strong candidates.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The book reports that he reviewed over a thousand resumes in a few years and, in one week of May 2020, more than 300, with feedback on each. It gives no hiring results for his advice.

blocks.label: Our reading
blocks.text: The book does not say how those resumes were chosen or whether his hunches were checked against outcomes. Treat the advice as an informed view, not a measured result.

card.rule: Separate the claim, the evidence offered and the strength the author gives it.
card.limits: Experience-based advice can still be wrong for your market. The author tells you to do your own research and ask your network.

concepts.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
concepts.title: Is this advice written for you?
concepts.question: Which jobs, regions and employers was this advice written for, and how far does it carry beyond them?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check that a resume tip was written for your kind of job, region and employer before you act on it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Put your effort into advice that is likely to fit your own applications.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author wrote for developer jobs at tech companies in the US, Europe and India where business is done in English, with well-known names and fast-growing startups especially in mind. He says other industries and companies follow other processes and look for other things.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (Our illustration) A software developer applying to a fast-growing US startup is the reader the book describes. Someone applying in another industry, or at a firm that does not work in English, is outside it and should treat each tip as a lead to check.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author calls everything in the book opinion that may not apply to your country, industry or company. He says to do your own research and ask your network, since no approach suits everyone.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: List your target companies and mark which ones match the audience described above.

card.rule: Match a tip to your job, region and employer before using it.
card.limits: The author's scope is a guide, not a wall: he thinks the principles likely carry over, but processes differ, so test them.

concepts.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
concepts.title: A guide, not a guarantee
concepts.question: What can this book promise about your results, and what can it not?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the book for context and structure in writing, not as a promise of a recruiter call; silence after applying does not show that the resume is bad.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Write your resume with more structure and confidence while keeping realistic expectations.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Hiring differs by company and even by hiring manager, and whether you get a follow-up call depends on factors nobody can predict. So the author says no template or content always leads to a recruiter call.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author compares resumes with software work: engineers know no single language suits every website and no single architecture suits every complex application. In the same way, no single resume template wins every time.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book cannot tell you why a particular company did not reply, and it is not an official guide for any company it mentions.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Before your next application, write what you control (content, tailoring) and what you do not.

card.rule: A good guide gives context and structure, not a guaranteed call.
card.limits: Our reading: Not being able to promise results does not make the advice useless; it still helps you avoid representing yourself badly.

concepts.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
concepts.title: A plan for reading the book
concepts.question: In what order should you read the book and write your resume to end with a better resume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Skim the whole book once, pick one or two resume templates, then write or rewrite your resume while you work through the Part 2 exercises.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Finish with an actual improved resume rather than only a finished read.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Part 1 explains why resumes matter and how hiring works. Knowing who reads your resume and how the process runs lets you write it on purpose. The author suggests starting with Part 1 if you have never been a hiring manager.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Part 1 gives context on resumes and hiring. Part 2 gives actionable advice, one area of the resume per chapter, heavy on examples and with a recap of actions at the end of each chapter. Part 3 gives templates and anonymised example resumes.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: If you have been a hiring manager yourself, the advice to start with Part 1 does not apply to you.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Skim the table of contents now and note which template you might start from.

card.rule: Skim once, choose templates, then write while doing the exercises.
card.limits: This is the author's recommendation, not the only possible route; his own reasoning for Part 1 depends on you not having hired.

concepts.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
concepts.title: Written for a scan of seconds
concepts.question: How long does a first reader give a resume, and what does that mean for how you write it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Write the resume so a reader who gives it only seconds can already see why you fit this job.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Pass the first scan so that someone reads on.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A hiring manager glances at a resume for 10 to 20 seconds to decide whether to read more, and the book cites a study putting the average recruiter at about 7 seconds. In that time the reader decides to reject or read further.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Going through over a hundred resumes in a hurry, the author says he would have passed on many strong, qualified candidates because their potential did not come across. He warns you may lose to someone equally qualified whose resume sells better.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The 10 to 20 seconds is the author's own habit as a hiring manager. The 7 seconds is credited in a footnote to an eye-tracking study reported by HR Drive; the book gives no further detail.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Seconds describe the first screen only. A resume that passes it can then be read in depth.

card.rule: Make the fit visible within a few seconds of reading.
card.limits: Our reading: The figures describe typical first reads; a particular reader may spend longer, and later reading is more thorough.

concepts.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
concepts.title: The goal is the interview
concepts.question: What is a resume for, and what is it explicitly not for?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Write each resume to win an interview for one specific position, not to record your whole history.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get a foot in the door with a recruiter or hiring manager at that company.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says the goal is the interview and nothing more. A resume is not meant to share a complete work history or to represent everything you did as accurately as possible; it is meant to sell you for that position. The rest of the book revolves around this goal.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Many people create a resume only because the application form needs an upload. They search for a template, fill in their experience and submit, doing the work without thinking about the goal.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The goal does not excuse exaggeration: the book's idea of a good resume is one that represents you as fairly as possible.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Write the interview you want in one sentence: which role, at which company.

card.rule: A resume exists to win the interview for that position.
card.limits: Our reading: Selecting what to include is not permission to mislead; the aim is the fairest picture that still sells you for the role.

concepts.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
concepts.title: Jump out of the pile
concepts.question: How does a busy hiring manager sort a large pile of resumes, and what does it take to land in the top pile?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Aim to jump out as a Yes-pile candidate by making your fit for the job clear on the first scan.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Be one of the few resumes that reach an interview.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A hiring manager with hundreds of resumes must cut them to a few interviews as fast as possible. The quoted manager sorts them into Yes, Maybe and No piles and looks mainly for reasons to put a resume in No.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The manager lists reasons for the No pile: poor spelling, poor grammar, no relevant experience in the last two years, or a different tech stack. The Yes pile holds at most five, and so does Maybe; everything else goes to No.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: One hiring manager with two decades of experience describes his own process. The author calls the Yes/Maybe/No approach typical of how hiring managers and recruiters screen; the book gives no counts of how many use it.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A Maybe can lose: if enough Yes candidates pass the phone screen, you may get no call even at the top of the Maybe pile.

card.rule: Make the match obvious enough to earn a Yes.
card.limits: Our reading: Even a strong resume may land in Maybe on a day with many strong rivals; the sort is quick and not fully in your control.

concepts.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
concepts.title: Good first, then great
concepts.question: What separates a good resume from a great one, and which of the two can you control?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: First make the resume good, meaning fair to you; then aim for great by showing rare, valuable experience that fits the specific role.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid losing chances through under-selling, and stand out for roles you suit.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A good resume represents you as fairly as possible and gives a qualified person the best chance of getting through screening. A great one makes the reader want to talk to you at once, and that depends on content, not on format.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book imagines an expert in a niche framework applying directly to a small company that is rebuilding its product in that framework; the recruiter would not believe their luck. A senior frontend developer from Google is not automatically great for a backend role that needs deep developer-tooling expertise.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Even a good resume will not win every time: your profile may not match, or stronger profiles may compete.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: Believing that a famous employer on the page makes any resume great.

card.rule: A good resume is fair; a great one is great for that specific role.
card.limits: Our reading: No resume is great for every role. Greatness depends on the match between your experience and what that job needs.

concepts.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
concepts.title: A famous name does not sell you
concepts.question: Can a well-known employer carry your resume, or must you show what you did there?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do not let a famous employer's name do the selling; pick out your most important personal contributions and put them on the page.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get interviews by showing what you did, not only where you worked.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The name of a well-regarded company catches the eye but will not always get you through the door. Hiring managers want people who can help with their current challenges of building software and shipping value.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An engineer with five combined years at Apple and Google, then at a small company, got few interviews. The resume linked a barely working prototype and said little about the big-company work. After a rework it named a complex backend system, leading a team of three on a Google project and a hard problem solved at Apple; interviews kept coming.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This is one case told by the author, who read the original resume and then talked with its owner. The book gives the result as the interviews that followed.

blocks.label: Our reading
blocks.text: A single case cannot show how much of the change came from the rewrite and how much from other factors.

card.rule: Show your best personal contributions; the employer's name is not enough.
card.limits: Our reading: A famous name still helps, but it does not replace evidence of what you did. A strong resume needs both.

concepts.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
concepts.title: Make growth visible
concepts.question: How does a resume show career progression, and why might its absence get you rejected?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Make growth visible: show promotions, more responsibility, vertical moves, initiative and harder problems, so your resume does not read as a journeyman resume.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Pass screens at high-growth companies that look for signs of progression.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says some great resumes show solid career progression toward the current role. A journeyman resume tells a story of little or no progression over long stretches, and for high-growth companies that can be a reason for rejection because they look for growth.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (Our illustration) A resume that traces promotions and widening responsibility year by year reads very differently from one that shows the same level of work across a long stretch.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Not every employer screens for progression; the author ties the rejection risk to high-growth companies.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Mark each promotion, scope increase or vertical move in your history on a timeline.

card.rule: Show the increase in responsibility, not only the list of jobs.
card.limits: Visibility helps only if growth happened; the author asks you to check honestly whether your story is badly told.

concepts.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
concepts.title: A LinkedIn export is not a resume
concepts.question: Why is an exported LinkedIn profile a poor substitute for a resume when you apply directly?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: For a direct application, send a resume tailored to that job instead of an exported LinkedIn profile.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Be easy for a recruiter to scan and show real interest in that particular job.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says LinkedIn is a tool for getting sourced when you are in demand and a poor one for applying directly. Its export wastes space, is not built for scanning, cannot be tailored to a position, keeps no versions and locks you into a feature that may change.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer with fullstack experience could apply to frontend, backend or fullstack roles. Each role calls for its own resume, but a LinkedIn profile gives one generic version.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Exported profiles can work when few people apply or your experience stands out. Keep your LinkedIn up to date regardless.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Open a PDF export of your profile and mark every line that does not help one target role.

card.rule: Tailor a resume for each direct application; do not rely on a LinkedIn export.
card.limits: Our reading: In a hot market or with standout experience, a thin application can succeed; the advice matters most when competition is real.

concepts.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
concepts.title: Necessary, not sufficient
concepts.question: Why can a well-written resume still fail to get a call, and what do you do about it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat a well-written resume as necessary but not sufficient: fix what you control and do not blame the resume for outside factors.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep realistic expectations and put effort where it can change the outcome.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says several things that decide a recruiter call are outside your control. Among them: the position may already be filled, you may face many stronger applicants, and your visa status can add cost and time for the company.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A reader wrote that he had applied to Facebook in London, Stripe in New York and Snap in Los Angeles, heard nothing, and asked for help fixing his resume to get an interview.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The book gives this message as one of several in which people think format is the only obstacle. It does not say how common the belief is.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The list is no reason to stop improving the resume: the author still calls a well-written resume required.

card.rule: A good resume is required, but it does not decide the outcome alone.
card.limits: Our reading: Knowing the limits of a resume does not excuse a weak one; it only stops you blaming it for what it cannot fix.

concepts.title: The hiring manager runs the show
concepts.question: Who runs a hiring process, and who makes the final decision?

paragraphs: The author calls the hiring manager the most important person in the process. This is the person who opened the position (a headcount, in company terms), set its requirements and usually wrote the job description.
The hiring manager also has the final hire or no-hire decision, and the aim is a team that excels. Candidates usually do not speak to this person until the onsite stage.
card.rule: The hiring manager sets the requirements and has the final say; everyone else works within them.
card.limits: Our reading: This describes the typical large-company process; at small companies the hiring manager also does the screening, as later ideas show.

media.alt: Diagram of recruitment roles drawn as avatar circles with labels. The hiring manager sits at the top. Below left, the recruiter has three roles beneath: sourcer, inbound sourcer and recruitment coordinator. Separately on the right, a group of three avatars forms the interview panel.

concepts.title: Recruiter and sourcer
concepts.question: How does a recruiter's job differ from a sourcer's?

paragraphs: The recruiter coordinates everything on the recruitment side. Once a profile looks promising, the recruiter is in touch with the candidate and guides them through the process. The aim is to fill the roles the hiring manager asks for with people who meet the bar.

The sourcer works earlier: reaching out on LinkedIn and other channels to get people interested in starting the process. At large companies sourcers only do reach-outs and sell the position in conversation, then hand interested people with good profiles to the recruiter.
card.rule: Sourcers bring people into the process; recruiters guide them through it.
card.limits: Our reading: smaller companies may spread these jobs across fewer people, since the author says dedicated roles exist mostly at larger companies.

concepts.title: Inbound sourcer, coordinator and interview panel
concepts.question: What do the inbound sourcer, recruitment coordinator and interview panel each do?

paragraphs: The inbound sourcer screens applications that arrive through the company jobs site. This is a specialised role at larger companies, where one role can draw hundreds of applications a week. The goal is to forward qualified candidates to the recruiter without wasting the recruiter's time.

The recruitment coordinator handles logistics: scheduling you and the panel, swapping interviewers, rescheduling and booking travel for onsites. The interview panel is the group of engineers who lead the technical interviews. They are trained and calibrated, and aim to keep the bar fair, consistent and as bias-free as possible.
card.rule: Inbound sourcers screen applications, coordinators run logistics, and the panel interviews.
card.limits: These are specialist roles at larger companies; the author notes that at very small companies the hiring manager does much of this work.

concepts.title: Recruiters are on your side, within limits
concepts.question: How should a candidate read the encouragement and rejections that recruiters and sourcers deliver?

paragraphs: The author says many candidates do not assume the recruiter and inbound sourcer are fundamentally on their side. Both need to make hires to hit their goals. They also balance the hiring manager's expectations, and if the manager asked explicitly for certain technologies or years of experience, they will most likely follow that.

A LinkedIn reach-out comes from a sourcer, who wants to get you into the pipeline. However encouraging, it does not guarantee a job: you still go through the interviews. A recruiter phoning about a rejection is often only the messenger.
card.rule: Treat recruiters as allies who are bound by the manager's requirements and who do not decide alone.
card.limits: These are the author's general points; the author adds that experiences vary widely between companies and individual recruiters.

concepts.title: The stages of the pipeline
concepts.question: Why is the process called a pipeline, and what are its stages in order?

paragraphs: Hiring managers and recruiters call the process a pipeline because at every stage a significant number of candidates drop out. At a typical tech company the order is: applicant tracking system queue, resume screen, recruiter screen, technical screen, onsite interviews, offer.
You can be rejected at each round or, if you do well, move on until you get an offer. The author's figure shows a large, well-known company; the actual process and numbers vary by role and company.
card.rule: Every stage removes candidates, so you must clear each stage in turn.
card.limits: The stages are typical, not universal: the author says the process and numbers differ by role and company, and later sections show shorter pipelines at small firms.

media.alt: Funnel diagram of a typical hiring pipeline at a large company, with counts from top to bottom: submitted resumes, applicant tracking queue, resume screen, recruiter screen, technical screen, onsite, offer. Numbers shrink sharply after the resume screen. Side callouts describe each stage, including a few seconds of scanning at the resume screen.

concepts.title: The queue: late resumes may go unread
concepts.question: Why might a qualified candidate's resume never be looked at?

paragraphs: The first stage is the applicant tracking system (ATS) queue. Not every application reaches the resume review. One reason is that the previous batch already gave enough qualified resumes; another is that the position has just been filled.

So, in general, the later your resume comes in, the higher the chance it will not be looked at, because enough qualified candidates are already further along the pipeline. Better companies still send a standard rejection notice when an application is not processed further.
card.rule: Apply early: a later resume has a higher chance of going unread.
card.limits: The author states a tendency, not a fixed rule, and whether a rejection notice arrives depends on the company's policy.

concepts.title: The resume screen: seconds, and the steepest drop
concepts.question: Who screens resumes, for how long, and where is the dropoff steepest?

paragraphs: In most companies recruiters do the resume screen; some larger companies, particularly in Silicon Valley, use a specialised inbound sourcer. They scan your resume for 5 to 20 seconds to judge whether you might be a match.

A promising first scan earns a longer, in-depth read. Otherwise you may get an automated rejection, if the company has a policy to send one. The dropoff is usually steepest here: from hundreds of resumes only a few dozen lead to a recruiter call, which is why the author says to tailor the resume.
card.rule: You have seconds to look like a match, so make your fit visible on the first scan.
card.limits: The 5 to 20 seconds is the author's typical range, and whether a rejection message is sent depends on company policy.

concepts.title: Recruiter, technical and onsite stages
concepts.question: What happens at the recruiter screen, the technical screen and the onsite?

paragraphs: Only profiles that look like a promising fit reach the recruiter screen: a phone call to confirm experience, motivation, and touch on soft skills. The technical screen is a phone screen and/or a take-home coding challenge, and candidates almost always deal with software engineers there.
The onsite has several interviews, such as coding, hiring manager and systems design. Each is a separate round at which a candidate can be rejected.
card.rule: Each later stage tests something different: fit, coding, then a full set of interviews.
card.limits: These are typical stages at large companies; the author says the real process varies by role and company.

concepts.title: What an applicant tracking system is for
concepts.question: What is an ATS for, and who moves candidates through it?

paragraphs: An applicant tracking system tracks the lifecycle of applications and helps recruiters coordinate. It keeps the status of each application and shows it to all recruiters. This is how a sourcer knows not to contact someone who is interviewing now or who recently declined an offer.

The workflow is human-based. An application starts as an unviewed applicant, and people (recruiters or hiring managers) move its status along, for example to In Review or Rejected. Statuses and workflows differ between companies, and flexible setup is a big focus of ATS features.
card.rule: An ATS is a status tracker that people operate; it does not make the decisions.
card.limits: Statuses and workflows differ by company, so the author's example boxes show one set-up, not a standard.

media.alt: Screenshot of an applicant tracking system pipeline view for one position, with Unreviewed and In Pipeline tabs and a search filter. A table lists candidates with columns for name, location, current role, highest education and number of job applications. Recruiters must open each candidate to process them.

Flowchart of statuses in an applicant tracking system. A grey Unviewed Applicant moves through four decision diamonds: recruiter review, hiring manager review, technical screens with onsite interviews, and offer extended. Passing leads to In Review, Interview and Offer boxes. Three of the first diamonds have arrows to a red Rejected box; the offer diamond leads to Accepted or Declined.

concepts.title: Do ATSes reject resumes? Humans do
concepts.question: Do the major ATSes reject or hide resumes automatically?

paragraphs: The author's answer is that ATSes do not reject resumes; humans do. As of 2020, none of the major systems rejected resumes automatically or hid them from recruiters. Resume processing in all major systems is basic.
Recruiters work through applications in the ATS interface. A recruiter quoted by the author calls the idea of a genius, AI-infused ATS crazy, and says anyone who has used one for work laughs at it.
card.rule: Humans, not the ATS, decide which resumes advance.
card.limits: Our reading: The claim is dated 2020 and concerns major systems used by tech companies; some newer niche systems offer more advanced parsing.

concepts.title: Who spreads the ATS myths, and why
concepts.question: What do the sources of ATS claims have in common, and why does the author distrust them?

paragraphs: The author says almost all claims about ATSes, from robots rejecting up to 75% of resumes to PDFs being inadvisable, are wrong. The misleading sites and people share two traits: they sell services to beat the ATS, and they cite sources that are not technical recruiters or hiring managers who use ATSes.

By contrast, the author says every claim in this section is backed by technical recruiters and hiring managers who configure and use ATSes daily. The conclusion: for tech resumes there is no ATS to beat.
card.rule: Ask who profits from a claim, and whether people who use ATSes back it.
card.limits: The author's test fits claims about tech hiring; it is one writer's judgment of those sources, not a rule that every seller is wrong.

concepts.title: Knockout questions: the one real automatic rejection
concepts.question: When can an ATS truly reject you, and where does that information come from?

paragraphs: Knockout, or prescreening, questions are the one place where the claim that the ATS rejects can be partly true. Recruiters add them to the application form to filter out people who are not eligible, whatever their resume says. For example, a company that does not sponsor visas may ask whether you will need sponsorship.
Even then, the recruiter set up the rule, and the answer comes only from the form you complete. The information is never taken from your resume.
card.rule: Only your form answers, never your resume, can trigger a knockout rejection.
card.limits: Our reading: Knockout questions screen for eligibility under the role's policy; they say nothing about how strong a resume is.

media.alt: Screenshot of a recruiter's form editor in an applicant tracking system. A yes or no question asks whether the applicant is legally eligible to work in the country. A ticked checkbox beneath the question text says to disqualify the candidate if the answer is no.

concepts.title: ATS-compatible resumes are a buzzword
concepts.question: What do ATSes actually do with the resume you upload?

paragraphs: Most ATSes try to parse resumes, but they do not use the contents to filter anything during screening. Parsing is done to auto-fill candidate details and to support searches later, outside the application process. Beyond matching personal details and indexing keywords, they do nothing clever.

Both PDF and Word documents are parsed well enough. The author compares calling a resume ATS-compatible with calling a website mobile phone compatible: all of them are, so the label is a meaningless buzzword.
card.rule: Every resume is ATS-compatible, so the label tells you nothing.
card.limits: Our reading: The claim concerns tech hiring with major systems as of 2020; parsing quality is described as good enough, not perfect.

concepts.title: Paid ATS optimisation and the Taleo rank
concepts.question: Why does the author reject paid bypass-the-ATS services, and what is the one partial exception?

paragraphs: ATS resume optimisation is sold for $100 to $500 and beyond, with the claim that matching the job description will let your resume bypass the ATS algorithm. The author calls this false for most tech jobs: there is no bypass, since your resume simply waits in a queue for a recruiter.

The one popular ATS that rates parsed resumes is Taleo. Its requisition rank is a percentage based on automated screening questions and how far your resume overlaps the job requisition. Recruiters can sort by it, but the score is off for developers, and none of the dozen-plus recruiters the author consulted used it to decide.
card.rule: There is no ATS algorithm to bypass for tech jobs; your resume waits in a queue for a person.
card.limits: The claims are dated 2020 and about tech roles. Taleo's rank exists; the author's point is that tech recruiters do not rely on it.

concepts.title: Why tailoring still works
concepts.question: If ATS tricks do not work, why does tailoring a resume to a job still help?

paragraphs: The author calls tailoring your resume for the position solid advice, and says it is why people see results after ATS-optimisation techniques. The ATS itself does not decide whether your resume advances: the recruiter or hiring manager scanning it does.

Those readers judge how relevant your experience is, and applications are almost always numerous. So tailoring the resume and grabbing attention on the first scan make a difference. The credit belongs to the human reader, not an algorithm.
card.rule: Tailor the resume for the human who scans it, not for a program.
card.limits: The author still advises against paying for algorithm tricks; tailoring works because people read for relevance.

concepts.title: What recruiters say: human filtering and PDFs
concepts.question: What do the three recruiters quoted say about ATS filtering and file format?

paragraphs: Three recruiters back up the point. A former Amazon, Google and Microsoft recruiter says the ATS list is organised by date applied, and a real person then decides: rejection on resume fit or knockout answers, or progress. A tech recruiter of over 20 years says none he knows would trust an ATS to filter, as the risk of losing good candidates is too high.

A London recruiter says ATSes are so poor at content filtering that firms receive badly formatted CVs, irrelevant profiles and blank pages, and suggests PDF as the best format. Word files can lose formatting in another Word version or operating system.
card.rule: Recruiters filter by hand and prefer PDF to protect formatting.
card.limits: These are three individual views quoted by the author, not company policy. PDF is the author's recommendation, backed by one recruiter.

concepts.title: Referrals, references and background checks
concepts.question: How do referrals, references and background checks differ, and when does each happen?

paragraphs: Referrals are employee referrals: employees refer candidates internally. Pretty much all tech companies have a referral programme that rewards employees for successful ones. References are reference checks, usually after the interviews but before an offer, and almost always run by the hiring manager. Candidates are often asked to supply them and should warn their referees.
Background checks usually come after you accept the offer, and the offer can be withdrawn if the check is unsatisfactory. They are almost always run by a specialist company.
card.rule: A referral comes before you apply, a reference after interviews, a background check after you accept.
card.limits: Our reading: the order is the usual one, not a fixed rule; the author says practice varies between companies, states and countries.

concepts.title: Why referrals get priority
concepts.question: Why do companies give referrals priority over other applications?

paragraphs: Referrals are treated with priority because they work remarkably well, says the author. Referred candidates are far more likely to go through interviews, get an offer and accept it, and less likely to turn out a bad hire who does not survive the trial period. Studies cited cover hiring in general, not only tech.

Referrals usually go to inbound sourcers or recruiters ahead of other applications. The flip side: without a referral, it is more difficult to get a human to look at your resume or to get a recruiter call.
card.rule: Referrals work better, so companies move them to the front.
card.limits: The author's evidence is cited studies of hiring generally; how much a referral helps varies by company, as later quotes show.

media.alt: Funnel diagram like the large-company pipeline, now with referrals. Of 250 submitted resumes, the resume screen holds 190 inbound resumes plus 10 referrals entering by a side arrow. The recruiter screen holds 20 from screened resumes, 8 from screened referrals and 2 strong referrals entering by a second arrow. Technical screen, onsite and offer follow.

concepts.title: Generic and strong referrals
concepts.question: How do a generic and a strong referral change your path through the pipeline?

paragraphs: The author separates a generic employee referral, where someone you do not know personally refers you with your resume after you asked, from a strong referral, where a colleague you have worked with actively vouches for you.

Referrals almost always guarantee an in-depth resume review, and often make the recruiter call easier to reach. For strong referrals you might get a recruiter call set up straight away. The extra context lets you skip part of the queue.
card.rule: A referral earns a closer look; a strong referral earns the fastest route.
card.limits: Employees quoted by the author say they do not speak for their companies and policies differ, so how much a referral helps varies.

concepts.title: How to ask for a referral
concepts.question: Where can you look for a referral, and how should you ask?

paragraphs: You get a referral by asking. First check whether anyone in your network works at the company. Then look for second-degree LinkedIn connections and ask for an introduction, doing the legwork yourself. The author likens job hunting to sales: you are selling yourself.

A cold request on LinkedIn can also work, although less well than via a shared connection. Send a clear, concise message about wanting a referral, and give the person an easy way out. For well-known companies you can also ask on Blind, an anonymous network of people working at larger companies.
card.rule: Ask through your network first, then cold, with a short message and an easy way out.
card.limits: Cold requests are less likely to work than ones through a shared connection, though the author says they still beat having no referral.

concepts.title: Ask for the referral before you apply
concepts.question: Why should a referral request come before your application?

paragraphs: Most tech companies' referral systems let employees refer only candidates who are not yet in the hiring pipeline. So if you apply first and then ask for a referral, you often will not be able to be referred.
That creates a trade-off: waiting for a referral slows your application, while applying at once can cost you the referral. The author says you must make that call yourself.
card.rule: If you want a referral, get it before you apply.
card.limits: Our reading: The rule holds for most, not all, companies, and the best balance depends on how likely you are to get a referral.

concepts.title: The priority order of resumes
concepts.question: In what order do hiring managers typically prioritise applications, and why?

paragraphs: With many applications, the author says, the more expensive a candidate is to hire in time or money, the lower the priority. The typical order: referrals, local candidates, candidates not needing visas, candidates needing visas and relocation, and last, candidates from countries that are unusually hard to get visas for.

Referrals are read in depth and are the likeliest place for exceptions. Local candidates need no paperwork or relocation, and carry little risk of backing out. Candidates who need no visa may still relocate, but that adds no uncertainty to the start date.
card.rule: The cheaper and quicker a hire, the earlier the resume is read.
card.limits: Our reading: this is the author's typical order, not a universal rule; companies decide position by position.

media.alt: Diagram of four circles rising like steps left to right: referrals, local candidates, candidates not needing visas, everyone else. Applicant numbers rise toward the right while cost and time to hire for the company rise too. Boxes under each circle list benefits such as acceptance likelihood, and for the last group relocation costs, more paperwork, slower start and higher withdrawal risk.

concepts.title: When companies sponsor visas and relocation
concepts.question: Which roles do companies sponsor for, and why is it rare for new grads?

paragraphs: Most companies decide visa and relocation sponsorship position by position; at larger companies policy is usually central. They typically sponsor only at senior and above levels and for roles hard to fill locally. Even Google or Facebook often hire entry-level positions locally, so sponsorship there is unlikely, though exceptions exist.

Rule of thumb: the more qualified local applicants, the less likely a company will sponsor. A hiring manager gives two reasons new grads are rarely sponsored: the time and money cost, and supply and demand. Large companies fill entry-level roles locally; with 2 to 3 years' experience this changes.
card.rule: Sponsorship follows scarcity: it is rare at entry level and common for senior, hard-to-fill roles.
card.limits: The author gives exceptions, such as specialised programmes for outstanding new grads, and notes policies differ by company and position.

concepts.title: Remote roles: employees versus contractors
concepts.question: How do remote hiring rules differ between larger and smaller companies?

paragraphs: For remote positions selection is usually more straightforward. Larger tech companies hire people as employees, and only in countries where they have a legal entity that can employ them. A US firm with entities in the UK and Singapore might hire remotely there, but only there.

Some smaller and mid-sized companies hire from anywhere and are open to contractors. A contractor sets up a business that the company contracts with, and handles their own taxes and benefits. The upside is being considered by different companies, if your timezone overlaps well enough.
card.rule: Remote does not mean anywhere: check whether the company can employ you in your country or takes contractors.
card.limits: Our reading: The contractor route depends on the company being open to it and on timezone overlap.

concepts.title: Why startups see few applications, and who hires
concepts.question: Why do little-known startups get few applications, and who runs their hiring?

paragraphs: Little-known startups and small companies often see few applications, for two reasons. Their job adverts are very specific about the technology that is a must. And they often want to hire in hot areas where large companies also recruit, but lack the reach those companies have. To offset this they often work with recruiting agencies.

Their recruiting is often run by the hiring manager. In very small companies, or those with minimal hiring resources, the hiring manager does all the work: the resume screen, the screening call and coordinating the onsite interviews.
card.rule: A small company means fewer applicants and a hiring manager who does the whole process.
card.limits: The author's figure shows a typical non-entry-level pipeline at a little-known company; the real process and numbers vary by role and company.

media.alt: Funnel diagram for a small company: ten resumes submitted, ten in the tracking queue, ten at the resume screen, then five at a hiring manager call, four at a technical screen, two onsite and one offer. Side callouts say even small firms use a tracking system and the hiring manager reads all resumes.

concepts.title: Outsourced coding screens at small companies
concepts.question: Why might a small, little-known company give you a hard algorithmic test?

paragraphs: Companies with little technical expertise, for example a non-technical founder and no hands-on hiring managers, almost certainly set algorithmic coding challenges, often hard ones. They lack the in-house skill to interview for these topics, so they buy a screening solution, such as Hackerrank.

Such tools are often built with Silicon Valley hiring in mind, so the bar can be high. Non-technical managers often use the score as the signal and do not look at your code, so a missing edge case could fail you. The upside: if you pass, you may be among the first hands-on technical hires.
card.rule: A hard test at a small company often reflects missing expertise, not the real work.
card.limits: The author says this applies to companies with little technical expertise; companies with technical founders often skip algorithmic challenges.

concepts.title: Technical founders: a nice pipeline with a catch
concepts.question: What is hiring like at a company with technical founders, and what is the catch?

paragraphs: With technical founders the hiring process can be one of the nicest. A technical hiring manager who works with developers daily reads your resume, and the first call is with that manager, probably your future boss. Technical screens rarely include algorithmic challenges and the onsite is shorter. There is less competition and you are more likely to get an offer.

The catch: these are small, lesser-known companies. They will almost certainly not sponsor visas, pay will almost certainly be below large tech companies, and the company may seem a risky bet. That is why so few people apply.
card.rule: Technical founders offer less competition at the price of lower pay, no visas and more risk.
card.limits: The author says the catch assumptions may not be true, so treat them as typical, not certain.

concepts.title: Case: the first mobile engineer at Uber
concepts.question: What does the story of Uber's first mobile engineer show about applying to very small companies?

paragraphs: The engineer had two years' experience in France and wanted a US job. He applied to over 20 jobs on a large job site and heard back from three: one said hiring abroad was complicated, one did not sponsor visas, and UberCab asked if he wanted to do the coding challenge.

After the challenge came one interview with the first engineer and the CEO, then an offer with visa sponsorship. His lesson: very small companies often have a lightweight process and move fast. He was hired from abroad because they could not find a mobile engineer.
card.rule: Very small, unproven companies can move fast and sponsor when they cannot find local talent.
card.limits: This is one person's story from 2011; the author's point is that applying to small companies can pay off, not that it always will.

concepts.section: Mid-Sized Companies with HR Support for Recruiting
concepts.title: Mid-sized companies and the HR generalist
concepts.question: How does hiring change at mid-sized companies, and what risk comes with a non-technical screener?

paragraphs: When a company outgrows the few-person stage, the hiring manager cannot do all the hiring, but the company is not big enough for a sourcer or dedicated recruiter. It usually hires an HR generalist to reduce the manager's load. This person screens resumes and organises interviews.

These companies see more applications than small ones, but far fewer than large ones. The pipeline resembles a startup's, but the hiring manager no longer reviews resumes. The HR generalist is not hands-on with tech and follows instructions: if the manager asks for four or more years of Java, they may reject resumes where this is not clear.
card.rule: Our reading: with a non-technical screener, make sure your resume plainly shows you meet the stated requirements.
card.limits: The risk depends on the instructions the screener received; the author's example is one case, not every mid-sized firm.

media.alt: Funnel diagram for a mid-sized company: twenty-five resumes submitted and in the tracking queue, twenty-five at the resume screen, then seven at a hiring manager call, four at a technical screen, two onsite and one offer. Callouts say an HR person scans resumes following the hiring manager's guidance, using a system aimed at small and medium firms.

concepts.title: Job boards versus job aggregators
concepts.question: How do job boards and job aggregators differ, and why does it matter?

paragraphs: Job boards are well-known brands where companies pay a hefty fee per advert; examples are LinkedIn Jobs, StackOverflow Jobs and AngelList. Most candidates search only on boards, which have far fewer tech listings.

Job aggregators also crawl company career pages, so they hold far more positions, including hidden gems with few applicants. They act as a search engine for jobs; examples are Indeed, Simply Hired, CareerJet and LinkUp. They are not specific to tech, so you narrow by title and location.
card.rule: Boards show paid adverts; aggregators also reveal listings that few candidates see.
card.limits: Our reading: Aggregators are not tech-specific, so you must narrow the search, and the sites named reflect the time of writing.

concepts.title: Apply directly with a tailored resume
concepts.question: After finding a role on an aggregator, how should you apply?

paragraphs: When a position looks interesting, find the company's career site and apply directly with a tailored resume. The author says to upload a generic resume only if you are already getting responses. If you struggle to get recruiter calls for jobs you seem qualified for, tweaking the resume for each job description gives better results.
Applying early to less visible jobs means your resume stands out among fewer applications, and the company spends less time and money on recruitment: a win for both sides.
card.rule: Go to the company's own site and send a resume tweaked for that job.
card.limits: Our reading: A generic resume is acceptable if you are already getting responses; tailoring matters most when calls are not coming.

concepts.title: Recap: the target reader, referrals and aggregators
concepts.question: Which recap actions concern the resume's target reader, referrals and aggregators?

paragraphs: The recap begins by asking you to keep in mind who your resume's target is: a recruiter, HR partner or hiring manager, who must see in a few seconds why you fit the position. Tactics follow later in the book.
It then says to seek out referrals, especially at well-known tech companies that likely see many applicants, and to browse job aggregators, not just job boards.
card.rule: Write for the person reading, ask for referrals, and search aggregators.
card.limits: Every company's process differs and some diverge from what the chapter describes.

concepts.title: Recap: build a prioritised application list
concepts.question: How should you plan which jobs to apply to, given how the pipeline works?

paragraphs: The author's fourth action is to list the jobs and companies you would consider. Add notes on how large each company is, how competitive its application process likely is, whether it is local, and whether you would need a visa.

Then prioritise by the likelihood of standing out. Do some long-shot applications, but also some safer bets. Every company's process differs, but knowing the typical one helps you tailor strategy before you submit.
card.rule: Rank applications by your chance of standing out and mix long shots with safer bets.
card.limits: Every company's process differs, and some diverge from what the chapter describes.

concepts.title: The five things a recruiter scans for
concepts.question: Which pieces of information does a recruiter look for in the first scan of a resume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Make five things easy to find: your years of experience, the technologies the job needs, your work experience and its impact, your work authorization if you apply from abroad, and anything that stands out.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stay out of the reject pile when a recruiter has many resumes to get through.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, recruiters collect these facts almost on autopilot. When one is hard to find and the pile is large, they may move on to the next resume.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For a backend role at a company that mostly uses Java and Go, the recruiter hunts for those two languages and for how well the candidate knows them. A candidate who hides them in a long paragraph makes that hunt harder.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Show your resume to a friend for ten seconds, then ask them what your years of experience and main languages are. The book asks you to make that answer easy to give.

card.rule: Make the five facts a recruiter scans for easy to find at first glance.
card.limits: Our reading: the list covers the first pass only. A resume that passes it is then read for detail, so the scan does not replace good content.

concepts.title: Making your years of experience easy to work out
concepts.question: How does a recruiter judge your experience against a job, and how do you make that easy?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Make your years of experience easy to work out, with dated roles and a graduation date placed where a recruiter will look for them.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let the recruiter place you against the level of the position quickly, so you are not rejected because the sum was hard to do.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Every job maps to an internal level that the advert may not show. The recruiter compares you with it, checks your graduation date and subtracts the time since. If that is hard to find or unclear, you may land in the reject pile.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: One level above entry-level at a large tech company is expected to suit someone with about three to five years, give or take. A resume with no graduation date makes the recruiter guess whether you fit.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Look at your resume for ten seconds and work out how long you have worked. If you cannot do it fast, the book suggests a recruiter cannot either.

card.rule: Make it fast to work out how long you have worked.
card.limits: Our reading: years are only a first filter. They are matched to a level the advert may not state, so the number does not decide the outcome alone.

media.alt: Chart comparing engineering career ladders at five large tech companies as five coloured columns. Each column stacks rungs from junior at the top to the most senior at the bottom, with different level codes and titles per company. Rung heights vary, so the same title sits at a different position at each company.

concepts.title: Page one, emphasis and work authorization
concepts.question: How do you make what recruiters want stand out, and what should a candidate from abroad state?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put most of the key information on the first page, draw the eye to it with clear formatting, colour and bold, and state your work authorization if your application may look as if it comes from abroad.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get the five scanned facts seen in a few seconds, and keep your application out of the pile reviewed only after local candidates.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says these are the facts recruiters look for, so putting them on page one and highlighting them answers the scan directly. A resume that seems to come from abroad with no authorization shown may go in a needs-visa pile.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer who lives outside the target country but already holds a valid work visa for it adds that fact near the top. Without it, the recruiter reviews local candidates first.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Check your first page: are your main languages and technologies and your last few positions on it? The book's recap asks this.

card.rule: Put the facts a recruiter scans for on page one, highlighted.
card.limits: Our reading: bold and colour work only when used sparingly. If everything is highlighted, nothing stands out.

concepts.title: Grammar, contact details and newest-first order
concepts.question: Which unwritten rules make a tech resume look professional?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Write with good grammar and no typos, put short contact details at the top, and list roles and education with dates, newest first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Look careful and professional, so the resume is not ignored for a reason that was easy to avoid.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author calls these rules that go without saying, so they are rarely written down. Typos and weak grammar suggest poor attention to detail or limited command of the language, and break the professional look.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A candidate puts an email address, a phone number and a city and country on one short line under their name, and lists the newest job first. No street address is given.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Run a spell checker and a grammar checker over your resume, then ask someone else to read it through for correctness.

card.rule: Follow the unwritten basics: clean language, short contact details, newest first.
card.limits: Our reading: the author presents these as norms for tech resumes, not laws. Breaking one signals less professionalism, which is the cost the author names.

concepts.title: Keeping the resume to two pages or less
concepts.question: How long should a tech resume be, and when can it run longer?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Aim for two pages or less, and cut anything that does not earn its place.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give a reviewer a resume that can be scanned in a short time and that matches the amount of experience behind it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author calls this not a strict rule but a very wise one. A page count beyond what your experience justifies adds reading with no extra information.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (Invented.) An engineer with four years of experience has a two-page resume whose second page is half empty. Cutting two weak sections lets the best material fill one tight page and a few lines.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Count your pages. If you are over two, ask which sections add little to no information and remove them.

card.rule: Aim for two pages or less unless you have lots of experience.
card.limits: The limit is not strict: the author allows more for people with lots of experience. Our reading: an exception is not a reason to include material that does not help.

concepts.title: Consistent formatting and single-level bullets
concepts.question: How should a resume be formatted so that reviewers read it rather than skim it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the same formatting throughout, list your experience in bullet points, keep to one bullet level, and use real bullets rather than dashes.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the resume easy to scan so that it is read, not skimmed.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says simple, concise, easy-to-read resumes get read more, while cluttered and wordy ones are skimmed at most. Tech recruiters are used to scanning bullets, which cost less effort than paragraphs.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (Invented.) A project entry written as a four-line paragraph becomes three short bullets, one point each, at the same size and indent as every other entry.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Check that you use bullets for your experience, with no sub-bullets, and that font sizes match across similar headings.

card.rule: Consistent format, one-level bullets, no paragraphs.
card.limits: Our reading: the author gives this as a reader-friendly norm. A bullet still needs to say something worth reading.

concepts.title: Writing dates that need no decoding
concepts.question: How should dates be written so a reviewer does not have to puzzle them out?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Write dates in one consistent, easy-to-read format, with the month spelled as a word and the year in full.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let the reader see your timeline and total experience without thinking.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says a date like 06/11—07/12 forces the reviewer to ask whether it means June 2011 or November 2006. Writing June 2011—July 2012 removes that doubt and keeps the year distinct from the month.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author's own example: replace the numeric span with month names and four-digit years, so the reader does not have to decode anything.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Look at your resume and ask whether someone could quickly tell how many years you have worked. The recap asks you to make dates stand out.

card.rule: Spell out the month and the year; keep one style.
card.limits: Our reading: the aim is the absence of doubt. Any format a reader cannot misread does the job, but month names with full years are the safe choice.

concepts.title: PDF only, and ruthless editing
concepts.question: Which file format should you send, and how do you decide what to cut from the resume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Send your resume as a PDF and in no other format, and edit it hard: drop sections that add little to no information and do not spell out trivial things.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make sure every reader sees the layout you built, and that the page holds only what helps your case.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says other formats can display inconsistently and mess up an otherwise well-formatted resume. Cutting is guided by one question: does this help make a good case that you are a fit for the position?

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (Invented.) A candidate sends a word-processor file, and bullets shift when a reviewer opens it on another computer. The same resume exported to PDF looks as the candidate designed it.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: For each section ask whether it helps make your case for the job. The book asks you to drop the ones that add little.

card.rule: Send a PDF, and cut what does not help your case.
card.limits: Our reading: the author states the PDF rule without exceptions. If an application form asks for another format, follow its instructions; the advice is about what you choose to send.

concepts.section: Avoiding Biases: Personal Details and Photos
concepts.title: Leaving out personal details and photos
concepts.question: Why does the author say to leave photos and personal details off a tech resume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Leave off your photo, date of birth, gender, nationality, relationship and family details, religion and similar non-essential facts; for most resumes your name and email are enough.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep the reader's attention on your skills and achievements, so that no personal detail becomes a reason to reject you.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says each non-essential personal detail is one more way for bias to act, with a recruiter or hiring manager, and that in tech the hiring criteria are skills and expertise. Tech recruiters he spoke to said photos add no value.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author shows two resumes with the same job content. The second shows age and young children, which could raise doubts about age, distraction and relocation. The first raises none, so the reader moves straight to skills.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Check your resume for a photo, date of birth, gender, nationality, family details or religion, and remove every one.

card.rule: Leave out photos and personal details that can only create bias.
card.limits: The author's examples are persuasion by scenario, not proof of how any one recruiter would act. Our reading: the rule is for tech resumes; in some countries photos are expected, so check local practice.

media.alt: Top part of a clean resume: name on the left and job title on the right above a green rule, then a short two-line summary paragraph of backend experience, a Work history heading, and the first role with dates on the right and one bullet. No photo or personal details.

Same resume top as the clean version, but the summary is squeezed left beside a large black-and-white headshot of a middle-aged man. Below the photo are lines giving nationality, age and marital status with children. The work history heading and first role follow unchanged.

concepts.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
concepts.title: The final checklist and the file name
concepts.question: What should you check before sending, and how should you name the file?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before sending, run the chapter's checks on your resume, then name the PDF with your own name and the word resume or CV.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Send a clean, scannable resume that a recruiter can identify and file at once.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says a file named with your name tells the recruiter whose it is. Version numbers or company names in the file name suggest you have several versions of the resume, which he advises not to show.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (Invented.) A file called Ana_Lopes_resume.pdf says who it belongs to. A file called Ana_Lopes_v4.pdf suggests there were at least three earlier drafts.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Go through the seven checks on your own resume and fix what each one finds.

card.rule: Run the checks, then name the file with your own name.
card.limits: Our reading: the checks collect rules from the chapter and add no new ones. They help only if you act on what they find.

concepts.section: Structure for Interns, New Grads and Bootcamp Grads
concepts.title: What a new grad should lead with
concepts.question: Which experiences catch reviewers' eyes most when a new grad has little to show?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: List your experience in the order reviewers notice: real software work, internships, sizeable open source work, school details, standout projects, then tutoring and student leadership.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the most of limited experience, so the strongest signals reach the reviewer first.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, these are the experiences that catch the eyes of people reviewing a CV most, in this priority order. Once you hold a first full-time job, your work experience and day-to-day skills take over.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student has a summer internship, a role as lab assistant and a school with a strong reputation. The internship goes first, with results, impact and the student's own contribution. Then comes the school, then the lab assistant role (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Write your experiences in a list and number each against the six levels. Note which levels you have nothing for.

card.rule: List your experience in the order reviewers notice: real software work, internships, sizeable open source work, school details, standout projects, then tutoring and student leadership.
card.limits: Our reading: The ranking is for people without full-time experience. After a first full-time job, work experience and professional skills matter more than school and projects.

concepts.section: Structure for Interns, New Grads and Bootcamp Grads
concepts.title: One page for a new grad
concepts.question: How long should a new grad's resume be, and why?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Fit a new grad's resume on one page, with the most relevant parts near the top.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get read at all among hundreds of other applicants.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, a new grad is up against hundreds of applicants and no one reads the second page. A second page starts to make sense as work experience grows.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A graduate with a summer internship and two projects drops a second page of course lists. The internship and projects stay at the top of a single page (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Print your resume. If it runs past one page, remove the lowest-priority item first until it fits.

card.rule: Fit a new grad's resume on one page, with the most relevant parts near the top.
card.limits: The one-page limit is for people starting out. The author's rule of thumb is one page for grads and two for everyone else.

concepts.section: Structure for Interns, New Grads and Bootcamp Grads
concepts.title: Section order for a new grad
concepts.question: In what order should a new grad arrange resume sections, and when should that order change?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Open with work experience and internships, then projects, education, languages and technologies, then interests; reorder when another section carries more weight for the job.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Put the strongest signs of fit towards the top, where reviewers look first.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, recruiters and hiring managers look for the most relevant things near the top, as signs you could fit the position. For most new grads the default order does that.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A graduate with a research award and top grades but no internship may lead with education, because it is the stronger signal for a research role (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: List your sections top to bottom. For each, ask whether it signals fit better than the one above it.

card.rule: Open with work experience and internships, then projects, education, languages and technologies, then interests; reorder when another section carries more weight for the job.
card.limits: Our reading: The listed order is a starting point. Change it when a section carries more weight or is more relevant to the job.

media.alt: Template for a new graduate resume with blue section headings and thin rules. Order from top: Experience with one internship entry, Projects with a link, Education and Certifications with a degree, expected graduation date and coursework, Languages and Technologies in three labelled bullets, then Interests. Placeholder text explains what each entry should hold.

concepts.section: Structure for Interns, New Grads and Bootcamp Grads
concepts.title: Projects with impact and links
concepts.question: How should a new grad describe projects so a reviewer can judge them?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Describe each project with its results, impact and your own contribution, and link to the source code when it is well organised and has a good README.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let a reviewer see what you built, why it matters and where to inspect it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, projects often fill the space new grads lack in work experience. The results, impact and contribution approach explains why they are important, and a link lets the reader check.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Instead of 'Built a chat app', write that 300 classmates use the app, what you wrote yourself (server and message storage), and add a link to a tidy repository (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Rewrite one project line in three parts: result, impact, your contribution. Then check that the repository has a README.

card.rule: Describe each project with its results, impact and your own contribution, and link to the source code when it is well organised and has a good README.
card.limits: Our reading: A link only helps if the repository is nicely organised with a good README. A messy repository can count against you.

concepts.section: Structure for Interns, New Grads and Bootcamp Grads
concepts.title: Make your availability clear
concepts.question: What timing detail do recruiters check closely in intern and student hiring?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: State when you can start, or how much time you have left in your studies, so it is crystal clear that you fit the role's timing.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Pass the timing check in intern recruiting before anyone looks at the rest.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Two recruiters who hired students and interns for Uber and other tech companies say they look closely at the timing of studies. A June internship only considers candidates ready to start in June.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A job ad asks for students with one year left. The resume states 'BSc Computer Science, graduating June next year; available from June', so the match is plain (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Add one line to your education entry that states your start availability or study end date.

card.rule: State when you can start, or how much time you have left in your studies, so it is crystal clear that you fit the role's timing.
card.limits: Our reading: This advice comes from recruiters of students and interns, where timing is part of the job requirements. It is their experience, not a proven rule.

concepts.section: Structure for Interns, New Grads and Bootcamp Grads
concepts.title: Leave out what big-tech recruiters ignore
concepts.question: Which header and grade details does a large-tech grad recruiter advise cutting?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Skip your street address and any objective statement, and show GPA or grades only if they are high.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Save space and avoid details that count against you among hundreds of applicants.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author quotes an opinionated thread by a grad recruiter at a Fortune 100 company. No one is sending you mail, it is clear you want the job, and low grades count against you.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A header shows a name, email and link to a code profile. It has no street address, no line saying 'Objective: obtain an internship', and no 2.8 GPA (invented illustration).

card.rule: Skip your street address and any objective statement, and show GPA or grades only if they are high.
card.limits: Our reading: This is opinionated advice for places with hundreds of applications per position, such as most large tech internships and new-grad roles.

concepts.section: Structure for Interns, New Grads and Bootcamp Grads
concepts.title: Include dates and numbers, send a PDF
concepts.question: Which details does the same recruiter thread say to include on a new-grad resume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Give a graduation date instead of an open range such as 2019-present, and use numbers to show what you did instead of generic responsibilities.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Be readable and credible among hundreds of applicants.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The thread gives these as directives without long reasons. The numbers point is that numbers demonstrate what you did, where generic duties do not. Treat the thread as one recruiter's opinion.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Replace 'Responsible for testing' with 'Wrote integration tests that cut reported bugs by a third', and replace '2022-present' with 'Expected graduation June 2027' (invented illustration).

card.rule: Give a graduation date instead of an open range such as 2019-present, and use numbers to show what you did instead of generic responsibilities.
card.limits: Our reading: The thread comes from one recruiter and is aimed at places with many applicants. It is opinion, not research.

concepts.section: Structure for Interns, New Grads and Bootcamp Grads
concepts.title: Mirror the posting, skip a cover letter that no one reads
concepts.question: How does the thread say to show fit for a role and what to do about cover letters?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Tailor the resume for the position and use language that mirrors the job posting, and skip the cover letter unless you can send it to the hiring manager or recruiter directly.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show you fit what the job asks for in a pile of hundreds, without spending time on documents nobody reads.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The thread says that with so many applications your resume should show a fit with the job. It adds that a cover letter has a high chance of not being read unless it goes directly to the person.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A posting asks for REST APIs in Go. A student rewords a real course project to say it exposed REST APIs in Go, matching the posting's terms and keeping the facts (invented illustration).

card.rule: Tailor the resume for the position and use language that mirrors the job posting, and skip the cover letter unless you can send it to the hiring manager or recruiter directly.
card.limits: Our reading: The advice is opinionated and for roles that see hundreds of applications. Mirroring a posting means describing your real work in its words, not claiming work you did not do.

concepts.title: Work experience at the top, tech on page one
concepts.question: Where should work experience and the technologies list go once you are past your first job?
