blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Once you have work experience, put your current title, company and last few years at or near the top, with a Languages and Technologies section on the first page.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let a reviewer glance at who you are now and what you work with.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, recruiters and hiring managers want to glance at your current title, company and recent work, so you make it easy by placing it at or near the top.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer with six years of experience opens with the current role, then a short technologies block, both on page one. Education follows lower down (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Look at only the top third of your first page. Can a stranger name your current role, company and main technologies?

card.rule: Once you have work experience, put your current title, company and last few years at or near the top, with a Languages and Technologies section on the first page.
card.limits: Our reading: The advice is for people no longer fresh from school. A new grad's default order differs, with internships and projects leading.

concepts.title: Let education shrink with seniority
concepts.question: How much education detail should stay as your work experience grows?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Shrink the education section as experience grows: details are fine with 1-3 years, but at 5+ years keep the degree, graduation date and at most one standout achievement.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Free space for work that is more relevant to the hiring manager.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, education details become less important with seniority. Grades, courses and activities say little about what you do now.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: After seven years of work, a developer's education reads: 'BSc Computer Science, 2017, summa cum laude'. Course lists, GPA and club memberships are gone (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Count your years of experience. If it is five or more, cut your education block to the degree, the date and one standout line.

card.rule: Shrink the education section as experience grows: details are fine with 1-3 years, but at 5+ years keep the degree, graduation date and at most one standout achievement.
card.limits: This is the author's guidance by years of experience; it does not mean hiding a degree. Keep the degree and date at any level.

concepts.title: Spend less space on old positions
concepts.question: How should you treat jobs from more than ten years ago?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you have 10+ years of experience, shorten sections on work from beyond ten years ago, and remove ones that are not relevant.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the resume sell you as you are now, not list every employer.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, what you did long ago is not representative of what you do now, and old, obsolete technologies are not worth listing.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer with sixteen years of experience writes five detailed bullets for each of her last two jobs. The jobs from twelve to sixteen years ago get one line each (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Mark every job older than ten years. Cut each to one line, or remove it if it has no bearing on the role you want.

card.rule: If you have 10+ years of experience, shorten sections on work from beyond ten years ago, and remove ones that are not relevant.
card.limits: Our reading: The advice covers work beyond ten years. Recent roles deserve detail. Older roles are shortened or dropped only when less relevant.

concepts.title: Extracurricular, projects and interests
concepts.question: Where do patents, talks, standout projects and hobbies fit on an experienced resume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put patents, publications, talks and standout open source or published projects in an extracurricular section, say why each matters, and end with a short hobbies line.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show attention-grabbing extras without crowding out work experience.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, these extras can grab attention. The more work experience you have, the less relevant projects outside work become, unless one really stands out.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer with nine years lists a conference talk and a library she maintains. Under the library she writes how many projects use it and her role, with a link (invented illustration).

card.rule: Put patents, publications, talks and standout open source or published projects in an extracurricular section, say why each matters, and end with a short hobbies line.
card.limits: Our reading: The extras come after your work experience and certifications. Keep hobbies short, and skip them if space is tight.

concepts.title: Certifications: relevant ones, below work
concepts.question: Which certifications help on a resume, and which can hurt?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: List certifications that are relevant to the job or industry below your work experience, and avoid ones that are trivial to get.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Add credible proof of skill without a negative impression.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, a trivial-to-get certification, such as a LinkedIn programming language certification built from about a dozen questions that can be repeated at any time, may create a negative perception.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A cloud engineer lists a professional cloud certification beneath her jobs. She leaves off a short online language quiz badge (invented illustration).

card.rule: List certifications that are relevant to the job or industry below your work experience, and avoid ones that are trivial to get.
card.limits: Our reading: Relevance decides. Some employers value certain certifications more, but a certificate anyone can retake gives little credit.

concepts.title: Show evidence of the must-haves
concepts.question: How do recruiters screen against a hiring manager's must-haves, and what should a resume show?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Show the role's must-haves, or close signs of them such as similar environments and problems or the same technology in projects, and write a resume tailored to each position.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Pass the recruiter's screen, which extends what the hiring manager asked for.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A recruiter in the chapter says the screen is usually an extension of the hiring manager's requirements. A tailored CV is what makes you stand out. This is one recruiter's account, told as lived experience.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The role needs Java or Go and the candidate has worked mainly in .NET. A recruiter would expect to see Java or Go in the projects or technologies section (the recruiter's example).

card.rule: Show the role's must-haves, or close signs of them such as similar environments and problems or the same technology in projects, and write a resume tailored to each position.
card.limits: Our reading: The advice is one experienced recruiter's view. Hiring managers differ in how strict their must-have lists are.

concepts.title: A separate languages and technologies section
concepts.question: What should a separate technologies section list, and what should it leave out?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: List the technologies relevant to the position that you are proficient in under a separate heading, and go neither only by the job advert nor overboard.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let a reviewer check, in seconds, what you share with the role.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, 'What languages and technologies is this person hands-on with?' is one of the first questions reviewers have. A separate section answers it fast. The heading matters less than the contents.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A full-stack ad wants one object-oriented language (JavaScript, Go or Java), React and API design. The candidate lists the ones she uses day to day and leaves out tools anyone learns in hours (the book's before and after case).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Write the job ad's technologies on one side and yours on the other. Keep the overlap where you could work on it day to day.

card.rule: List the technologies relevant to the position that you are proficient in under a separate heading, and go neither only by the job advert nor overboard.
card.limits: Our reading: Use good judgment. Skip trivial or niche technologies that have nothing to do with the job, and applications that are trivial to learn.

concepts.title: Do not label your level
concepts.question: Why does the author advise against rating yourself on each technology?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Avoid listing your expertise level or a points score; list only languages you feel proficient with, strongest first, and drop tools anyone can pick up quickly.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep the list credible and easy to scan.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says labels such as expert and proficient are double-edged, because they imply you are not an expert in the rest. Technical recruiters told him that people who rated themselves experts were often rejected after being grilled on depth.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the book's before version, a full-stack candidate's list is a dump with expert and proficient labels and tools like Eclipse, Rational Rose, phpMyAdmin, Trello and Word. The after version is grouped in tabs and holds only hands-on items.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Strip every level label from your list. Reorder so your strongest languages come first, and delete anything a colleague could learn in a few hours.

card.rule: Avoid listing your expertise level or a points score; list only languages you feel proficient with, strongest first, and drop tools anyone can pick up quickly.
card.limits: The author allows a level only for extremely deep knowledge of a relevant technology. Otherwise let the order show strength.

media.alt: Before version of a skills section titled Relevant Skills, with three bullets: programming languages, databases and technologies. Some items carry self-rated labels in parentheses such as expert or proficient. The technologies line is a long, mixed dump of tools, editors, design software and office programs.

The same skills section as an annotated critique, with pink highlights on the self-rating labels, two older languages near the start of the language line, and a run of generic tools in the final bullet. A note says those tools are either trivial or overly specific. Core language names are unhighlighted.

After version of the skills section, tidied into three tab-aligned bullets: Languages, Technologies and Other. Each list is short and uses no self-rating labels. The Other line is highlighted green, with a note saying it adds skills relevant to the job listing.

concepts.title: Two other ways to show your technologies
concepts.question: How can technologies be shown without one list, and when does each approach help?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Show technologies inside each role's description, in a consistent place, to convey recency, or split a group of rusty technologies from the hands-on ones.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Tell the reader how current you are, which a single list cannot do.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, a list does not differentiate technologies you use now from ones you have not touched lately. Naming technologies in each role shows recency.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A candidate applying to a Ruby-heavy company uses JavaScript and Java every day. Ruby is rusty. In the book's example, Ruby is shown separately from the two daily languages.

card.rule: Show technologies inside each role's description, in a consistent place, to convey recency, or split a group of rusty technologies from the hands-on ones.
card.limits: Our reading: Each approach has a cost: weaving needs discipline in where technologies appear, and splitting out rusty ones is useful only when the job values them.

media.alt: Excerpt of two job entries, each with italic title and two achievement bullets that mention measured results such as cost or support reduction. The final bullet of each entry is a Technologies line naming the stack used in that role, kept in the same place each time.

Same two job entries rewritten so technology names are woven into the achievement sentences themselves, for example built with a named framework or deployed on a cloud stack, and no separate Technologies line appears. Measured results are unchanged and the stack is still easy to spot.

Skills block with three tab-aligned bullets. Languages and Technologies list the candidate's regular stack, while a third bullet labelled working knowledge lists a few other languages and a framework, separating hands-on skills from rusty ones.

concepts.title: Tell a story backward in time
concepts.question: What should a reader see at a glance in your work history, and how are promotions shown?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Make the work history a story that runs backward in time and can be understood at a glance, with each promotion shown as its own titled entry and projects listed under it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show progression and clarity so promotions are not missed.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, a promotion shows you can create impact and be recognised, and reviewers should see it. Treat each promotion as a sub-section with the projects of that period.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer joined as Engineer in 2019 and became Senior Engineer in 2022 at the same company. The resume shows two titled lines under one employer, each with its projects (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Look at your last employer. If you were promoted, give each title its own entry with dates and the projects from that period.

card.rule: Make the work history a story that runs backward in time and can be understood at a glance, with each promotion shown as its own titled entry and projects listed under it.
card.limits: Our reading: A long stay without a promotion calls for key projects and titles instead. The story must stay readable at a glance.

media.alt: Plain bullet listing of career history, newest first, with three columns: title, employer and years. A senior role is at the top, followed by two consecutive entries at one employer with different titles and adjacent date ranges. Two summer internships and a mathematics degree complete the list.

concepts.title: Clarify titles that describe your role poorly
concepts.question: When may you change or add to a job title, and when is that not honest?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Clarify an official title that describes your role poorly, but change it only if your real work for three months or more did not match it, or if it is too company-specific to transfer.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let skimmers understand your level and role, without bending facts.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: An experienced recruiter in the chapter says these are the only ethical exceptions. The author agrees: a title that says Associate for a software developer may need a clarifying description.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A finance firm's Associate is a software developer. The resume says Software Developer (Associate). An iOS engineer who moved to backend for a year and a half could write Software engineer (iOS and backend) (the book's cases).

card.rule: Clarify an official title that describes your role poorly, but change it only if your real work for three months or more did not match it, or if it is too company-specific to transfer.
card.limits: Our reading: The recruiter would not change titles outside those exceptions. Do not give yourself a grander title for the sake of the job you want.

concepts.title: Dates, and what to leave out of the story
concepts.question: Which date detail and which jobs should you drop to keep the story clean?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Drop the months from dates more than a few years old, and omit work that does not support your story, giving recent roles far more detail than early ones.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep the story easy to scan and focused on what is relevant.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, past 2-3 years of experience readers do not care about month-level details, so they are noise. Jobs that do not support the story distract from it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author has seen non-technical jobs such as pizza delivery on profiles and a person with 15 years listing all four internships from over a decade earlier. Both should go.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Rewrite your dates as years for any role over three years old. Remove one job that does not support your story.

card.rule: Drop the months from dates more than a few years old, and omit work that does not support your story, giving recent roles far more detail than early ones.
card.limits: Our reading: The advice is for experienced people. Months can help for recent roles, and a relevant early job may stay.

concepts.title: Why most readers skip the summary
concepts.question: Who reads a resume's summary section, and when does it do more harm than good?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: With a few years of experience, leave out the summary unless you customise it for the listing, and do not state ambitions that could make a reader pass.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid spending space on a section few read, and avoid ruling yourself out.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, recruiters and hiring managers rarely read the summary on the first scan, however much effort you put in. They read it only after they have decided to proceed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer's summary says she is looking for opportunities to lead. The role is for an individual contributor, so the manager may think the team cannot offer that growth and not call (the author's case).

card.rule: With a few years of experience, leave out the summary unless you customise it for the listing, and do not state ambitions that could make a reader pass.
card.limits: This is the author's advice for less experienced candidates. Senior and standout profiles are the exception, covered next.

concepts.title: When a summary is worth having
concepts.question: In which situations does the reader actually read a summary?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use a summary when the reader will want context: a senior or standout profile, a fully remote role, or a change of direction such as manager back to individual contributor.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Answer the question your resume raises before the reader asks it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, in these cases hiring managers are curious and will read the section, as long as it is easy to spot.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A candidate with four years at a well-known company applies to a smaller one. The summary says she wants her next challenge in a high-growth, smaller environment (the author's case).

card.rule: Use a summary when the reader will want context: a senior or standout profile, a fully remote role, or a change of direction such as manager back to individual contributor.
card.limits: A summary is not a tiebreaker for senior roles. The author says the rest of the resume will be.

concepts.title: Write a short, specific summary, and write it last
concepts.question: How should a useful summary be written?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you include a summary, keep it short and specific: your years of experience, especially if they do not match your graduation date, and highlights that show why you fit the position.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make a reader want to keep reading by showing results for their company.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author gives a rule, and an experienced developer adds that the best summary is written last, once the resume is airtight, using its most impressive details. Her view is persuasion based on experience, not proof.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A candidate applying for a mobile job does not stress years as a frontend developer. She writes that she taught herself Swift and Objective-C quickly to fill a role her company needed (the quoted developer's example).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Finish your resume first. Then pick its two strongest results and write two sentences for the summary around them.

card.rule: When you include a summary, keep it short and specific: your years of experience, especially if they do not match your graduation date, and highlights that show why you fit the position.
card.limits: Our reading: The summary should not be too short or too long. Hobbies like gardening or hiking do not make the case; results do.

concepts.section: Structure for Senior and Above People
concepts.title: Two pages is a guide, not a wall
concepts.question: How long may a senior resume be, and what do two recruiters and a CTO say?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: With more than ten years of experience, list your relevant major deliverables and accomplishments, and do not be hung up on the two-page limit, but keep the resume focused.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give a hiring manager enough relevant detail without losing the reader.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, at this level the hiring manager reads your resume more often and wants to understand more of your history. The one-page resume is for grads and two pages for everyone else, but the limit is not a hard one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A CTO with 20 years of hiring says reviewers are often left without enough detail, and recommends listing major deliverables for each role. A recruiter says one to two pages is ideal (the quoted experts).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: List the deliverables for your last role. Keep those a hiring manager would find relevant and cut the rest.

card.rule: With more than ten years of experience, list your relevant major deliverables and accomplishments, and do not be hung up on the two-page limit, but keep the resume focused.
card.limits: Opinions differ. They agree on relevance. The author's recap says even with a lot of relevant experience, the length should not go above three pages.

concepts.section: Structure for Senior and Above People
concepts.title: Separate resumes for manager and individual contributor
concepts.question: How should someone open to both management and hands-on roles present themselves?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you are open to both management and individual contributor roles, write two separate resumes, each telling its own story, rather than one hybrid.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give a hiring manager a clear answer to where you are headed.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, companies rarely hire hybrid roles. A hybrid resume with no clear next step is put in the unsure pile.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: One person's two resumes differ in summary, in titles (Senior Engineer or Team Lead, Senior Engineer for the same job) and in highlighted achievements, though every fact is correct (the book's example).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Decide the role you most want. List which achievements and which title wording support that story only.

card.rule: If you are open to both management and individual contributor roles, write two separate resumes, each telling its own story, rather than one hybrid.
card.limits: Our reading: Be very careful not to bend facts. Different emphasis is fine, but facts that contradict across versions are damaging.

media.alt: Top of a resume aimed at returning to an individual contributor role: name in large red type, an email, a Summary row with dates in a left column, and a three-line summary about leaving leadership. A Head of Engineering entry has four short bullets on building and technical foundations, then an older senior engineer line.

Top of the manager-track version of the same resume: same red name and layout, but the summary presents a leader of engineering teams looking to scale a group. The head of engineering entry has five bullets on hiring, career ladders, budgeting and shipping. The older role title is extended to show team leadership.

concepts.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
concepts.title: The chapter's seven-point audit
concepts.question: Which seven checks should you run on a resume's structure before sending it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check section order, relevant technologies, your story, a tailored summary, detail on recent versus old work, date readability and length against your experience.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make sure the most relevant details reach the first page of the resume.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The chapter's recap turns its advice into seven questions. Agreeing with a practical book means acting on it, and this audit is the place to do that.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Walk through a draft: key details first, only relevant technologies, titles showing progression, a short tailored summary, more detail on recent jobs, tidy dates, and a length that fits the experience (invented walk-through).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Run the seven checks on your own resume in the chapter's order. Write one change for each, then make the three most useful ones.

card.rule: Check section order, relevant technologies, your story, a tailored summary, detail on recent versus old work, date readability and length against your experience.
card.limits: The audit follows the chapter's advice and is not a guarantee of results. Judge each check against the job.

concepts.title: Write what you achieved, not what you did
concepts.question: Should a resume bullet describe the tasks you carried out, or the results you produced?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Describe what you achieved, with its impact and business result, instead of only listing what you did.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show the reader that you are self-sufficient, that your work made a difference on your team, and that you know what impact it had.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, most resumes stop at duties. A resume that shows how you added value on purpose is the kind that gets sought after, while people who only follow directions are easy to find.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A bullet that says a tool was widely adopted tells the reader little. The author's rewrite says you led three developers to build a framework that fifteen teams and over fifty developers used.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Pick one bullet from your own resume and ask what changed because of it. The book asks you to put that change in the bullet.

card.rule: Write each bullet around the result you produced, not only the task you were given.
card.limits: Our reading: a resume still has to say what your role was. Results with no sense of the job can leave the reader unsure what you were responsible for.

concepts.title: The impact, number, contribution formula
concepts.question: What three parts can a strong resume bullet contain, and in what order?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Shape a bullet as: accomplished some impact, as measured by a number, by doing a specific contribution.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the impact obvious to the reader, show what you personally contributed, and add specifics wherever you can.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, the formula puts the result first and then backs it with a measure and your own action.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A sample bullet in the chapter reduces an open ticket backlog from 500 to 20 in three months. The impact is a smaller backlog, the number is 500 to 20, and the action would follow.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Take one of your bullets and label which of the three parts it has, then fill in any that is missing.

card.rule: Write bullets in the shape: accomplished impact, measured by a number, by doing a specific contribution.
card.limits: Our reading: the order is a guide, and a bullet that is stiff to read can be loosened as long as all three parts survive.

concepts.title: Put numbers in your bullets
concepts.question: Why does the author want numbers in resume bullets, and what can count as a number?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Quantify your impact wherever you can, so that the bullets carry numbers.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stand out from the many resumes that give no figures.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, most resumes do not contain numbers, so adding specifics sets yours apart. A figure also lets a reader who never worked at your company judge the size of your result.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: One sample bullet in the chapter says a new task tracking system reduced schedule creep by forty percent. The number turns a claim into something a reader can weigh.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Choose a bullet without a figure and ask how many people, users or hours were involved. The book asks you to add one number.

card.rule: Quantify the impact of your work wherever you can.
card.limits: Our reading: Limits: do not invent a number you cannot stand behind. If you cannot measure it, give the clearest specific detail you truthfully can.

concepts.title: Use active verbs for your bullets
concepts.question: Which kind of verbs should open a bullet, and how much does the exact verb matter?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Start bullets with active verbs that show what you did and how you were proactive.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show that you drove the work yourself rather than having things happen to you.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, active verbs make you look proactive, while passive wording sounds like events that merely occurred around you.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author prefers verbs such as led, managed, drove, improved and rolled out over forms such as improving or rolling out.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: A list of fancy action words is not the goal. The point is details, not a showy verb.

card.rule: Open each bullet with an active verb that shows what you did.
card.limits: Limits: the book warns against agonising over which impressive verb to use. The detail of the work matters more than the choice of word.

concepts.title: Name technologies at the end of a bullet
concepts.question: Where in a bullet should technologies go, and which ones?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Mention the languages and technologies you used toward the end of a description, after the impact and your contribution.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give detail-oriented readers, such as hiring managers and interviewers, proof that you were hands-on.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, impact and contribution are more important to convey than technologies. Calling out tools at the end is still powerful for people who read in detail.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A bullet could end with 'using Kotlin and Room' after stating a launch time improvement. The tools support the result instead of replacing it.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A bullet that is only a list of tools gives a reader nothing about what you achieved.

card.rule: Put the technologies near the end of the bullet, and keep them matching your Languages and Technologies section.
card.limits: Our reading: Limits: you need not mention a technology in every bullet. The tools support the result and never replace it.

concepts.title: Collect your bullet material early
concepts.question: How can you gather the raw material for strong bullets before you write them?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Start early and write down everything you remember doing, then prune later.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make sure you have enough detail to build specific bullets rather than scrambling at the last minute.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the advice the chapter quotes, it is easier to delete extra information than to invent one more bullet at the last minute, and ordering and phrasing can wait.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The quoted author suggests carrying a sheet of paper and scribbling ideas as they come back to you, without worrying about order.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Spend ten minutes listing what you did on one project, including numbers if you have them. The book asks you to focus on the story, not buzzwords.

card.rule: Write down everything you can recall doing, early, and cut it down later.
card.limits: Our reading: Limits: this is a first pass. The result is still a pruned set of specific bullets, not a long list of everything.

concepts.title: Case: from vague bullet to specific bullet
concepts.question: What did the author find wrong with a vague platform bullet, and what did the rewrite add?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check each bullet for what an outsider can understand, whether it has numbers, and whether it shows what you did.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn a description that only a colleague would follow into one a recruiter can weigh.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, the before version names a platform that only colleagues know, has no numbers, sounds assigned to the person, leaves the effect of a refactoring unclear, and ends with an etc.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The after version adds numbers, actions and specific technologies. The author says it shows a person who moved the needle for the business and can get things done.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: Do not read the case as a call for long bullets. The fix is more specific, not simply longer.

card.rule: Read your bullet as an outsider: if it needs company knowledge, has no figure or sounds assigned, rewrite it.
card.limits: Limits: the case is a single before-and-after pair. Our reading is that the same problems apply to other bullets, but the book shows this one only.

media.alt: Short job entry on a resume: an italic role line followed by four plain bullets. They describe billing microservices, automated error handling, third-party integrations for a platform and a legacy reverse-engineering effort. Wording is vague, mostly team-oriented, with no figures or clear results.

The same four-bullet job entry with pink highlights and short bracketed notes. Notes flag missing specifics, team-centred words such as our, trailing filler words, a passive description that makes the person seem told what to do, and unclear impact of the refactoring work.

Rewritten job entry with five bullets and green highlights on strong parts: action verbs, numbers such as availability improvements, load, percentage drops in support tickets and conversion gains, plus named technologies. Each bullet states what the person did and the measurable effect.

concepts.title: Write about yourself, not the team
concepts.question: Should a resume bullet say we or I, and what should the page be about?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Talk about yourself rather than your team: avoid we and use the first person, and in most cases drop the I.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make clear what you personally brought to the table before, and what a company would get by hiring you.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, the resume is about you. Team wording hides which part of the result was yours, so the reader cannot tell what you added.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The before version of the chapter's case has several references to the team over the person. It also calls the candidate a team member who took part, which the author reads as undersell.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: Dropping we does not mean claiming the whole team's result as yours. State what you did.

card.rule: Write what you did in the first person, and leave we and the team's name out of your bullets.
card.limits: Limits: say that a result came from a team when that is true, and name your own part within it. The book asks for your contribution, not for credit for work you did not do.

concepts.title: Be concise but not humble
concepts.question: How should you weigh modesty against selling yourself when you write your achievements?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Be concise but not humble, and do not hide your achievements.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make your resume stand out from an already competitive crowd.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, the resume should sell the professional you for the position, and the readers are a recruiter and a hiring manager who will not guess at hidden strengths.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The chapter's before version used wording such as sometimes and occasionally, which the author says made the person's contribution look small.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The same section tells you not to claim untrue things. Selling yourself is not the same as making things up.

card.rule: State your achievements plainly and fully; do not shrink them with soft wording.
card.limits: Limits: the advice to lean toward claiming credit is the author's opinion, and it stops at the truth. Claims you cannot support invite trouble in an interview.

concepts.title: Sell your side projects and open-source work
concepts.question: How should you describe a side project or open-source contribution so a reader opens it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Describe side projects and open-source contributions with the results, impact and contribution approach, and do not leave a bare link.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the reader curious enough to look at the work in detail.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, if you do not sell the project, the person reading the CV may not look at it. A link with no explanation gives them no reason to click.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The chapter contrasts a bare link with an entry that explains the project, and says the explained version is the one a hiring manager will want to open.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: A project is not sold by its name alone. A generic description could hide anything from a simple demo to a complex build.

card.rule: Describe each side project by its goal, impact and your approach, not by a bare link.
card.limits: Limits: this applies where you have something worth showing. Our reading: a thin project may be better left out than padded.

concepts.title: Add tech-adjacent activities with impact
concepts.question: Which outside activities belong on a resume, where do they go, and how should you describe them?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put tech-adjacent extracurricular activities at the end of your resume and describe their impact.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Add colour to a dry resume with standout activities.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, many resumes are dry, and showing high-quality or standout activities can make a good resume even better.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If you organised a meetup with 100 participants, say so. If you keep a technical blog, link one specific article of high quality for the reader to open.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Choose one activity and write one line with a number and a link. The book asks you to pick activities that are neutral and would not trigger bias.

card.rule: At the end of the resume, list tech-adjacent activities with their impact and a specific link.
card.limits: Limits: pick activities that are neutral. The author warns that some interests can trigger bias, and says the activity should be one that adds value to the reader.

concepts.title: Mention what you learned and why
concepts.question: What can a resume say about learning that makes a candidate more interesting?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Mention why and how you picked up a skill, how it affected a role, and what you want to do with it next.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show proactive learning, which hiring managers value.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, hands-on recruiters and hiring managers value hearing this.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the chapter's case, the improved version explains why the person picked up Groovy and Scala, what they achieved with them and what they hope to achieve next.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Write one line about a skill you learned: the reason, the result and the next goal.

card.rule: Add a short note on why you learned a skill, what it changed and what you want to do with it.
card.limits: Our reading: Limits: keep it short and relevant. A learning note supports the results in your bullets and does not replace them.

concepts.title: Leave out what does not help you
concepts.question: Which weak points may you leave off your resume without being dishonest?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: You do not need to list things that do not show you in a good light, such as failed projects or a low GPA.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep the page focused on the strengths you want the reader to weigh.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, the resume is a sales document for the position. Leaving a weak point out is different from claiming something untrue.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A project that was cancelled, or a grade average that is low, can safely be left out, the author says.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: Leaving out is not lying. Do not claim things that are not true.

card.rule: Leave out failed projects, low grades and similar points; do not claim anything untrue.
card.limits: Limits: omission is for things that do not help your case. Our reading: a gap that the reader will notice anyway, such as a break, may need a short honest line, which later chapters discuss.

concepts.title: Case: from an undersold resume to a confident one
concepts.question: What did the author fix when turning an undersold resume into a confident one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check your work, volunteer and project entries for team-first wording, soft modifiers, missing data and generic descriptions.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn entries that undersell you into entries that make a hiring manager want to click.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, the before version put the team ahead of the person, used passive roles and soft words, and gave no data.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The volunteer entry in the rewrite says the person built a local group of 500 developers and ran over 30 events and hackathons. It left out partnerships and pointed to press coverage.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: The case is not about longer entries. The after version is more specific and more focused.

card.rule: Replace team wording, passive roles and soft modifiers with your own actions, data and links.
card.limits: Limits: this is one before-and-after pair. The book shows the changes for this candidate, so apply them as a checklist, not as a template to copy.

media.alt: A resume section before editing. Work experience has four bullets that speak of we or my team, passive participation and soft words like occasionally. Below, a projects list has a verbose volunteer entry with three sub-bullets, then two project entries with brief descriptions and underlined names.

The before section with pink highlights and bracketed comments. Comments mark missing specifics, underplayed achievements, team wording instead of personal contribution, passive language, a question whether one event or many took place, an overly verbose volunteer entry and casual project descriptions.

Improved section with green highlights. Work experience has five bullets giving the person's own actions, team sizes, usage counts and technologies, including a learning bullet. Projects show a community lead role with audience size and event count, plus two named projects with a purpose, key concepts and source links.

concepts.section: Write a Resume for That Job
concepts.title: Write the resume for that specific job
concepts.question: Why should you write a separate resume version for each job, and what should it copy from the job description?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Write your resume for the specific job description, using similar language to the one the job uses.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Grab a recruiter's attention when many qualified people apply for few openings.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, for most advertised positions there are far more qualified job seekers than headcount. Recruiters see many inbound resumes, so yours needs more work to stand out.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For an Android role that focuses on Kotlin, show your Android and Kotlin work first. If you also have web experience, move it further down the page.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Read one job description and underline the phrases you could truthfully echo. The book asks you to use that language in your descriptions.

card.rule: Re-edit your resume for each job so it echoes the job description and puts the matching experience first.
card.limits: Limits: echo only experience you really have. Our reading: tailoring changes emphasis and wording, not the facts.

concepts.section: Write a Resume for That Job
concepts.title: Keep a master resume and trim it per job
concepts.question: What is a master resume, and how do you turn it into a version for one job?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep a master version full of detail, then cut it down and re-edit it for each job description.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make tailoring quick, so each application gets a version that suits it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, you do the hard work of writing results, impact and contribution once. Then you only choose which parts to keep and how to word them for each job.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer with Android, Kotlin and web projects keeps all three in the master. For an Android role she keeps the first two and moves the web work out of the way.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Start a master file with every project in results-impact-contribution form. The book asks you to copy it and trim it for one real job.

card.rule: Write one detailed master resume, then trim and reword a copy for each job description.
card.limits: Our reading: Limits: only the trimmed copy is sent. A master is a working file, not the version a recruiter should receive.

concepts.section: Write a Resume for That Job
concepts.title: Be ruthless about what you remove
concepts.question: What should you do with bullets that do not help you for this job, and why is it safe?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Remove bullets that do not help convey why you fit the position instead of cramming everything in.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep the resume focused on what gets you the interview.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A headhunter quoted in the chapter says most people are nervous about cutting and cram the content instead. She argues the resume exists to get you the interview.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An invented case: a candidate applying for a role in the frontend team drops two backend bullets from the master and keeps the three that show frontend impact.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The advice is about relevance. Cutting a bullet that supports the match removes the reason you fit.

card.rule: Cut every bullet that does not show why you fit this job.
card.limits: Limits: the headhunter's advice is an expert's opinion from recruiting practice, and the book gives no study. Cut for relevance, not to shorten for its own sake.

concepts.section: Write a Resume for That Job
concepts.title: Work out why the job was opened
concepts.question: How can you tell whether a company wants something new built or an existing system kept running?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Read the job description carefully to work out whether the role is new or a replacement, and shape your resume to match.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show the strengths that fit the real reason the company is hiring.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A headhunter quoted in the chapter says to ask whether the company is hiring someone to build something brand new in a new team, or whether there is something to maintain, perhaps replacing a person who left. The answer shapes what to show.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For a small company, search for its staff on LinkedIn. If someone already has the skills the advert asks for, you would likely work with that person, who may be on your interview loop.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: This is a clue, not proof. For large tech companies the headhunter says it can be hard to tell.

card.rule: Read the advert, and for a small company check its staff, to infer why the role exists.
card.limits: Limits: the book calls this hard for large tech company adverts. The staff check is the headhunter's tip for small companies.

concepts.section: Write a Resume for That Job
concepts.title: Case: the same content, mirrored to one advert
concepts.question: What changed between the generic and tailored versions of the Amazon example, and what stayed the same?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Mark the keywords and key areas in the job description, then reflect that wording in the matching parts of your resume.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make a recruiter who compares versions more likely to move your application ahead.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, the generic version is not bad but does not reflect the job description at all. The tailored one uses the phrasing the listing uses.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author highlighted keywords and key areas in an Amazon job description and rewrote the resume text to echo them, assuming the person has experience in those areas.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: Mirroring is not inventing. The author says to reflect these only if you do have the experience.

card.rule: Highlight the advert's key phrases, then echo them in your own matching experience.
card.limits: Limits: the case shows one candidate and one advert. Our reading: the technique helps only where the experience is real.

media.alt: A job advert for a payments software engineer at a large online retailer, with an overview, responsibilities, basic qualifications and preferred qualifications. Yellow highlights mark key phrases about critical services, availability, scale, design verbs, performance, scalability, languages and collaboration that a candidate could mirror.

A generic resume snippet: a skills summary with four bold-labelled lines (languages, databases, tools, other) and a job entry with four short bullets about back-end work, a dashboard generator, a testing proxy and a beta environment. No wording echoes a particular advert.

The skills summary and job entry rewritten to echo a job advert. Yellow highlights mark mirrored phrases such as distributed systems, best practices, reliability, testing practices and rollouts. The job entry now has three bullets stating team size, ownership and adoption by other teams.

concepts.title: Show breadth and fundamentals for generalist employers
concepts.question: What do large tech companies and fast-growing start-ups look for when they hire generalist engineers?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: For generalist roles, show a language you know well and the fundamentals the advert asks for, such as data structures and algorithms.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Match what big tech and fast-growing venture-funded companies screen for.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, these companies almost always look for generalists because their tech stack can be varied and change quickly. They care less about the specific language and more about engineering skill.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A resume for such a role names the languages the advert mentions, and shows work on distributed systems, object-oriented design or scale, backed by numbers.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: Generalist does not mean no language. The author wants good understanding of at least one language.

card.rule: For generalist employers, lead with fundamentals, a strong language and the areas the advert asks for.
card.limits: Limits: this is the author's profile of large and fast-growing firms. Companies that hire for one named technology weigh the stack more, as the next ideas show.

media.alt: A job advert for a generalist engineer. Minimum qualifications have four bullets: a degree or equivalent, coding in any one of three named languages, web markup and scripting, and full-stack features. Three preferred front-end items follow, then paragraphs about wide-ranging fields, versatility, switching teams and owning delivery.

concepts.title: Use engineering metrics and open-source ties
concepts.question: Which kinds of numbers and open-source links catch the eye of recruiters at generalist tech companies?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Focus on impact and engineering metrics, and mention open-source frameworks by the company that you know or contribute to.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Speak the language of engineering-minded recruiters at generalist employers.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, strong resumes at these places tend to carry engineering numbers, which tell a technical reader how large and how good the work was.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Metrics include requests per second for a system you built, test coverage increases, infrastructure cost savings, user counts and latency reductions.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Look at the employer's public repositories. The book asks you to mention any framework of theirs you use or have contributed to.

card.rule: Show engineering metrics, and name the company's own open-source frameworks you use.
card.limits: Limits: mention only what you use. Our reading: a framework named without real use will not survive an interview question.

concepts.title: Do not list too many tools, or trivial ones
concepts.question: What should you leave out of a resume aimed at a generalist tech employer?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do not list too many technologies and tools, and do not list trivial tools that need little engineering knowledge.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep the resume credible to engineering-minded recruiters.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, hiring managers at these places assume you can pick up any tool quickly, and recruiters are more sensitive to keyword stuffing, which reduces the value of your resume.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author says a hiring manager frowns when Trello or JIRA appears in a technology list.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: At companies hiring for one set stack the advice changes, as a later idea shows.

card.rule: Leave out long tool lists and trivial tools when you apply to generalist employers.
card.limits: Our reading: Limits: this applies to generalist employers. Companies hiring for a specific technology often want the relevant technologies listed, with care.

concepts.title: Advice from an inbound sourcer
concepts.question: What does a recruiter who screened thousands of resumes at a large tech company look for first?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Highlight the experience and technologies relevant to the company, keep the resume clean and short, and apply to generalist employers only if you are open to their stack.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Grab the attention of the recruiter who first reads your resume, and avoid wasted calls.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A former inbound sourcer quoted in the chapter says relevant experience catches her eye, and that she prefers clean and easy-to-read resumes above anything else.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For senior backend roles she looked for engineers who had split large monoliths into microservices or built large distributed systems. Work on scalability and reliability also caught her attention.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The advice reflects one recruiter's practice. The book presents it as an expert's view, not as a study.

card.rule: Show the experience the company needs, keep the page clean, and apply only to stacks you are open to.
card.limits: Limits: this is one recruiter's view, from a large tech company. Our reading: it describes generalist hiring, not every kind of employer.

concepts.title: List the stack when the job names one technology
concepts.question: How does your resume change when a company hires for one set technology?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: For companies hiring for a specific technology, list the relevant technologies from the advert, state your years with the main language, repeat the tools in your experience, and keep it readable.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get past screeners who look for named technologies and then convince the hiring manager that you are hands-on.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, many of these companies work with less technical recruiters who screen for specific technologies or phrases as the hiring manager instructs.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Non-tech-first and smaller companies often hire this way. Their adverts list the required technologies at length and use traditional wording such as duties and responsibilities. A short summary can state your years of experience.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Do not invent sentences just to repeat tools. Unrelated or trivial technologies should be removed.

card.rule: Mention the advert's technologies you are comfortable with, state your years, repeat them in your experience and keep the page readable.
card.limits: Limits: the author says to be pragmatic. Keyword stuffing is more relevant here, but going overboard still hurts, and unrelated tools should go.

media.alt: A job advert for Java developers at a growing company. Sections are duties (three bullets), required technical expertise (six bullets naming Java years, testing, object-oriented design, Linux, Docker, build and messaging tools, databases) and desirable technical skills (seven bullets of further tools and languages).

concepts.title: Agencies: list everything you are good at
concepts.question: What changes in your skills list when you apply to a consultancy or agency?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you apply to an agency, consider listing all technologies you are proficient with, not only those in the advert, and list all your certifications.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show agencies more ways they could place you with their clients.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, agencies hire developers and contract them out to client work, so they may be flexible about extra technologies they could sell.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A consultancy advert lists Java. A candidate who also knows Python and AWS lists all three, since either could suit a client.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The other advice for set-stack employers still applies: keep the resume easy to read.

card.rule: For agencies, list all the technologies you are proficient with and all your certifications.
card.limits: Limits: proficient means proficient. Our reading: the list is longer than for a one-technology employer, not unlimited.

concepts.title: Why the exact words of the job matter
concepts.question: Why can a resume that describes the right experience still be thrown out?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the exact terms of the job description for the experience you really have, because a less technical screener may look for the words, not the meaning.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get through the first resume screen, where many qualified people fail.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, at companies where recruiters are not very technical, filtering is done by discarding resumes that lack certain keywords.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For a backend role on a Java team, a resume without Java or backend would be disregarded in most cases. A resume describing microservices and message queues but never the word distributed may be dropped by a screener hunting for that term.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A screener who reads for meaning does not need the exact word, but you cannot know in advance who reads yours.

card.rule: Say it in the job's own words wherever the experience is real.
card.limits: Limits: it helps only where the experience is real. The practice is the author's account of screening by less technical staff, and it is less common where recruiters are technical.

concepts.title: Keywords without stuffing
concepts.question: How can you make sure the right keywords appear without making the resume look unprofessional?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Include the most relevant keywords in a human-readable way: a short skills section plus specifics in the experience section.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Pass the first screen and still read as professional to the person who comes next.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, throwing in every possible keyword, called keyword stuffing, can make a resume look unprofessional. A technical hiring manager may put it in the maybe pile.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author's fix cuts a long list down to the technologies relevant to the job and shows in the work experience which ones were used to get specific projects done.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Take your skills list and cross out everything the job does not ask for. The book asks you to give an example of each remaining skill in your experience.

card.rule: List the relevant keywords once in a short section and prove them in your experience, without stuffing.
card.limits: Limits: the author calls keyword stuffing controversial. Where recruiters are less hands-on it may work, but it works less well where requirements are clear and recruiters are technical.

media.alt: A dense technical skills block written as one run-on paragraph. Many underlined bold categories are separated by double bars, covering languages, databases, back-end and front-end technologies, frameworks still being learned, build tools, testing, editors, CI, API styles, infrastructure, queues and a final other-tools category containing task trackers and office applications.

A trimmed resume snippet. A short languages and technologies section has three compact lines (languages and frameworks, tools, other topics). Beneath, a backend engineer entry has two bullets in which relevant technologies are highlighted green inside sentences about the work done and its measured result.

concepts.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
concepts.title: The five checks that make a resume stand out
concepts.question: Which five questions should you ask of your resume to make it stand out?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check your resume for numbers and impact, active language, technologies in your examples, a version tailored to the job, and your own voice instead of we.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn the chapter's advice into actions on your own resume.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, expressing the impact of your work and tailoring to the job are the two most impactful changes you can make.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A bullet that says what you did, shows a figure, names the tool, echoes the advert and speaks for you passes all five checks.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Run the five checks on one bullet and one resume version. The book asks you to act on them, since agreeing with a practical book means doing what it says.

card.rule: Ask five questions: numbers, active verbs, technologies, a tailored version, and I rather than we.
card.limits: Limits: the checks are a list, not a guarantee. They help the resume stand out, but the author does not promise results.

concepts.title: One column, plain style
concepts.question: Why does a simple one-column layout get read in more detail than a crammed multi-column one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Choose a simple one-column layout with a restrained style, so the reader can scan it fast.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get your resume read in detail, so that good and relevant experience is not lost in the layout.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, multi-column formats are far harder to scan, and squeezing a lot onto one page often means the resume is read in less detail. A developer resume is about 95% content and 5% style, and loud contrasts make relevant facts hard to find.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: a candidate fits three columns and a coloured sidebar onto one page. A recruiter glancing for seconds cannot tell where the latest job starts. The same facts in one column, newest role first, can be found at once.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Count the columns on your resume. If there is more than one, try moving everything into a single column and see whether the key facts are easier to find.

card.rule: Choose a simple one-column layout with a restrained style, so the reader can scan it fast.
card.limits: The problem is readability: the author says that if a fancy design does not get in the way of scanning, that is fine.

concepts.title: Bold only the labels
concepts.question: Which parts of a resume deserve bold, and which do not?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use little bold, apply it the same way throughout and keep it to key labels such as dates, titles and companies.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let the eye find the structure of your career at once, without random emphasis that distracts from it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says bold in the middle of a sentence looks arbitrary and leaves the reader asking why that part matters. Concise descriptions and a clean format work better, and one has to be careful with bolding inside sentences.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: a candidate bolds the words various tools and on time inside bullets. A reviewer wonders why those words matter. Bolding only job titles, company names and dates makes the career easy to follow.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Mark every bolded word on your resume. If it is not a date, title or company, or it sits in the middle of a sentence, try removing the bold.

card.rule: Use little bold, apply it the same way throughout and keep it to key labels such as dates, titles and companies.
card.limits: Our reading: Bold is not banned: the point is restraint and consistency, so a few labels stand out and nothing else competes.

media.alt: Top of a resume with name and role at left and phone, email and profile link at right. A bold skills paragraph follows. Two jobs list six and four bullets. Many phrases inside bullets are bold, including tax and payroll terms, and date styles differ between jobs.

concepts.title: Consistent fonts and alignment
concepts.question: What does uneven formatting tell a reviewer about the candidate?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep font sizes, alignment and spacing consistent, and align elements with tabs rather than spaces.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show attention to detail, and present yourself in a polished way.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, different font sizes, misaligned key information and elements pushed into place with spaces make a resume look like amateur formatting. The reader may conclude that you have little attention to detail and do not know how to present yourself.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: two job entries list dates at the right margin, but one was lined up with a tab and the other with spaces, so they sit a few characters apart. The company names are in different sizes. The page looks hurried.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Zoom out and check that headings, dates and bullets line up from job to job. Fix any spacing done with the space bar.

card.rule: Keep font sizes, alignment and spacing consistent, and align elements with tabs rather than spaces.
card.limits: The author puts style at about 5% of a developer resume, so tidy formatting supports good content and does not replace it.

media.alt: The resume with hand-drawn red annotations and arrows. Label one, too much bolding, points at the skills paragraph and bold bullet phrases. Label two, inconsistent formatting, boxes the contact block and the differing date styles. Label three, sloppy phrasing, underlines filler endings in bullets.

concepts.title: No sloppy phrases
concepts.question: What kind of wording should you remove from a resume, and what goes in its place?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Replace etc., and so on and slang with specific items and clear, neat full sentences.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the resume read as professional and precise.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author lists sloppy phrases, such as etc., and so on, slang or unprofessional language, among the format mistakes that make a resume with good and relevant experience hard to understand.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: Built APIs, tested stuff, etc. becomes Built three REST APIs and wrote the integration tests for each one.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Search your resume for etc., and so on and casual words. Replace each with the specific items, or delete it.

card.rule: Replace etc., and so on and slang with specific items and clear, neat full sentences.
card.limits: Neat does not mean long: the author also asks for concise descriptions and for large blocks of text to be avoided.

concepts.title: Spell out internal names
concepts.question: Why will a recruiter not follow internal project names, and what should you write instead?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do not rely on internal acronyms, project names or jargon; describe the work in terms an outsider can follow.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Convey your skills and tell the story of your work to a reader who knows nothing about you.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says you write for recruiters and hiring managers you do not know, so you should assume they know nothing about you. Names that mean something inside your company mean nothing to them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: Led QA for Project Heron v3 becomes Led QA for a fraud-detection service used by two million customers.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Underline every acronym and project name on your resume. For each, ask whether a stranger could say what it is. If not, replace it with a plain description.

card.rule: Do not rely on internal acronyms, project names or jargon; describe the work in terms an outsider can follow.
card.limits: Our reading: The test is whether an outsider can follow, not whether a word is technical: terms every developer knows are fine.

concepts.title: Lead with what the job needs
concepts.question: In what order should you present experience that covers more than the job asks for?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put the experience most relevant to the position you are applying for first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let the recruiter for that specific job see a fit straight away.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says the audience of your resume is the recruiter hiring for the specific position you apply for, so keep that reader in mind and show what they are looking for first.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: a candidate with mobile and backend jobs applies for a backend role. In each job entry the backend work is listed first and the mobile work after it.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Name the position in one phrase. Check that the first example under each job matches that phrase.

card.rule: Put the experience most relevant to the position you are applying for first.
card.limits: Our reading: It changes the order of what you show, not the facts: what you did stays exactly as it was.

concepts.title: Evidence beats cliches
concepts.question: How can a reader learn you are a team player without being told so?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Replace trait claims such as team player with specific results from your experience entries.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give the reader facts, examples and specifics to judge, instead of self-description.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says a sentence like I am a team player and a fast learner tells a recruiter nothing, because it contains no facts, examples or specifics. Showing what you delivered demonstrates the trait.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: hard-working and detail-oriented becomes Reviewed 150 pull requests in a year and wrote the team's testing guide.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Underline each trait word on your resume. Replace it with the result that shows the trait, using the results, impact and your contribution structure.

card.rule: Replace trait claims such as team player with specific results from your experience entries.
card.limits: Our reading: The cliche is the problem, not the trait: if a quality matters, the proof must come from what you delivered.

concepts.title: Short enough for a glance
concepts.question: How much text can a reader take in when they only glance for seconds?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Write short sentences, avoid large blocks of text and edit your descriptions ruthlessly.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let a recruiter with only seconds take in your experience.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says recruiters have limited attention and glance at a resume for seconds, so large blocks and long sentences go unread. Optimise for quick, easy reading.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: a five-line bullet on a service redesign becomes two short lines naming what changed and the result.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Read your longest bullet aloud once. Cut every word that does not carry a fact.

card.rule: Write short sentences, avoid large blocks of text and edit your descriptions ruthlessly.
card.limits: The author admits it is not easy to distil years of experience into a few short sentences, but says you still need to.

concepts.title: Skip the photo, cap the contacts
concepts.question: Should a resume carry a photo, and how many contact details or profile links belong at the top?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Leave off your photo and list no more than four contact details or profile links, compact at the top.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid bias and wasted space, so attention goes to the content of the resume.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author recommends skipping the photo because of the biases it creates. Most recruiters and hiring managers will not click through most contact links, so anything beyond four is irrelevant.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: a header with phone, email, LinkedIn, GitHub, a website, Medium and Instagram is cut to email, phone, LinkedIn and GitHub.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Count the contact details and links in your header. If there are more than four, keep the four a recruiter is most likely to use.

card.rule: Leave off your photo and list no more than four contact details or profile links, compact at the top.
card.limits: Four is a ceiling, not a target: the author says to stick to few, relevant links, so drop any that adds nothing for the job.

media.alt: A densely filled one-page resume header and tail. A red name with a rule sits above a location and seven profile links in blue, with a large smiling portrait at right. A grey placeholder box stands for normal content. A spoken languages list and a references section with two praise quotes follow.

A cleaned-up resume header: a red name with a rule beneath, then a single line with city, email and two link labels, LinkedIn and GitHub, separated by vertical bars. A grey placeholder box below stands for the normal content.

concepts.title: Drop spoken languages and skill scores
concepts.question: Why do a spoken-languages list and self-rated skill scores add little or backfire?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Leave out the spoken-languages section and any self-rating, and list only the technologies you are proficient with.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Spend the space on what an English-first tech employer cares about: your programming languages and technologies.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says people assume you are fluent in English for such an employer, so the languages section adds little. A self-rating can only backfire, since it gives the reader a number to doubt.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: Languages: Portuguese (native), English (fluent) is removed, and Python and Go with star scores becomes Python, Go, SQL listed by name.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Delete any score bars or stars on your resume. Keep only the names of technologies you can work with.

card.rule: Leave out the spoken-languages section and any self-rating, and list only the technologies you are proficient with.
card.limits: Skills can still be tested: the author says that if people want to probe them in an interview, that is fair game.

concepts.title: No references, no praise quotes
concepts.question: Why do references, and quotes praising you, not belong on a resume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Leave out the references list, the line references available on request, and quotes from others praising you.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Use the space for your own selling, because the resume is your pitch.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, references only matter after you pass the interviews, and tech expects you to supply them anyway. Quotes from others look out of place, since the resume is about you selling yourself.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: a references line and a quote from a manager are removed, freeing three lines for another result.

blocks.label: Try it
