blocks.text: Find a references line or a quoted praise on your resume. Replace it with one more result from your experience.

card.rule: Leave out the references list, the line references available on request, and quotes from others praising you.
card.limits: References still come up later: the author says tech expects you to be able and willing to provide them.

concepts.title: Clickable, named, quiet links
concepts.question: How should a link appear on a resume so it is usable but does not steal attention?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Make links clickable, show a descriptive name instead of the full address, and let them blend in with the text.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep the reader's eyes on the content that matters while still letting them click through.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says no one prints a resume and types in the address, and a link left in default blue is often the only colour on the page, pulling eyes to details.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: a long repository path becomes underlined text reading Order tracker, source code, in the same colour as the body text.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Click each link in your exported PDF. Check that each shows a descriptive name and does not use a colour seen nowhere else.

card.rule: Make links clickable, show a descriptive name instead of the full address, and let them blend in with the text.
card.limits: Links are details: the author says recruiters click them only after the first scan has found the key information.

media.alt: A resume section with centred name, email and website link, then work experience and personal projects. Employer names are bold blue links, long web addresses are typed out in blue, projects show monospace blue addresses, and dates sit right-aligned. Colour pulls the eye toward links.

The same kind of section with calm links. All text is black, links appear as short underlined words like mobile app or on GitHub, and job titles and dates are bold with employers on a separate line. Project names are bold. Nothing blue competes for attention.

The resume with restrained colour: the name, section headings and rules beneath them are blue, while body text stays black. Job titles and dates are bold, employers sit on their own lines, and links are short black underlined phrases. Colour guides the scan to structure.

concepts.title: Link only to current, professional pages
concepts.question: When does a link help you, and when is it better removed?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Link to GitHub, LinkedIn or a website only if it is up to date and shows good work; otherwise remove it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make sure that the thorough recruiters who do click through see work that supports your application.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says most recruiters will not click, but the thorough ones will, and few things disappoint more than a GitHub untouched for years, pinned repositories with no READMEs, or a site last updated years ago.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: a candidate whose GitHub has not changed in four years removes the link. The resume points only to a current LinkedIn profile.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Click every link on your resume and judge each page as a stranger would. Fix it or delete the link.

card.rule: Link to GitHub, LinkedIn or a website only if it is up to date and shows good work; otherwise remove it.
card.limits: The author says you do not need these links on your resume, especially when their contents add no value to the application.

concepts.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
concepts.title: The nine checks before you send
concepts.question: Which checks catch the classic mistakes before a recruiter does?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before sending, run the chapter's nine checks: photo, contact count, working links, professional pages, scannability, simplicity, concision, bolding and consistency.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Catch the classic mistakes before a recruiter rolls their eyes at them.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says the nine questions turn the chapter's mistakes into actions. The photo should go, contacts stay at four or fewer, links work and lead to good pages, and the page reads easily, with little bold and one steady format.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: a candidate finds a photo, six contact links, a dead website and full addresses. They remove the photo, keep four contacts, delete the website link and name the rest.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Try to give your resume to a friend for five seconds, then ask for their immediate impression.

card.rule: Before sending, run the chapter's nine checks: photo, contact count, working links, professional pages, scannability, simplicity, concision, bolding and consistency.
card.limits: Our reading: The checks need your own judgement. The five-second friend test is a way to get an outside view.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Seek internships while you study
concepts.question: Which student experience does the author rate among the best, and when should you start pursuing it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Seek out internships well ahead of time and prepare for their interviews.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Arrive at graduation with real industry experience, so your resume has more than coursework to show.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, working as an intern on real-world problems in an industry setting is one of the best experiences a student can have. Places usually take applications well ahead of the start date, and the interviews need preparation. The author adds a personal note: skipping internships at college is something they regret.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A second-year student wants a summer placement. In autumn she looks up which companies take interns, sets aside weekends to practise interview questions, and applies months before the summer (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: List three companies near you that take interns and note when their applications usually open.

card.rule: Seek out internships well ahead of time and prepare for their interviews.
card.limits: Not every student can land an internship. The author lists other ways to grow in the same section: campus activities and published projects.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Extracurriculars and published projects
concepts.question: Beyond internships, which two student activities does the author recommend, and what does each build?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Step up for campus activities such as helping professors or running events, and publish your class projects online.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Gain hands-on experience in mentoring, leading groups and taking initiative, and give reviewers something to try.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says campus life offers openings to help professors, lead laboratory practices and organise events, which build mentoring and leadership. Class projects can also be published so others can download or try them. Final projects suit this best, because they are more complex than usual.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student leads a weekly lab practice for first-years, then puts the final-year web app online with a short description and a download link (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Choose one finished class project and note what it would need before others could try it.

card.rule: Step up for campus activities such as helping professors or running events, and publish your class projects online.
card.limits: These activities take extra effort on top of coursework. The author presents them as ways to grow faster and stand out, not as a requirement.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Publish projects with a strong README
concepts.question: What should the README of a published bootcamp project contain?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Publish your projects on GitHub with a README that has a summary, screenshots, how to run and how to test.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stand out from other bootcamp grads, whose course projects look alike.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, a bootcamp grad has little that sets them apart, and many competitors list similar course projects. Projects are a key place to differ. A published project with a good README shows reviewers what it does and how to try it. The author suggests taking inspiration from projects with excellent READMEs.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A grad publishes a to-do app. The README opens with two lines on what it does, shows three screenshots, lists the commands to run it and ends with how to run its checks (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Open one of your repositories and tick off the four README parts. Write down which are missing.

card.rule: Publish your projects on GitHub with a README that has a summary, screenshots, how to run and how to test.
card.limits: A README alone does not make a weak project strong. The author pairs it with tests, open source work and finished takehomes as ways to stand out.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Tests you can run, and say so
concepts.question: Why add runnable tests to a bootcamp project, and how should the resume and README show them?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Give your project automated tests, add a Running tests section to the README, and state the code coverage percentage.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show you can build software that is checked, which the author says most bootcamp projects lack.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author notes most bootcamp projects have no automated tests such as unit or end-to-end tests, and many grads have not heard of test-driven development. A tested project helps you stand out. The README should say how anyone can run the tests, and the project description can give the coverage percentage.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A grad adds unit tests to a recipe app, writes a short Running tests section and states in the project line that coverage is 78 percent (invented figures).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Add one test to a project of yours and write the command that runs it in the README.

card.rule: Give your project automated tests, add a Running tests section to the README, and state the code coverage percentage.
card.limits: Coverage is only a number the author suggests quoting and raising; it says nothing on its own about how good the tests are. Our reading: tests that never run help nobody.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Merged open source work as proof
concepts.question: How can an open source contribution be turned into a resume claim?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Get a pull request merged into a popular open source project and state how many developers use it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show that experienced engineers accepted your code in real software used by many people.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says that once your pull request is merged, you can claim a contribution to a project used by a large number of developers, and stars on the project are one metric to use. For example, a project with 28,000 stars can be described as used by more than 28,000 developers. Raymond Gan, a bootcamp graduate quoted in the book, adds that few juniors make such contributions and calls it more valuable than puzzle sites or student projects.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A grad fixes a small bug in a mapping library and has it merged. The resume says: Contributed to a leading open-source mapping library with more than 28,000 developers using it (modelled on the book).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Find one beginner-friendly issue in a library you use and read how a past fix was written.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A pull request that is rejected gives no claim, though the comments can still teach you.

card.rule: Get a pull request merged into a popular open source project and state how many developers use it.
card.limits: Our reading: The claim only works after the pull request is merged. Raymond Gan's strong view that open source beats puzzle sites is a guest opinion, not a tested finding.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Turn a takehome into a full project
concepts.question: What should a bootcamp grad do with a coding challenge after submitting it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do not stop at submitting a coding challenge: keep working, publish a polished version, and put it on your resume.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get a lasting project out of effort you have already made, even when the challenge did not lead to the next round.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says a coding challenge usually follows a passed resume screen. After handing it in, you can keep going: publish a more polished solution with code on GitHub, tests and a pleasant user experience. A small spend on a domain and hosting lets anyone try it. If the company turns you down, ask for feedback and build it in.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: After a rejection, a grad asks the company what to improve, adds the feedback, publishes the app on a bought domain and emails a short note with the new version (invented, loosely modelled on the book).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Pick one past challenge and list three things that would make it ready for a stranger to try.

card.rule: Do not stop at submitting a coding challenge: keep working, publish a polished version, and put it on your resume.
card.limits: The author says not to hold your breath on the follow-up email to the company. The main gain is the project itself.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Grow your experience while job hunting
concepts.question: Which activities in the book's before-and-after example added to a bootcamp grad's resume over five months?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: While you search, build new experience: contribute to open source, finish a takehome, take a paid freelance project and publish what you learned.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Change what your resume can say by growing your experience, not only its wording.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author's before-and-after example differs from other examples because it shows growth, not rephrasing. Over five months of job hunting the person made open source contributions, published a takehome, took a paid freelance job and shared coding challenge learnings as a public project with a tidy README.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A grad who struggled with data structures in interviews implements several of them with tests, publishes them with a README, and adds the repository to the resume (modelled on the book).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Choose one of the four activities and write a first step you could take this week.

card.rule: While you search, build new experience: contribute to open source, finish a takehome, take a paid freelance project and publish what you learned.
card.limits: It takes months and effort, and a freelance job can be hard. In the book's example the client argued about price and the grad took the job for experience, not profit.

media.alt: Two project bullets under a projects heading. Each has an underlined project name, the technology stack in brackets and a one-sentence description of a small web app.

Five project entries under a projects heading, each with a bold name, stack in brackets and a short description with proof. Proof includes an open-source contribution to a widely used library, a site with tests and public praise, a tool used by many businesses, and fully covered code. Underlined code links follow.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: A career changer's summary and projects
concepts.question: What should a career changer put first, and why do working projects matter so much?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Open with a summary that says you changed careers and why, then show languages and linked working projects near the top.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give the reader context at once, and prove you can build software without a long university education behind you.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, recruiters and hiring managers like to know they are reading the resume of someone who recently moved into software development, so the summary states the change and the motivation. Next come languages, projects or a portfolio that show hands-on skill. With no years-long degree in the field, the working projects and source code are what convince a hiring manager an interview is worth their time.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A former nurse opens with two lines on moving into software after a bootcamp. A block of languages follows, then three linked projects with source code, before any mention of hospital work (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Write a two-line summary that states your earlier field, your move and your reason for it.

card.rule: Open with a summary that says you changed careers and why, then show languages and linked working projects near the top.
card.limits: The advice assumes you lack professional software experience. The author also says the bootcamp advice for strengthening projects applies whether or not you attended one.

media.alt: One-page career changer resume. A centred name and contact line lead to a one-sentence summary mentioning the earlier finance career. Purple headings follow: languages and technologies, projects with bold stacks, two finance experience entries with two bullets each, education with a bootcamp and a degree, and an interests line.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Keep the old career short
concepts.question: How much space should a career changer give to past work and degrees, and which details are worth keeping?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Summarize past work in one sentence, add bullets only for skills that transfer, and keep the resume to one page.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Spend the reader's attention on projects and relevant experience, not on a previous profession.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says to describe each past job in one sentence, and use extra bullets only for skills that could carry over to software work: learning new things on your own, teamwork, mentoring or public speaking. You may want to say more, but the recruiter will care less. Aim for one page and do not go past one and a half.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A former project coordinator writes one line on the job, then bullets on training a new team and presenting to clients. The resume fits one page, with projects given more room (invented illustration).

card.rule: Summarize past work in one sentence, add bullets only for skills that transfer, and keep the resume to one page.
card.limits: Our reading: This is advice for people with no software job behind them. Someone with relevant paid experience would use the experience structures from earlier chapters.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: When a career break needs no explanation
concepts.question: How does the age and position of a career break decide whether to explain it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Explain a break only when it is recent: skip one from more than four or five years ago, and judge one that does not lead to the present.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep scarce resume space for current evidence while avoiding needless questions.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, there is no one-size-fits-all advice. A break from more than four or five years ago rarely matters to hiring managers, and if it does, it will come up in a screening call, so do not spend space on it. For a recent break followed by employment, judge whether it is still relevant; a gap from earlier might not be, but you may add a clarification.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer paused for eight months seven years ago and has worked steadily since. The resume leaves the pause unexplained. A different developer had a four-month gap last year followed by a new job, and weighs a one-line note (invented illustration).

card.rule: Explain a break only when it is recent: skip one from more than four or five years ago, and judge one that does not lead to the present.
card.limits: The author gives no formula. When a recent break leads up to the present, it needs a story, which the next card covers.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Tell the story of a recent break
concepts.question: How should a break that leads up to the present be presented on a resume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: For a recent break that runs up to now, take the lead and tell a short story, matching the answer you would give a hiring manager.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Control how the gap is read, instead of leaving the reader to guess the reason.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says that if you are currently out of full-time work, you should lead the narrative on the resume. The resume should say something close to what you would answer if the hiring manager asked about the break. Reasons the book names include not wanting regular employment, not finding a suitable job at the time, and leaving or being let go.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer laid off five months ago writes one line: Took time to care for a relative, now returning and building a side project in the open. The same sentence works as the answer in a screening call (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Say your break aloud in one sentence, then write down exactly that sentence.

card.rule: For a recent break that runs up to now, take the lead and tell a short story, matching the answer you would give a hiring manager.
card.limits: The story must be one you would say aloud; the author warns that no one-size-fits-all advice exists.

media.alt: A resume fragment with a bold title for a break lasting several months in 2020 and a single bullet giving a family reason. A previous position heading with an ellipsis placeholder sits underneath.

A resume fragment with a bold title for travelling and writing, dated from early 2020 to the present, and one bullet saying the person took a longer break for long-wanted goals. A previous position entry with a placeholder sits below.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Present study time like work, with proof
concepts.question: How should a career break spent studying be shown, and what proves the skills were mastered?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: List a study break like a work experience, and prove your skills with something in production, teaching or open source, not only courses.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show new skills as real ability, so the break reads as growth rather than a gap.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, work running in production speaks louder than finishing a course or self-study. Portfolio projects are common and, if only you use them, weak evidence. To stand out, ship something in production, teach what you learned through articles or mentoring, or contribute to open source in the same technology.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer spends six months learning Kotlin. Besides a portfolio app, they publish two articles, mentor a learner, and get a fix merged into a Kotlin library, describing each plainly (invented illustration).

card.rule: List a study break like a work experience, and prove your skills with something in production, teaching or open source, not only courses.
card.limits: The author says recruiters usually value work experience above full-time study, so proof helps but does not fully replace a job.

media.alt: A resume entry titled self-study, running from early 2020 to the present, above a software developer role. Six bullets cover taking a break to learn a stack, a tested scraping tool, an open-source contribution, blog posts with readership, mentoring juniors and books read.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Turn study time into freelance work
concepts.question: Why does the author prefer a freelance entry to a study break, and what can you do if you cannot name a client?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do a freelance project on your new stack, even for little or no pay, and present the time as freelancing instead of a break.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show delivery of real-world work, which screeners value over self-study.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says freelancing speaks to a specialist who can deliver in production, and screeners value it more than self-study alone. You can make it a resume entry instead of a break. If you struggle to find work, offer to help a friend or a small business for free or at a steep discount by building a feature that ships.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Over a study break, a developer builds a booking feature for a friend's bakery in the new framework. The resume lists it as freelance work and describes the result in one line (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Name one person or small business who could use a feature built with your new skills.

card.rule: Do a freelance project on your new stack, even for little or no pay, and present the time as freelancing instead of a break.
card.limits: The feature has to ship to count, and the author prefers real use over a demo. Free work still takes time you could spend elsewhere.

media.alt: A resume with a freelancer entry running from March 2020 to the present, with five bullets: a reporting tool with measured speed-up, a shipped API with monitoring, an open-source contribution, posts and mentoring. Below it a shorter self-study entry covers only the earlier months, with three bullets.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Senior resumes: show promotions, results and a tailored summary
concepts.question: What should an experienced engineer add so the resume stays relevant and shows growth?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Make promotions visible, state results and impact, and add a summary tailored to the position.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep a long career relevant to the one job in front of you, and show how you have grown.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, a person with a senior title but only a few years of work should make any promotion visible and be clear about the results and impact of their work. With eight to ten years or more you have likely used many technologies, so the challenge is relevance. A summary written for the position tells both recruiter and hiring manager about your motivation and how you can help their team.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An engineer promoted twice at one company shows both titles with dates under a single employer heading, and opens with three lines on why the role at the new company suits them (invented illustration).

card.rule: Make promotions visible, state results and impact, and add a summary tailored to the position.
card.limits: Our reading: A summary is useful only when it is tailored. A generic one wastes the space it takes.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Show soft achievements and influence
concepts.question: Besides business results, what two kinds of evidence do senior engineers add, and who looks for them?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Add soft achievements and influence to your business results: mentoring, leading teams, and which teams you moved.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Meet the expectation that senior people help others and affect more than their own work.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, many companies want seniors with a track record of doing their work and of helping the people around them. So add mentoring junior developers and leading teams. Also mention influence: the impression your work made and the teams or organisations you shaped toward specific outcomes. The author says the more senior you are, the more you are expected to influence.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A senior engineer writes: mentored three junior developers, led a team of five, and convinced two neighbouring teams to adopt the same release process (invented illustration).

card.rule: Add soft achievements and influence to your business results: mentoring, leading teams, and which teams you moved.
card.limits: The author's claim about what employers expect rests on experience, not a cited study. Soft achievements add to results; they do not replace them.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Move education back and shorten old roles
concepts.question: Where does education go on a senior resume, and how do older jobs change in size?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put Education on the second page with only standout details, and give older jobs proportionally less space.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Fill page one with current evidence and reduce age bias while the reader forms a first judgment.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says a senior has enough work to fill page one, and education matters less. Moving it to page two also reduces age bias, since the reader cannot do the math on graduation dates until they have probably judged your skills. Keep education to one or two lines: school, degree and date, plus a standout such as top honours. Older jobs should take proportionally less space.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A resume's page one holds the summary and three recent roles in detail. Page two lists two earlier roles in two lines each, then one line for the degree and date (invented illustration).

card.rule: Put Education on the second page with only standout details, and give older jobs proportionally less space.
card.limits: Moving education reduces age bias but does not remove it, since the dates can still be done on page two. The author says it is for people with plenty of experience.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Go around the application form
concepts.question: How can an experienced engineer make contact beyond the standard application channel?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Find the recruiter and hiring manager on LinkedIn and message them directly to ask about applying.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reach the decision-makers directly instead of waiting in the queue.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says that with plenty of relevant experience you can consider sidestepping the direct application channel. Look for the recruiter and hiring manager on LinkedIn and message them to ask about applying. According to the author, the people doing the hiring are more likely to respond to experienced engineers.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An engineer with nine years of experience finds the hiring manager for a role on LinkedIn, sends a two-line note about their relevant work, and asks how best to apply (invented illustration).

card.rule: Find the recruiter and hiring manager on LinkedIn and message them directly to ask about applying.
card.limits: The author says responses are more likely for experienced engineers, not certain. Our reading: a vague mass message would not follow this advice.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Show how you helped a team beyond coding
concepts.question: Why would a company hire a tech lead rather than another engineer, and what proof should the resume carry?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Show on your resume how you made a team succeed beyond what a senior engineer does: faster delivery, better quality, mended relations.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Match the problem the hiring manager is trying to solve, which more coders cannot fix.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, a tech lead role focuses less on technical contribution and more on delivery and team leadership. Hiring managers advertise it when a team is behind on delivery, loses people or ships poor quality, and adding engineers will not solve it. So show what you did: did you speed up delivery, improve quality, or repair stakeholder relationships? Make the evidence easy to find.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A candidate writes: took over a team that missed releases, introduced a review routine, and cut late deliveries from monthly to rare in two quarters. A second line shows a repaired relationship with the sales team (invented illustration).

card.rule: Show on your resume how you made a team succeed beyond what a senior engineer does: faster delivery, better quality, mended relations.
card.limits: Our reading: The advice fits roles whose posting describes a team problem. Where a posting asks mainly for technical depth, a senior engineer resume may suit better.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Give team context and show outcomes
concepts.question: Which specifics and outcomes should a tech lead resume include, beyond saying you led a team?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: State the team's size and make-up, the context it worked in and its main technical choices, and give outcomes as well as activities.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let recruiters judge the scale of what you led and see that it delivered.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says recruiters want the size and make-up of the team, the setting it operated in, and the major technical choices. Say both what you did and what came of it. Knowing you ran daily scrums is reassuring, but did the team deliver on time? Give proof points for delivery, for team leadership and for technical leadership.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A candidate writes: led a team of two front-end, two back-end and one test automation engineer inside a 50-person programme, delivered the payments project on time and coached two graduates to senior (modelled on the book).

card.rule: State the team's size and make-up, the context it worked in and its main technical choices, and give outcomes as well as activities.
card.limits: Specifics must be real and checkable. The author's sample figures are examples, not targets.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: A manager's story and sharp summary
concepts.question: How should an engineering manager use the resume to tell a story, and what makes the summary strong?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Tell the story of how you made teams better, and write a specific, tailored summary that works as your cover letter.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show you can lead and communicate, and say clearly what you would do for this organisation.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says engineering managers need to be good storytellers, so the resume should tell how you improved teams, what results you achieved and what you will help the organisation achieve. As a manager, your summary is your cover letter: craft it carefully for the position, avoid buzzwords and generic wording, and make it represent you well.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A manager opens with three lines about turning around two struggling teams, then lists in the work history the numbers behind each turnaround (invented illustration).

card.rule: Tell the story of how you made teams better, and write a specific, tailored summary that works as your cover letter.
card.limits: A story that is not supported by the work history is only persuasion. The author asks for the summary's claims to be backed in the experience section.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Check values and fit before you apply
concepts.question: Why research a company's values and keep to roles where you can play to your strengths?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Research the company's values, link them to your achievements, and only pursue roles where you can deliver your best results.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Land at an organisation where the fit is real for you and for them.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says engineering managers are hired to help teams thrive and reach the next level, so learn the culture and think about which values you already represent. Role fit is a two-way street: companies hire for a specific gap, and you may be tempted to reshape your resume to look like that fit. Think carefully. Aim to reach a hiring manager conversation only where your strengths apply.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A manager who thrives where early teams are hands-on declines to stretch the resume for a large organisation that needs someone to drive alignment across many groups (invented illustration).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Write the type of environment where your best results came from, in one sentence.

card.rule: Research the company's values, link them to your achievements, and only pursue roles where you can deliver your best results.
card.limits: The advice assumes you can afford to be selective. The author also notes that moving to manager from senior engineer is harder than staying a senior engineer.

concepts.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
concepts.title: Make achievements about the team, and seek outside views
concepts.question: Which people-focused results should a manager list, and where can a manager find examples and feedback?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Pair business results with results about your people, and look at other managers' profiles and feedback for ideas.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Paint the full picture of leading people, since people are at the heart of engineering management.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says shipping impactful projects and meeting hard goals is great, but ask about the team: did you support people, help them get promoted, hire for diversity, keep attrition low, or coach and mentor beyond your team? To improve the resume, browse the LinkedIn profiles of fellow managers to see how they describe work, impact and results.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A manager adds under a launch: promoted two engineers to senior, kept yearly attrition under five percent, and mentored a manager in another department (invented figures).

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Write two team results from your last role that no dashboard shows.

card.rule: Pair business results with results about your people, and look at other managers' profiles and feedback for ideas.
card.limits: Our reading: the people-focused questions are prompts, not a checklist you must fill. List only what is true.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Start a second resume from scratch
concepts.question: Why does the book ask you to write a second resume that looks nothing like the first?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Write a second resume on a different template, with different achievements and structure, without copying from the first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reach a significantly better resume than you would by polishing one draft again and again.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, people who write great resumes have written several, while people with weaker ones keep tweaking one. A fresh start forces you to find new material.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented example: a developer's first resume is a tidy two-column page about a payments migration. Her second uses a bold layout and leaves the migration out, describing on-call tooling and a data clean-up instead.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Try to put the first resume away, pick a clearly different template, and write a new one with different bold choices. This quiz does not grade it.

card.rule: Write a second resume from scratch on a different template, with new achievements, and do not copy the first.
card.limits: The second draft is raw material. The book does not say to send it as it is: it asks you to combine the best of both into a third.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Combine the two drafts into a third
concepts.question: What do you do once two very different resumes exist, and what do you gain?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Compare the two drafts, note what is good in each, and build a third resume from the strongest parts of both.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep the best material from two independent attempts instead of one.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The second draft is written without the first, so it contains choices you would not have made by editing. Comparing shows which of them are better.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented example: the first draft has a crisp summary; the second has a clearer project section with numbers. The third uses the summary from the first and the project layout from the second.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Ask of each section: which draft says it better? Copy that version across. This quiz does not grade it.

card.rule: Compare the two drafts and build a third from the best parts of both.
card.limits: The book does not say how to settle a tie between two good sections. Our reading: judge by what the target job needs.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.section: Find Out the Impact of Your Past Projects
concepts.title: Ask others what your projects achieved
concepts.question: Where do you look for the impact numbers that most resumes lack?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Find the real impact of each project by asking your team and manager, or your former colleagues and managers.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Replace a list of responsibilities with results: reach, revenue, speed or size changes.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, many resumes name tasks but give no impact, often because the writer never learned it. Others close to the project may know the numbers.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A line saying you built and shipped a website rewrite can gain views, extra revenue, a loading-time gain or a smaller codebase, if you find the figures.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: For the current job, ask your team and manager what the launch achieved. For old jobs, contact the old team or manager. This quiz does not grade it.

card.rule: Ask your team, your manager or former colleagues what your projects achieved, then add the figures.
card.limits: People may not remember or may not share figures. The book then says to estimate, which the next idea covers.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.section: Find Out the Impact of Your Past Projects
concepts.title: If you cannot find it, estimate
concepts.question: What should you do when the exact impact of a project cannot be found?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When no exact figure exists, estimate the impact to a good approximation.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give the reader some specifics rather than none.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says you do not need to be exact; being close enough is better than nothing.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented example: a developer cannot find the exact traffic gain from a redesign, so she writes a figure she can defend as close.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: An estimate has to stay honest and close; the book allows approximation, not invention.

card.rule: If the exact impact is unknown, give a good approximate estimate.
card.limits: Our reading: the estimate should be one you can defend in an interview, since the book asks only for a good approximation.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.section: Do a Grammar Check, Not Just a Spellcheck
concepts.title: Check grammar and readability, then re-read
concepts.question: Which checks does the book add beyond spelling, and why not rely on tools alone?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check grammar and readability with tools, keep sentences short, and then re-read the resume yourself several times.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A resume that reads naturally, with no typos and clear grammar.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author names a free grammar checker (Grammarly) and a free readability editor (Hemingway Editor) but warns against relying on them alone.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented example: a line with correct spelling can still be a long, tangled sentence. A readability tool flags it so you can split it.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Run the text through both tools, then read it again from the top at least a few times. This quiz does not grade it.

card.rule: Use grammar and readability tools, but also re-read the resume yourself, more than once.
card.limits: The tools can miss meaning or flag good lines. The book says to use them as help, not as the final judge.

media.alt: Screenshot of the Hemingway Editor writing app. The left pane shows a sample paragraph with sentences highlighted in yellow, red, purple, blue and green. The right pane shows a readability grade and a stack of coloured counters for adverbs, passive voice, simpler word choices and hard sentences. It shows a tool that flags long, complex or weak writing so you can simplify it.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.section: Ask for Friends or Family to Proofread
concepts.title: Get a fresh pair of eyes
concepts.question: Why should someone else read your resume before you send it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask a friend or family member to read the whole resume thoroughly and give feedback.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Catch grammar slips, typos and logic errors you have stopped seeing.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, as you write you develop tunnel vision and overlook obvious inconsistencies; a fresh reader notices what looks or sounds wrong.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented example: an author reads his own resume ten times and misses that two jobs overlap on dates. A friend sees it in one pass.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Hand the resume to someone you trust and ask them to mark anything that looks or sounds off. This quiz does not grade it.

card.rule: Have a friend or family member read your resume thoroughly before you send it.
card.limits: The book names friends and family for catching errors; it does not claim they judge hiring fit.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Use forums with low expectations
concepts.question: How should you use free online resume review forums, and which suit which reader?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Join resume feedback communities ahead of time, read feedback on other resumes, and treat the advice with a grain of salt.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Gain extra opinions on your resume at no cost without being misled by them.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says free feedback comes from members doing a favour, so hopes should stay modest. Reading other people's feedback first shows how useful it tends to be.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book names a Slack channel for engineering managers and review offers from community members on Dev.to, Twitter and LinkedIn.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Pick one community, read a few reviews of other resumes, and then decide what to post. This quiz does not grade it.

card.rule: Join feedback communities early, read other reviews, and take advice with a grain of salt.
card.limits: The book gives no quality guarantee for any forum; each reviewer's advice is one opinion.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Remove personal details before posting
concepts.question: What should you take out of a resume before you post it for review online?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Remove personal information from any resume you submit to a public forum.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep your private details safe while you collect feedback.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author notes the resume might be circulated well beyond your control once it is on a forum.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented example: before posting, a developer deletes her phone number, home address and email and replaces her name with a placeholder.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Anonymising does not stop the content from spreading; it only removes the details that identify you.

card.rule: Strip personal information from a resume before posting it for public feedback.
card.limits: The book gives the reason as loss of control over where the resume goes; it does not list which fields to remove, so the field choice here is our reading.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Compare your resume with the job description
concepts.question: How do you check that your resume uses the keywords of the job you are applying for?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Compare the job description with your resume and make sure its key terms appear, if you really have that experience.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stand out for the position by mentioning what the posting treats as key.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, a resume that mentions the keywords of a job is more likely to stand out.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For a Java backend position, the resume should mention Java and backend, assuming you have experience with both.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Underline the key terms in the posting and look for each in your resume. This quiz does not grade it.

card.rule: Compare the posting and your resume, and mention the job's key terms where they are true for you.
card.limits: The condition is real experience. The book's example says to mention both terms only if you have both.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Treat ATS scan services with caution
concepts.question: How much should you trust paid ATS scan services and their match scores?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use a scan service only for rough pointers on word overlap, and do not pay for premium tech-role advice.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid spending money on advice that is not likely to help a tech application.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says most scans rest on ATS fallacies and aim to upsell; the scores are guesswork and an ATS will not reject your resume.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A free scan of a resume against a posting never shows a full 100 percent match, which nudges you toward the paid plan.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: the author says a quick check can still give ideas for tailoring, so the free pointers can be useful.

card.rule: Use a free scan only as a rough pointer, and do not pay for ATS optimisation for tech roles.
card.limits: The book says the quick check can still suggest how to tailor your resume. Its criticism is aimed at paid upgrades and the scores.

media.alt: Screenshot of a scan service's report comparing a resume with a job posting. A large ring shows a low overall match rate under twenty percent. Beside it, horizontal bars rate several check groups: the recruiter-findings bar is full while the skills-match bar is almost empty. Below, a findings table marks missing skills and job title with red crosses, and education and section headings with green ticks.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Your LinkedIn is found, your resume is sent
concepts.question: How do recruiters find LinkedIn profiles, and how should that change what you write there?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Build your LinkedIn profile for recruiter search, and invest in it as much as in your resume.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let opportunities come to you while the resume handles your direct applications.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author likens the two to yin and yang: you apply directly with a resume, and recruiters find you through a profile. Recruiters search for a skillset in a certain location and may add filters such as companies or schools.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A recruiter filling a backend role searches for a skillset in one city and narrows by past employers. Profiles that match show up as search cards.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A profile tuned for search still does not replace a resume when you apply directly.

card.rule: Treat LinkedIn as a search profile for recruiters and give it as much effort as the resume.
card.limits: The book says the two are not identical, and that differences come from how recruiters use the search view.

media.alt: Yin-yang style diagram with two halves labelled Resume and LinkedIn profile. Crossing arrows on the left lead to applications to positions, which you start with a resume. Crossing arrows on the right lead to reachouts from recruiters, which come through the profile. It shows the two documents as complementary routes to a job: you apply with one, and opportunities find you through the other.

Screenshot of LinkedIn's recruiter search view: a left filter panel for job titles, locations, skills, companies and schools, and a result card on the right. Six numbered callouts point at the headline, title, location and industry line; the current title with its date; past titles with dates; school names; a Boolean skills search; and the other filters. It shows what recruiters glance at and filter by.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Headline and title: say what you want to be found for
concepts.question: What should your headline and current job title say on LinkedIn?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Set a headline that says what you want to be found for, and word your current title to describe your real role.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give recruiters a reason to click your profile in the first line they see.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The headline is the first thing a recruiter sees. If you set none, your current position appears there instead. A LinkedIn title need not match your contract title.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer leads a team but is officially a Software Developer. On LinkedIn her title can read Frontend team lead, since that is what she does.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The title has to be both true and how you want to be found, such as Backend engineer specializing in Go.

card.rule: Make the headline and current title state the role you want recruiters to find you for.
card.limits: The book allows a title different from your contract only when it is what you really do and how you want to be found.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Write the words recruiters search for
concepts.question: Why put technologies and practices in your profile text, and how do recruiters search?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Mention in your summary and job descriptions the technologies, frameworks and practices you want recruiters to find you for.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Appear in the results of the searches recruiters run.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, recruiters use Boolean search, combining AND, OR and NOT, and you appear if your profile contains the phrases. Closer matches and closer connections rank higher.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A search might ask for software developer OR software engineer, or for React.js AND Python while excluding managers with NOT.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Words only count when true; the author asks for terms you can back up.

card.rule: Put the terms recruiters would type into their searches into your headline, summary and job entries.
card.limits: Our reading: the approach depends on recruiters searching by words. A profile with the right words still has to read well to a person.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Tell your story in a longer summary
concepts.question: How does LinkedIn differ from the resume on summary length and on which jobs to show?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Write a summary of up to two paragraphs on the value you bring and your motivation, and leave out jobs that do not support your story.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Tell a clear professional story to hiring managers who do read the LinkedIn summary.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says recruiters and managers barely look at a resume summary but are likelier to read it on LinkedIn; he reads it and the last one or two job entries. More content may also rank higher.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer's part-time job from years ago has nothing to do with her profession. The author says to remove it as noise.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Draft two short paragraphs on the value you bring and why you want the work. Then delete positions that do not support that story.

card.rule: On LinkedIn write a fuller summary and remove jobs that do not support your professional story.
card.limits: The author says a LinkedIn profile does not have to fit one page; a longer text helps only if it stays on your story.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Signal a job search the right way
concepts.question: How should you show you are job hunting on LinkedIn, and what else helps when searching?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When job hunting, switch on the Open to Job Opportunities feature instead of writing it in your headline, and keep a current position listed.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Be found by recruiters without wasting your headline.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says phrases like Open for a new role add little and take space you could use for skills. He also says LinkedIn ranks a profile lower when it has no current position.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer between jobs lists a current role that shows the technologies and languages she is an expert in. A profile adviser quoted in the book suggests this.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Turn on the feature, add a current position, add colleagues and recruiters you know, and update your location if you have a destination in mind.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: If a move needs a visa, use judgment; confirm sponsorship once a company reaches out.

card.rule: Use the Open to Job Opportunities setting, not the headline, and always show a current position.
card.limits: Changing your location can bring local inbound messages, but the author says to use judgment where a visa is needed.

media.alt: Screenshot of a LinkedIn settings panel about letting recruiters know you are open to opportunities. A switch is turned on, set to Yes, with a Saved confirmation. Small print says LinkedIn tries not to reveal this to your current company but cannot guarantee complete privacy. It shows the built-in feature for signalling a job search without writing it in your headline.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Link GitHub only if you are proud of it
concepts.question: When is a GitHub link an asset on a resume, and when does it hurt?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Link your GitHub only if there is work on it you are proud to show, and tidy it first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn a click-through into a positive impression instead of a doubt.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says there is no expectation of a GitHub link, but as a hiring manager he often clicks it after the first scan. Other managers confirmed that. Recruiters click less. At the onsite, developers on the panel often raise the projects as talking points.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A candidate links an empty profile. The manager clicks, finds nothing, and the link has done harm. Do not link an empty profile or one with poor code visible.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Open your profile as a stranger would. If the first view embarrasses you, tidy it or leave the link off.

card.rule: Include a GitHub link only when the work visible there is worth showing, and clean it up first.
card.limits: Having no GitHub link is not penalised: the author never explicitly looks for one.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Show what a hiring manager scans for
concepts.question: What does this hiring manager look for on a GitHub profile?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Make the profile show context, code quality, tests, contributions to larger projects and how you handle issues and pull requests.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give a manager reasons to think you write clean, tested code and work well with others.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author names five checks: a clear project description and README with how to run and test; readable, well-named code; unit or integration tests; contributions to larger open source projects; and polite handling of pull requests and issues on a popular repository. He does not pay attention to followers, repository counts or contributions in the last year.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented example: a manager opens a pinned project, finds a README that explains how to run it and a test folder, and sees the owner answering an issue calmly.

card.rule: Arrange your GitHub so a quick visit shows context, quality, tests, outside contributions and collaboration.
card.limits: Our reading: these are one hiring manager's checks. The book says others confirmed the click-through habit, not this full list.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Set up your profile page to sell you
concepts.question: Which steps turn a GitHub profile into one a hiring manager wants to explore?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Add a profile README, pin your best repositories, describe each one, and give each pinned project a good README.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the few clicks a manager gives your profile count.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says hiring managers will probably open only a few pinned repositories, so those should be your best. A short repository description should say what the project does and why it is interesting.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A personal README is created by making a repository named like your username and starting it with a README. Pinned projects have READMEs that say what they do and how to use them.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Create the profile repository, pin your best work, write a lively description for each, and compare your READMEs with those of popular projects.

card.rule: Build your profile page: a personal README, pinned best repositories, clear descriptions and strong READMEs.
card.limits: The tidy-up supports good work but does not replace it, since the author says to link only what you are proud of.

media.alt: Screenshot of GitHub's Create a new repository form. The owner field and the repository name field hold the same username. A green box announces a special repository whose README is shown on the owner's profile, if it is public and initialised with a README. The Public option is selected. It shows how a personal profile README is created.

Screenshot of a GitHub profile Overview page. On the left are a profile photo, a name and a short bio. On the right is a grid of six popular repository tiles, each with a title, one-line description, language dot, stars and forks. A callout arrow points at the link for customizing pins, urging you to show your best repositories.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Point to the one or two articles that prove your skill
concepts.question: How should a technical blog appear on a resume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Link the one or two most relevant technical articles you wrote, with a short description, instead of only your blog's address.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Steer the reader to proof of the skill the job asks for.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says linking a whole blog hands control to chance: the reader lands on whatever you posted last. Naming articles lets you choose what they read first.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For a frontend role asking for Angular, the before version links a blog whose latest two posts are non-technical, with two solid Angular articles buried deep. The after version links those two articles directly.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Pick the one or two posts that best match a target job, and write a line saying what each covers. This quiz does not grade it.

card.rule: List one or two relevant articles with a short description rather than just linking the blog.
card.limits: The advice assumes you have good articles. The book frames a blog as a bonus, not an expectation.

media.alt: Excerpt from a resume's Projects section: a single bullet saying the person writes about technical concepts on a blogging platform, with only the platform's name as a link. This is the before version. The link leads to the blog as a whole, so the reader lands on whatever was posted most recently rather than on chosen articles.

Excerpt from a resume's Projects section: a single bullet saying the person writes a technical blog, with a green highlight on a phrase announcing popular articles, followed by two underlined links to individual articles about the Angular framework. This is the after version, pointing straight at the two articles most relevant to the job.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.section: StackOverflow, Twitter, Instagram, Quora and Other Social Sites
concepts.title: StackOverflow sometimes, social media no
concepts.question: Which of the other sites belong on a resume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Link StackOverflow only if you are active and your profile supports your story; leave Twitter, Instagram and Quora off.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Add credibility where it shows relevant expertise and avoid weak signals.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says an active profile can support your credibility, such as many badges in a technology you want to be known for. He says other social sites convey professional value poorly.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A JavaScript expert with many JavaScript badges has a StackOverflow profile that backs a JavaScript story.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: An inactive or unrelated profile adds nothing; the author's advice is conditional on activity and fit.

card.rule: Include StackOverflow only when active and on-story, and keep other social media off the resume.
card.limits: The author gives these as his view as a hiring manager.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Write cover letters where someone will read them
concepts.question: For which employers is a cover letter worth the effort?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Prioritise cover letters for smaller companies where the hiring manager screens resumes, or when you can reach the manager directly.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Spend effort where a letter is read and skip it where it is not.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says big tech rarely asks for them and tech recruiters rarely read them. At smaller companies and startups the hiring manager screens, and fewer applicants make a letter likelier to be read.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer applies to a ten-person startup, where the manager reads every application, and sends a letter. For a large firm that asks only for a resume, she does not.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Your tailored resume should already work like a cover letter, which makes the letter less important.

card.rule: Write cover letters mainly for small companies or direct contacts with the hiring manager.
card.limits: The author says small companies may allow letters but few ask for them, and the tailored resume already does much of the work.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Keep a developer cover letter short and specific
concepts.question: What should a short cover letter for a developer role contain?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep the letter short and show you read the job ad and the company's site, name the company, briefly say why you fit, and check the spelling.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the company feel a little special and raise your odds of passing the CV screen.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The recruiter quoted in the book says firms want to feel that an offer would likely be accepted, and a coherent letter that shows you read their material stands out.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A letter names the company, refers to something on its website, and gives two lines on qualifications linked to the role.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The same recruiter notes some firms may not read letters; for competitive junior or very senior roles motivation matters more.

card.rule: Keep it short, name the company, show you understand the role and why you fit, and spell check.
card.limits: The advice comes from one recruiter's view; she says some companies may not find letters useful and that the style should suit the company and country.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Personal beats templated
concepts.question: Why do templated cover letters fail, and what does a strong personal one do?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Skip the template and write a personal letter for that position and company, only where someone will probably read it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Win attention at companies that read letters.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says templated letters are frequently ignored in tech, since they add little beyond the resume. A strong letter talks about the company first and the applicant second, sounds sincere and not copy-pasted, and reads with energy.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book praises a letter by an engineer to a bold US startup: it shows he followed the company and shares its mission, and he says why he is excited and what he offers.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A personal letter costs time; do it where the reader exists, such as smaller firms or direct contact with the manager.

card.rule: Write a sincere, personalised letter about the company first, and only where it will be read.
card.limits: The book says to write such letters only when someone will probably read them, since they take time.

media.alt: Plain-text cover letter template full of curly-brace placeholders: a greeting with a name slot, an opening line with slots for position, site, skills, years and a problem to solve, then three bullets each pairing a job requirement with proof of having done it, a polite closing request and a name slot.

A long, informal cover letter addressed to a company, opening with a waving-hand emoji. It has short paragraphs, bold lead-in lines, two bullets contrasting what the writer is and is not good at, and an enthusiastic, challenging tone that talks about the company first. It illustrates a bold, non-traditional letter aimed at a startup.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.title: Match the tone to the company, level and country
concepts.question: What risks does a bold cover letter carry, and how do you judge them?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Match the letter's tone to the company, your level and the country, and weigh the risk of coming across as over the top.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get your foot in the door without putting off a reader.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says the praised letter also breaks unwritten rules: it is over the top, can make an applicant sound junior, and its tone suits the US but not a traditional firm in the UK or Australia.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The same exuberant letter that wins a US startup could land in the bin at a conservative UK firm, where a professional tone is expected.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author says to use good judgment, and that a tactful, personalised letter can make the difference at small companies.

card.rule: Weigh a letter's tone against the company's culture, the level you apply for and the country.
card.limits: The book says a casual style may suit a young US startup and a reserved one a large UK or Australian firm. It is the author's view.

concepts.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
concepts.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Application Beyond the Resume
concepts.title: Where to spend effort beyond the resume
concepts.question: Which of the extras beyond the resume matter most for a software developer, and what is the action for each?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put effort first into LinkedIn, GitHub and technical blogs, then into a tailored cover letter where it will be read.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Increase the chance of a recruiter call.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The recap says LinkedIn, GitHub and technical blogs are usually the most relevant for developers, and StackOverflow and cover letters can also play a part.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: LinkedIn: update the profile for what you want to be found for. GitHub: pin high-quality projects with good READMEs. Blog: name specific articles. Letter: tailor and keep brief.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Pick the one extra you have neglected most and do its action this week. This quiz does not grade it.

card.rule: Prioritise LinkedIn, GitHub and technical blogs, and add a tailored cover letter where it will be read.
card.limits: The ranking is the author's view of what matters for developers; individual employers differ.

concepts.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
concepts.title: Why flashy templates work against developers
concepts.question: Why does the author advise developers against flashy resume templates that promise to make you stand out?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Choose a plain template from a source with a record of working for software developers, not a flashy one that promises to make you stand out.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get a resume that recruiters and hiring managers can read easily and that pushes you to share specifics.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, flashy templates are usually harder to read, and in his experience as a hiring manager they push people towards fewer specifics and more buzzwords.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A popular template site sells its templates on a promise to make you stand out. The author calls that kind of flashy template a poor choice for software engineers and engineering managers.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Look at the template you use now and ask whether it hides your specifics behind decoration.

card.rule: Prefer plain templates from sites with a track record for software developers over flashy templates that promise to stand out.
card.limits: The advice is the author's judgment as a hiring manager, not test data, and it is aimed at software engineers and engineering managers.

media.alt: Marketing graphic from a resume-builder site. On the left, a card about memorable design above a list of six features such as no learning curve and content analysis. In the centre, a column of coloured circles for choosing a colour theme. On the right, a sample resume with a coloured accent, a photo, skill bars, a pie chart and icons in two columns. It shows a flashy, designer-style template.

concepts.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
concepts.title: Top-to-bottom reading
concepts.question: In what direction do recruiters and hiring managers read a resume, and what should that mean for its layout?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Lay out your resume so that it reads in one pass from the top to the bottom.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let a recruiter or hiring manager take in the resume without hunting for where to begin.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says that every hiring manager and tech recruiter he has talked with reads resumes top to bottom, himself included, and that a well-known hiring guide recommends the same.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The guide for hiring managers, Hiring Geeks that Fit, tells its readers: “Start reading each resume at the top.” The book treats this as a recommendation as well as a habit.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Cover your resume with a sheet of paper and pull it down: does each line you reveal build on the one above?

card.rule: Make your resume readable in a single pass from top to bottom.
card.limits: The evidence is the author's conversations and one hiring guide, not a survey of all recruiters.

concepts.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
concepts.title: Most relevant things first
concepts.question: Where on the page should the most relevant parts of your resume go, and where do the less relevant parts belong?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put the sections most relevant to the position near the top and the less relevant ones towards the end.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make sure the details that matter for this role are seen first and the minor ones come last.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Good nonfiction opens with an introduction that sets the context. A resume works in a somewhat similar fashion, so the most relevant things go towards the top.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author compares a resume to nonfiction: a good book starts with an introduction and often explains the chapters to come, and a good resume starts with what matters most.

blocks.label: Look-alike
