blocks.text: Do not read this as putting your oldest or most impressive item first; relevance to the position decides.

card.rule: Order your resume so that the parts most relevant to the position come first.
card.limits: Our reading: Relevance depends on the position, so the order is not fixed for every application.

concepts.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
concepts.title: Strategic use of colour and bold
concepts.question: How should bold and colour be used on a resume, and how do they help a reader?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use bold and colour strategically to point the reader at the few things you want to stand out.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Guide the reader's eye to key details without adding clutter.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says bolding can draw attention and colours can also pull your attention, so used strategically both guide the reader.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the author's improved template, the details a recruiter scans for, such as years of experience, technologies, titles and location, stand out clearly at a glance.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Pick the two details a recruiter must not miss on your resume and check that they are the ones that catch your eye first.

card.rule: Use bold and colour strategically to guide attention to what should stand out.
card.limits: The book says strategic but gives no count of how much bold or colour is right; that is left to your judgement.

concepts.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
concepts.title: How a hiring manager reads for fit
concepts.question: What does a hiring guide say a manager does with the strong points a candidate puts at the top?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat the top of your resume as the place where a hiring manager learns what you think your strong points are, and make them match the role.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let a manager compare your resume with the job's requirements quickly.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A hiring guide says that seeing what a candidate presents as strong points tells you a lot about the candidate, and the author reads resumes the same way.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The guide's author reads each resume from the top to its final line. As she reads, she makes a mental note to compare later with the actual job's requirements.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: One guide and one author describe this method; other managers may weigh things differently.

card.rule: Show your strongest, role-relevant points where a top-to-bottom reader begins.
card.limits: It is one manager's method, backed by the author's own practice, not a rule that every manager follows.

concepts.title: The familiar LinkedIn-style top-down layout
concepts.question: Which layout do recruiters know best, and what must a developer add to it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Pick a top-down template shaped like a LinkedIn profile, adjusted to show your languages and technologies.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give recruiters a layout they know while stressing what developers need to show.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Recruiters read LinkedIn profiles day in, day out, so the format is familiar. LinkedIn's generic format does not stress languages and technologies, which matter for developers.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book first shows a LinkedIn profile as recruiters see it, then an adjusted format for developers. The adjusted version keeps the familiar top-down layout and gives languages and technologies a place.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Find where your languages and technologies appear on your resume and see whether a recruiter could spot them in a glance.

card.rule: Follow the familiar top-down profile layout and add emphasis on languages and technologies.
card.limits: Our reading: A copy of LinkedIn's generic layout leaves out what developers most need to show.

media.alt: Wireframe of a LinkedIn-style profile as one column of white boxes on blue: a photo beside name and details, then Summary, Work Experience with three inner entries, Education, Projects, Skills and Expertise, and Honors and Awards. It shows the top-down structure recruiters read daily; languages and technologies have no block of their own.

Wireframe of an adjusted top-down resume template: one column of white boxes on blue, with a long arrow down the side meaning read top to bottom. From the top: name and details, Summary, Languages and Technologies, Work Experience with three entries, Education, Projects, then Interests or Honors and Awards. It adds a dedicated technologies block to the LinkedIn-style order.

concepts.title: Top-down for long resumes
concepts.question: Does the top-down layout still work when the resume runs past one page, and what is the cost?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the top-down layout even for a multi-page resume, and accept its one downside.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep enough room for detail while the layout stays familiar and easy to read.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says top-down layouts work well for multi-page resumes too. Given how familiar and easy to read the format is, he sees little reason not to use it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book weighs one possible downside of the top-down layout against its familiarity and ease of reading, and ends up recommending it.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: If page space is the only thing that matters, a multi-column layout seems to do better.

card.rule: Use the top-down layout, even over several pages, because it is familiar and easy to read.
card.limits: Our reading: It may use page space less efficiently than a multi-column layout.

concepts.title: Why two columns are harder to read
concepts.question: What does a two-column resume do to the reader's path, and why does that hurt?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Avoid a two-column layout, because the reader must read down one column and then start again in the other.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let a recruiter find education or work experience at once, without working out where to look.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says a two-column layout gains something at the cost of readability. The reader goes top to bottom, then starts again, and key sections are in no fixed place.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book shows two popular two-column examples. Their columns are in a different order, even compared with the first example, so a recruiter cannot rely on where things sit.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: A tidy, compact page is not the same as an easy-to-read one.

card.rule: Avoid two columns: the reader has to restart, and key sections move around.
card.limits: The layout's goal is real, but the book finds the readability cost too high for developers.

media.alt: Wireframe of a two-column resume. A top row holds a photo with Summary beside a Contact box. Below, a narrow left column holds Relevant Skills and a wider right column holds Work Experience with three entries above Education. Arrows at the side say to read top to bottom and then left to right, so the reader must restart in the second column.

Two wireframe two-column resumes side by side. The left one has name with photo, Summary, Work Experience and Education in its wide column, and Contact, Interests and Skills in the narrow column. The right one has Name and Contact with photo, Projects and Work Experience in its wide column, and Life Philosophy, Toolbox and Education in the narrow one. Section order and placement differ between them.

concepts.title: Two columns and thin detail
concepts.question: How does a two-column layout affect how much you say about your work?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Prefer a layout with room for several bullet points per position, so you can describe results instead of buzzwords.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Describe the impact of your work with the technologies you use.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, none of the two-column designs he shows cater for several bullet points per position, so such resumes are more likely to fill with buzzwords and cliches.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author looks at the two-column examples in the book and finds no space in them for several bullets under a job or a project.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: This describes the designs in the book; a particular two-column template could differ.

card.rule: Choose a layout that lets you write several bullets for each job and project.
card.limits: The claim is about the two-column designs the author reviewed, not a proof about every design.

concepts.title: When two columns can fit
concepts.question: For which jobs does the author think a two-column resume can be a good choice?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use two columns only when the layout itself is part of the application, as in design or UX; for software roles stay with a single column.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Match the layout to what the reader will judge.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The book says two-column can be a great choice for design or UX positions, where the layout is part of the application. For software developers it sees no advantage, only drawbacks.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A UX designer's resume layout shows the craft the employer wants to judge. A backend developer's does not, so the same layout buys the developer nothing. (Our illustration of the book's point.)

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: Do not read this as two columns being bad in general: it fits where the layout is itself on show.

card.rule: Choose two columns only when your layout is itself part of what is being judged.
card.limits: The advice is addressed to software developers; elsewhere the author only says two columns might work.

concepts.title: A technical recruiter's view of layouts
concepts.question: Why does a technical recruiter consider top-down best, and what does he say about the two-column layout?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Judge a layout by whether it lets a recruiter take in your career story in about ten seconds.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Earn the time to discuss more by telling your career story briefly and right.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The recruiter, who has worked at Facebook and Andela and seen thousands of resumes, finds top-down most readable and says it starts with skills and relevant experience, which the hiring team wants first.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: He calls a resume a brief story of your career, a ten-second elevator pitch. If you tell it right in that time, you get time to talk further.

blocks.label: Persuasion
blocks.text: This is one recruiter's testimony from experience. It supports the view but is not a measurement.

card.rule: Pick the layout that tells your career story fastest and most clearly.
card.limits: Our reading: It is one recruiter's opinion, offered as an expert view, not data about all recruiters.

concepts.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
concepts.title: The four details of the first scan
concepts.question: Which details do recruiters and hiring managers look for in the first few seconds?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Make four details easy to find: years of experience and dates, relevant technologies, titles and companies, and where you are based.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Pass the recruiter's first quick check so that they go on to read the rest.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In the first few seconds, recruiters and hiring managers want a few key details. These tell them quickly whether the candidate is worth reading in full.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the book's sample resume, the recruiter first notes at least two years of experience. If that matches the hiring manager's guidance, the scan continues.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Ask a friend to look at your resume for five seconds, then ask them to name your years of experience, main technologies, latest title and location.

card.rule: Make years and dates, relevant technologies, titles and companies, and your location easy to see.
card.limits: These four are the book's list for a first scan, not everything a recruiter will ever want to know.

media.alt: Full-page text resume of a software developer in a plain single-column format: centred header with name and contact, then ruled headings for tech stacks, work experience, volunteer work, education, awards, skills and interests, and personal projects. Company names are blue links, dates sit at the right edge, and bullets are dense. It is the original resume used for the book's scan walkthrough.

The sample resume blurred, with callouts. One arrow points at the city in the header, labelled as location, with a note on whether a visa or relocation might be needed. Arrows to the latest job's date range, an earlier job's start and the graduation year show quick date maths for years of experience, concluding with two to three years.

The blurred sample resume again, with boxed words pulled out: the city, two programming languages from the tech stack, three job titles with their years, and the degree with its graduation year. Notes say the recruiter checks whether technologies overlap what the hiring manager wants, and reads titles and companies for career progression and standout employers or schools.

concepts.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
concepts.title: The staged read: scan, then skim, then page two
concepts.question: In what order does a recruiter move from first glance to reading page two?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Expect a staged read and make sure what matters shows up at each stage before attention drops.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep the recruiter reading by passing each stage in turn.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The book describes a first scan for key details with a glance at technologies and titles. If most match, the recruiter starts reading top to bottom with a short scan, and only then looks at the second page or reads in depth.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book walks through a sample resume in stages. Each stage highlights what a recruiter would see, and each pass is shorter than a full read.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Mark on your own resume which details a recruiter would see at each of the three stages.

card.rule: Put what matters where each stage of the read will reach it, starting with the first scan.
card.limits: The sequence is the author's account of how recruiters read, not a measured timing.

media.alt: The sample resume blurred, with many short phrases boxed from top to bottom: key technologies, actions such as re-architecting, managing a team, building an app and designing an API, a scholarship, and practices such as design patterns. A note says the recruiter asks how good a fit the person is, and sees varied mobile and backend experience.

concepts.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
concepts.title: What a good template does for the recruiter
concepts.question: How does a good template help the recruiter, and what else must the resume have?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Pick a template that makes the key details very easy to find and that steers attention to a few extra points.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Free the recruiter's time for reading what you want to say.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A good template makes the key pieces of information easy to find, and it can guide attention to a few additional points. The recruiter then gets the facts faster and spends more time on what you share.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the book's walkthrough, the same four details are found at a glance with a good template, and the recruiter's time goes into reading the content.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A template alone cannot make weak content strong.

card.rule: Choose a template that makes the key details easy to find and steers attention to a few more.
card.limits: Our reading: A template does not replace content; it only makes good content quicker to reach.

media.alt: The revised resume, blurred, with four boxed regions and callouts: the city line at the top, the technologies block under the header, the date column at the right of each job, and the aligned titles, companies and school name on the left. Notes say location is immediately clear, dates stand out, relevant technologies are listed upfront, and titles and companies stand out.

concepts.section: The Results of Using a Good Resume Template
concepts.title: Template and content together
concepts.question: What difference does a readable template with strong content make to a tired, hurried recruiter?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Pair a readable template with well-written, specific content so that your chances do not depend on the recruiter's mood.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get your information across even to a recruiter who is tired or in a hurry.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says a hard-to-read format makes the recruiter work hard and leaves your chances to luck. A recruiter who sees a resume late in a big pile may be tired and short of time, and may set it aside.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book shows the same candidate twice. In the updated resume the key details stand out, and the content is more specific about the impact of the candidate's work.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Ask a friend to read your resume at the end of a long day and tell you what they remember.

card.rule: A readable template plus specific content gets your information across even when the reader is hurried.
card.limits: The book gives this as the author's reasoning from experience, not as a measured effect on hiring rates.

media.alt: Full-page revised resume of the same developer in a single-column template: large centred name, a one-line contact row, blue ruled headings for technologies and languages, work experience, education, and projects and volunteer work. Titles, companies and dates share one aligned bold line, and bullets lead with outcomes and figures such as percentages and team sizes.

The revised resume with the body blurred and short phrases boxed down the page: figures such as a conversion gain, team size, number of apps served and scholarship selectivity; action words like re-architected and built; tool names; and project results with audience numbers. A note says impact is clear from the first words, numbers draw attention, and the resume reads easily top to bottom.

concepts.title: The four template principles together
concepts.question: Which four principles should a resume template satisfy, and how do they fit together?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Choose a template that reads top to bottom, uses a single column, puts important things first and uses bold and colour with purpose.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Pick a template quickly and be able to give reasons for the choice.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The principles support each other: a single column keeps the reading path simple, order puts relevant items first, and emphasis steers attention. A single-column layout also leaves room to share enough about your work.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The chapter's recap lists four principles. Apply them to any template in turn, and a template that fails one, such as a two-column design, is a weaker candidate.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Score your current template against the four principles and note the first one it fails.

card.rule: Choose templates that read top to bottom, use one column, put important things first and use emphasis strategically.
card.limits: The recap is the author's checklist for developer resumes, not a rule for design or UX roles.

concepts.title: Generators built for everyone
concepts.question: Why do most paid resume generators fit a software developer poorly?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before trusting a resume generator, check whether it is built for developers or for every profession at once.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get a resume in a format that technical hiring managers find familiar and easy to read.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, the big generator sites promise professional, proven resumes, but they are tuned for resumes of everyone, from finance and accounting to teaching and sales. Tech is a small slice of what they offer.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author counted the templates of one popular site: of 277, ten focus on tech and three on software development. Judged as a technical hiring manager, he would strongly recommend none, and they mostly use two columns.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Open any generator you are considering and count how many templates are for developers. Look at the sample content: does it read like a developer resume?

card.rule: Prefer a generator or template made with developers in mind over one optimised for all professions.
card.limits: This is the author's review of the sites he looked at. A generator built for tech and checked with hiring managers can still earn his approval.

media.alt: Screenshot of a resume site's category filter: a three-column list of professions, each followed by a count of examples. All categories is highlighted with 277; information technology shows only 10, a small slice beside many unrelated fields such as medical, sales and education.

Grid of eight thumbnail resume templates in two rows, each labelled with a job title and a star rating. Most use a narrow side column beside a wider main column, with tiny text and varied header styles, so none looks tuned to developer work.

concepts.title: Check the sample content
concepts.question: What can the example text inside a template tell you about whether it suits developers?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Read a template's sample content, and reject it if it shows no sign of real developer work.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid a template made by someone who has never written or hired for a developer resume.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says most such sites use content writers for developer resumes, and these are not checked with engineering managers or recruiters in tech. The gap shows in the details.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author's look at one site's Programmer example: it lists no programming language, yet lists spoken languages. Its skills section is weak, and it uses two columns.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: A good-looking page is not the same as a good template: the sample can look professional and still miss what tech readers want to see.

card.rule: Judge a template by its sample content: it should look like something a developer would really write.
card.limits: Our reading: Sample text is only a clue to who made the template. You will replace it with your own content, which matters more.

media.alt: Full-page generator template for a programmer: large name header, then a narrow left column with contact info, a skills list drawn with thick bars, and spoken languages with level bars. The wide right column holds profile, two jobs and education.

concepts.title: Ask a paid generator for evidence
concepts.question: What evidence should a paid resume generator show before you trust its claim that it gets you interviews?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Trust a paid generator only if it shows evidence: tech-ready templates, hiring-manager testimonials and real, successful resumes.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Spend money on a service whose results are backed by people who hire developers, not by marketing.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author lists three tests: templates made with the real audience and easy reading in mind; testimonials from real hiring managers or recruiters in the industry; and real, even anonymised, resumes that got people hired.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author applies these tests to the generators he reviewed and finds that most fail them for software developers.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Open a generator's site and look for named hiring managers or recruiters speaking about it, and for resumes of people who got hired.

card.rule: Ask a paid generator to show hiring-manager testimonials and real, successful resumes, not only claims.
card.limits: The tests are the author's own criteria for developer resumes. Passing them shows evidence, not a promise that you will get an interview.

concepts.title: Clear pricing, no ATS myths
concepts.question: Which two warning signs in a generator's pricing and sales pitch suggest it lacks industry expertise?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Avoid a generator whose pricing is unclear or whose pitch leans on ATS myths.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Pay only for a service with a clear value and a pitch you can trust, so you do not buy on fear.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says some sites advertise as free and then use dark patterns to charge, or have unclear tiers. Sites that quote ATS myths to upsell often have no industry expertise.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author gives a typical myth used to sell: that 75% of resumes are never seen by humans.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: A scare tactic is not evidence. A pitch that raises fear of the system is trying to persuade you, not to inform you.

card.rule: Choose a service with clear pricing and a clear value beyond a PDF, and walk away from pitches built on ATS myths.
card.limits: Clear pricing is one of the author's criteria, not a sign of quality alone. A fair price can still sit beside weak templates.

concepts.section: Standard Resume: By Developers, for Developers
concepts.title: What Standard Resume offers
concepts.question: What four benefits does the author give for paying for Standard Resume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you pay for a generator, choose one that gives you tech-ready layouts, a web version, view tracking and real developer examples.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Send a clean, readable resume in whatever channel you are using, and learn whether anyone opened it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author names four benefits: clean tech layouts whose spacing was set by UX designers, so fonts cannot be crammed; a web-only version you can send before applying; tracking of web views; and real resumes of developers who got hired.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: When you message someone on LinkedIn you often cannot attach a PDF. A link to a web resume with the same layout as the PDF solves it, and the platform shows whether it was opened.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: It is a paid subscription. The author also lists free recommended templates, so payment is a choice, not a requirement.

card.rule: Pay for a generator only for concrete benefits, such as uncramped layouts, a shareable web version, view tracking and real examples.
card.limits: These are the author's reasons for one paid tool, and he recommends it alongside free templates. If you do not need the web link or tracking, a free template can do.

media.alt: Gallery of twelve thumbnail resume templates in two rows, each with a style label below and one marked as selected. Nearly all are single-column, top-to-bottom pages with generous spacing; a few add a narrow side column or accent colour.

concepts.section: Standard Resume: By Developers, for Developers
concepts.title: Do not cram the page
concepts.question: What does a Standard Resume cofounder say is the number one issue with software engineering resumes?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep whitespace between sections and a readable font size; focus on the critical parts or accept a second page.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the resume easy to read, because a recruiter who skips a hard-to-read page never reaches your content.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A cofounder of Standard Resume says cramming a lot onto one page is the number one issue he sees. Removing space between paragraphs and sections, or using tiny fonts, makes a resume harder to scan, and if it is skipped nothing else matters.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: a candidate shrinks the font and deletes the gaps to keep four jobs on one page. The recruiter sees a dense block and moves on. Cutting to the critical roles, or using two pages, would have kept it readable.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Check your font size and the gaps between sections. If you have shrunk either to fit one page, cut the least relevant lines first.

card.rule: When the content does not fit, cut to the critical parts or use two pages; do not shrink fonts and spacing.
card.limits: This is a cofounder's view, not a law. The earlier chapters of the book give the author's own advice on length and what to cut.

concepts.title: Content beats template
concepts.question: How much should the choice of template matter compared with the content you write?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Start from a tried and proven template, customise it, and spend most of your effort on the content.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get a strong resume built quickly without waiting for a perfect layout.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, a template is a great help for getting started, and customising a proven one to your own style is good practice. But what the resume says counts for more than the template it sits in.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: a candidate spends two weeks comparing layouts and an hour on bullet points. A better split would use a proven template on day one and spend the time on results and impact.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Pick a recommended template today and set a deadline. Spend the time you saved rewriting your weakest bullet points.

card.rule: Pick a proven template early, customise it lightly and put your effort into writing strong content.
card.limits: This does not make layout irrelevant: the book's chapter on template principles still applies. It says the template is not where the main work lies.

concepts.title: How to read a template review
concepts.question: What does each part of the author's template reviews tell you, and how should you use it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Read each review for its rating, strengths, drawbacks and fixes, and borrow the good parts even from templates you reject.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Choose and adapt a template with a clear view of its trade-offs rather than by looks alone.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The reviews share one format: a link; a rating for software developers on how well it follows good developer template principles; the good, the bad, and ways to improve it. The good parts can inspire you even if you do not use the template.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A review that lists a drawback such as no room for personal details also lists a fix, so you can judge whether you can live with it or must customise.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Write your own review of your current template in this format, then act on the single most useful fix.

card.rule: Use a review's rating to compare, its bad points to find risks and its ways to improve to customise.
card.limits: A rating is the author's judgment for software developers, not a verdict for every profession or a guarantee of results.

concepts.title: The Pragmatic Engineer's template
concepts.question: Why does the author rate this clean one-column developer template so highly?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the Pragmatic Engineer's template when you want a clean developer layout that US tech recruiters already know how to scan.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get your titles, dates and achievements read quickly, in a format that feels familiar to the reader.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author's review gives it five stars. It resembles the CareerCup template, so US tech recruiters find it familiar. Consistent formatting and good use of bold make it easy to scan, and dates and titles are easy to read.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book shows this template as page images; we rely on the author's commentary. His review lists these strengths and one drawback: it does not cater to people who want to add more personal information.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Compare your current resume with the strengths listed: can a reader find your dates and titles at a glance?

card.rule: Choose this template for a clean, scannable layout that US tech recruiters recognise.
card.limits: The review's one drawback is that it leaves little room for extra personal information, though the author says that can be customised.

media.alt: Resume template page with centred name, contact details left and profile links right. Headings in blue with rules: work experience, education and certifications, technologies and languages. Each job shows title, employer, team, location and dates, with bullet counts shrinking from newest to oldest job.

concepts.title: The Mono Engineer's template
concepts.question: When does shifting the emphasis toward titles or companies help your resume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Choose the Mono variant when your job titles or your employer names are your strongest selling point and should draw the eye.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Put the stronger of your two signals, company or title, in front of the recruiter first.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, this template is a slight modification of the Pragmatic one that draws more attention to the company or the job title. It suits people with standout companies, and people whose employers recruiters will not recognise, since focusing on titles then makes more sense.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Invented illustration: an engineer at a little-known startup holds a senior title. A layout that gives the title weight tells the reader the level at once, even though the company name means nothing to them.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: It is a variation on the Pragmatic template and shares its drawbacks, such as limited room for personal details.

card.rule: Pick the variant that emphasises the signal that is strongest for you: standout companies or, if they are unknown, your titles.
card.limits: Our reading: It is a slight change to the Pragmatic template, so it keeps that template's strengths and its drawbacks. Pick it for the emphasis, not for a different structure.

media.alt: Single-column resume page with a centred name, a contact line with links, and a short summary. Headings are capitals over thin rules. Each job opens with a bold employer line and dates at the right, with the job title in plain type below.

concepts.title: The Markdown to PDF template
concepts.question: Why might a developer keep a resume in Markdown on GitHub rather than in a word processor?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you are comfortable with the command line, write your resume in Markdown and build the PDF from it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep a single source of truth and many versions of your resume under version control.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says this template generator treats Markdown as the source for your resume and lets you store different versions on GitHub or another source. You build the resume from the command line.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author lists these as the template's good points: a clean template, Markdown as the data source, versions stored in GitHub and building from the command line.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Copy your resume into a text file in Markdown form and commit it, so your next edit leaves a history.

card.rule: Use Markdown as the source of your resume when you want versions in a repository and a build from the command line.
card.limits: Our reading: The review is rated five stars for developers, but it suits those who like working with code. Its drawbacks are the same as those of the Mono template.

media.alt: Plain black-and-white resume page rendered from Markdown: centred serif name and contact line, bold capitalised section headings over rules, then experience, projects, education and skills. Jobs have bold titles, right-aligned dates and bulleted lines with no colour.

concepts.title: The Experienced Engineer's template
concepts.question: For whom is a two-page template with deliberate empty space and links a strong choice, and for whom a weak one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the Experienced Engineer's template only if your career has standout features; otherwise pick a plainer one.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make a candidate with standout companies, titles or contributions stand out across two pages.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: It is a two-page template for experienced developers with standout experience, such as principal, staff or distinguished engineers, standout employers or open source work. Company names and titles get extra attention and links invite the reader to click.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author rates it five stars with standout experience and three without. Its empty left side and the technologies section landing on page two are deliberate: they push attention to names and titles.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: It works poorly for people with less experience or few standout areas, who gain little from what it emphasises.

card.rule: Match the template to your profile: a two-page layout that stresses names and titles pays off only if you have standout names and titles.
card.limits: The ratings are the author's. A layout whose trade-offs are deliberate is a strength only for the profile it was built for.

media.alt: Two-page-style resume first page: centred name and links, a one-line summary, then section labels in a narrow left margin. Entries sit in a wide right column, with the employer and title bold on one line and dates right-aligned; the area under the labels is empty.

concepts.title: Parker and Venables ports
concepts.question: What do the Standard Resume ports Parker and Venables add to the original templates, and what do they cost?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Consider the paid Parker or Venables version when you want the original layout with designer spacing, a web link and tracking.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get a proven layout that is hard to break and easy to share.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Parker is Standard Resume's port of the Pragmatic template and Venables is its port of the Experienced template. Designer touches make them slightly more readable, and Venables needs less fiddling with tables.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author finds Parker easier to scan than the original. Both ports give a shareable web version with the same layout, with views tracked by the platform.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Locations cannot be set per position, so the author added them to the company name field. They are also paid.

card.rule: Prefer a port when you value its spacing and web features more than the freedom to edit the layout.
card.limits: Our reading: Their ratings equal those of the originals, so the gain is polish, not a new idea.

media.alt: Single-column resume page with a bold name and blue section headings with long rules to the right. Each job has the title bold on the left, employer and city in bold beside it, and dates right-aligned; education and technologies follow in aligned rows.

Resume page with a centred name over a short red rule. Section titles stand in a left margin; entries to the right show the employer with its city in brackets in bold, the title in regular type, and dates at the right. Education and technologies follow in aligned rows.

concepts.title: The CareerCup template
concepts.question: Why does a four-star template still need adjusting for non-US jobs and for a modern look?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the CareerCup template for US tech applications, and adjust it for non-US employers or a modern look.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Be easy to read for recruiters who see this format every day, without inheriting its dated habits.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author gives it four stars. US tech recruiters are used to it, dates and titles are easy to read, formatting is consistent and your experience is easy to work out. It dates from 2014, when printing resumes was still common, and is geared to top US tech companies.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Its black-and-white style looks dated, and the format encourages crowding content onto the page.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: If you apply outside the US, move the languages and technologies section up to page one.

card.rule: Use this template where US tech recruiters expect it, and adapt it elsewhere.
card.limits: Our reading: The review flags a dated style, a US focus and a tendency toward crowding. Two pages work if the most important details sit on the first page.

media.alt: Dense one-page resume in small black serif type, all in black and white. Small-caps bold headings with rules, then jobs, education, projects, awards and technologies. Each entry has employer and dates on one line, with tight, crowded bullet lists.

concepts.title: Match template to profile
concepts.question: Given your own career, which of the author's seven recommended templates should you start from?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Choose from the recommended list by your profile: a standout career, a recognised or unrecognised employer, a US or non-US target, a taste for code.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Spend less time choosing and begin with the template that suits your profile.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The seven recommendations differ in what they emphasise. Pragmatic and CareerCup suit US recruiters. Mono shifts emphasis to company or title. Experienced, and Venables as its port, suit standout careers. Markdown to PDF suits those who want versions in GitHub.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A staff engineer with an open source project fits Experienced or Venables; a mid-level engineer with a little-known employer might choose Mono.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: More stars do not mean better for you: the same template can be five stars with standout experience and three without.

card.rule: Start from the recommended template whose emphasis matches your strongest asset and your target.
card.limits: The author says content matters more than the template. Treat the list as a set of starting points, not a ranking.

concepts.title: Fix an 'other' template before use
concepts.question: When can a template the author hesitates to recommend still work for a developer?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use a not-recommended template only after fixing its stated drawbacks, and only if your content fits the space it gives you.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reuse a template you already have or like, without carrying its weaknesses into your resume.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author hesitates to recommend the second list but says those templates could work well enough once their drawbacks are addressed, or for certain use cases. Content matters more than the template.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The Google Docs Serif template is a two-column layout rated three stars. The author calls it an okay choice if you change Skills to Technologies and remove Awards and Languages.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: He says to use it only if everything definitely fits on one page, since the format gives little room for experience.

card.rule: Treat a hesitant-list template as a draft: apply the review's fixes, and drop it if your content will not fit.
card.limits: These are the author's cautions, not bans. For some use cases a fixed template works; a two-column one still scans worse than a single column.

media.alt: Two-column resume template with sample placeholder text: large name header and address block at the top, then a wide left column with experience, education and projects in blue headings, and a narrow right column with skills, awards and languages. The right column is cut off at the page edge.

concepts.title: Borrow the Swiss section order
concepts.question: Which section order does the author like in the Swiss template, and why does he still reject the template?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Take the section order from the Swiss template (technologies, then work experience, then education) but not the template itself.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Lead with what a hiring manager wants first, using a layout that is easy to scan.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says this order works well for software engineers. But the template is rated two stars: it wastes space on the left and makes it hard for recruiters to scan the dates for work and education.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: He advises against using it for software engineering roles.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Check your own section order against technologies, experience, education.

card.rule: Copy a good idea from a poor template; do not copy the poor template.
card.limits: Our reading: The order is his preference for software engineers, and the section order is not the only factor that decides a resume's quality.

media.alt: Resume page with section titles set in small bold capitals in a narrow left margin, with entries in a wide area to their right. Each job shows employer, title and right-aligned dates; large blank space sits under the left-hand labels, and education follows work experience.

concepts.title: Canva: choice without guidance
concepts.question: Why is a huge template library, like Canva's, a risk for a developer resume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In a large template library, filter hard: look for single-column templates with clear formatting.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find a readable developer resume among hundreds of designs made to look good.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author notes Canva may have the largest selection, but it is overwhelming, hard to narrow to tech, and most templates are optimised for looks over content. Ratings range from one to three stars.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A Canva Pro subscriber has hundreds of resume templates, and a few decent ones exist if you search more.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Most are not built with readability in mind, so a pretty pick is likely to be a poor one.

card.rule: When choosing among hundreds, use criteria (single column, clear formatting, no photo) instead of looks.
card.limits: Our reading: The rating spans one to three stars because the library varies, so a good pick is possible but takes effort.

media.alt: Gallery of nine colourful resume templates from a design tool. Most carry a round or square portrait photo, bold colour blocks, patterns or decorative shapes, and two-column arrangements, so looks dominate the page and text is small.

concepts.title: The cost of two columns
concepts.question: What do two-column resume.io templates cost a developer in space, relevance and consistency?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Reject a template whose columns limit the detail you can give on your work experience, or whose sections are not about tech.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep room for the experience and impact that decide your application.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author rates both resume.io templates he reviews at two stars. The two-column layout limits the details you can share. The software engineer one has no languages and technologies section but has a references section, and its skills have little to do with what tech hiring managers look for.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The example copy in the software engineer template seems written by someone who has not worked in software. For both templates the author advises not using them for software engineering positions.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: The single good point the author finds in each is that it is a one-page resume, which does not outweigh the lost room for detail.

card.rule: Do not use a template whose sections ignore what tech employers look for; the author advises against using these.
card.limits: The author's verdict covers software engineering positions. The same layouts may suit other fields, but his complaint is the loss of room for experience.

media.alt: Two-column resume template for a software developer: wide left column with profile, employment history with bullets, education and a references block with named referees; narrow right column with contact details, nationality and a skills list underlined in blue.

concepts.title: Drop the skill stars
concepts.question: Why do star or point scores for your technologies work against you?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: List the technologies you are proficient with and leave out any star, point or bar rating.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show only skills that help you, without handing the reader a reason to doubt you.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author gives three reasons. A score of three of five or lower begs the question why you list it. A four or five is a given, since readers assume you are proficient with whatever you list. And self-ratings are often off.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A template with a skills section scored in points is the web developer template. The author advises not using it for software engineering.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Delete any bars or stars in your skills section and keep only the technologies you could work with tomorrow.

card.rule: Drop star ratings and keep every relevant technology you are proficient with.
card.limits: Our reading: The advice is about self-scored ratings on a resume. It does not forbid listing technologies; it asks you to list those you are proficient with.

media.alt: Two-column resume template with a full-width boxed name and a grey side column on the left. It holds info and a skills list in which every entry has a row of five dots; wide column holds profile, employment history, education and references.

Close-up of a resume skills section: spaced-capital heading with a rule, then seven skill lines, each with a row of five dots beneath it. Every dot in every row is filled, so all skills show the top score, one entry appearing twice.

concepts.title: The VisualCV standard template
concepts.question: What makes the VisualCV standard template a solid alternative to CareerCup, and what does it cost?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the VisualCV standard template as an alternative to CareerCup, but pay to remove its branding and add what it lacks.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get a clean, two-page-ready layout that still shows dates and titles well.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author gives it three stars. It is clean, works well for two pages, separates sections clearly and highlights job titles while keeping dates easy to read.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: On the free service a logo is added, which makes the resume look cheap.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Look at your dates and job titles: can a reader find both at a glance?

card.rule: Use it as a CareerCup alternative if you pay to remove the logo, adding technologies on the first page.
card.limits: Our reading: The review is three stars and calls it a solid alternative, but only when the branding is gone; paid removal is part of the real cost.

media.alt: Resume template with name and job title at top, a contact block at the right, and a long summary paragraph. Experience entries show the bold title with dates at the right and the company in blue below, with bullet lists; education follows.

concepts.title: Pretty to you, hard to scan for them
concepts.question: Why does a resume that looks stunning to its owner often fail with the recruiter?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Judge a template from the reader's seat: pick it for how fast a recruiter can scan it, not for how pretty it looks to you.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep your resume readable for the technical hiring manager who decides its fate.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author lists the EnhanCV software engineer resume as a cautionary example of sites making resumes job seekers find pretty. It looks stunning to the candidate, but technical hiring managers find it hard to scan. It also pushes a photo, which leads to bias.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Some sections make little sense, such as Life Philosophy, and the two columns discourage enough detail about your experience.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The review rates it two stars, with looking stunning to the candidate as its one good point.

card.rule: Choose the template your reader can scan fastest, even if another looks more striking to you.
card.limits: The author's complaint is about scanning, bias and low-value sections in this template, not about attractive design as such.

media.alt: Busy two-column resume: large name with a coloured headline and a round portrait photo at the top. Left column has IT projects with links and corporate experience; right column has a life philosophy quote, a toolbox of technology tags, power skills tags and education.

concepts.title: Europass: avoid it
concepts.question: Why does the author advise against Europass for tech jobs, in Europe or anywhere else?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do not use the Europass CV template for tech jobs.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid details that invite bias, and keep space for what matters.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author gives it one star and says there is nothing good about it. It encourages adding photos, birth dates and gender, which lead to bias, and it uses a dated table format that wastes space and represents tech professions poorly.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: He says every tech recruiter he spoke with advised against it, and he agrees.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: It is not required to apply for jobs in Europe, though some assume it is.

card.rule: Skip Europass for tech applications.
card.limits: The author's advice covers any positions, tech or not. The claim about its origin is hearsay he could not confirm.

media.alt: European-format CV with a logo at top and labels in a left column. It shows a passport-style photo beside personal details, a job-applied-for line, work experience and education blocks, and a table grading spoken languages by listening, reading, speaking and writing level.

concepts.title: Skip templates that ask for a photo
concepts.question: Which template features should make you reject it because they invite bias?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Reject any template that has a place for a photo, birth date or gender, or that pushes you to add one.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep your application judged on skills and experience, not on personal details.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author flags this in several reviews: Canva templates often carry photos, EnhanCV encourages a photo that leads to bias, and Europass invites photos, birth dates and gender.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Choosing a single-column developer template without a photo slot removes the temptation.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Check any template you like for photo, birth date and gender fields. If it has them, pick another.

card.rule: Pick templates without a photo slot or personal-detail fields.
card.limits: The rule is the author's advice for tech resumes; local norms may differ, but he sees these details as leading to bias.

concepts.title: Cut sections tech readers do not need
concepts.question: Which template sections tell a tech reader nothing and should be removed or renamed?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Remove or rename sections that tell a tech reader nothing: awards, spoken languages, references, Life Philosophy, Power Skills.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Spend page space on technologies, experience and impact.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The reviews flag sections that are noise in a tech resume: Awards, spoken Languages, References, Life Philosophy and Power Skills. They take space from what recruiters look for.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In place of the Serif sidebar, the author suggests Technologies; in place of Toolbox, Skills.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: List your sections and ask of each: would a tech recruiter miss it?

card.rule: Keep sections a tech reader looks for, and cut the rest.
card.limits: Our reading: The advice is for tech resumes. A section that is noise for one field may matter in another.

concepts.title: Lead with the stack the posting asks for
concepts.question: Which of your skills should the reader see first on a resume for this particular job?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: List first the languages and tools that the target posting names and that you have really worked with.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the reader see a match with this position at first glance, instead of sending one resume to every job.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author wants a resume built on your own experience but tailored to the specific position; leading with the posting's own stack shows the fit at once.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A two-year engineer applied to a rotation programme whose posting named C++, Java, PHP and JavaScript. Being hands-on with PHP and JavaScript, they listed those two first in the refactored resume.

card.rule: List first the languages and tools that the target posting names and that you have really worked with.
card.limits: Our reading: List only what you have used: the example puts first the posting's languages the person works in, not all of them.

media.alt: Refactored resume, compact, with blue section headings and thin blue rules. Name centred, with location, email and a website link on one line. A technologies section of three bullet rows comes first, then work experience. Each role has job title at left, employer centred and dates in bold at right, followed by bullets that open with results and numbers. Education starts at the bottom.

concepts.title: Keep formatting consistent and spacing sensible
concepts.question: What do uneven fonts, alignment and margins say about the writer of a resume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the same font sizes and alignment in every section and keep margins and spacing no larger than they need to be.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Look careful, and use the page for content.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says inconsistent formatting gives the resume a sloppy feel, and very large margins reduce what fits on each page.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the 2-year example, font sizes and alignment differed between sections and the side margins were unusually large. In the 8-year remote example, the refactored resume still had a strange layout of spacing and bullets, and a header repeated on page two.

card.rule: Use the same font sizes and alignment in every section and keep margins and spacing no larger than they need to be.
card.limits: Our reading: Good spacing can help a resume; the complaint is against very large spacing at the top and sides, not against spacing.

media.alt: Page two of the same plain resume, with sections for volunteer work, education, awards, skills and interests, and personal projects. Organisation and project names are blue underlined links. Dates sit at the right margin in some sections but inline or on their own line in others, and the page switches between bullets and plain paragraphs, so formatting looks uneven.

Second page of the refactored CV. The name, phone, email and the two link labels are repeated in a banner at the top, then job entries continue from the previous page in the same format: title, centred employer, year range at right, bullets and a technologies line. The last entries are earlier roles ending with an intern entry.

concepts.title: Steer the reader's eye with links and bold
concepts.question: Where will a recruiter's eye land on your resume, and did you choose that place?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Link and bold only what you want read first, so the eye goes to your title, dates and results.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Draw attention to the things that show your value, not to decoration.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A glancing reader is pulled to links and bold text, so whatever carries them gets read first.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: One resume linked every past employer, so the eye went to company names rather than job title and date. The refactor also replaced a bare blog link by two chosen articles. Another resume bolded every technology, some results and even W4 forms.

card.rule: Link and bold only what you want read first, so the eye goes to your title, dates and results.
card.limits: Our reading: Company links bring little value, since a reader can search the name; a link still serves if it points to work you want opened.

media.alt: Page one of a plain single-column resume on white. Centred name and contact lines with a website link, then a short bulleted tech stacks section, then work experience. Every job heading begins with the employer name as a blue underlined link, followed by the job title and a date range at the right margin, with bullet points beneath.

Closing section headed projects and volunteer work, in blue with a rule. Four bullets, each opening with a bold label for a community role, two software projects and technical blogging. Each adds one or two lines of description and underlined links, such as to the source code or to two specific articles, instead of one bare link to a whole blog.

First page of an original resume with teal headings. A technical skills block of long bold lines lists many tools in one run. Work experience entries show title, employer, city and dates, with bullets in which many phrases are bold: percentages, feature names and some tools. Contact details are at top right and give no home city. Education is at the end and shows no dates.

concepts.title: Write what your work achieved, not just what you did
concepts.question: For each job on your resume, can the reader see why your work mattered beyond the code?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: For each role, state what your work achieved and why it mattered, in active language, with the impact first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show the reader a person who takes initiative and gets results, rather than someone who followed instructions.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says companies, especially in newer fields like machine learning, look for people who take initiative and get results.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A bullet said only that the person built a mobile app. The refactor, about the same person and the same work, went deeper to say how the work mattered beyond coding. Another refactor opened each role with its impact instead of burying it.

card.rule: For each role, state what your work achieved and why it mattered, in active language, with the impact first.
card.limits: Our reading: Impact has to be true to the work: the examples describe the same work more fully, not invented work.

media.alt: Refactored resume with teal headings and thin rules. Header has location and a profile link at left, name centred, phone and email at right. Technical skills form three short bullet rows. Each job shows title, team, employer, place and dates aligned right, with bullets that open with measured results. Dates show years only, and education lines now carry date ranges.

concepts.section: Machine Learning Engineer with 5 Years Experience
concepts.title: Add technologies, numbers and your role to each bullet
concepts.question: What would a hiring manager ask about each bullet, and does the bullet already answer it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put into each bullet the tools used, a number where one exists, and what your own role was.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the work concrete enough for a reader to judge its scale.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A general statement leaves the reader with questions; tools, numbers and role answer them without a call.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author suggested turning 'created a full-stack web application for internal stakeholders' into a line naming Vue.js, Django and AWS, or into 'designed, implemented and deployed 4 microservices serving 100 RPS'. For a tool that raised support efficiency by 30%, he asked which languages, whose idea, whether a team was led and how many customers used it.

card.rule: Put into each bullet the tools used, a number where one exists, and what your own role was.
card.limits: Add only numbers and details you actually have: the author's figures are illustrations of the kind of detail, not facts for your resume.

concepts.section: Machine Learning Engineer with 5 Years Experience
concepts.title: Leave out skill self-ratings
concepts.question: What does a score or star rating next to your own skill tell a hiring manager?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: List your skills without scores, stars or levels.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid giving a reader a reason to doubt your skill.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says self-rating can only work against you: a reader may take a middling score to mean you are not proficient, which is not what you meant.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A machine learning resume opened with 4 out of 5 for Python and 3 out of 5 for JavaScript. The author, as a hiring manager, could assume a weak developer or an over-modest one. An 8-year engineer gave stars, one star for Node.js, though proficient on most tools; the advice was to drop the rating.

card.rule: List your skills without scores, stars or levels.
card.limits: Our reading: The rule is about the writer's own ratings of their skills; listing the tools you know is still wanted.

media.alt: Top of the first page of a black and white two-column resume. A dark banner with diagonal stripes holds the name, job title and contact links. Section headings are white spaced capitals in solid black boxes: experience and frameworks on the left; education, programming languages, cloud, tools and design patterns on the right. Five languages each carry a row of five dots, partly filled as a self-rating.

concepts.section: Machine Learning Engineer with 5 Years Experience
concepts.title: Write about yourself, not your employer, in bullets
concepts.question: In each job entry, how many words describe the employer and how many describe your results?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Spend each entry's words on your own results, one point per bullet, and drop the description of the company.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let the reader find your achievements on a quick scan.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Readers scan rather than read, so text about the company crowds out your achievements.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In one machine learning resume, each position had nearly as much text about the company as about the person's achievements, in paragraphs. The author advised dropping the company part and using bullet points.

card.rule: Spend each entry's words on your own results, one point per bullet, and drop the description of the company.
card.limits: Our reading: A company link or name still tells where you worked; the rule is against long descriptions of the employer in place of your results.

media.alt: Page two of the same resume, under a black bar headed detailed experience. Each job has title, employer, place and dates, then a paragraph describing the employer and its business, then a dashed list of responsibilities, then a stack line of technologies. The page is dense grey text with no emphasis on results.

concepts.section: Remote Software Engineer With 8 Years Experience
concepts.title: Make page one carry your strongest proof
concepts.question: If a recruiter stops after page one, what will they have seen of your best work?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put your strongest evidence and key skills on page one, with experience in reverse chronological order and old education lower down.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Win the first scan, because many readers stop after page one.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says recruiters and hiring managers likely never got past the first page and moved a weak first page to the reject pile.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A machine learning resume opened with buzzwords and self-ratings, while the depth sat on pages two and three. A remote engineer's resume began with education, and listed work oldest first, with the proper experience on page two.

card.rule: Put your strongest evidence and key skills on page one, with experience in reverse chronological order and old education lower down.
card.limits: Our reading: A first page of key skills suits a candidate chasing specific stacks; the rule is about what the first page proves, not about a fixed order.

media.alt: Page three of the same resume. It continues the job entries in the same pattern: a paragraph about the employer, then a stack line of technologies for each job. A wide black bar labelled additional information follows, with a spoken languages block rated by rows of dots and a short talks list.

Full-page template in blue and pale cyan with a round portrait photo at top left, name, contact lines and a banner offering remote work. Two columns: left holds education, profile links and an other skills list with leadership and a driving licence; right lists five employers from earliest year at the top to 2020 at the bottom, then a skills block of dot rows. Icons sit beside headings.

Second page of the same blue template, headed detailed experience with a small document icon. Five employers are listed from the latest at the top to the earliest at the bottom, with dates at right. Under each are several short uppercase bullets on duties and tools, set in a narrow column with blue bars at the sides.

concepts.title: Cut what does not help the job you want
concepts.question: Which lines of your resume would you delete if the target job were the only reader?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Leave out positions, skills and intros that do not help the job you are after.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep the resume focused so the strong parts stand out.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says a hiring manager cares about recent results, so older or off-target items add little and crowd the useful ones.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An infrastructure engineer aiming at an SRE role had listed a training consultant job from 2004 to 2008, early system admin jobs, and skills such as training course design. The refactor cut the old positions. The author would not care what the person did before their master's degree, given a decade of results since.

card.rule: Leave out positions, skills and intros that do not help the job you are after.
card.limits: Our reading: Cutting works when the recent record is strong; do not cut a position that the job asks about or that explains your growth.

media.alt: Page one of an original two-page CV with a grey running header, shaded section bars and a name followed by degree letters. Below the address block is a personal profile of several prose paragraphs. Key skills sit in two columns: operating systems, training and support, programming languages and technologies. The career summary opens with the current senior role and a long list of square bullets. Dense and dated.

Second page of the refactored CV. It starts with an earlier, lower-titled role at the same employer, with an earlier date range. Then education as three bold degree lines with years, a projects and community section whose open-source tools link to repositories, a teaching and training section with course topics, and a short interests list.

concepts.section: Remote Software Engineer With 8 Years Experience
concepts.title: Drop the photo, the irrelevant skills and the cliches
concepts.question: Which lines on your resume add no information or give a reader grounds for bias?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Remove the photo, skills that do not matter for the job, and cliches such as excellent communication, or swap them for specifics.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep the reader on your evidence and away from bias or noise.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says a photo introduces bias, and irrelevant skills or cliches without specifics add nothing a reader can use.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A remote engineer's resume had a photo, a leadership skill, and a Cat-B driving licence on a remote developer application; all were flagged for removal. An SRE resume listed excellent interpersonal skills and excellent communication; the advice was to remove them or replace them with specifics.

card.rule: Remove the photo, skills that do not matter for the job, and cliches such as excellent communication, or swap them for specifics.
card.limits: Our reading: A claim becomes useful when backed by a specific; the cliche is removed or replaced, not just reworded.

concepts.section: Machine Learning Engineer with 5 Years Experience
concepts.title: Match the length to your experience and your market
concepts.question: How many pages does your experience honestly need for the job market you are applying in?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep the resume as short as your meaningful experience allows, and go to two pages only when both experience and market support it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Be read to the end, with no padding.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says readers scan and many never leave page one, so padding costs you; a long career in a market that expects length can fill two pages.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A machine learning engineer cut a 3-page resume to one page and saw many more leads, including from firms that had not replied before; a job at a target firm followed. A backend developer with five or six years fitted the key parts on one page. A 20-year SRE candidate kept two pages.

card.rule: Keep the resume as short as your meaningful experience allows, and go to two pages only when both experience and market support it.
card.limits: Our reading: The one-page default bends for long careers: the SRE resume stayed at two pages because of the UK market and enough meaningful experience.

media.alt: Refactored one-page resume in black and white, single column. Bold centred name with contact links, then thin-ruled headings for employment, education and technologies. Each job has title at left, employer and city centred and dates at right, with short achievement bullets and no employer description. A three-column technologies table at the bottom groups languages, frameworks and tools.

concepts.title: State your location and make dates easy to scan
concepts.question: Can a recruiter tell in two seconds where you are, when you worked and when you studied?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Give your city and country, put dates on the right, show education dates, and drop the months from dates four or more years back.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Remove doubts and make the timeline quick to read.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says a missing address may make recruiters assume you are abroad, and missing education dates raise questions about whether you graduated.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A backend developer in Vancouver had left out their location, and education dates were missing. The refactor added Vancouver, Canada, put dates where they were easy to scan, dropped months from dates four or more years old, and added education dates.

card.rule: Give your city and country, put dates on the right, show education dates, and drop the months from dates four or more years back.
card.limits: Our reading: Seasons suit short periods like an internship; for jobs a month format such as Jun 2019 to Mar 2020 reads more clearly.

media.alt: First page of a refactored two-page CV with purple-blue headings. Centred name with phone, email and two link labels. It opens with a skills section of bullets, then a one-line education entry, then work experience newest first. Each role has title, centred employer and a season-based date range at right, then bullets and a technologies line. One entry is a sabbatical break. Bullet indents and spacing are uneven.

concepts.title: Make promotions and leadership visible
concepts.question: If you stayed at one employer for years, can the reader see how your role grew?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Show promotions and leadership inside a long role, so tenure reads as growth.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Prevent the question of whether you stood still.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says a reader who sees ten years at one employer with no change will wonder whether the person was promoted; the resume should answer that.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An HPC systems administrator had a decade at one employer with no sign of advancement. The refactor called out a promotion after two years, with the person now leading the HPC team and likely the most senior HPC administrator.

card.rule: Show promotions and leadership inside a long role, so tenure reads as growth.
card.limits: Our reading: State only real changes of role; where there was none, other specifics must carry the story.

media.alt: First page of a refactored CV with blue headings and thin rules. Location and links at the top left, name centred, phone and email right. Technologies and languages appear as four labelled rows (languages, technologies, tools, other). Work experience starts with the current senior role, bold title, employer centred, dates at right, then a long list of bullets, many with numbers and measurable results.

concepts.title: Pick a clean, modern template
concepts.question: What does your template say about you before anyone reads a word?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Choose a template that is easy to scan, makes titles, dates and skills stand out, and feels current.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let the layout help the reader and avoid a dated or unprofessional impression.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says layout is judged at a glance, and a dated look can make some hiring managers wonder about keeping up with technology.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The 20-year SRE resume felt dated just by its template. Its refactor used an easier to read, more modern template where technologies jumped out. The 5-year ML resume had black headers that drew attention needlessly. A DIY layout on the remote resume still felt amateur.
