card.rule: Choose a template that is easy to scan, makes titles, dates and skills stand out, and feels current.
card.limits: Our reading: A template cannot replace content: the examples show template changes alongside rewritten content.

media.alt: Page two of the original CV, with grey section bars. It continues the career summary with earlier jobs: a co-founded training business, a training consultant role and two early systems administrator posts, each with employer, dates and a few square bullets. Education lists three degrees, followed by an IT certifications box in two columns. The page looks dated, and the old roles take most of the space.

concepts.title: Check grammar, tense and file type before sending
concepts.question: Before you send, have you run a grammar checker, checked your verbs and exported to PDF?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Run a grammar check, write past roles in the active past tense, and send a PDF, not a docx file.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Remove small flaws that make a strong record look careless.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says a grammar checker would have surfaced sentences that read awkwardly, and that PDFs are a much better choice than docx.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A backend resume's line about troubleshooting tools read awkwardly, and a checker would have caught it. The original was a docx; PDFs were advised. A remote engineer's 'Creating backend microservices' was to become 'Created backend microservices'.

card.rule: Run a grammar check, write past roles in the active past tense, and send a PDF, not a docx file.
card.limits: Our reading: A grammar check polishes but cannot add what is missing: it does not supply specifics or results.

concepts.title: Use real examples as inspiration, not as templates to copy
concepts.question: How should you use someone else's improved resume when writing your own?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Compare your resume with the examples to spot similar improvement chances, and do not copy any line one-for-one.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Improve your own resume so it is about your experience and tailored to the position.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The examples are other people's experience; copying them would put someone else's story on your page.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The examples are real resumes sent to the author, often from people not getting the response they hoped for. Each shows an initial analysis, then the improved version the person used as their master resume. Names, companies, schools, locations and dates are altered; the other features are as they were.

card.rule: Compare your resume with the examples to spot similar improvement chances, and do not copy any line one-for-one.
card.limits: Our reading: The examples are not a script: anonymising altered the facts, so learn from structure and wording choices.

concepts.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
concepts.section: Know that your screening process is broken
concepts.title: Resume screening misses good people
concepts.question: If a resume is a weak signal of ability, what should a hiring manager expect from a resume screen?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Accept that any resume screen will reject some good people, and choose how you screen with that in mind.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep strong candidates from being lost just because they wrote a poor resume.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, a cover letter and resume together are a weak way to introduce a candidate, so they give only a faint clue to quality. As long as resume screening exists, good people with poor resumes will be rejected; only relaxing or dropping the screen would change that.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (Our illustration) A manager reads a bare, two-line resume from a person who may be an excellent engineer and rejects it in seconds. The resume said little, so the manager's choice rested on very little.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author still defends the filter: it cuts the number of applicants and removes people who are likely not a fit. The point is to know its cost, not to scrap it.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Look at the last five resumes you rejected and write down which signal made you reject each one.

card.rule: Accept that any resume screen will reject some good people, and choose how you screen with that in mind.
card.limits: Our reading: The screen has a purpose: it reduces the applicant pool. The lesson is to see its error, not to conclude that screening has no value.

concepts.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
concepts.section: Know that your screening process is broken
concepts.title: Yes, Maybe and No piles
concepts.question: How can a hiring manager avoid rejecting a promising person too early at the resume stage?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Place each resume in a Yes, Maybe or No pile on purpose, and re-read the Maybe pile if the role stays open.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid early rejection of people who might turn out to be strong.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Because a resume can hide a good candidate, the advice the author quotes from Rothman is to give each person the benefit of the doubt. Doubtful resumes go to a middle Maybe pile instead of straight to No, and you make that choice consciously for every resume.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (Our illustration) A manager has one opening. She phone-screens her Yes pile, nobody fits, and she then re-reads the Maybe pile. A candidate who explained their work poorly turns out to have strong linked code.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The Maybe pile is a second look, not a promise. Rothman re-reads it only after phone-screening the Yes candidates, when the opening is still unfilled.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: While you screen, say the pile aloud for each resume before you open the next one.

card.rule: Place each resume in a Yes, Maybe or No pile on purpose, and re-read the Maybe pile if the role stays open.
card.limits: Our reading: It only helps if you actually re-read the Maybe pile; a pile you never reopen is the same as a No.

concepts.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
concepts.section: Know that your screening process is broken
concepts.title: Assess skills instead of only reading resumes
concepts.question: How can a hiring manager find people a resume screen would have rejected?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Consider an assessment of what people can do, either to replace the resume screen or to re-check the resumes you rejected.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reject fewer people who would thrive on your team.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, several startups are moving from a resume-based first screen to an assessment-based one. Woven takes your rejected resumes and runs an hour-long hands-on exercise; Triplebyte gives developers a tailored assessment before onsites; Hackerrank offers coding challenges that can replace the resume screen.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (The book's, shortened) A founder keeps screening resumes as usual for strong matches, and sends the rejected ones to a hands-on exercise. People who do well move on, and the team sees people it would have turned away.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Assessments cost time and effort. Woven spends more of both on the people who would have been rejected, in return for fewer lost hires.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: List the people you rejected last month and decide which of them a short hands-on task could have re-checked.

card.rule: Consider an assessment of what people can do, either to replace the resume screen or to re-check the resumes you rejected.
card.limits: An assessment adds cost. The author presents it as a hybrid: keep the quick resume pass for strong resumes and spend effort on the rest.

concepts.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
concepts.section: Know that your screening process is broken
concepts.title: Low-budget ways to screen more fairly
concepts.question: What can a hiring manager do with no extra budget to reduce unfair resume rejections?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Without extra budget, screen the same resumes with a second person, set aside real hiring time, and watch for your own bias.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reject fewer otherwise great applicants purely on their resume.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, comparing your Yes pile with another person's, from the same resumes screened independently, calibrates expectations and reduces bias. Without dedicated time you will be rushed and get poor results. You are also likely to favour people similar to yourself, without noticing it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (Our illustration) Two team leads each screen the same 60 resumes alone, then compare Yes piles. They disagree on eleven resumes, discuss why, and find that one of them had been favouring a certain kind of employer.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author says that if you cannot find the time, you should delegate the process to someone who has it.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Pick ten resumes and ask a colleague to sort them separately from you, then compare.

card.rule: Without extra budget, screen the same resumes with a second person, set aside real hiring time, and watch for your own bias.
card.limits: Our reading: A second reader reduces bias only if the reading is independent; agreeing with the first reader's notes copies the first bias.

concepts.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
concepts.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
concepts.title: Treat recruiters as true partners
concepts.question: What should a hiring manager do with recruiters and sourcers from the day hiring starts?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Build a strong relationship with recruiters and sourcers from the start: sit with them, explain what makes people succeed, and hold regular check-ins.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get better hiring results through shared understanding of how each side works.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, if you do not reach out, HR or recruitment may assume you are not interested in their work. Hiring managers and recruiters working in silos waste a chance to improve the process. The more each side understands the other, the better the results.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (Our illustration) A new engineering lead books a weekly half hour with a recruiter, explains what past strong teammates had in common, and asks what signals the recruiter looks for in a resume.

blocks.label: Limit (our reading)
blocks.text: Our reading: the book names no case where this partnership fails; its warning is about the opposite, working in silos.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Book a first check-in and bring two questions about how candidates move between stages.

card.rule: Build a strong relationship with recruiters and sourcers from the start: sit with them, explain what makes people succeed, and hold regular check-ins.
card.limits: Our reading: it takes time that busy managers must protect. The next ideas show what the author wants that time to include.

concepts.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
concepts.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
concepts.title: Let recruiters champion standout candidates
concepts.question: Why should a hiring manager allow recruiters to bring in people who miss a listed requirement?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Set sensible guidelines, then encourage recruiters to champion people who stand out, and read some rejected resumes yourself.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find hidden gems that strict hiring criteria would screen out.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, recruiters try not to waste engineering time on candidates who miss any requirement you set. Over time they learn who gets an onsite and an offer. Rigid demands leave them no room to take a chance, so give them guidelines and the initiative.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (A story, not proof) In the story the author cites from a tech recruiter, a person messaged the recruiting team for weeks. The recruiter finally spoke to them, took a chance, and the person did very well in interviews and later joined full time.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author asks for sensible guidelines, not none. The room for exceptions is added to requirements; it does not replace them.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: This week, re-read five rejected resumes and note any you would send to the next round.

card.rule: Set sensible guidelines, then encourage recruiters to champion people who stand out, and read some rejected resumes yourself.
card.limits: The stories are the author's and his sources', told to persuade; they show it can work, not how often.

concepts.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
concepts.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
concepts.title: The story of BusyManager and MakeTimeManager
concepts.question: What did the author see that made one manager hire well and the other fail with the same recruiters?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat hiring as a priority you protect: meet recruiters weekly, stay reachable, and help with every part of the process.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Fill your headcount quickly and well, as the author claims MakeTimeManager did.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, two managers worked with the exact same recruiters over a year. BusyManager delegated the headcount and rarely checked in; recruiters found it hard to understand what to hire for. MakeTimeManager met them weekly, said hiring came first and stayed involved.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (The book's story, shortened) BusyManager wrote a short job description, then rejected almost every onsite candidate and changed recruiters several times. MakeTimeManager had less headcount, held a weekly meeting and was open to interruptions, then hired well and earned more headcount.

blocks.label: Limit (our reading)
blocks.text: Our reading: this is one story seen by one observer, offered to persuade. It shows a pattern the author noticed, not a controlled test.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Put a recurring slot in your calendar for a recruiter check-in and tell them they may interrupt.

card.rule: Treat hiring as a priority you protect: meet recruiters weekly, stay reachable, and help with every part of the process.
card.limits: It is a persuasive story, not proof: no numbers or controls are given. Weigh it as an illustration of the rule the author argues for.

concepts.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
concepts.title: Write the job description with your recruiters
concepts.question: What should you decide before writing a job description, and why not copy an old one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Write and revise the job description with your recruiters, deciding first what the person must do and which skills are truly non-negotiable.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Attract a larger pool of qualified people and give candidates, recruiters and interviewers a better experience.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, copy-pasting an old job description gives candidates, recruiters and interviewers a poor experience. Sit with recruiters first and ask what the person will do in the first month and the first year, and which skills are truly needed or can be learned on the job.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (The book's, shortened) For a tech lead on an ads team using Node.js, having led a small team is probably a must-have; having worked in ads probably is not. The language may be negotiable for a fast learner with backend experience.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Some constraints are real. In the author's example, leading a team is likely a must-have for a tech lead, so challenge the list but do not empty it.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Before writing the next advert, write what the person should achieve in month one and year one.

card.rule: Write and revise the job description with your recruiters, deciding first what the person must do and which skills are truly non-negotiable.
card.limits: Our reading: Challenging a requirement does not mean dropping all of them; some are must-haves for the role.

concepts.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
concepts.title: Remove gendered wording from adverts
concepts.question: How can the wording of a job advert change who applies?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Write job adverts in inclusive, welcoming, de-biased language and avoid gendered phrasing.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Widen the pool, so that people are not turned away by the language alone.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, job descriptions with masculine wording attract fewer female applicants, and many of them are turned away by the language alone. The author's evidence is a company that rewrote its adverts and saw the share of female applicants rise.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (Cited from an article) Accenture in the UK changed its job descriptions to be more inclusive. The author, citing an HR Magazine article, says female applicants rose from 34% to 50%.

blocks.label: Limit (our reading)
blocks.text: Our reading: the figure shows a rise in applicants after a change; it does not show who was hired or that wording alone caused the rise.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Read your latest advert aloud and mark phrases that sound narrow in who they invite.

card.rule: Write job adverts in inclusive, welcoming, de-biased language and avoid gendered phrasing.
card.limits: Our reading: One company's figure supports the rule but does not prove it for every advert.

concepts.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
concepts.title: Monitor the pipeline and hold retrospectives
concepts.question: How can a hiring manager keep learning from the pipeline rather than just running it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Track how people progress through each stage, look behind the numbers, and hold open retrospectives with recruiters.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Spot problem areas early and widen the funnel to more people like those who succeed.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, ask what percentage progress through each stage and how it changes over time, but do not rely only on the numbers. Check diversity at each stage too; without data you cannot act. Talk openly with recruiters about response rates, referrals and interviews.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (Our illustration) A lead notices that fewer people pass the resume screen than last quarter. She asks the recruiters what changed and learns that referrals have fallen, and then agrees a plan to bring more in.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Numbers alone mislead. The author asks you to keep your ears on the ground and follow hiring case by case.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Write down each stage of your pipeline and the share of people passing it this quarter.

card.rule: Track how people progress through each stage, look behind the numbers, and hold open retrospectives with recruiters.
card.limits: Our reading: Retrospectives only help if people speak openly, and numbers need conversation to be understood.

concepts.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
concepts.title: Agree a feedback policy for candidates
concepts.question: What should a hiring manager settle about the feedback candidates receive at each stage?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Agree with your recruitment team a clear policy on feedback at each stage and on when people may re-apply.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give candidates a consistent experience within the limits of your company.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, you should ask what happens when someone is rejected at the resume stage, and after the technical phone screen, then confirm the process with your recruiters. A sensible policy takes the limits of company and law into account and gives candidates the same experience.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (Our illustration) A team agrees that resume-stage rejections get a standard note, phone-screen rejections get a short message, and close calls are told when they may apply again.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author admits that honest feedback on every single resume is not feasible, so the policy has to be honest about what it offers.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Ask your recruiter what a person rejected at each stage hears today.

card.rule: Agree with your recruitment team a clear policy on feedback at each stage and on when people may re-apply.
card.limits: The policy cannot promise detailed feedback to everyone; the author sets sensible limits instead.

concepts.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
concepts.title: Read books devoted to hiring
concepts.question: Where should a manager who needs a full hiring strategy turn, given that this book is about resumes?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you lack a hiring strategy, read books devoted to hiring developers, since this one is about resumes.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Build an organised hiring process.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says this book is not about hiring developers well, though several books cover it in detail. He recommends Spolsky's Smart and Gets Things Done, which he calls concise and opinionated, and Rothman's Hiring Geeks That Fit, a must-read for first-time hirers.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: (Our illustration) A first-time manager with no organised strategy reads Rothman before opening the role, then plans the hiring steps from the book's outline.

blocks.label: Limit (our reading)
blocks.text: Our reading: both books state their authors' opinions, and the author himself calls Spolsky's opinionated, so weigh them against your own setting.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Choose one of the two books and write three questions you want it to answer.

card.rule: If you lack a hiring strategy, read books devoted to hiring developers, since this one is about resumes.
card.limits: The recommendations are one author's picks; the list is short and not a survey of hiring advice.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: One end behind many rules
concepts.question: What single end do all the book's resume rules serve, and what does that end leave out?

paragraphs: The book gives dozens of rules about layout, bullets, dates, templates and referrals. The author says they all serve one end: an interview for that specific position with a recruiter or hiring manager. A resume is not meant to share your complete work history or represent everything you did as accurately as possible.

The reader is the reason. A recruiter decides in seconds and a hiring manager in 10 to 20, sorting resumes into Yes, Maybe and No piles. Your aim is to jump out as a Yes, so each rule either makes your fit visible fast or gets your resume read at all.
This gives a test for any tip you meet: does it help a hurried reader see that you fit this job? If not, leave it out.
card.example: A developer is proud of a six-month side contract in an unrelated field and wants a full paragraph on it. Applying the test, that paragraph does not help this reader see a fit for a backend role, so it is cut or shortened to a line. (Our illustration.)
card.rule: Judge each resume choice by whether it helps a hurried reader see that you fit this job and call you in.
card.limits: Choosing what to show is not permission to mislead; the author says not to claim anything untrue. Even a well-aimed resume carries no guarantee: competition and luck still play a part.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Write for the person, not the software
concepts.question: Why does the author tell you to write for a person, and which rules follow from that?

paragraphs: The author argues that an applicant tracking system (ATS) is a status tracker that people operate. It parses resumes to fill in your details and to index keywords for later searches, but it does not rank or reject resumes by their content. People decide which resumes advance.

That claim sets the target of the whole book: a hurried recruiter, inbound sourcer or hiring manager. A plain layout, a PDF, the facts a recruiter scans for on page one and wording that mirrors the job all serve that person. The author treats paid ATS optimisation, sold for $100 to $500 and beyond, as a myth.

One place where a program does act is the application form. Knockout questions, such as one on visa status, use your form answers and are never read from your resume. Readers also differ: a less technical screener may look for exact terms, so use the job's own words where they are true.
card.example: A candidate is offered an ATS-proof rewrite for $200. Using the author's claim, the candidate asks who actually rejects resumes, hears that people do, and spends the time on a clear page one and a version tailored to the job. (Our illustration.)
card.rule: Write for the hurried person who reads your resume, and answer form questions carefully because only they can trigger an automatic rejection.
card.limits: Our reading: this is the author's claim about tech hiring. A company can configure its tracker differently, so weigh any seller's promise against how recruiters say they work.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Layout, order and emphasis as one scan
concepts.question: How do the layout, ordering and bold rules combine for a reader who scans in stages?

paragraphs: The author describes a reader who moves in stages. First comes a glance for years and dates, relevant technologies, titles and companies, and location. Then a short top-to-bottom skim for anything relevant. Only after that does the reader look at page two or read closely.

The separate rules are parts of one design for these stages. A single column lets the reader go top to bottom in one pass. Putting the most relevant parts first and the key facts on page one means each stage meets what it needs. Bold and colour, used sparingly and the same way each time, steer the eye to a few details.
When two rules seem to pull apart, the scan decides: emphasise only what the current stage needs.
card.example: A resume lists languages on page two, bolds whole bullets and splits the page into two columns. The first glance finds no technologies. The fix is to move the languages to page one, bold only dates, titles and companies, and use one column. (Our illustration.)
card.rule: Put each fact where the stage of reading that needs it will reach it, and emphasise only what that stage needs.
card.limits: Our reading: the staged scan describes a typical hurried read. The author notes that a recruiter early in a pile may take longer and a tired one later may set a resume aside.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Claims against proof
concepts.question: What do the bullet, skills and cliche rules have in common, and what do they ask you to do?

paragraphs: Several rules in different chapters ask for the same move: show instead of assert. A bullet states the impact you accomplished, a number that measures it and your own contribution. Trait claims such as team player give way to results from your entries. Skill stars and level labels are dropped, and technologies you are proficient with are shown in use.

The reasons are the reader's. A hurried reader cannot check a claim, but a figure or a named tool can be compared. According to the author, numbers such as visitors, requests per second or a percentage improvement translate across employers better than a qualitative description.
If you do not know the figure, ask your team or manager, and if that fails, give a good estimate. Close enough beats nothing.
card.example: Instead of 'excellent communicator who works well in teams', a candidate writes: 'Ran weekly demos for three teams and cut review turnaround from four days to two.' The second line can be checked and compared. (Our illustration.)
card.rule: Wherever you are about to claim a quality, replace the claim with a result, a number or a named technology a reader can see.
card.limits: The author allows an estimate but says not to claim anything untrue. Proof must be real, and each bullet still has to stay short enough to scan.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Tailor, trim and stay true
concepts.question: How do the tailoring, cutting and keyword rules work together, and where do they stop?

paragraphs: The book's answer to what to include is a routine. Keep one detailed master resume, written with results, impact and your contribution, which may run past two pages. For each job, copy it and re-edit: echo the posting's language where it is true, put the matching experience first, and remove what does not help.

Three rules seem to pull in different directions: add the job's words, be ruthless about cutting, and stay short. They fit because the master holds everything and each version is cut to one job. A headhunter the author quotes says you lose little by cutting, since you can speak about the rest at the interview.
Two limits apply. Stuffing in every possible keyword makes a resume look unprofessional, and you may leave out what does not flatter you but must not claim what is untrue.
card.example: A developer with Android, Kotlin and web experience applies to an Android role focused on Kotlin. The Android and Kotlin work moves to the top with the posting's wording, and the web work moves lower or shrinks. (From the author's own example, retold.)
card.rule: Keep one full master, then build each application by echoing the job's own words in true experience and cutting the rest.
card.limits: Our reading: the two-page guide is for most people; the author lets very senior people with 10+ years run longer. Keyword care matters most with less technical screeners, and stuffing can backfire with technical ones.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Choosing rules by stage and employer
concepts.question: Which rules change with your career stage and the type of employer, and which stay fixed?

paragraphs: Two things decide which rules you lean on: who you are and who is reading. Some rules stay fixed: write for a hurried reader, make the fit visible, show impact, and tailor to the job. The variants sit on top of these.

By stage: a new grad keeps to one page with work, internships and projects first. A career changer opens with a short summary of the switch and its reason, shows languages and linked working projects, and gives the old career one sentence. A senior engineer shows promotions and results with a tailored summary, and a manager open to both paths writes two resumes.

By employer: a generalist tech company wants fundamentals, engineering metrics and a short tool list. A company hiring for one technology wants the advert's technologies, your years with the main one and certifications. An agency wants every technology you are proficient with.
card.example: A developer with 8 years sends one resume to a large generalist firm and another to a Java consultancy. The first leads with fundamentals and impact metrics with few tools; the second lists the stack and certifications in full. (Our illustration.)
card.rule: Fix the reader, the scan and the proof first, then pick the variant that matches your stage and the type of employer.
card.limits: Our reading: stage and employer type are labels, and many people sit between them. The author says processes differ by company, so test advice against the firm and your own market.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Where effort goes beyond the resume
concepts.question: In what order should effort go across referrals, the resume, LinkedIn, GitHub, a blog and a cover letter?

paragraphs: The author says a good resume is required but does not decide the outcome alone. Other routes change how and whether it is read. A referral moves you ahead of other resumes and almost guarantees an in-depth review, and he names referrals as the biggest way to cut down luck. Ask before you apply, because many firms only accept referrals for people not yet in the pipeline.

Resumes are also read in an order. Referrals come first, then local candidates, then those not needing a visa, then those needing a visa and relocation. The costlier the hire, the later the read, so if you sit far down this order, referrals and direct contact matter more.
After that, the author finds LinkedIn, GitHub and technical blogs most relevant for developers. A cover letter is worth writing mainly for small companies or when you can reach the hiring manager.
card.example: A developer finds a role at a large firm where a former colleague works. The developer asks the colleague for a referral first, tailors the resume to the job, and only then applies. (Our illustration.)
card.rule: Spend effort where it moves you up the queue or puts proof in the reader's path: a referral first, a tailored resume, then LinkedIn and GitHub.
card.limits: The author says referral value varies: one engineer he quotes says a referral gets an interview faster but does not help get an offer. Cover letters can be skipped at large firms.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: A working order from draft to send
concepts.question: In what order do the book's steps run from first draft to sending, and why does the order matter?

paragraphs: Our reading: the book's separate steps fall into a working order. Choose targets and rank them. Gather the results of your past work by asking others. Pick a proven template early and put your effort into content, writing a master resume and, if you wish, a second one from scratch to merge. Then tailor a copy to each job, check it, and send it, ideally after a referral.

The order follows the logic of the book. A template is not worth much without content, so content comes first. Tailoring needs the master, and the checks should be made on the version you will send: grammar tools, a fresh pair of eyes, the chapter checklists and a PDF named with your own name.
A practical book asks to be acted on. The hiring chapter adds a reason to do the work well: resume screens miss good people.
card.example: A candidate spends a week picking between 20 templates with three bullets written. Following the order, the candidate picks a proven template, asks former colleagues for project results, writes the master, and then tailors one copy per job. (Our illustration.)
card.rule: Work in order: choose targets, write one strong master, tailor it per job, check it with outside eyes, and ask for the referral before you send.
card.limits: Our reading: this order is a synthesis, not a list the author gives in one place. Adjust it to your time and keep a step out only when you know it is not needed.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A hiring manager writes a resume guide. Which evidence would you expect behind its advice?
options: A controlled trial comparing thousands of resumes across employers
His own experience of reading many resumes as a hiring manager
A legal standard that every employer must follow when screening
Scoring rules published by the makers of recruiting software
optionExplain: Plausible for a rigorous guide, but a manager's book seldom has one, and this one does not claim it.
Right: guides like this usually rest on the writer's experience. The card shows what this author offers and how he labels it.
Resume screening is not set by one legal standard, so this does not describe the source.
Software rules may matter elsewhere, but they are not the base of this author's advice.
questions.explain: Guides by practitioners usually rest on experience. The card next shows what this author offers and how he labels it.
questions.rule: Ask what a tip rests on.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: The book reports that in one week of May 2020 the author reviewed more than ____ resumes in detail.
questions.explain: He reports reviewing over 300 resumes in that week, spending far more time on each than a recruiter would. That is the core of his stated evidence.
questions.rule: Know what the evidence is before you weigh it.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Which claim does the author's May 2020 week of reviewing resumes support?
options: Recruiters spend around seven seconds on each resume they scan
A well-written resume is enough to guarantee an interview call
An exported LinkedIn profile is the best format for direct applications
Most developer resumes he saw under-represented the person
optionExplain: This figure is real in the book but comes from a study cited in a footnote, not from his review.
The book says the opposite: a resume is required but not sufficient.
The book argues against this in a later section; the review is not used for it.
Right: this is the claim the review is used for.
questions.explain: He uses the review to say that many developer resumes under-represent the person. The seven-second figure and the LinkedIn point have other sources.
questions.rule: Match each piece of evidence to the claim it is used for.
questions.hint: Which claim is about what the resumes showed?

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Which is the stronger support for the claim that most developer resumes represent the person poorly?
options: His account of closely reading 300+ resumes with feedback on each
The fact that his newsletter is read by many engineering managers today
A footnote explaining that FAANG names five large and well-known tech companies
A footnote explaining that CV is a Latin phrase meaning the course of life
optionExplain: Right: it is the experience the claim is drawn from.
A readership says who follows him, not what he found in resumes.
That is a definition and supports no claim about resumes.
That explains a word, not what resumes look like.
questions.explain: The claim is about what he saw in resumes, so only his review bears on it. The other items are background.
questions.rule: Evidence must bear on the claim it is offered for.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it matches what the book reports about the author's evidence.

items.t: He reviewed more than 300 resumes in one week in May 2020
He calls the content opinions that may not fit every country
A controlled study proves his tips raise interview rates
He says the writers of the resumes put in time and effort
Hiring results confirm every tip in the book
He read each of the 300 resumes for only ten seconds

questions.explain: The book reports his reviews and calls its advice opinion. It cites no outcome study, and his May 2020 week was far slower than a ten-second glance.
questions.rule: Do not credit the book with evidence it does not give.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A friend says: the author read 300 resumes, so recruiters must study each one closely. What does the book's account suggest?
options: Recruiters match his time, because both are hiring professionals who face big piles of resumes
He rushed the review, which is why he found so many problems in it
It was far slower than a recruiter's scan, so it shows what feedback is possible
He reviewed them the way applicant tracking software does, in bulk
optionExplain: The book says the reverse: recruiters scan in seconds.
The book says he took more time, not less.
Right: the book says he spent far more time on each than a recruiter or hiring manager would.
No such link is made in the book.
questions.explain: In the May 2020 review he spent far more time on each resume than a recruiter or hiring manager would. His detailed feedback is therefore not a picture of real screening.
questions.rule: Check whether the evidence was gathered under the conditions of the claim.
questions.teaches: In the May 2020 review the author spent far more time per resume than a recruiter or hiring manager would, so the detailed feedback is not a picture of real screening.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A developer in Berlin uses a resume guide written mostly for US tech jobs. What is a sensible stance?
options: Use it as a starting point and check it against local practice
Follow every tip as a fixed rule that holds for every employer there
Skip the guide entirely because Europe differs from the US in hiring
Use only the parts that talk about the best-known companies it names
optionExplain: Right: advice from one market can help, but it needs a check against the market you apply in.
Tempting for its confidence, but employers differ in what they look for.
The scope may overlap, so dropping all of it wastes useful context.
Famous names are a small part of what any hiring market looks like.
questions.explain: Advice made for one market can still help in another, but it needs a check. The card gives this author's stated scope.
questions.rule: Check advice against the market you are in.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: The book is written for developer jobs at tech companies in the US, Europe and ____.
questions.explain: The author names the US, Europe and India as the target regions, for companies that do business in English.
questions.rule: Know the stated scope.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A civil servant in a non-English-speaking country asks if the book's rules apply to her. What does the author's scope imply?
options: They apply to every industry, because resumes work the same way in every country and sector
They apply once she removes the mentions of the FAANG companies from them
They do not apply at all, so she should not bother reading the book
They target English-language tech hiring, so she should test each tip locally
optionExplain: The author says different industries follow different processes.
The names are examples; the scope is about industry and language, not only brands.
This goes too far: the book is aimed at English-language tech hiring, but its tips can still be tested locally.
Right: the scope is tech jobs where business is in English, and the author says processes differ elsewhere.
questions.explain: She is outside the stated scope, so the book is a source of leads, not rules. The author's own caveat is to do your own research.
questions.rule: Outside the scope, test each tip.
questions.hint: Which two things define the book's audience: industry and what else?

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Sort each reaction by whether it uses the book with care or over-trusts it.

items.t: Asks two people who hire locally whether a tip matches practice
Treats every tip as a law for any employer
Remembers that the author calls the content opinion
Assumes a startup tip also fits a government agency
Compares a tip with feedback from her network
Skips her own research because the author has hired many people

questions.explain: The author asks for your own research and feedback from your network. Treating his tips as universal laws ignores that.
questions.rule: Opinion plus your own check, not blind trust.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, the book's principles likely carry over to some companies outside its target group, though practices differ.
questions.explain: He says the principles likely translate to other companies, while adding that different industries and companies may follow other processes.
questions.rule: Principles travel better than details.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A beginner hopes the book will make up for missing experience for senior roles. What does the book assume about its readers?
options: That readers can invent the experience that a given job requires of them
That they already have the experience for the positions they target
That every reader is already a senior engineer at a large firm
That readers want managerial roles only and nothing technical at all
optionExplain: The book is about representing you fairly, not about invention.
Right: the book helps present experience, it does not supply it.
The book covers new grads up to experienced developers, leads and managers.
Managers have dedicated sections, but most content is for developers.
questions.explain: The author assumes you already have the experience for the roles you apply to. The book helps you show it, not make it.
questions.rule: A resume guide presents what you have.
questions.teaches: The book assumes you already have the relevant experience for the positions you apply to; it helps you present it fairly and does not replace it.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: You send a polished resume to ten companies and hear nothing. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: Your resume must be bad, since a good one always gets a call back
Many unseen factors also affect replies, so silence does not explain itself
Your template is the cause, so changing it will end the silence for good
Companies ignore resumes sent online, so nothing at all explains it
optionExplain: Tempting, but no resume guarantees a call.
Right: replies depend on much more than the document.
Template changes are one lever, not a cure for silence.
Many do read them; the book says outcomes vary by company.
questions.explain: Silence has many possible causes. The card next shows what this author says he can and cannot explain.
questions.rule: Silence is not a diagnosis.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: There is no one-size-fits-all resume ____ that will yield the best results.
questions.explain: The author uses the point that no single language or architecture suits every project to say no single template suits every application.
questions.rule: No template wins everywhere.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Sam has rebuilt his resume in five templates after each silence from employers. What is the flaw in this approach, per the author?
options: Template changes do not work, so only rewriting the content helps
He should apply to fewer companies so each reply is more reliable to read
No template guarantees a call, and replies depend on more than the resume
Silence after applying means the resume was rejected for its format
optionExplain: The author does not say templates never matter, only that none always wins.
Fewer applications do not make replies more predictable.
Right: the author denies a template always works.
Silence has many causes; the book does not tie it to format.
questions.explain: The author says nothing predicts a call, so chasing the perfect template misreads the problem. Look at what you control.
questions.rule: Do not chase a magic template.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Which of these can the book help with, according to the author?
options: Context on how hiring works and advice for writing with more structure
Explaining why a specific company never answered your application to it
Guaranteeing a recruiter call if you follow each of its steps closely
Speaking officially for the companies that it names in its pages
optionExplain: Right: this is what the author says the book offers.
He says the book cannot answer why you do not hear back.
He says no content always results in a call.
He says it is not an official guide for any of them.
questions.explain: The author limits the promise to context, structure and confidence. The other three are claims he explicitly disowns.
questions.rule: Know what the book does not promise.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, hiring can differ between hiring managers, so one resume may get different responses for different openings.
questions.explain: He says hiring can differ not only per company but also per hiring manager, which is one reason outcomes are hard to predict.
questions.rule: Different managers, different outcomes.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A designer sends one portfolio to three agencies and hears nothing. Which factors named by the author could explain it?
options: Only the visual polish of the portfolio and the file type she used to send it to each agency
Only whether she followed up by phone within a week of applying to each agency, one by one
How many other qualified applicants there were, how soon roles must be filled, and how many are open
Only the agencies' brand reputation and how well known their clients are in the design field
optionExplain: These are within her control; the author stresses factors she cannot see.
Follow-up may help but is not one of the factors he names.
Right: these are the factors the author lists as impossible to predict.
Reputation is not among the factors he names.
questions.explain: The author says the chance of a follow-up depends on how many other qualified applications there are, how soon the position must be filled and how many are open. The same logic reaches a designer.
questions.rule: List what you cannot see before blaming the document.
questions.teaches: The chance of a follow-up call depends on how many other qualified applications there are, how soon the position must be filled and how many positions are open.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: You have recently bought a resume guide. Which plan fits an author who wants you to end with a better resume?
options: Read it cover to cover before you touch your own resume at all
Copy a template and stop reading once your resume is filled in
Skim first, pick a template, then rewrite while doing exercises
Read only the chapter for your seniority and skip all the rest of it
optionExplain: Reading everything first delays the real work and tests nothing.
A template alone skips the reasons that make a resume work.
Right: reading is tied to producing the resume.
This misses the hiring context that the other parts supply.
questions.explain: A guide works best when reading leads to writing. The card gives this author's order.
questions.rule: Read to produce.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Put the author's recommended steps in order.
items: Choose one or two resume templates
Write or rewrite your resume while working the Part 2 exercises
questions.explain: The author recommends skimming once, choosing one or two templates, and then writing as you go through the Part 2 exercises.
questions.rule: Skim, choose, write.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Imani has not worked in recruiting and wants to know how her resume will be read. Where does the author suggest she begins?
options: Part 1, on why resumes matter and how hiring works
Part 3, because the templates matter most to her first draft
The Part 2 chapter that matches her level of seniority
The footnotes, which define the key terms used in the book
optionExplain: Right: he recommends it for readers who have not been hiring managers.
Templates come after the context, and he says to choose them after skimming.
Part 2 is about writing, which he wants to rest on understanding the process.
Footnotes define words like FAANG but do not explain hiring.
questions.explain: He suggests Part 1 for readers who have not been hiring managers, since knowing who reads the resume helps you write it on purpose.
questions.rule: Know your reader, then write.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Match each part of the book to what it contains.
pairs: Context on why resumes matter and how hiring works
Actionable advice by area of the resume, with examples and recap actions
questions.explain: Part 1 sets the context, Part 2 teaches the writing area by area and Part 3 gives templates and examples to start from.
questions.rule: Context, advice, templates.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: In Part 2 Imani meets pairs of resume snippets with highlighted improvements. According to the book, what are they?
options: Invented samples written by the author to show ideal wording for each area
Real, anonymised snippets as first written, with improvements highlighted
Templates she should copy word for word into her own resume
Opinions from recruiters about how the hiring process works at their firms
optionExplain: The book says the snippets are real, not invented.
Right: the book says they are real snippets, anonymised.
Templates sit in Part 3 and are starting points.
Recruiter opinions appear in other boxed sections.
questions.explain: Before-and-after examples are real snippets as their authors originally wrote them. Highlights mark what needed improving.
questions.rule: Learn from real before-and-after cases.
questions.teaches: The before-and-after examples are real but anonymised resume snippets, shown as their authors first wrote them, with improvement areas highlighted.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A reader finds a boxed section written by a hiring manager. How should she treat it?
options: As an exercise that she must complete before moving on to the next chapter
As a template that she should copy into her own resume this week
As an anonymised before-and-after sample of a real resume snippet
As one insider's view on how and why things are done
optionExplain: Exercises are in the recap sections, not these boxes.
Templates are in Part 3.
Samples are resume snippets, not commentary.
Right: the book presents such boxes as extra perspectives from people in the process.
questions.explain: The book includes about a dozen boxed sections with the thoughts of hiring managers, tech recruiters and others in the process on how and why things are done.
questions.rule: Treat boxes as added perspectives.
questions.teaches: About a dozen boxed sections give the views of hiring managers, tech recruiters and others in the process on how and why things are done.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: About how long does the book say a recruiter gives a resume on the first scan?
options: About 2 minutes
About 30 seconds
About 7 seconds
About 5 minutes
optionExplain: That is closer to a full read than a first scan.
Longer than the book's cited figure.
Right: this is the figure the book cites.
No first scan takes this long according to the book.
questions.explain: The book cites a study of around 7 seconds. The card gives the source.
questions.rule: First scans are short.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A hiring manager in the book glances at a resume for ____ seconds to decide whether to read on.
questions.explain: The author says 10 to 20 seconds is his own glance; the 7 seconds is the cited recruiter figure. Both are short.
questions.rule: Different readers, same short window.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A developer fits ten years of work on one page in long paragraphs. Which change best serves a seconds-long scan?
options: Add every task from every role so that nothing at all is lost along the way
Put the roles and results that match the job first, in short lines
Expand each project into a paragraph so that depth shows from the start
Place the strongest match last so that readers keep going to the end
optionExplain: More detail slows the scan and buries the match.
Right: fit must show immediately.
Depth is for the second read, not the first.
Many readers stop before the end of the first scan.
questions.explain: The first reader decides in seconds, so the best match must come first and be quick to read.
questions.rule: Strongest match first.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Sort each approach by whether it fits a seconds-long scan.

items.t: Opens with the experience most relevant to the role
Lists every task from the past ten years
Assumes the reader will read it all before deciding
Makes the fit visible within the first lines
Cuts details that do not help this application
Hides the best result in the middle of a long paragraph

questions.explain: A scan of seconds rewards a visible match and punishes hidden results and padding.
questions.rule: Make it easy to see the fit.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: True or false: According to the book's figures, a recruiter's first scan is usually longer than a hiring manager's glance.
questions.explain: The recruiter figure is about 7 seconds; the author's own glance is 10 to 20. The recruiter's is shorter, which makes the first lines more important.
questions.rule: Shorter scans make openings matter more.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Lena's best project is described in specialist terms only an expert follows. Given who may read first, what is the risk?
options: Specialist terms make the resume look weaker to the engineers who read it
Nobody reads past the first line, so the project is lost anyway for everyone
A recruiter, often less technical, may pass on it without seeing its value
Recruiters score jargon highly, so the project is safe from rejection
optionExplain: The book does not say engineers dislike specialist terms.
The scan is short but not limited to the first line.
Right: the author notes recruiters are often less technical.
The author says the opposite about recruiters' technical knowledge.
questions.explain: The author says recruiters, who are often less technical, would have passed on even more of the strong candidates than he would. Write so a non-expert can see the value.
questions.rule: Write for the least technical first reader.
questions.teaches: Recruiters are often less technical than hiring managers and, the author says, would have passed on even more of the strong candidates he would have passed on in a hurry.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: What is the main job of a resume?
options: Record everything you have done in your career
Get you an interview for a specific position
Satisfy the upload field so the application is complete
Give recruiters a reason to remember your name later
optionExplain: A full record is not the goal; it can bury what matters.
Right: the book names the interview as the goal.
Many treat it this way; the author says that skips the goal.
The aim is a specific position now, not a lasting memory.
questions.explain: Resumes get you to an interview. The card gives the author's statement of the goal.
questions.rule: The goal is the interview.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: The goal of a resume is to get you to an ____ for that position.
questions.explain: The author calls it getting your foot in the door: the interview, nothing more and nothing less.
questions.rule: Goal: interview.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Priya has twelve years of varied roles and applies for a backend job. How should the goal shape her resume?
options: Include every role equally so that nothing is misrepresented or lost
Describe the whole career in order and let the reader choose what matters
Keep one generic version for all roles to save time on each application
Select what sells her for that backend role, even if some history is left out
optionExplain: Completeness is explicitly not the goal.
That leaves the selling to the reader in seconds.
The goal is tied to one specific position.
Right: the aim is the interview, not completeness.
questions.explain: A resume sells you for that position. Selecting what supports the match serves the goal; listing everything does not.
questions.rule: Choose content to fit the position.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Sort each action by whether it serves or misses the goal of a resume.

items.t: Cuts a detailed job from 2009 that does not help this application
Fills in a template with every duty and submits
Chooses content to fit this specific position
Treats completeness as the aim
Asks whether each line helps win the interview
Writes one resume to send to all roles and companies

questions.explain: Serving the goal means choosing for the interview. Listing everything or sending one generic version aims at something else.
questions.rule: Each line must help win the interview.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A European recruiter asks for a CV. According to the book, what does that term mean?
options: The same kind of document as a resume, named a CV in Europe and Asia
A longer academic document listing every job, paper and conference talk
A cover letter explaining in prose why you want the job
A LinkedIn profile export saved as a PDF file for applications
optionExplain: Right: the book uses the two words for the same document.
Elsewhere that may be true, but the book treats the terms as the same.
A cover letter is a different document.
An export is a different artefact, discussed later as a poor choice.
questions.explain: The book says that in Europe, Asia and several other places a resume is called a CV, short for Curriculum Vitae.
questions.rule: CV and resume name the same document here.
questions.teaches: In Europe, Asia and several other places the document is called a CV, short for Curriculum Vitae, Latin for course of life, and the book treats it as the same document.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Dana emails a one-page pitch to win a first meeting with a client. By the author's goal logic, how should the pitch be judged?
options: By whether it covers everything the firm has ever done for clients
By whether it gets the meeting, as it need not tell the whole story
By whether it follows the standard template of the whole industry
By its length compared with the pitches that competing firms send
optionExplain: Completeness is not the goal.
Right: it plays the same role as a resume.
A template is a tool, not the test.
Length matters only if it helps win the meeting.
questions.explain: The test is the next step, not the full story. The author expects the selling to happen in under 10 seconds of reading, so a resume works like a quick pitch.
questions.rule: Judge by the next step.
questions.teaches: The author expects the resume to sell you in less than 10 seconds of reading, so it works as a quick pitch rather than a full record.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A hiring manager faces 300 resumes. Which approach does the book's quoted manager use?
options: Read every resume in full and rank all three hundred of them
Sort them quickly into a few piles, looking for reasons to reject
Interview the first twenty people who applied for the role
Choose by the brand of the employer on each resume only
optionExplain: That would take more time than he has.
Right: he sorts fast and looks for reasons to say no.
He does not sort by order of arrival.
Brand alone is not his method.
questions.explain: He sorts fast to cut the pile. The card gives his three piles.
questions.rule: Sort fast, reject on small grounds.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: The quoted manager's three piles are Yes, Maybe and ____.
questions.explain: He sorts into Yes, Maybe and No, and the No pile receives everything beyond the first two.
questions.rule: Yes, Maybe, No.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A resume has spelling errors and no relevant work in the last two years. Where does the quoted manager put it?
options: The Yes pile, since he values potential over polish
The Maybe pile, because he reads past errors to judge talent
The No pile, because these are quick reasons to reject
None, because he reads every resume equally
optionExplain: He lists poor spelling as a reason for No.
He is looking for a reason to say no, and these are two.
Right: he names both as reasons.
He sorts quickly and does not treat all equally.
questions.explain: Poor spelling and no relevant recent experience are two of his stated No-pile reasons. A single one can be enough when the Yes pile is full.
questions.rule: Small flaws are reasons to reject.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Sort each resume feature by whether it helps toward the Yes pile or risks the No pile.

items.t: Careful spelling and grammar
Typos in the first lines
Relevant experience in the last two years visible at the top
No relevant experience in the last two years
Experience matching the stack in the posting
A tech stack unlike the one the job uses

questions.explain: The quoted manager names spelling, grammar, recent relevant experience and the tech stack as what moves a resume between piles.
questions.rule: Fix the quick reasons to reject.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: You top the Maybe pile, but enough Yes candidates pass the phone screen to fill the interviews. What may follow, per the author?
options: You may get no call even though you topped the Maybe pile
You move into the Yes pile for being first among Maybes
The manager starts again with fresh resumes including yours
The phone-screen result does not affect the Maybe pile
optionExplain: Right: the author warns of exactly this.
He does not describe promotion in this way.
No restart is described.
The author says it does: Yes candidates may fill the slots.
questions.explain: If enough Yes candidates pass the phone screen, a Maybe may not get a call even at the top. That is why the Yes pile is the aim.
questions.rule: Aim for Yes, not near-Yes.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: How does the book present the Yes/Maybe/No process?
options: As a measured industry standard backed by survey figures from many firms
As a rule that applicant tracking software enforces on every employer
As the author's private method that most managers decide to avoid
As one manager's account the author calls typical of how screeners work
optionExplain: No survey figures are given.
The book does not tie it to software here.
The author calls it typical, not unusual.
Right: one account, described as typical.
questions.explain: The evidence is one manager's description. The author calls it typical, but gives no counts, so the strength is that of an expert account, not a survey.
questions.rule: Weigh a single account as a single account.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A bakery owner has 60 applications for one counter job. Using the quoted manager's logic, what is a realistic aim?
options: Interview all 60 applicants so that none of them is missed by chance
Cut the pile to a handful to meet quickly, not hunt for perfection
Find the single perfect candidate first and stop reading there
Read each application twice in full before sorting any of them into piles
optionExplain: That is not how a busy screener works.
Right: this is the logic he describes.
He says he does not have time for that.
The sorting is meant to be quick.
questions.explain: The manager says his aim is not to find the unique snowflake who would be perfect, because he has no time. He wants a handful to interview.
questions.rule: Aim to shortlist, not to find perfection.
questions.teaches: The quoted manager says his aim is not to find the one perfect candidate, since he has no time for that; he wants to reduce the pile to a handful quickly.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: What mainly makes a developer resume great rather than only good?
options: A polished template with consistent fonts and spacing
Rare, valuable skills that match what the job needs
A long list of every technology the person has ever used
A well-known employer shown on every line of the history
optionExplain: Good formatting helps but does not make a resume great.
Right: the author puts the difference in content, not looks.
Length adds noise; it does not make the match.
A famous name does not make a resume great for every role.
questions.explain: The author ties greatness to content that fits the role. The card gives his reasoning.
questions.rule: Great is about content and match.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Great resumes depend less on format and more on ____.
questions.explain: The author says greatness has little to do with format and everything to do with content.
questions.rule: Content over format.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Ana's resume is neat but generic. Her real strength is a niche payments library a target firm is rebuilding around. What lifts the resume toward great?
options: A new template with a bolder heading and tidier columns for her skills
A longer list of every library she has touched in her career so far
A line saying that she is a fast learner who adapts quickly to teams
Placing that rare expertise where the firm's reader will see it for the role
optionExplain: Format does not change the match.
More items dilute the one that matters.
A claim of general quality is not the rare experience the role needs.
Right: great is rare, valuable and exact for the role.
questions.explain: Great resumes show rare, valuable experience that fits the job. Her library knowledge is exactly that, and it must be easy to find.
questions.rule: Show the rare fit first.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Sort each description by whether it fits a good resume or a great resume.

items.t: Represents you as fairly as possible
Makes the reader want to talk to you at once
Shows rare, valuable skills the job needs
Gives a qualified candidate the best chance of passing screening
Fits one specific role exactly
Avoids missing chances by under-selling

questions.explain: Good is about fairness and getting through screening; great is about grabbing attention with a rare, exact match.
questions.rule: Good is fair; great is a specific fit.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a good resume guarantees that a recruiter will want to talk to you.
questions.explain: He says that even with a good resume you will not win over a recruiter every time, since your profile may not match or stronger profiles may compete.
questions.rule: Good opens doors; it does not force them.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Lena's first job gives her little to show and she feels her resume cannot become great. How does the author link good and great?
options: Great resumes come from layout, so she should redesign it now before applying
A great resume is unrelated to the jobs that a person has held before
A good resume lands a good job, which supplies experience for a great one
She must wait until a famous employer decides to hire her first
optionExplain: The author says greatness depends on content, not format.
Great resumes show valuable experience, so jobs matter.
Right: good is the first step toward great.
The author says a famous name does not make a resume great.
questions.explain: The book frames a good resume as the first step: it helps you get a good job, which provides the experience a great resume is built on.
questions.rule: Good now, great later.
questions.teaches: A good resume is the first step: it helps you get a good job, and that job provides the experience a great resume is built on.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: An engineer with five years at Apple and Google gets few interviews. What is the likely issue?
options: The resume lists too many different employers over the years
The resume does not show the person's own best contributions
Big names put recruiters off from reading further
The font was hard to read on the screens of recruiters
optionExplain: Employers were not the problem.
Right: the name alone did not do the selling.
The book does not say this.
Nothing in the story suggests format was the cause.
questions.explain: Well-known employers do not sell the person. The card gives the author's reading of the case.
questions.rule: Names do not sell; contributions do.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A famous employer's name alone is not enough; the resume also has to ____ you.
questions.explain: The author says the resume of the engineer did no selling, it only did underselling.
questions.rule: A resume must sell.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Rahul spent four years at a big-name firm. His resume says only: worked on the search team. What should he add?
options: His own contributions and results, such as what he built or led
More logos of the products that the firm makes and sells
A longer list of everyone else who sat on the same team
A note that the firm is highly regarded by most engineers
optionExplain: Right: personal contribution is what the reader cannot see.
Logos repeat the name, not his work.
That shows the team, not him.
Readers already know that; it does not show what he did.
questions.explain: The employer's name is already known. The missing piece is what he did there.
questions.rule: Add the personal contribution.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Which claim is the Apple and Google story used to support?
options: Backend engineers should leave frontend work off the resume they send
Working at a famous company is a handicap when the interviews begin
Presenting personal contributions matters even with strong companies listed
Open-sourcing a component guarantees an interview at most employers
optionExplain: The story mentions frontend work but not as the lesson.
The name catches the eye, per the author.
Right: this is the lesson the author draws.
One component was open sourced, but the book draws no such guarantee.
questions.explain: The author's lesson is that structuring past experience to show best personal contributions is key, even with strong names.
questions.rule: Match the story to its claim.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Sort each resume line by whether it sells the person or undersells them.

items.t: Links to a barely working prototype as the main project
States that they led a team of three on an internal project
Says little about specific work at the famous employers
Describes a hard problem solved and its impact
Lets the employer logo carry the page
Describes a complex system built end to end

questions.explain: Lines that name personal leadership, difficulty and results sell. Lines that rely on the name or on weak work undersell.
questions.rule: Name what you did.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: The first resume linked frontend work the engineer rarely did. What did that choice do?
options: It proved that they were a strong full-stack engineer who was able to do both kinds of work
It showed weak work outside their real strength and hid their backend work
It balanced the resume well between the two kinds of work they did
It showed that they enjoyed frontend work a great deal and chose it
optionExplain: It showed the opposite.
Right: the reader judged the engineer on the wrong evidence.
The book says it hid the real strength.
The engineer did not enjoy it.
questions.explain: The most visible work was a few weeks of frontend. Their real strength, backend research and systems, was missing.
questions.rule: Show your best evidence, not the nearest.
questions.teaches: The first resume's most visible work was a few weeks of frontend that this backend engineer rarely did, so it hid the real strength in backend research and systems.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, the weak first impression came from poor work rather than from how the resume presented it.
questions.explain: The author says the engineer did remarkable research and built a solid system but the resume mentioned none of it; the problem was the presentation.
questions.rule: Under-selling can look like weak work.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A friend says: reword your resume and interviews will follow, as in this story. What caveat does the author's ending add?
options: He says anyone who rewrites a resume gets interviews as a direct result of the rewriting
He says the rewrite worked because it listed more employers than the first version did
He says the case proves that format beats content in every case that it covers
He notes it was not hard for an ex-Google engineer, so presentation is the lesson
optionExplain: He does not claim this.
It worked because it showed contributions.
The book says the opposite about format.
Right: his own ending limits the claim.
questions.explain: The author admits the success was not hard for a Google alumnus; it reminds us that presentation and storytelling make a big difference. One case does not show this works for everyone.
questions.rule: Read the author's own limits.
questions.teaches: The author concedes that success is not exactly hard for someone who has worked at Google; the case reminds readers that presentation and storytelling make a big difference.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Which resume pattern might worry a fast-growing company?
options: Several years in one role with no visible change in the scope of the work
Two jobs held at the same company over the years
A short summary placed at the top of the first page of the resume
A promotion recorded in the third year of the same job
optionExplain: Right: it can read as little progression.
Staying at a company can still show growth.
A summary is not a progression signal.
A promotion is a progression signal.
questions.explain: Fast-growing companies look for progression. The card names the pattern.
questions.rule: Growth should be visible.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A resume showing little or no progression over long stretches is called a ____ resume.
questions.explain: The author calls such resumes journeyman resumes; they tell a story with zero or close to zero progression.
questions.rule: Name the pattern.
