questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Tomas held the same title for six years but led an onboarding redesign, mentored two juniors and ran the on-call rota. What helps?
options: Changing his title so that it matches the work he does
Deleting the early years to shorten the whole resume
Keeping only the titles and dates of each position held
Showing how his scope grew within the role
optionExplain: That would misrepresent him; the aim is to show growth fairly.
Cutting years hides the progression.
Titles alone show no growth.
Right: this makes the growth visible without changing the title.
questions.explain: The growth is in the work, not the title. Showing wider responsibility counters a flat look.
questions.rule: Show scope, not only titles.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Sort each resume line by whether it shows progression or hides it.

items.t: Notes a promotion and the bigger scope that followed
Lists identical duties for every year
Shows a move to a team lead role
Omits that she took over a harder system
Describes taking initiative on a problem nobody owned
Gives only titles and dates with no scope

questions.explain: Progression shows through promotions, wider scope and initiative. Omitting those hides it.
questions.rule: Make growth show.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, rejection for little progression is a risk at high-growth companies.
questions.explain: The author says that for high-growth companies journeyman resumes can be a reason for rejection, since they look for signs of progression.
questions.rule: Know which employers screen for growth.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A freelance designer's portfolio shows eight years of similar logo jobs. By the author's diagnostic, what should she ask first?
options: Am I telling my story badly, or have I really not grown?
Which template hides the dates of each role best?
Should I claim a senior title that I never actually held?
Should I drop my oldest work so that I look newer?
optionExplain: Right: the author gives these two possibilities.
Hiding dates avoids the question, it does not answer it.
That would misrepresent her.
That does not address growth.
questions.explain: The author says to ask whether you are not telling your story right or have not been growing. He thinks it unlikely that you have not grown at all.
questions.rule: Check the telling before assuming no growth.
questions.teaches: The author thinks it unlikely that you have not grown at all, so the first suspect is how the story is told, and the remedy is to visualise growth.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: You have only a LinkedIn profile and are applying directly to a backend role. What is the best move?
options: Export the profile as a PDF and send it
Send nothing and wait to be sourced
Write a resume tailored to the backend role
Message the recruiter your profile link only
optionExplain: It will work only in some markets, and it is not tailored.
That works when in demand, not when applying directly.
Right: a direct application deserves a tailored document.
That still leaves the document untailored.
questions.explain: Direct applications favour a tailored resume. The card gives the author's reasons.
questions.rule: Direct application, tailored resume.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Which are downsides the author lists for using LinkedIn as your resume? Select all that apply.
options: It cannot be tailored to a position
It keeps no versions of earlier drafts
It cannot show job titles
It ties you to one platform's feature
Recruiters refuse any PDF
optionExplain: Right: a generic profile cannot be tailored.
Right: there is no versioning.
Not listed: profiles show titles.
Right: lock-in to a feature that may change.
Not listed: PDFs are what people send.
questions.explain: The author lists poor tailoring, no versioning, wasted space and lock-in. Titles and PDF refusal are not among his points.
questions.rule: Know the listed downsides.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A fullstack developer applies for a frontend job, then a backend job. What follows from the author's reasoning?
options: Reuse the same export, since fullstack covers both of the roles being applied for
Prepare a separate resume for each role
Edit the LinkedIn headline before each separate application is sent
Apply only to fullstack roles from now on, and skip the others
optionExplain: That ignores tailoring.
Right: a single profile cannot be tailored to each role, so prepare a separate resume for each.
A headline edit does not tailor the document.
That narrows options instead of solving the problem.
questions.explain: Different roles want different emphasis. A generic profile cannot give that.
questions.rule: One role, one tailored resume.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: When does the author say a LinkedIn export can still work as a resume?
options: When the company uses applicant tracking software to screen
When the role is a management one at a large firm
When few people apply or the candidate has standout experience
When the profile has many recommendations from colleagues
optionExplain: He does not tie it to software.
He does not limit it by role.
Right: he names these cases.
He does not mention recommendations.
questions.explain: He says it works when there are few applicants or the experience stands out. Otherwise it does not serve you well.
questions.rule: It works when competition is low.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, in a market where companies struggle to find any applicants, resume formatting matters far more.
questions.explain: In such a market you need to worry far less about resume formatting. The advice matters most when competition is real.
questions.rule: Weak competition lowers the stakes.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A developer in a hot hiring market sends only name, email and years of experience in a text file. When did the author say this could work?
options: In the late 1990s before the Dotcom bust, and partly in the early 2010s
Only during the Dotcom bust itself, when firms were cutting back on hiring
Whenever the applicant has a LinkedIn profile that is kept up to date
In any market, since content beats format whenever the hiring is done
optionExplain: Right: those are the periods he names.
The bust is when it stopped working.
A profile is not the cause.
He says it depends on the market.
questions.explain: When hiring is frantic, thin applications can get technical interviews. The author names the late 1990s and the early to mid 2010s.
questions.rule: The market sets how much the resume must do.
questions.teaches: Thin applications worked when hiring was frantic, as in the late 1990s and the early to mid 2010s; how much a resume must do depends on the market.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: You applied to three big companies and heard nothing. What should you conclude about your resume?
options: A good resume is needed, but other factors also decide replies
That its format is the only possible problem with the whole application
That a resume has no effect on whether companies reply to anyone
That applying to more companies will fix whatever is wrong with it
optionExplain: Right: it is necessary and not sufficient.
Many people think so; the author says other factors are outside your control.
A well-written resume is still required.
More applications do not fix format.
questions.explain: A resume is needed but not enough on its own. The card lists outside factors.
questions.rule: Required is not sufficient.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A well-written resume is required, but it is not ____ to get a recruiter call.
questions.explain: The author calls it required but not sufficient, since several factors are outside your control.
questions.rule: Required, not sufficient.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Mo hears nothing about a job posted three months ago. Which outside factor from the book fits?
options: His resume format has too many columns for recruiters to follow
Recruiters stop reading resumes once a posting is a month old
Recruiters favour candidates who have shorter names
The position may already have been filled without him knowing
optionExplain: Format is within his control and not a listed outside factor.
The book does not say this.
Nothing in the book supports this.
Right: this is the first factor listed.
questions.explain: The author lists whether the position is still open as the first outside factor.
questions.rule: Check whether the job is open.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: Sort each factor by whether it is outside your control or within it.

items.t: Whether the position is still open
How well the resume shows your fit for the role
How many stronger applicants compete
Whether your visa needs company sponsorship
Which achievements you put first
Whether you tailor the resume to the posting

questions.explain: Openness of the position, competition and visa status are outside your control; content choices and tailoring are within it.
questions.rule: Spend effort on what you control.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, competition is likely to be tougher for remote-friendly jobs than for jobs requiring office presence.
questions.explain: The author says that for remote-friendly and remote-only jobs the competition will be far more intense.
questions.rule: Wider pools mean more rivals.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A role gets hundreds of applications and two candidates have equal skills, one local. Which way may the preference go, per the author?
options: Toward the candidate who relocates, since that shows more commitment
Toward the local candidate, who needs no relocation and costs less
Toward the candidate with the longer and more detailed resume
Neither, since location plays no part in a decision of this kind
optionExplain: The author does not give this reasoning.
Right: that is his reasoning.
Length is not a factor he names.
He says local candidates may get preference.
questions.explain: He says that with hundreds of applications local candidates might get preference because they can start faster and cost the company less.
questions.rule: Cost and speed can tip close calls.
questions.teaches: Where a position sees hundreds of applications, local candidates may get preference because they need no relocation, can start faster and cost the company less.

questions.unitTitle: Why resumes and CVs are important
questions.q: A nurse applies to a popular hospital post with hundreds of applicants and worries it comes down to luck. By the author's logic, what lowers the role of luck?
options: A referral from someone inside, which can matter most against luck
Sending more applications in the same week as the first one
Making the resume longer with more detail on each role she held

questions.explain: People update statuses.

questions.q: An application starts as an unviewed applicant and eventually becomes Rejected, Accepted or ____.
questions.explain: The author lists Rejected, Accepted or Declined as the eventual statuses.
questions.teaches: Application statuses start at Unviewed applicant and eventually become Rejected, Accepted or Declined, as people move them along.
questions.rule: An ATS is a status tracker that people operate; it does not make the decisions.

questions.q: A recruiter has forty candidates at different stages. What problem does the ATS solve for her, according to the author's quoted recruiter?
options: Choosing the best candidate from among the forty at once
Writing the interview questions for each stage of the process
Predicting which of the offers made will be accepted
Knowing who is waiting on whom and what to do next
optionExplain: The ATS does not pick candidates.
Interview questions are not its job.
The chapter describes no prediction feature.
Right: without an ATS she would not know who is waiting on whom, doing what.
questions.explain: An ATS keeps a recruiter organised.
questions.teaches: A recruiter uses the ATS to see, for each candidate, what has been done and what must happen next, such as whether an interview is set up or an offer approved.
questions.rule: An ATS is a status tracker that people operate; it does not make the decisions.

questions.q: Which statement about ATSes and resume rejection does the author support?
options: Most ATSes reject resumes that fall below a certain keyword score
Humans reject resumes; major ATSes do not do so automatically
ATSes hide the resumes they cannot read from the recruiters
Most rejections come from algorithms rather than from people
optionExplain: The author calls keyword-score rejection a myth.
Right: the author's answer is that ATSes do not reject resumes; humans do.
The author says none of the major systems hide resumes from recruiters.
The author attributes rejections to people.
questions.explain: The author's answer is plain and surprising. The card next gives the detail.
questions.rule: Humans, not the ATS, decide which resumes advance.

questions.q: True or false: As of 2020, none of the major ATS systems rejected resumes automatically or hid them from recruiters.
questions.explain: That is the author's statement about the major systems.
questions.rule: Humans, not the ATS, decide which resumes advance.

questions.q: A friend says robots threw out her resume. The author would say the one who moved her application to Rejected was a ____.
questions.explain: People, either recruiters or hiring managers, move statuses; rejection comes from the resume or from knockout answers.
questions.rule: Humans, not the ATS, decide which resumes advance.

questions.q: Some recruiters predict AI-assisted hiring decisions. What outcome does the author expect even then?
options: A hidden ranking of all resumes that no human ever opens
An end to human interviews, with hiring decided by software alone
A new rule under which only Word files would be accepted
Much like a recruiter's quick scan ending in Yes, Maybe or No
optionExplain: The author expects no hidden ranking to replace the scan.
Interviews are not discussed in this prediction.
File format is not the point of the prediction.
Right: the outcome should not differ from a quick human scan.
questions.explain: Even future systems resemble a quick scan.
questions.rule: Humans, not the ATS, decide which resumes advance.

questions.q: True or false: Because ATS functionality is advanced, resume parsing is the main way they add value.
questions.explain: Resume processing is basic in all major systems; most added functionality lies elsewhere.
questions.rule: Humans, not the ATS, decide which resumes advance.

questions.q: A vendor boasts of its ATS features. Which kind of feature does the author say vendors mostly add?
options: Integration with company systems and reporting
Smarter automatic rejection of the weaker resumes in the queue
Rating of coding skill directly from the resume text
Automatic scheduling of interviews run by an AI
optionExplain: Right: most added functionality is outside the resume processing phase.
The author says resume processing stays basic.
The author makes no such claim.
The text describes no such feature.
questions.explain: Extra features sit around the resume, not on it.
questions.teaches: Most of the added functionality of ATSes is outside the resume processing phase, in integration with other company systems and in reporting.
questions.rule: Humans, not the ATS, decide which resumes advance.

questions.q: Which two traits does the author say ATS-myth sites share?
options: They are run by recruiters who give their name and experience
They give away free advice and cite peer-reviewed hiring studies
They sell beat-the-ATS services and cite sources that no recruiter backs
They sell Word templates and cite surveys from job seekers online
optionExplain: The author says the reverse: no recruiter backs them.
The author says they promote paid services.
Right: a sales motive and no insider sources.
The key traits are the sales motive and the missing recruiter backing.
questions.explain: Motive and sources are the two tests. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Ask who profits from a claim, and whether people who use ATSes back it.

questions.q: The misleading sites promote services you can ____ to beat the ATS.
questions.explain: They sell services; that gives them a reason to exaggerate the problem.
questions.rule: Ask who profits from a claim, and whether people who use ATSes back it.

questions.q: A site offers a 200-dollar ATS fix and quotes only its own customer surveys. What would the author conclude?
options: Trust it, because the customers themselves confirm the problem
Trust it, because a high price suggests a quality service to buy
Ignore the claim only if the resume is submitted as a PDF file
Be suspicious: it sells a service and has no recruiter backing
optionExplain: Surveys run by the seller are not recruiter backing.
Price is not evidence.
File format is not the author's test.
Right: both of the author's traits are present.
questions.explain: Check motive and sources.
questions.rule: Ask who profits from a claim, and whether people who use ATSes back it.

questions.q: True or false: The author treats claims backed by technical recruiters who use ATSes daily as more credible than claims from sellers of ATS services.
questions.explain: First-hand users, with no product to sell, are the author's standard of evidence.
questions.rule: Ask who profits from a claim, and whether people who use ATSes back it.

questions.q: Which source would the author trust most on how ATSes work?
options: A website that sells paid resume optimisation packages to job seekers
A technical recruiter who sets up and uses one every day
A career coach's blog post about how to beat the hiring bots
A vendor page listing which fonts are supposedly ATS-friendly
optionExplain: It sells the cure, which gives it a motive to exaggerate.
Right: first-hand daily use is the author's standard.
It has no recruiter backing.
It sells advice and repeats the myth.
questions.explain: First-hand users beat sellers.
questions.rule: Ask who profits from a claim, and whether people who use ATSes back it.

questions.q: A news article claims 75% of resumes are not read by a human, quoting only resume-service firms. What does the author say about this kind of article?
options: It is correct, because several firms agree with each other
It is correct, but only for resumes that are saved as PDFs
No hiring manager or tech recruiter backs the claim up
It proves that ATSes are advanced AI-driven screening tools
optionExplain: Several sellers repeating a claim are not independent backing.
The author calls the PDF claim false.
Right: the author criticises exactly this pattern in a business news article.
The author says ATSes are far simpler than that.
questions.explain: Many sellers are not many independent sources.
questions.teaches: The author's example, a business news article claiming 75% of resumes are never read by a human, cites only sources from companies that sell resume services.
questions.rule: Ask who profits from a claim, and whether people who use ATSes back it.

questions.q: In which case does the claim the ATS rejected me have some truth, according to the author?
options: Your resume used an unusual font that the system could not read
Your resume contained too few keywords from the job advert text
Your answers to knockout questions on the application form
Your file was saved as a PDF instead of as a Word document
optionExplain: Fonts do not trigger rejection.
The author says keyword scoring does not decide screening.
Right: knockout questions are the one real automatic filter.
The author says PDFs are fine.
questions.explain: Form answers can filter you. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Only your form answers, never your resume, can trigger a knockout rejection.

questions.q: True or false: Knockout questions use information taken from your resume.
questions.explain: The information is never taken from your resume; you provide it on the form.
questions.rule: Only your form answers, never your resume, can trigger a knockout rejection.

questions.q: A form asks whether Sam will need sponsorship. He says yes and is rejected at once. Who set that rule up?
options: The recruiter, following the policy for the role in question
The ATS vendor, which decides who counts as eligible
The hiring manager's assistant, who reviews every application
Sam's own resume, which listed his previous employers
optionExplain: Right: the recruiter configured the question.
The system only applies what recruiters configure.
The chapter names the recruiter as the one who sets such questions up.
Resumes do not feed knockout rules.
questions.explain: Recruiters configure the rules.
questions.rule: Only your form answers, never your resume, can trigger a knockout rejection.

questions.q: Sam improves his resume but gives the same answer on the form. The knockout outcome stays the same, because it uses the form ____.
questions.explain: Knockout rules look at the information given on the form, never at the resume.
questions.rule: Only your form answers, never your resume, can trigger a knockout rejection.

questions.q: A blogger says: your resume was knocked out because it did not mention your visa needs. What is wrong?
options: Knockout questions do not exist in any of the major ATSes
Knockout data comes from the form you fill in, not the resume
Visa questions are not asked of candidates on application forms
Resumes are ignored by every recruiter and hiring manager
optionExplain: They exist in the major ATSes under various names.
Right: the data must be explicitly provided by the candidate on the form.
The author's own example is a visa question.
Recruiters and hiring managers do scan resumes.
questions.explain: Form answers, not resumes.
questions.rule: Only your form answers, never your resume, can trigger a knockout rejection.

questions.q: A candidate reads the Greenhouse documentation and finds custom questions. What does the author say these correspond to?
options: A resume scoring feature that ranks candidates by keyword overlap
The same kind of knockout question, but under a different name
An interview scheduling tool used by the recruitment coordinator
A form for collecting reference checks from past colleagues
optionExplain: The author names no such scoring feature in this context.
Right: each ATS has its own name for them.
Scheduling is a coordinator task.
References come after interviews.
questions.explain: Same feature, different names.
questions.teaches: ATSes name knockout questions differently: Taleo calls them prescreening questions, iCIMS screening questions, Greenhouse custom questions and Workable form application questions.
questions.rule: Only your form answers, never your resume, can trigger a knockout rejection.

questions.q: Why do most ATSes try to parse a resume?
options: To decide automatically whether the resume should be rejected
To grade the writing style and quality of the resume text
To check the facts in the resume with former employers
To auto-fill details and to allow searches at a later date
optionExplain: The author says parsing is not used to filter.
The chapter describes no grading.
Verification is a later step, after an offer.
Right: parsing helps convenience and later searching.
questions.explain: Parsing is convenience, not judgement. The card next details it.
questions.rule: Every resume is ATS-compatible, so the label tells you nothing.

questions.q: True or false: Most ATSes use the contents of your resume to filter candidates during screening.
questions.explain: They parse it to auto-fill details and for later searches, not to filter.
questions.rule: Every resume is ATS-compatible, so the label tells you nothing.

questions.q: A site sells ATS-compatible resume designs at a premium. How does the author's comparison apply?
options: Like selling mobile-compatible websites, since all of them already are
It proves that your resume needs a special layout to be read
It is true only for Word files, because PDFs cannot be parsed
It shows that the ATS rejects files that are not compatible
optionExplain: Right: the label is a meaningless buzzword.
The author says the opposite.
Both PDF and Word are parsed well enough.
The author denies that ATSes reject on compatibility.
questions.explain: All resumes are ATS-compatible.
questions.rule: Every resume is ATS-compatible, so the label tells you nothing.

questions.q: Dev uploads a PDF and a friend uploads a Word file. The author expects the ATS to have ____ both well enough.
questions.explain: Both formats are parsed well enough, so format is not a barrier.
questions.rule: Every resume is ATS-compatible, so the label tells you nothing.

questions.q: True or false: To pass screening, a resume must be saved in the one format that ATSes can read.
questions.explain: Both PDF and Word are parsed well enough, and the ATS does not screen on contents.
questions.rule: Every resume is ATS-compatible, so the label tells you nothing.

questions.q: Months after a hiring round, a recruiter searches the ATS for developers who mention Go. What makes this possible, per the author?
options: The ATS rates every resume for Go skills when it is uploaded
Recruiters retype each resume into the system by hand later
Candidates must tag their own skills in the application form
Keywords are indexed from parsed resumes, which supports boolean search
optionExplain: The author says the ATS does nothing clever.
Parsing automates this step.
The chapter does not say candidates must tag skills.
Right: the parsed text is indexed for boolean searching later.
questions.explain: Parsing feeds later search.
questions.teaches: Resume parsing also allows boolean searching in the ATS later, outside the application process, by indexing the keywords found in the resume.
questions.rule: Every resume is ATS-compatible, so the label tells you nothing.

questions.q: What do ATS optimisation services typically charge, according to the author?
options: Anywhere from $100 to $500 and sometimes beyond
Under $10 for a complete resume review
A flat fee of $20 for the whole service
Free of charge for new graduates only
optionExplain: Right: the author gives $100 to $500 and beyond.
Far below the author's figure.
Still far below it.
The author describes paid services only.
questions.explain: The sums are sizeable. The card next explains why the author doubts the pitch.
questions.rule: There is no ATS algorithm to bypass for tech jobs; your resume waits in a queue for a person.

questions.q: Taleo can assign a percentage score called the requisition ____.
questions.explain: Taleo's requisition rank compares screening answers and resume with the requisition.
questions.rule: There is no ATS algorithm to bypass for tech jobs; your resume waits in a queue for a person.

questions.q: An ad says: pay $300 and your resume will bypass the ATS algorithm. How would the author respond?
options: Agree, because beating the algorithm is the best tactic for any applicant
There is no bypass for most tech jobs: the resume waits in a queue
Agree, but only if the resume is submitted in Word format instead
Agree for entry-level jobs only, where algorithms matter more
optionExplain: The author denies there is an algorithm to beat.
Right: the author calls bypass claims false in most cases for tech jobs.
Format is not the point.
The author does not limit the claim to entry-level jobs.
questions.explain: No algorithm gates the queue.
questions.rule: There is no ATS algorithm to bypass for tech jobs; your resume waits in a queue for a person.

questions.q: A tech recruiter uses Taleo. What does the author expect about relying on its rank for developer resumes?
options: Most recruiters rely on it fully when choosing which to read
It replaces the recruiter's first scan of each resume completely
Few if any recruiters rely on it to decide what to read
It is always more accurate than a human reading the resume
optionExplain: The author says none of those consulted used it.
The scan by a person still happens.
Right: the score is off for software developers and the recruiters consulted did not use it.
The author doubts its accuracy for developers.
questions.explain: Even Taleo's score is not trusted for developers.
questions.rule: There is no ATS algorithm to bypass for tech jobs; your resume waits in a queue for a person.

questions.q: Which statements about Taleo's rank match the author? Select all that apply.
options: It can be a percentage based on screening answers and resume overlap
Recruiters can sort resumes by it
It is accurate for software developers
Every major ATS has one
optionExplain: This matches the author's account of Taleo.
This matches the author's account of Taleo.
The author says it is off for developers.
It is the only popular ATS that rates resumes.
questions.explain: Taleo is the exception, and even there the rank is not trusted for developers.
questions.rule: There is no ATS algorithm to bypass for tech jobs; your resume waits in a queue for a person.

questions.q: A vendor says its ATS can tell that Kotlin experience implies Java. What does the author say about ATS sophistication as of 2020?
options: They can infer related skills reliably from your job titles
They check your code samples on GitHub before the screening
They are simpler than even working out which languages you have listed
They compare you against all the other applicants for the role
optionExplain: The author denies this level of sophistication.
The chapter makes no such claim.
Right: the author says they are far simpler than that.
Comparing applicants is done by the recruiter.
questions.explain: ATSes are simple.
questions.teaches: As of 2020, ATSes were far simpler than even working out which programming languages you have listed on your resume.
questions.rule: There is no ATS algorithm to bypass for tech jobs; your resume waits in a queue for a person.

questions.q: People report better results after following ATS optimisation tips. What explains this, according to the author?
options: Tailoring makes the resume more relevant to the human scanning it
The ATS algorithm ranks tailored resumes higher in the queue for review
The ATS rewards a high keyword density with a better internal score
Saving the resume in PDF format avoids rejection by the applicant system
optionExplain: Right: tailoring helps because a person judges relevance.
The author denies a ranking algorithm in tech hiring.
Keyword density is not the cause.
Format is not the cause.
questions.explain: Humans reward relevance. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Tailor the resume for the human who scans it, not for a program.

questions.q: True or false: The ATS itself decides whether to move forward with your resume.
questions.explain: The recruiter or hiring manager scanning your resume decides.
questions.rule: Tailor the resume for the human who scans it, not for a program.

questions.q: Nia applies to ten jobs with one generic resume and hears nothing. What does the author's point suggest?
options: Buy an ATS optimisation service to help bypass the algorithm
Switch to a Word document so that the ATS can read it better
Add every keyword you know to the resume you send each time
Tailor the resume to each position for the human reader
optionExplain: The author says there is no ATS to bypass.
Format is not the problem.
Keyword stuffing is a separate warning later in the book.
Right: tailoring is solid advice.
questions.explain: Tailor for the reader.
questions.rule: Tailor the resume for the human who scans it, not for a program.

questions.q: A role gets hundreds of applications. The author expects a tailored resume that grabs ____ at the first scan to make a difference.
questions.explain: With numerous applications, quick relevance is what makes a resume stand out.
questions.rule: Tailor the resume for the human who scans it, not for a program.

questions.q: A coach says: tailoring works because the ATS ranks tailored resumes higher. Where does this reasoning go wrong?
options: Tailoring does not work, because recruiters ignore the content
The ATS does not decide; a person judging relevance does
Recruiters do not read resumes themselves, since only the ATS does
Only the hiring manager ever reads resumes, not the recruiter
optionExplain: The author calls tailoring solid advice.
Right: the benefit comes from the human reader.
Recruiters almost always scan resumes.
The recruiter or hiring manager scans the resume.
questions.explain: Right result, wrong cause.
questions.rule: Tailor the resume for the human who scans it, not for a program.

questions.q: A recruiter is scanning a tailored resume. How does the author describe the time they take to judge relevance?
options: About ten minutes
A full hour
They never judge it
A few seconds
optionExplain: That is far longer than the author's scan.
The author says recruiters decide in a few seconds.
They judge relevance by scanning.
Right: they judge how relevant the experience is in a few seconds.
questions.explain: Readers decide in seconds.
questions.teaches: The recruiter or hiring manager who scans the resume judges how relevant your experience is in a few seconds.
questions.rule: Tailor the resume for the human who scans it, not for a program.

questions.q: Why might a recruiter suggest PDF as the best CV format?
options: Word files can lose their formatting on another version or system
PDFs receive a higher score from the ATS than other formats
Word files are rejected automatically by most applicant systems
Hiring law in several countries requires CVs to be sent as PDFs
optionExplain: Right: PDF keeps the layout intact.
The author denies score-based ranking of formats.
The author calls claims about format removal false.
The chapter mentions no legal rule.
questions.explain: Layout safety is the reason. The card next gives the quotes.
questions.rule: Recruiters filter by hand and prefer PDF to protect formatting.

questions.q: True or false: One quoted recruiter says the ATS list is organised by date applied and a real person then makes the decision.
questions.explain: That recruiter describes filtering as human.
questions.rule: Recruiters filter by hand and prefer PDF to protect formatting.

questions.q: A candidate frets over converting a PDF into Word to please the ATS. What do the quoted recruiters suggest?
options: Convert it to Word, because ATSes cannot read PDF files properly
Send both versions and let the ATS pick whichever it prefers
Keep the PDF: it protects the layout and filtering is human
Remove all the formatting so the file is as plain as possible
optionExplain: The author calls this advice poor.
The chapter does not propose sending both.
Right: PDF is suggested as the best format.
Layout still matters to the human readers.
questions.explain: PDF is the safe format.
questions.rule: Recruiters filter by hand and prefer PDF to protect formatting.

questions.q: Why would no recruiter the quoted professional knows trust an ATS with filtering?
options: ATSes are too expensive for most hiring teams to use
ATSes cannot store the resumes that candidates upload
Hiring managers forbid automated filtering by company policy
They could lose otherwise good candidates by mistake
optionExplain: Cost is not the reason given.
ATSes do store applications.
No such policy is mentioned.
Right: the risk of losing good candidates is too high.
questions.explain: Risk of losing good people.
questions.rule: Recruiters filter by hand and prefer PDF to protect formatting.

questions.q: Which are reasons given for preferring PDF to Word? Select all that apply.
options: Word may break the layout on another version or operating system
Agency recruiters may use Word CVs to strip your contact details
ATSes can only parse PDF
PDFs bypass the ATS queue
optionExplain: The quoted recruiter gives this as a reason.
The quoted recruiter gives this as a reason.
The author says both parse well enough.
The author says there is no bypass.
questions.explain: The reasons are layout and contact-detail safety, not parsing.
questions.rule: Recruiters filter by hand and prefer PDF to protect formatting.

questions.q: Mia emails a Word CV to a recruiting agency. What risk does one quoted recruiter warn about?
options: The agency may strip her contact details for its own business use
The agency may lose the file when it moves between systems
The employer's ATS may reject the Word file automatically
The employer may be shown an older version of her CV later
optionExplain: Right: agency recruiters can reuse Word CVs after removing contact details.
The quoted recruiter does not raise lost files.
The author denies automatic ATS rejection.
Version problems are not what the recruiter warns of.
questions.explain: Word CVs are easy to edit and reuse.
questions.teaches: Agency recruiters may use Word CVs to remove your contact details and reuse them as business development material.
questions.rule: Recruiters filter by hand and prefer PDF to protect formatting.

questions.q: At what point are background checks usually run?
options: Before you apply to the position at all
After you have accepted the offer that was made to you
Right after the resume screen is complete
Before the technical screen takes place
optionExplain: Applications come before any checks.
Right: they usually come after acceptance, and an unsatisfactory result can withdraw the offer.
The resume screen is far earlier in the pipeline.
The technical screen is an early stage.
questions.explain: Background checks come late. The card next separates the three terms.
questions.rule: A referral comes before you apply, a reference after interviews, a background check after you accept.

questions.q: Match each term to what it means.
pairs: An employee recommends a candidate internally
Usually after interviews, before an offer
Usually after you accept the offer
questions.explain: The three terms differ in who acts and when.
questions.rule: A referral comes before you apply, a reference after interviews, a background check after you accept.

questions.q: After her final interview, a company asks Priya for two professional contacts to call. What is this?
options: A referral
A background check
A reference check
A knockout question
optionExplain: A referral is an employee's internal recommendation.
Background checks come after acceptance and are run by a specialist company.
Right: references are usually requested after interviews and before an offer.
Knockout questions are on the application form.
questions.explain: Tell your referees to expect a call.
questions.rule: A referral comes before you apply, a reference after interviews, a background check after you accept.

questions.q: A candidate has accepted an offer, but the background check turns out unsatisfactory. What can happen?
options: The offer is final regardless
The candidate restarts at the resume screen
The offer can be withdrawn
The hiring manager must resign
optionExplain: Acceptance does not protect against a failed check.
The chapter does not describe restarts.
Right: the offer can be withdrawn.
This has no bearing on the question.
questions.explain: Acceptance is not the end.
questions.rule: A referral comes before you apply, a reference after interviews, a background check after you accept.

questions.q: True or false: Referrals and references mean the same thing.
questions.explain: A referral gets you into the process; a reference check confirms fit after interviews.
questions.rule: A referral comes before you apply, a reference after interviews, a background check after you accept.

questions.q: Two candidates both accept offers: one at a retail design agency, one at a bank. Where does the author expect stricter checks?
options: At the bank, since finance is stricter
At the agency, since design is regulated
Equally, since checks are uniform
Neither, because checks are voluntary
optionExplain: Right: finance and government are stricter than other industries.
The author names finance and government.
Checks vary by industry, country and company.
The chapter does not call them voluntary.
questions.explain: Strictness varies by industry.
questions.teaches: Background checks often verify employment history for the past few years and may include criminal records; finance and government are stricter than other industries, and rules vary by country, state and company.
questions.rule: A referral comes before you apply, a reference after interviews, a background check after you accept.

questions.q: Why do tech companies give employee referrals priority?
options: Referrals cost the company nothing to process, unlike other leads
The law requires companies to read referral resumes before the rest
Employees insist on it in their contracts of employment terms
Referred hires tend to do better in interviews and on the job
optionExplain: Referrals carry bonuses, so they are not free.
The chapter mentions no law.
The chapter mentions no contract rule.
Right: referrals work remarkably well.
questions.explain: Results explain the priority. The card next gives the evidence.
questions.rule: Referrals work better, so companies move them to the front.

questions.q: True or false: The author says referred candidates are far more likely to go through interviews successfully.
questions.explain: Referred candidates are more likely to pass interviews, get an offer and accept it.
questions.rule: Referrals work better, so companies move them to the front.

questions.q: A recruiter has two similar resumes and one came by referral. Which of the author's reasons supports reading it first?
options: Referral resumes tend to be shorter and so quicker to read through
Referred hires are less likely to fail their trial period
Referred candidates do not need a visa or relocation support
The ATS flags referral resumes as perfect matches automatically
optionExplain: Length is not part of the evidence.
Right: a lower chance of a bad hire is part of the evidence.
Referrals can still need visas.
The ATS does not rate resumes this way.
questions.explain: Referrals carry lower risk.
questions.rule: Referrals work better, so companies move them to the front.

questions.q: You apply with no referral. The author says it is more ____ to get a human to look at your resume.
questions.explain: Without a referral, getting a human to look at your resume is more difficult.
questions.rule: Referrals work better, so companies move them to the front.

questions.q: True or false: The studies the author cites show that referral benefits apply only within tech.
questions.explain: They confirm the benefit for hiring in general, not just within tech.
questions.rule: Referrals work better, so companies move them to the front.

questions.q: A manager at a Dutch software firm wonders why her engineers push friends' resumes into the referral system. What do employees receive when a referral is hired?
options: A trip to another office of the company
Nothing beyond a thank-you note from the team
A share of the new hire's first-year salary
A bonus, often in the thousands of dollars
optionExplain: The chapter mentions no such perk.
Programmes reward employees with money.
The chapter mentions no salary share.
Right: referral programmes pay a bonus on a successful hire.
questions.explain: Referral programmes pay a bonus, which gives employees a reason to take referrals seriously.
questions.teaches: Employees who refer a candidate that is hired are paid a bonus, often in the thousands of dollars.
questions.rule: Referrals work better, so companies move them to the front.

questions.q: Which referral is likeliest to get a recruiter call set up straight away?
options: One from a colleague who worked with you and actively vouches for you
One from a stranger that you messaged once on a public forum
One from an employee who read your resume once but never met you
One from a recruiter at another company who saw your profile
optionExplain: Right: a strong referral comes with first-hand vouching.
That is a generic referral at best.
Reading a resume is not vouching.
Someone at another company is not an employee referral.
questions.explain: Vouching matters. The card next names the two types.
questions.rule: A referral earns a closer look; a strong referral earns the fastest route.

questions.q: True or false: A generic referral comes from someone who has worked with you and vouches for you.

questions.rule: A referral earns a closer look; a strong referral earns the fastest route.

questions.q: Omar asks a stranger on LinkedIn for a referral; Lia asks an ex-teammate. Whose referral does the author call strong?

Both, because each of them asked an employee for a referral

Only vouching by someone who knows your work counts.

questions.rule: A referral earns a closer look; a strong referral earns the fastest route.

questions.q: A referral usually secures an in-depth resume ____.
questions.explain: Referrals almost always guarantee an in-depth resume review.
questions.rule: A referral earns a closer look; a strong referral earns the fastest route.

questions.q: Which statement fits a strong referral but not a generic one?

The referrer submitted your resume through the internal system
The referrer is an employee of the company that is hiring
The referrer's company pays a bonus for successful referrals

Both generic and strong referrals submit a resume.
Both come from employees.
Bonuses apply to both.

questions.rule: A referral earns a closer look; a strong referral earns the fastest route.

questions.q: A developer in Cape Town gets a referral from an engineer at a large search company who does not know her. Beyond getting an interview, what does a Google employee quoted by the author say such cold referrals do?

questions.q: What should you check first when hunting for a referral?

The posted salary range for the open position
Whether anyone you know works at the company
How old the recruiter is and how long they have worked

Pay is not a way in.
Right: the network comes first.
The recruiter does not give referrals.

questions.rule: Ask through your network first, then cold, with a short message and an easy way out.

questions.q: When messaging someone cold, give them an easy way ____.
questions.explain: An easy way out lets them decline without awkwardness.
questions.rule: Ask through your network first, then cold, with a short message and an easy way out.

questions.q: Sam sends a cold LinkedIn request that says only: Hi, let's connect. What does the author advise adding?
options: A copy of the address and phone number of every past employer
A request for the hiring manager's personal mobile phone number
A clear, concise message that you are looking for a referral
A long essay on your whole career history since university
optionExplain: Nobody needs that to give a referral.
That is inappropriate for a first message.

The advice is to be concise.

questions.rule: Ask through your network first, then cold, with a short message and an easy way out.

questions.q: True or false: Ben knows nobody at the firm, but a friend is connected to someone there. The author suggests Ben ask the friend for an introduction.
questions.explain: Second-degree connections can introduce you; do the legwork when asking.
questions.rule: Ask through your network first, then cold, with a short message and an easy way out.

questions.q: Which approach goes against the author's advice on cold referral requests?
options: Sending a clear, concise message asking for a referral
Offering the person an easy way out of the request
Naming the role you are interested in at the company
Demanding a referral and giving no easy way out
optionExplain: That is advised.
That is advised.
Naming the role fits being clear.
Right: the author advises giving the person an easy way out.
questions.explain: Make it easy to say no.
questions.rule: Ask through your network first, then cold, with a short message and an easy way out.

questions.q: You post a referral request on Blind for a well-known company. What should the post include?
options: Your resume alone and a request to forward it to the recruiter
Company tag, LinkedIn link, why you fit, job post link
Only the job title and a request that someone reply to you
A warning that you will apply elsewhere if nobody replies
optionExplain: That leaves out the details the author lists.
Right: these four items make the request easy to act on.
Too little for a referrer to act on.
A threat is not appropriate.
questions.explain: Give the referrer everything they need.
questions.teaches: On Blind, tag the company name, include your LinkedIn profile, describe why you are a good fit for the job, and link the job description.
questions.rule: Ask through your network first, then cold, with a short message and an easy way out.

questions.q: When should you ask for a referral compared with applying on the company site?
options: After you apply
Before you apply
At the same hour
Only after the recruiter call
optionExplain: Once you have applied, you are an active candidate and often cannot be referred.
Right: referral systems often only accept people not yet in the pipeline.
Being already in the system is the problem.
A referral cannot be requested for someone already in the pipeline.
questions.explain: Order matters. The card next gives the reason.
questions.rule: If you want a referral, get it before you apply.

questions.q: True or false: If you apply on a company's website and then ask for a referral, you often will not be able to be referred.
questions.explain: You count as an active candidate once you have applied.
questions.rule: If you want a referral, get it before you apply.

questions.q: Zoe applied on the site yesterday; a friend inside offers a referral today. What does the author expect?
options: The friend can still refer her, as the system has no limits
The system will merge both entries into one candidate file
The referral will double the chances of her application succeeding
The system may refuse, as she is already in the pipeline
optionExplain: The author says it is often not possible.
The chapter does not describe merging.
The author makes no such claim.

questions.explain: Apply later in time, not earlier.
questions.rule: If you want a referral, get it before you apply.

questions.q: Hana waits two weeks to arrange a referral. The cost is that her application goes in ____.
questions.explain: Waiting delays your application, which is the trade-off the author describes.
questions.rule: If you want a referral, get it before you apply.

questions.q: Which decision does the author say is yours to make?
options: Which ATS the company uses to track its applications
Which statuses the recruiter assigns to each candidate
Whether to apply sooner or to wait for a possible referral
Which engineers are picked to interview the candidates
optionExplain: The company chooses its ATS.
Recruiters set statuses.
Right: the balance between a faster application and a referral is the candidate's.
The hiring manager picks the interviewers.
questions.explain: Weigh speed against a referral.
questions.rule: If you want a referral, get it before you apply.

questions.q: A developer in Warsaw finds a bank role she likes. She plans to submit her application tonight and ask a friend inside the bank for a referral tomorrow. What goes wrong with this order?
options: The friend cannot see roles that were already applied to
The ATS deletes her resume once a referral is requested
The hiring manager refuses referrals from people who applied first

questions.rule: If you want a referral, get it before you apply.

questions.q: Which candidates typically get the lowest priority?

Local candidates who need neither paperwork nor relocation help
Referred candidates, whose resumes are normally read in depth first
Candidates not needing visas, though they may need to relocate

Local candidates rank near the top.
Referrals come first.

questions.rule: The cheaper and quicker a hire, the earlier the resume is read.

questions.q: Put the typical priority first to last.
items: Candidates from countries with unusually hard visas
questions.explain: The order follows time and money cost to hire.
questions.rule: The cheaper and quicker a hire, the earlier the resume is read.

questions.q: Two near-identical resumes: one local, one needing a visa and relocation. Which is read first and why?
options: The visa one, because the extra paperwork shows more diverse skills
The local one: no paperwork, no relocation and a low risk of backing out

questions.rule: The cheaper and quicker a hire, the earlier the resume is read.

questions.q: A strong referral needs a visa and relocation; the manager has a policy against such hires. What is likely?

The candidate drops to the bottom of the list, below all other visa cases

The chapter describes no company-wide change.

questions.rule: The cheaper and quicker a hire, the earlier the resume is read.

questions.q: True or false: Priority is decided mainly by how well written the resume is.
questions.explain: The ranking in this section rests on local status and visa needs, i.e. time and cost.
questions.rule: The cheaper and quicker a hire, the earlier the resume is read.

questions.q: A retailer in Manchester has two equally strong finalists, one local and one who would need a visa and a move from abroad. Why would the second hire rank lower on cost?
options: It needs a full year of training before the new hire can start
It costs the company twice the new hire's yearly salary

questions.rule: The cheaper and quicker a hire, the earlier the resume is read.

questions.q: Who is most likely to be sponsored for a visa by a large tech company?
options: A senior engineer for a role that is hard to fill locally
A new graduate from abroad applying for an entry-level role

Entry-level candidates are rarely sponsored.

questions.q: Companies typically sponsor visas only at ____ and above levels.
questions.explain: Sponsorship usually starts at senior level.
questions.rule: Sponsorship follows scarcity: it is rare at entry level and common for senior, hard-to-fill roles.

questions.q: A new grad abroad applies to thirty large US firms' entry-level roles. What outcome does the author expect?

questions.rule: Sponsorship follows scarcity: it is rare at entry level and common for senior, hard-to-fill roles.

options: It rises
It falls
It stays the same
It becomes certain

questions.rule: Sponsorship follows scarcity: it is rare at entry level and common for senior, hard-to-fill roles.

questions.q: True or false: The hiring manager advises new grads to avoid applying abroad completely.

questions.rule: Sponsorship follows scarcity: it is rare at entry level and common for senior, hard-to-fill roles.

questions.teaches: Recruiters follow the company's policy and the hiring manager's instructions, and will not spend time talking to people for whom the company or manager would not sign off on an offer.
questions.rule: Sponsorship follows scarcity: it is rare at entry level and common for senior, hard-to-fill roles.

questions.q: A developer in Brazil compares four job adverts for a Berlin role and wants to avoid wasting an application if the company cannot sponsor her. Which advert follows what better companies do?
options: It tells candidates about sponsorship only after an offer is made

questions.rule: Sponsorship follows scarcity: it is rare at entry level and common for senior, hard-to-fill roles.

questions.q: A US company has legal entities only in the UK and Singapore and hires remote staff as employees. Who can it hire?

questions.rule: Remote does not mean anywhere: check whether the company can employ you in your country or takes contractors.

options: She will be hired as a salaried employee working from Brazil

The chapter describes no automatic visa.

questions.explain: No entity, no hire.

questions.q: A small company will hire from anywhere. A contractor must set up a ____ that the company contracts with.

questions.rule: Remote does not mean anywhere: check whether the company can employ you in your country or takes contractors.

options: Remote roles are open to anyone with good internet

True: the author says they hire only where they have an entity.

questions.rule: Remote does not mean anywhere: check whether the company can employ you in your country or takes contractors.

questions.q: A Canadian developer is offered remote work by a Dutch startup that has no company set up in Canada, so it proposes a contractor agreement. Why might the startup be reluctant to keep this going long term?

optionExplain: Cost is not the reason the author gives.

questions.rule: Remote does not mean anywhere: check whether the company can employ you in your country or takes contractors.

questions.q: Which is a reason little-known startups often see few applications?

questions.rule: A small company means fewer applicants and a hiring manager who does the whole process.

questions.q: True or false: In very small companies the hiring manager often does the resume screen, screening call and onsite coordination.

questions.rule: A small company means fewer applicants and a hiring manager who does the whole process.

questions.rule: A small company means fewer applicants and a hiring manager who does the whole process.

questions.rule: A small company means fewer applicants and a hiring manager who does the whole process.

questions.q: A candidate assumes his resume at a five-person firm goes to an inbound sourcer. What is wrong with this?

questions.explain: Small firm, manager screens.
questions.rule: A small company means fewer applicants and a hiring manager who does the whole process.

questions.q: A candidate in Lagos assumes that a startup that recently raised a Series A is flooded with resumes, so she sends only a polished long shot. What do the recruiting agencies the author spoke with say about this assumption?
options: It holds: funding news draws more resumes than a small team can read

The chapter does not say this.

questions.rule: A small company means fewer applicants and a hiring manager who does the whole process.

questions.q: Why might a barely known company use a hard algorithmic coding test?
options: Its engineers enjoy algorithm puzzles and want to see them solved

questions.q: Non-technical founders may outsource technical screening to a tool such as ____.
questions.explain: The author names Hackerrank as an example.
questions.rule: A hard test at a small company often reflects missing expertise, not the real work.

questions.q: A non-technical founder's startup sends you a test. You solve it but miss one edge case. What does the author warn?

questions.rule: A hard test at a small company often reflects missing expertise, not the real work.

You are automatically given a senior title and a higher salary band

questions.rule: A hard test at a small company often reflects missing expertise, not the real work.

questions.q: A candidate in Ohio applies for a developer role at a small manufacturer and receives an algorithm test from an outside firm. She assumes only Silicon Valley companies screen this way. How common is it outside major tech hubs?
options: Practically unknown outside the largest technology companies

questions.q: Who typically reads your resume at a startup with technical founders?

A non-technical inbound sourcer hired for the purpose
A trained interview panel drawn from a large pool of engineers

optionExplain: The ATS does not read resumes for the company.
Such firms do not have that role.

questions.rule: Technical founders offer less competition at the price of lower pay, no visas and more risk.

questions.q: True or false: At such companies the first phone call is usually with a recruiter.

questions.rule: Technical founders offer less competition at the price of lower pay, no visas and more risk.

Many difficult algorithmic challenges at every screening stage

questions.rule: Technical founders offer less competition at the price of lower pay, no visas and more risk.

questions.q: Why would a tiny company sponsor a visa for someone from abroad?
options: It could not find any mobile engineer to hire locally

questions.q: True or false: Two of the three companies that replied to him also offered sponsorship.
questions.explain: One said hiring abroad was complicated and one did not sponsor.

questions.q: A friend abroad applied to twenty jobs and three replied. Which type of company does the story suggest might move fastest?
options: A company with a long, heavily structured process of many rounds
A company that needs three or more rounds of interviews first
A large company with a dedicated inbound sourcer team

optionExplain: Long processes are slower.

oe: Hobbies are not among the author's examples of things that pop.
