questions.explain: The author lists contact details, location of last work or study, and even your name as signals. If any applies and you have authorization, add it.
questions.rule: Any one of three signals can lead the recruiter to assume you need a visa.
questions.teaches: An application can seem to come from abroad because of its contact details, the location of the last work or study, or even the candidate's name.

questions.q: A new graduate in Manila applies to a Singapore bank and has no jobs to list yet. What must her first page include?
options: A blank space where her work experience can be added later on
Only her contact details, with everything else moved to page two
Her education details, since there are no jobs to show
A list of every course taken in the degree, with its grade
optionExplain: A blank space wastes the page the recruiter reads first.
Contact details are needed, but the facts being scanned would then be missing.
Right: with no experience, the education details take the first page.
A full course list adds length; the recap asks for education details, not every course.
questions.explain: Page one carries languages, technologies and your last few positions; if there are no positions, education replaces them.
questions.rule: No experience yet: lead with education.
questions.teaches: If you do not yet have work experience, the recap says to make sure your education details are on the first page.
oe: A blank space wastes the page the recruiter reads first.
Contact details are needed, but the facts being scanned would then be missing.
Right: with no experience, the education details take the first page.
A full course list adds length; the recap asks for education details, not every course.

questions.q: Which contact details belong at the top of a tech resume, according to the author?
options: Your full street address, phone and email, so employers can reply by post
Your name and a photo, with your email as the only other line
Your name alone, since a recruiter will find the rest online
Email, phone number, and city and country of residence, kept short
optionExplain: A full address seems thorough, but no one will post a letter based on a resume.
A photo is advised against, and a phone number or location is normally included.
Recruiters need a way to reach you on the page itself.
Right: a short line with email, phone and city and country is what the author recommends.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card lists the basics, including what the contact block holds.
questions.rule: Follow the unwritten basics: clean language, short contact details, newest first.

questions.q: List your work and education with the ____ one on top and earlier ones underneath.
questions.explain: Reverse chronological order puts the newest entry first.
questions.rule: Newest first.

questions.q: A friend's resume starts with a job from 2012 and ends with their current role. What do you suggest?
options: Keep the order and bold the current role so it still pops
Reverse the order so the current role sits at the top, with dates visible on each entry
Group the jobs by company size rather than by date
Sort the jobs alphabetically by company name
optionExplain: Bold may help, but it leaves the order against the rule.
Right: newest first is the unwritten rule, and dates mark each entry.
Grouping by size hides the timeline recruiters scan for.
Alphabetical order scatters the timeline.
questions.explain: Putting the latest experience on top and earlier ones underneath is one of the unwritten rules.
questions.rule: Latest on top.

questions.q: Sort each resume habit: does it follow the ground rules, or break one?

items.t: Email, phone and 'Lisbon, Portugal' on one line
Newest role listed first
Same punctuation style on every bullet
Full street address with postcode at the top
Education listed oldest first
A typo left in because the content is strong

questions.explain: A short contact line, newest-first order and consistent punctuation all follow the rules. A full postal address, oldest-first order and a left-in typo break them.
questions.rule: Short contact, newest first, clean language.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a typo is likely to be forgiven when the rest of the resume is strong.
questions.explain: The author says typos and poor grammar can easily cause a resume to be ignored, because they suggest poor attention to detail.
questions.rule: A typo can sink a good resume.

questions.q: A developer in Lagos wonders whether to print her full street address under her name. What does the author advise?
options: Leave it off: nobody will post a letter, and full details come later
Add it, since postal addresses are checked against records before any interview
Add it, because a complete address looks more thorough to the recruiter
Add it in place of a phone number, since recruiters prefer to reply by post
optionExplain: Right: the author gives these two reasons, and says offers come far later.
Nothing in the text says addresses are checked at this stage.
Modern looks are not the author's reason.
The author lists email and phone together as expected contact details.
questions.explain: The resume needs contact details that let a recruiter reach you, not an address for letters. The full details come at the offer stage, a long way ahead.
questions.rule: Contact details, not a mailing address.
questions.teaches: The author says a full mailing address is unnecessary because no one will send a letter based on a resume, and that all personal details are requested only if an offer follows.
oe: Right: no one will send a letter based on a resume, and you give full personal details if an offer comes.
Postal addresses are not checked this way; the text gives no such step.
Thoroughness is not the aim; the author asks you to keep contact details short.
The author asks for a phone number and email; an address is not needed.

questions.q: In your resume some bullets end with a full stop and others do not. According to the author, what should you do?
options: Leave it, because only spelling mistakes are held against a candidate
Use full stops on the first page and none on the second
Pick one punctuation style and apply it across the whole resume
Rewrite the bullets as paragraphs, where full stops are expected
optionExplain: Spelling matters most, but the author extends the rule to punctuation.
Switching styles by page is itself inconsistent.
Right: the author says punctuation must be consistent across the resume.
Paragraphs go against the bullet-point advice.
questions.explain: Consistency applies to punctuation as well as to spelling and grammar. Mixed styles look careless.
questions.rule: Consistent punctuation.
questions.teaches: The author's advice on correctness extends to punctuation: it must be consistent across the whole resume.

questions.q: True or false: A longer resume signals more seniority, so an engineer with three years' experience should aim for three pages.
questions.explain: The author advises two pages or less, and says more is justified only by lots of experience. The next card gives the reasoning.
questions.rule: Aim for two pages or less unless you have lots of experience.

questions.q: The author calls the two-page limit not a strict rule, but a very ____ one to follow.
questions.explain: It is advice with a reason behind it, not a requirement.
questions.rule: A wise limit, not a strict one.

questions.q: An engineer with three years' experience has a three-page resume. What does the author's advice point to?
options: Keep three pages, because the limit is strict only for new graduates
Keep three pages, as detail shows thoroughness to a recruiter
Cut to two pages or fewer, since the limit holds unless experience is extensive
Shrink the margins until three pages fit on two
optionExplain: The limit is not tied to graduates alone; it relaxes only with lots of experience.
The author says reviewers skim cluttered and verbose resumes.
Right: with only three years, the limit should hold.
This keeps the clutter and the length while trading away readability.
questions.explain: A resume longer than two pages needs the experience to justify it. With three years the better step is to edit.
questions.rule: Edit down unless experience justifies more.

questions.q: Sort each approach to resume length: does it follow the author's guidance, or break it?

items.t: Two pages for an engineer with six years' experience
Cutting a section that adds little to stay within two pages
Treating two pages as a wise limit, not a legal rule
Padding the resume to three pages to look senior
Adding filler sections so page two looks full
Believing every company rejects a three-page resume

questions.explain: Staying within two pages and cutting weak sections follow the advice. Padding or filler works against it, and treating the limit as an absolute misreads the author, who calls it not strict.
questions.rule: Cut, do not pad; the limit is wise, not absolute.

questions.q: A graduate in Dublin has one internship and wonders about padding to two pages. What does the author say about length?
options: Two full pages, to match what experienced candidates send
One page, with no need to fill a second
Three pages, to make room for coursework
No limit, as there is little to cut at that stage
optionExplain: Two pages is the upper guide for the experienced, not the aim for graduates.
Right: new graduates should fit everything on one page.
The author does not suggest coursework should push the length up.
The advice includes a page target for graduates.
questions.explain: With few years of experience there is not enough material to fill a second page, so one page is better.
questions.rule: New grads: one page.
questions.teaches: New graduates should fit their resume on one page, and anyone with fewer than a few years of experience is not expected to fill the second page.

questions.q: An engineer with twelve years' experience has a three-page resume. What does the author's guidance allow?
options: Nothing: the two-page limit applies in exactly the same way at every career stage, whatever the history
Only if the extra page holds a photo and references, which senior people usually add
Only after more than twenty-five years of experience behind the resume
Going past two pages can be fine with lots of experience, typically over eight to ten years
optionExplain: The author says the limit is not strict for people with lots of experience.
Photos and references are not what justify extra pages, and the book advises against photos.
Twenty-five years is not the author's figure.
Right: the author gives eight to ten years as the typical point beyond which more pages can be fine.
questions.explain: The longer the career, the more material there is worth including, so the author allows more than two pages after roughly eight to ten years.
questions.rule: More pages need lots of experience.
questions.teaches: The author puts the point at which more than two pages becomes acceptable at typically beyond eight to ten years of work experience.

questions.q: You must list four achievements for your latest job. Which format do tech recruiters find easiest to scan?
options: A paragraph of four sentences telling the story of the job
Four bullet points at one level, each on its own line
Four dashes in a row, to save space on the page
Two bullets, each followed by two indented sub-bullets
optionExplain: A paragraph feels natural, but the author says to avoid paragraphs.
Right: single-level bullets are less effort to read.
Dashes save space, but the author calls them out of place.
Sub-bullets add a level the author says clutters the resume.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card gives the author's reasons for bullets and the single level.
questions.rule: Consistent format, one-level bullets, no paragraphs.

questions.q: Use bullet points to list your experience, and avoid ____.
questions.explain: Recruiters in tech are used to scanning bullets, which take less effort than paragraphs.
questions.rule: Bullets, not paragraphs.

questions.q: Each bullet in an entry has sub-bullets listing the tools used. What fix fits the author's advice?
options: Keep the sub-bullets but indent them less
Turn the sub-bullets into dashes under each bullet
Turn the whole entry into one paragraph
Fold tool names into the bullets
optionExplain: A smaller indent still leaves two levels.
Dashes are also advised against, and the nesting remains.
Paragraphs are advised against.
Right: fold the tool names into the main bullets and keep a single level.
questions.explain: Sub-bullets clutter the page and add words. Folding their content upward keeps the entry flat and short.
questions.rule: One level only.

questions.q: Sort each formatting habit: does it follow the author's advice, or break it?

items.t: The same font size for all section headings
Experience listed as one level of bullets
Each point on its own short bullet
A paragraph describing a project
Sub-bullets under each main bullet
Different sizes for headings of equal rank

questions.explain: Matching sizes, flat bullets and one point per bullet follow the advice. Paragraphs, sub-bullets and uneven headings add clutter.
questions.rule: Flat, even and scannable.

questions.q: Priya starts a first resume from a blank page. What does the recap give as the first action for a neat, consistent result?
options: Choose a simple, easy-to-scan template, from the book's list or online
Design your own layout from scratch, mixing fonts for variety and personality
Copy a friend's resume closely, changing only the name and dates
Use whatever default layout your word processor opens with, unchanged
optionExplain: Right: the recap starts with picking a simple, consistent template.
Variety works against consistency.
Copying is not what the recap suggests, and layouts differ by person.
A default is not chosen for scanning.
questions.explain: A good template takes care of consistent sizes and spacing. The recap points to the templates listed at the end of the book or another source online.
questions.rule: Start from a simple template.
questions.teaches: The recap's first action is to choose a template that is simple, consistent and easy to scan, either from those listed at the end of the book or another found online.

questions.q: Short on space, a developer swaps bullets for dashes in the experience section. What does the author say?
options: It is fine, because saving space is the main goal of the page
It is fine as long as the dashes are used throughout
Avoid it: dashes look out of place and are harder to read than bullets
Only the first role should keep real bullets
optionExplain: Space matters, but the author puts readability first.
Consistency helps, but dashes are the problem.
Right: the author tells you to avoid dashes even to save space.
Mixing styles breaks the consistency rule.
questions.explain: Dashes save a little room but cost readability, which the author ranks higher.
questions.rule: Real bullets, even when space is tight.
questions.teaches: The author specifically warns against using dashes in place of bullets to save space, since they look out of place and are harder to read.

questions.q: A resume says 04/09—05/10. What problem does the author see with dates like this?
options: The reader must stop to work out which number is the month and which the year
Slashes are not allowed in a PDF and break the file
Dates in a resume must include the day to be valid
Only the end date of a role should be shown
optionExplain: Right: the author says such dates make the reviewer think.
Slashes display fine; the problem is readability.
The author does not ask for days.
The author shows a start and an end date.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card shows the author's fix for this kind of date.
questions.rule: Spell out the month and the year; keep one style.

questions.q: In 'June 2011—July 2012' the year is easy to tell apart from the ____.
questions.explain: Month names separate the month from the year, so the reader does not need to decode anything.
questions.rule: Month as a word.

questions.q: Which is the best way to write a role that began in March 2019 and ended in August 2021?
options: March 2019—August 2021
Mar'19–Aug'21
optionExplain: Dots do not say which number is the month.
Slashes recreate the original problem.
Right: month name and four-digit year leave nothing to decode.
The apostrophe form is shorter but still makes the reader work out the century and year.
questions.explain: The author's fix is month name plus year, so the reader does not need to think.
questions.rule: Month name plus year.

questions.q: Sort each date style: is it easy to read, or does it need decoding?

items.t: March 2019—August 2021
Spelled-out month names throughout
The same date style on every role
2019 in one role and 03/19 in another
A bare 10/11 with no hint of month or year

questions.explain: Month names with full years are quick to read, and one style throughout keeps them so. Numeric spans and mixed styles make the reader stop.
questions.rule: Make dates unambiguous and uniform.

questions.q: A role ended twelve years ago. According to the author, how exact must its dates be?
options: Exact days are needed to prove the length of the role
Months must stay, so that every role matches the others
The dates should be removed altogether
Exact months can be dropped, as they become irrelevant for dates well in the past
optionExplain: The author does not ask for days anywhere.
Consistency is valued, but the author allows dropping months for older spans.
Dates stay; the old ones can be simpler.
Right: for spans beyond a few years, the months can go.
questions.explain: Precision matters for recent roles. For older ones, especially those four or five years back, the year alone is enough.
questions.rule: Old spans can lose their months.
questions.teaches: For date spans beyond a few years the exact month can be dropped, because it becomes irrelevant, especially for dates more than four or five years ago.

questions.q: A resume prints dates in small pale text at the far right. What does the recap say to check?
options: Whether the dates are faint enough not to distract from job titles
Whether the dates stand out so total years can be seen quickly
Whether dates have been moved to a footnote on page two
Whether the dates can be left out, as the summary gives your years
optionExplain: Faint dates hide the very fact the recruiter scans for.
Right: the recap asks for dates that are easy to scan.
Moving dates away from the roles makes the sum harder.
The recruiter scans dates for years, not the summary.
questions.explain: Recruiters look at dates to work out experience, so they should stand out and be easy to find.
questions.rule: Dates should stand out.
questions.teaches: The recap asks you to make the dates of your work experience stand out, so that someone can quickly tell how many years of total experience you have.

questions.q: You finish your resume in a word processor. Which file do you send to recruiters, according to the author?
options: The editable word-processor file, so the recruiter can adjust it
A PDF export of it
A rich text file, because it opens on most computers
A link to an online document the recruiter can open
optionExplain: Editability seems helpful, but the layout may break on other machines.
Right: the author says to use PDF and no other format.
Rich text seems universal, but the author names it among the formats to avoid.
The author advises sending the file in PDF form.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card gives the author's rule and a way to decide what to cut.
questions.rule: Send a PDF, and cut what does not help your case.

questions.q: The author says to use the ____ format and no other.
questions.explain: PDF keeps the layout the same for every reader.
questions.rule: PDF only.

questions.q: Your resume has a section of school-age hobbies that says little about your fit for a backend role. What do you do?
options: Remove it, since sections that add little to no information are dropped
Keep it, since a longer resume shows more commitment
Shrink the font so it takes less space
Move it to the top, since it shows personality
optionExplain: Right: the advice is to drop sections that add little.
Length is not a goal; the author says to edit ruthlessly.
Shrinking keeps content that does not help.
A section that adds little should not take prime space.
questions.explain: The test is whether a part makes a good case for the position. If it does not, cut it.
questions.rule: Cut what does not help your case.

questions.q: Sort each item: keep it on the resume, or cut it?

items.t: Main languages used in your last role
A measured result from a project
Dates for each role
A section that adds little to no information
A line explaining that you can use email
Detail the job does not need and that makes no case for you

questions.explain: Facts that answer the recruiter's scan stay. Trivial lines and low-value sections dilute the case.
questions.rule: Keep the case, cut the clutter.

questions.q: A friend sends her resume as a .doc file to a US startup. Why does the author advise against .doc and .rtf?
options: Company email filters block them before a recruiter ever gets to see them
They cannot hold bullet points or bold text, so formatting is lost on saving
They are too large to attach to most emails, so the message bounces back
They display inconsistently on machines without software such as Word
optionExplain: The text says nothing about filters.
These formats can hold bullets and bold; the issue is how they display elsewhere.
File size is not the reason given.
Right: display differences between machines are the author's reason.
questions.explain: A resume that looks fine in your word processor can shift on a computer without it. PDF avoids that.
questions.rule: PDF looks the same everywhere.
questions.teaches: The author names .doc and .rtf as formats to avoid because they display inconsistently on machines that do not have software such as Word installed, which can mess up a well-formatted resume.
oe: The author gives no email-filter reason.
These formats can hold bullets and bold; the issue is inconsistent display.
File size is not the author's reason.
Right: they display inconsistently where Word-type software is missing, which can mess up the formatting.

questions.q: Your resume has a section on a side project in an unrelated field. For a backend role, what does the author's test suggest?
options: Keep it, because any project, in any field, shows initiative to a reader
Keep it but move it to the end of page two, where it takes no space
Ask whether it helps make the case you fit this role, and cut it if not
Keep it only if the project was finished and has a link to a live demo
optionExplain: Initiative is a fair point, but it does not answer the author's test.
Moving it hides it without testing whether it belongs.
Right: the author's test is tied to the position you are applying for.
Whether a project was finished is not the author's test.
questions.explain: The author phrases the test around the position being applied for, so the same section can stay for one job and go for another.
questions.rule: Judge each section against this job.
questions.teaches: The author's editing test is tied to the specific position: whether a section makes a good case for why you are a good fit for the position you are applying for.

questions.section: Avoiding Biases: Personal Details and Photos
questions.q: Which of these belongs on a resume for a tech job, according to the author?
options: A recent photo, so the recruiter can put a face to the name
Your marital status and number of children
Your name and email address, which are often the only personal details needed
Your date of birth, so your years of experience can be checked
optionExplain: The author says photos add no value and can distract.
Family details are among the items that invite bias.
Right: name and email are enough for most resumes.
Years of experience come from dates of work and study, not from your age.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card gives the author's reasons, with his example of two resumes.
questions.rule: Leave out photos and personal details that can only create bias.

questions.section: Avoiding Biases: Personal Details and Photos
questions.q: Every non-essential personal detail adds one more way for ____ to kick in.
questions.explain: The author's point is that unnecessary details give bias a chance to act on the reader.
questions.rule: Extra details give bias a way in.

questions.section: Avoiding Biases: Personal Details and Photos
questions.q: A candidate wants to list marital status and children to show stability. What does the author's advice suggest?
options: Leave it out, since it invites assumptions about distraction or relocation
Add it, since employers value settled workers
Add it, but only on the second page
Add it only if the company advertises family benefits
optionExplain: Right: such details only create chances for negative bias.
The author's example shows family details raising doubts, not trust.
Moving it to page two keeps the detail on the resume.
The advice is to leave such details off, whatever the employer offers.
questions.explain: Family details are in the author's list of items to leave out, because they can only lead to negative bias.
questions.rule: Leave out family details.

questions.section: Avoiding Biases: Personal Details and Photos
questions.q: Sort each item: keep it on the resume, or remove it?

items.t: Email address
City and country of residence
Phone number
A photo of yourself
Date of birth
Religion
Number of children

questions.explain: Contact details let a recruiter reach you. A photo, date of birth, religion and family details only give bias a way in.
questions.rule: Contact details stay; identity details go.

questions.section: Avoiding Biases: Personal Details and Photos
questions.q: True or false: If a recruiter rejected you because of your age, you would normally be told so directly, according to the author.
questions.explain: The author says you will not get a call like that, because a company would be in trouble if it admitted discrimination. So bias works unseen, which is why you leave the details off.
questions.rule: Bias is silent, so remove its triggers.

questions.section: Avoiding Biases: Personal Details and Photos
questions.q: A developer prepares a CV for a tech job in Dubai. What does the book's UAE recruiter say about photos?
options: Photos are banned by law on every CV sent there, whatever the role
Photos are expected only for non-tech roles, so tech CVs leave them out
Recruiters there ignore photos in tech applications and read the text only
Photos are expected for all roles, though a cultural shift is under way
optionExplain: The text does not mention any ban.
The recruiter says expectations cover tech roles too.
The recruiter says the opposite: photos are expected.
Right: the recruiter says photos are expected for all roles, even tech roles, and that this is beginning to change.
questions.explain: The author's rule is aimed at tech hiring generally, but local practice can differ. The recruiter advises tailoring your CV to local practice in the countries you apply to.
questions.rule: Local practice can differ; tailor to it.
questions.teaches: In the UAE and most of the Middle East, photos are expected on CVs for all roles, even tech roles, though a recruiter there reports a cultural shift toward inclusive hiring; the advice is to tailor your CV to local practice.

questions.section: Avoiding Biases: Personal Details and Photos
questions.q: You apply to a Berlin tech startup, and many German CVs carry photos. What does the recruiter quoted for Berlin and London say?
options: A photo is required in Germany, so add one to match what local firms expect
No client has rejected a CV for lacking a photo; research each country and ask local recruiters
German companies reject CVs that carry photos
One rule applies in every country, so no research into local practice is needed
optionExplain: The recruiter says photos are not necessary, even though most German companies receive CVs with them.
Right: the recruiter says no client has rejected a CV for lacking a photo, and advises country-specific research.
The text does not say German firms reject photos.
The text advises researching specific countries and asking local recruiters or hiring managers.
questions.explain: Even in a market where photos are common, this recruiter reports no rejections for leaving one out. The author adds that tech is an area where a missing photo is rarely an issue.
questions.rule: Check local practice; a missing photo is rarely a problem in tech.
questions.teaches: A recruiter with nearly two decades in London and Berlin says no client has ever rejected a CV because it lacked a photo, even though most German companies receive CVs with photos; the author advises researching specific countries and asking local recruiters and hiring managers.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume

options: Ana_Lopes_resume.pdf
resume_final_FINAL.pdf
CV.pdf
Resume_Draft_v3.pdf
optionExplain: Right: your name and the word resume make it easy to tell whose it is.
This tells nothing about the owner and hints at drafts.
This could belong to anyone.
A version number suggests several drafts.

questions.rule: Run the checks, then name the file with your own name.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: Name the file yourname_resume.pdf or yourname_____.pdf so it is easy to identify.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: Sam Okoye is about to send a PDF. Which file name follows the author's advice?
options: Sam_resume_latest.pdf
resume_Sam_2.pdf
Sam_Okoye_CV.pdf
Okoye_new_version.pdf
optionExplain: 'Latest' signals other versions exist.
A number suggests drafts.
Right: full name plus CV tells whose it is.
'New version' signals other versions exist, and the first name is missing.
questions.explain: Aim for a name that identifies the owner and hides any sign of several versions.
questions.rule: Your own name, no version words.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: Which of these actions are on the author's list of checks? Select all that apply.
options: Choose a simple, consistent template
Add a photo so you are recognisable
Put relevant technologies and work experience on the first page
Use sub-bullets for extra detail
Run spelling and grammar checks
optionExplain: Right: the first action is to choose a simple, consistent template.
Photos are among the items the list removes.
Right: the key facts belong on page one.
The list says not to use sub-bullets.
Right: the list asks for spelling and grammar checks.
questions.explain: The checks gather the chapter's advice: a simple template, no personal details, key facts on page one, readable dates, flat bullets, language checks and a PDF with a clear name.
questions.rule: Every check traces back to a rule from the chapter.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: Sort each file name: does it follow the naming advice, or break it?

items.t: Mei_Tan_CV.pdf
Jo_Lee_resume.pdf
Jo_Lee_v4.pdf
Mei_Tan_Acme.pdf
resume_new.pdf

questions.rule: Name plus resume or CV; no versions.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: A developer finishes her draft and wants it checked beyond spelling before sending. What does the recap name?
options: Only the word processor's built-in spell checker
Grammarly and the Hemingway Editor, both free
A paid proofreading service and a thesaurus
Hemingway Editor alone, as Grammarly checks only spelling
optionExplain: A built-in checker is the spell check; the recap asks for more.
Right: the recap names Grammarly and the Hemingway Editor as free tools.
The recap names free tools.
The recap names both tools.
questions.explain: The recap asks you to fix all issues the tools raise, not only spelling errors.
questions.rule: Fix what the tools raise.
questions.teaches: Besides a spell check, the recap names two free tools, Grammarly and the Hemingway Editor, and asks you to fix all the issues they raise.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: You tailor your resume for Acme and want to name the file Priya_Nair_Acme.pdf. What does the author say?

optionExplain: That changes the facts rather than the wording.
Copying whole phrases adds nothing about you.
The work stays the same; only the wording matches the posting.
Slogans say nothing about your work.
questions.explain: Mirroring is about wording true facts in the reader's terms. It is not about adding skills.
questions.rule: Match the words, keep the facts.

questions.section: Structure for Interns, New Grads and Bootcamp Grads
questions.q: True or false: According to the thread, a cover letter sent through a general application form has a high chance of not being read.
questions.explain: The thread says to skip it unless you can send it directly to the hiring manager or recruiter.
questions.rule: Tailor the resume for the position and use language that mirrors the job posting, and skip the cover letter unless you can send it to the hiring manager or recruiter directly.

questions.section: Structure for Interns, New Grads and Bootcamp Grads
questions.q: Two recruiters say what makes a resume stand out from hundreds. Which candidate fits their view?

The one with projects that match the job description, as well as internships
The one with the longest list of courses
The one who sends the same generic resume quickly to as many roles as possible

They say projects count as relevant experience just as internships do.
They look at relevant courses, but a long list alone does not stand out.
They tell students to read the job description and amend the resume.
questions.explain: The two recruiters say standout resumes match the job description and show relevant experience, whether internships or projects.
questions.rule: Match the job and show relevance.
questions.teaches: Recruiters say relevant experience can come from projects as well as internships, as long as it matches the job description.

questions.q: Sam has six years of experience, but the resume opens with education, then projects, then jobs. What would the author advise?
options: Move work experience to the top and add a technologies section on page one
Keep education first because a degree is what employers trust most in a candidate
Move projects first since they show passion
Keep the order and add a long personal summary

Education matters less as seniority grows.
Projects get less relevant with more work experience.
A summary does not fix a buried work section.
questions.explain: Past the first job, work experience is what reviewers want to glance at. The card gives the full structure.
questions.rule: Once you have work experience, put your current title, company and last few years at or near the top, with a Languages and Technologies section on the first page.

questions.q: Put work experience at or near the ____ of the page.
questions.explain: The current title, company and past few years should be easy to spot, so they go at or near the top.
questions.rule: Work experience goes up top.

questions.q: Which top-to-bottom order fits a developer with four years of experience?
options: Education, hobbies, work experience
Work, skills, then education
Hobbies, languages and technologies, then work experience at the end
Projects, education, work experience

Work leads and the technologies list sits on page one, with education moving lower.
Hobbies at the top waste the best space.
Work experience should come first once you have some.
questions.explain: Lead with work, keep the technologies list on page one, and let education drop.
questions.hint: What does the reviewer want to see first?
questions.rule: Once you have work experience, put your current title, company and last few years at or near the top, with a Languages and Technologies section on the first page.

questions.q: Sort these layouts for a developer five years into their career.

items.t: Current role in the top third of page one
Education block above all jobs
Technologies list on page one
Technologies list only at the end of page two
Recent years of work easy to spot
Hobbies placed above current job

questions.explain: Current work and the technologies list belong near the top of page one.
questions.rule: Current role and tech up top.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, once you have work experience, the Languages and Technologies section can be left to the second page.
questions.explain: The author asks for a Languages and Technologies section on the first page.
questions.rule: Once you have work experience, put your current title, company and last few years at or near the top, with a Languages and Technologies section on the first page.

questions.q: A job ad mentions payments and Go. What does the author say a technologies section can list?
options: Every tool you have touched, so none is missed
Only the job's technologies, whether or not you know them
Domains, languages or frameworks from the job that you know well
Each technology followed by a score out of ten

The author asks for areas where you are an expert or proficient.
The author names domains, languages and frameworks mentioned by the job, listing only expert or proficient areas.
The author says not to list skill levels.
questions.explain: Domains can count, not only languages. The section should hold what the job mentions and what you know well.
questions.rule: List relevant strengths only.
questions.teaches: The technologies section may include domains as well as languages and frameworks, limited to those you are expert or proficient in.

questions.q: Eight years into a career, a developer's education block lists GPA, courses and clubs. What should happen?
options: Reduce it to the degree, graduation date and at most one standout achievement
Keep all of it, since education details keep mattering to hiring managers at any level
Remove education completely
Add more courses to look current
optionExplain: At 5+ years the block shrinks to those three elements.
The block is no longer what hiring managers want.
The degree and date should stay.
More courses add noise.
questions.explain: The block shrinks as experience grows. The card gives the details.
questions.rule: Shrink the education section as experience grows: details are fine with 1-3 years, but at 5+ years keep the degree, graduation date and at most one standout achievement.

questions.q: At 5+ years of experience, keep your degree, date of graduation and no more than one standout ____.
questions.explain: The author allows one standout achievement, if it is still relevant.
questions.rule: Degree, date, one achievement.

questions.q: Arjun has seven years of experience. His education block has a degree, summa cum laude, a GPA, a chess club and a course list. What stays?
options: The degree and the GPA only
Everything, because honours deserve a full record of grades and courses
The degree, the graduation date and perhaps summa cum laude, but no grades list
Only the chess club, to show personality
optionExplain: The author says the GPA should disappear.
Courses and activities go after five years.
The author says summa cum laude can probably stay while GPA, courses and activities go.
Activities should disappear at this stage.
questions.explain: Keep the degree, the date and at most one standout line such as summa cum laude.
questions.hint: Which single line is a standout?
questions.rule: Shrink the education section as experience grows: details are fine with 1-3 years, but at 5+ years keep the degree, graduation date and at most one standout achievement.

questions.q: Sort these education blocks by years of experience.

items.t: Degree and date after eight years
Course list after eight years
Full details with two years of experience
GPA after six years
Student activities after ten years
Summa cum laude kept after six years

questions.explain: Details are fine for 1-3 years. Beyond five, only the degree, date and one standout line stay.
questions.rule: Years up, education down.

questions.q: Tomas's experience grows from two years to six. What should happen to his education section?
options: It grows, because he has more achievements and courses to add to it
It stays identical in every version
It moves to the top of the page
It shrinks to a few lines
optionExplain: The block shrinks as work experience grows.
The author asks you to reduce it slowly.
Work experience takes the top.
Education matters less with seniority, so details are removed.
questions.explain: Shrink education slowly as work experience grows.
questions.rule: More experience, less education.

questions.q: A manager with twelve years of experience finished a degree with honours. What does the author say about the honours?
options: It must go with the rest, because all education details disappear at that level
Summa cum laude can probably stay, while GPA, courses and activities should go
It should be bold at the top, as proof of ability
It stays with GPA and courses for context
optionExplain: The author says it can probably stay.
Honours are the one standout line the author expects to survive.
Education loses weight with seniority.
GPA, courses and activities should disappear.
questions.explain: The author names summa cum laude as an example of what can stay.
questions.rule: Keep one standout line.
questions.teaches: Summa cum laude can probably stay for experienced people, while GPA, courses and activities should disappear.

questions.q: A developer with fourteen years of experience gives every job equal detail. What would the author suggest?
options: Keep equal detail for every job so the career looks complete to readers
Remove the most recent job to shorten
Give the older jobs less space and drop those that are not relevant
Expand old jobs to show breadth
optionExplain: The author says the resume should sell you, not show every employer.
The recent job matters most.
Old roles are less representative of current work.
Adding detail to old jobs adds noise.
questions.explain: Old work is less relevant than recent work. The card shows what to do.
questions.rule: If you have 10+ years of experience, shorten sections on work from beyond ten years ago, and remove ones that are not relevant.

questions.q: For people with 10+ years, work experience beyond ____ years is less interesting.
questions.explain: The author sets the line at ten years.
questions.rule: Ten years back is the line.

questions.q: Mei has sixteen years of experience, including three short jobs from fourteen years ago that do not connect to her goal. What should she do?
options: Shorten them or remove them, and spend the space on recent work
Keep each in full to avoid gaps
Move them to the top as proof of range
List them with expanded technology lists to show the range of her skills
optionExplain: The author advises shortening and considering removing irrelevant old jobs.
The author says the resume should sell you, not list every place.
Old, irrelevant work should not lead.
Obsolete technologies are not worth listing.
questions.explain: Shorten or drop old and less relevant roles so the resume focuses on current strengths.
questions.hint: The resume should sell you.
questions.rule: If you have 10+ years of experience, shorten sections on work from beyond ten years ago, and remove ones that are not relevant.

questions.q: Sort these choices for a developer with fifteen years of experience.

items.t: One line for a job from thirteen years ago
Five bullets for an unrelated job from thirteen years ago
Five bullets for the current job
A list of obsolete tools from a role twelve years ago
Dropping a short, unrelated job from long ago
Listing every employer to avoid gaps

questions.explain: Recent work gets depth; old work gets a line or nothing.
questions.rule: Depth for recent, brevity for old.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, what you did more than ten years ago is not representative of what you do now.
questions.explain: This is the author's reason for shortening older sections.
questions.rule: If you have 10+ years of experience, shorten sections on work from beyond ten years ago, and remove ones that are not relevant.

questions.q: A candidate's resume shows five short jobs from a decade back, but a long recent tenure. What does the author say about the old ones?
options: Keep them to show a wide range of stacks
Consider skipping those that are not relevant, especially if it was job-hopping
Rewrite them with extra detail to explain
Move them to a separate second resume that has to be sent along with the main one
optionExplain: The author warns that it is not the aim to show everything.
The author says to consider removing or skipping irrelevant old ones, especially job-hopping from a decade back.
Extra detail from an old period adds noise.
The advice is to shorten or skip, not to add documents.
questions.explain: Skipping old job-hopping is the author's suggestion; the resume should focus on what is relevant now.
questions.rule: Skip old and irrelevant jobs.
questions.teaches: The author suggests removing or skipping irrelevant old jobs, especially job-hopping from a decade ago, and not listing obsolete technologies.

questions.q: A developer with nine years of experience built a popular open source library. Where does the author suggest listing it?
options: Under extracurricular, with impact
At the very top of the first page, above all of her work experience
Nowhere, since projects stop mattering
In a long list with all student projects
optionExplain: A standout project goes in the extras with a reason and a link.
Work experience should lead.
A project that really stands out can be listed.
Only a standout belongs, with a clear reason.
questions.explain: A standout project can be listed under extracurricular with a link. The card gives the format.
questions.rule: Put patents, publications, talks and standout open source or published projects in an extracurricular section, say why each matters, and end with a short hobbies line.

questions.q: Which items does the author place in an extracurricular section? Select all that apply.
options: Patents
Conference talks
A standout open source project
A part-time retail job from age eighteen
A long list of every hobby
optionExplain: They are one of the author's examples.
Talks are named by the author.
Yes, with the reason it is important.
Old unrelated work is trimmed rather than moved.
The author asks to keep hobbies short.
questions.explain: Patents, publications, talks and standout open source or published projects belong in the extras.
questions.rule: Extras that grab attention.

questions.q: Imani lists her open source library as Maintainer of a caching library. How can she improve the line?
options: Add more of the technologies used to build it, and the languages it supports
Say what it is used for, by how many projects, and her role, with a link to it
Add 'passionate about open source' after it
Move it above her current job
optionExplain: The reader wants importance, not a tool list.
The author asks to be specific on why open source projects are important.
A feeling does not show importance.
Work experience stays near the top.
questions.explain: Explain why the project matters with results, impact and your contribution.
questions.hint: The author says to be specific on why it is important.
questions.rule: Put patents, publications, talks and standout open source or published projects in an extracurricular section, say why each matters, and end with a short hobbies line.

questions.q: Sort these lines for an extracurricular section.

items.t: Conference talk with the audience size
Open source project with no description of its use
A short line on two hobbies
A paragraph on every hobby
Published app with its user numbers and a link
A school assignment from year one

questions.explain: Specific, attention-grabbing extras fit; vague or long entries do not.
questions.rule: Specific and short.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, the more work experience you have, the more relevant outside-work projects tend to become.
questions.explain: The author says the opposite: they become less relevant, unless one really stands out.
questions.rule: Put patents, publications, talks and standout open source or published projects in an extracurricular section, say why each matters, and end with a short hobbies line.

questions.q: A developer's two-page resume is full and she is short on space. What does the author say about interests?
options: Keep them, since they are required to show personality on a resume
Replace work experience bullets with them
Move them to the top to be noticed
Skip them if short on space
optionExplain: The author makes them optional.
Work experience matters far more.
Interests close the resume.
Interests are optional and the first thing to go when space is short.
questions.explain: Interests depend on length: add a few if there is room, skip them if you stay on one page and space is short.
questions.rule: Interests are optional.
questions.teaches: Interests can be skipped when you keep to a one-page format and are short on space.

questions.q: A developer holds a short online quiz badge for a programming language. How might it look to a reviewer, according to the author?
options: It can leave a negative impression, because it is trivial to get
It shows initiative and always helps
It matters most to reviewers and should lead the page above everything else
It is ignored and never harms
optionExplain: A badge that can be retaken at any time proves little.
The author warns about the opposite for trivial ones.
Certifications go below work experience.
The author says it can create a negative perception.
questions.explain: Trivial certifications carry a risk. The card explains.
questions.rule: List certifications that are relevant to the job or industry below your work experience, and avoid ones that are trivial to get.

questions.q: List certifications below your ____ experience.
questions.explain: Certifications that are relevant to the job go below your work experience.
questions.rule: Certifications go below work.

questions.q: Sofia holds a respected professional certification in her field and a language quiz badge. What should she list?
options: Both, with the quiz badge listed first because it is the newer of the two
The respected certification, below her work experience, not the quiz badge itself
Neither, since certifications never help
Only the quiz badge, as it is easy to verify
optionExplain: The trivial badge can hurt.
It is relevant and credible, while the badge may leave a negative impression.
Relevant ones can help.
Easy to verify does not make it meaningful.
questions.explain: List relevant, credible certifications and leave trivial ones off.
questions.hint: Which one is trivial to get?
questions.rule: List certifications that are relevant to the job or industry below your work experience, and avoid ones that are trivial to get.

questions.q: In the author's LinkedIn example, what makes the certification trivial to get?
options: It is awarded only to people with several years of professional experience
It is graded by a manager who knows the candidate
It is a series of about a dozen questions that can be repeated at any time
It requires a paid course of several months
optionExplain: The author's point is that it takes little to obtain.
The example is a short repeatable quiz, not a manager's assessment.
Anyone can retake the short quiz until they pass.
The example is quick and repeatable, not a long course.
questions.explain: The author calls it trivial because it is a dozen questions that can be repeated at any time.
questions.rule: Check how hard a certificate is to earn.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a certification anyone can retake at any time, such as a short programming-language quiz, can create a negative perception.
questions.explain: This is the author's warning about trivial certifications.
questions.rule: List certifications that are relevant to the job or industry below your work experience, and avoid ones that are trivial to get.

questions.q: A candidate applies to a company working with governments, where certain professional certifications are required. What does the author say?
options: Certifications no longer matter for them
They only care about quiz badges
They ignore any certifications that sit below the work experience section
Such firms may weigh them more

Trivial certifications still carry risk.
Placement below work is the author's general rule and does not make them invisible.
The author says companies working with governments that require certain certifications might focus more on them.
questions.explain: Employers that need certain certifications may focus on them, so relevant ones matter more there.
questions.rule: Relevance decides.
questions.teaches: Companies that work with governments requiring certain professional certifications might place more focus on those certifications.

questions.q: What decides what a recruiter screens for, according to the recruiter in the chapter?
options: The recruiter's own personal taste in resume layout and style
What the manager asked for
The number of pages the resume has
The company's logo on the resume
optionExplain: The recruiter works from the manager's requirements.
The recruiter's screen is usually an extension of the manager's requirements.
Length is not the screening criterion described.
Logos are not the point.
questions.explain: Recruiters screen against what the hiring manager wants. The card shows how to respond.
questions.rule: Show the role's must-haves, or close signs of them such as similar environments and problems or the same technology in projects, and write a resume tailored to each position.

questions.q: What recruiters look for in a resume is usually an extension of what the hiring ____ asked them to screen for.
questions.explain: The hiring manager sets the requirements.
questions.rule: Manager sets the screen.

questions.q: A job needs Java or Go. Rahul has worked mainly in .NET but built a hobby service in Go. What should he do?
options: Leave the Go project out, as it is a hobby and not paid work for an employer
Rewrite his work history to mention Go jobs
Make sure the Go project appears in his projects or technologies section
List Go as an expert-level skill
optionExplain: The recruiter says personal projects count.
That would bend the facts.
The recruiter expects to see missing must-have languages somewhere else on the resume.
The author advises against expertise labels.
questions.explain: Show the missing must-have where you do have it, such as in projects or the technologies section.
questions.hint: Where else could Go appear?
questions.rule: Show the role's must-haves, or close signs of them such as similar environments and problems or the same technology in projects, and write a resume tailored to each position.

questions.q: The hiring manager listed five must-haves and a candidate has three or four. What can a good recruiter do?
options: Advise the manager that the team may be able to train or mentor the gap
Reject the candidate automatically
Ask the candidate to add the missing items
Rank the candidate first, because three out of five must-haves is enough
optionExplain: A flexible recruiter weighs resources to train someone who is close.
The recruiter described advising flexibility.
A resume should not claim what is missing.
The recruiter said a person might still be considered, not ranked first.
questions.explain: A good recruiter can advise the market and resources, so a near match is not always rejected.
questions.rule: Near matches can pass.

questions.q: True or false: According to the recruiter, someone applying for 20 different jobs should have 20 different CVs.
questions.explain: She says each CV should be specific to its role, and this is necessary rather than bad.
questions.rule: Show the role's must-haves, or close signs of them such as similar environments and problems or the same technology in projects, and write a resume tailored to each position.

questions.q: A flexible hiring manager still wants evidence of fit. What might a recruiter look for?
options: Awards and recognition that have no direct link to the job on offer
Work at scale, multidisciplinary teams and the technologies used
A long hobbies list
The longest job title
optionExplain: The recruiter did not mention these.
The recruiter's examples were scale, multidisciplinary teams and technologies.
Hobbies are not part of the screen described.
Titles are not the signal described.
questions.explain: When must-haves are flexible, recruiters look at similar environments and problems.
questions.rule: Show similar environments.
questions.teaches: When a hiring manager is flexible, recruiters look for similar environments or problems, such as work at scale, multidisciplinary teams and the technologies used.

questions.q: What is the first question about technologies that a reviewer has, according to the author?
options: Which tools the person uses hands-on
Which technologies the person has read about
Which certifications the person holds for each technology they list

Hands-on use matters, not reading.
Certifications are a separate matter.
Desire is not what reviewers check first.

questions.rule: List the technologies relevant to the position that you are proficient in under a separate heading, and go neither only by the job advert nor overboard.

questions.q: The name of the technologies section matters less than its ____.

questions.rule: Contents over name.

Only Kubernetes, as it is the rarest skill
Nothing, because the ad already shows the needs
optionExplain: Listing a tool you only touched in a tutorial overstates it.

questions.explain: List what you can use day to day, not everything you have touched and not only what the ad says.

questions.rule: List the technologies relevant to the position that you are proficient in under a separate heading, and go neither only by the job advert nor overboard.

questions.q: Sort these items for a full-stack developer's technologies section.

items.t: JavaScript, used daily at work
Microsoft Word
React, used in two recent projects
Trello
A niche tool unrelated to the job
API design, done in the last job

questions.explain: Relevant, hands-on items belong. Trivial tools and unrelated niches do not.
questions.rule: Relevant and hands-on only.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a technologies section should list only the technologies named in the job advert.

questions.rule: List the technologies relevant to the position that you are proficient in under a separate heading, and go neither only by the job advert nor overboard.

questions.q: Ben has a skills section. He wonders whether to also name key technologies inside his work descriptions. What does the author say?
options: No, that duplicates the section and wastes space
No, because descriptions should hold only soft skills and team results
Yes, name key ones there too, as it reinforces hands-on experience
Yes, but only for technologies you rate as expert

The author wants specifics in descriptions.
The author says to mention key technologies in your work experience as well.
The author advises against expertise labels and does not limit it this way.

questions.q: A resume lists Python as expert and Go as proficient. What is the problem, according to the author?

Length is not the objection.

questions.rule: Avoid listing your expertise level or a points score; list only languages you feel proficient with, strongest first, and drop tools anyone can pick up quickly.

questions.q: As a rule of thumb, avoid listing your ____ level.

questions.q: Which technologies section follows the author's advice?
options: Java (expert), Go (proficient), Eclipse (expert)
Java 9/10, Go 7/10, JavaScript 6/10
Every language and tool touched since university, in alphabetical order
Go, Java and JavaScript, strongest first, with no level labels

Points systems are advised against.
A dump of everything reduces credibility.
It lists proficient languages and uses order to show strength.

questions.hint: Order, not labels, shows strength.
questions.rule: Avoid listing your expertise level or a points score; list only languages you feel proficient with, strongest first, and drop tools anyone can pick up quickly.

questions.q: Sort these items from a technologies section.

items.t: Strongest languages first
Expert and proficient labels
Eclipse listed next to Java
Items grouped in tabs for scanning
Word and Trello as skills
Only hands-on languages

questions.q: True or false: According to the recruiters in the chapter, people who rated themselves experts in a language were sometimes rejected after being questioned on its depth.

questions.rule: Avoid listing your expertise level or a points score; list only languages you feel proficient with, strongest first, and drop tools anyone can pick up quickly.

questions.q: A 50-year-old developer lists Perl and C++ that she has not used in years and rates herself rusty. What might the author's advice add?

Keep them but label them rusty
Move them to the top of the list as proof of depth

Strongest languages go first.

Alphabetical order hides which are recent.

questions.q: Ravi wants a Ruby-heavy company to see that he has used Ruby before but is stronger in JavaScript and Java. Which approach fits?

List Ruby first in the main list
Rate Ruby as expert to match the ad
Hide Ruby, as the company will teach it to him on the job
optionExplain: The book's third approach splits out less hands-on technologies.
That would suggest it is his strongest language.

questions.q: A developer's official title is Associate, a finance-industry title. What does the author suggest?
