options: Relevant technologies and date readability
Only the summary check, because it is missing from the draft
Only the length check
None of them
optionExplain: Expert labels fail the technologies check, and month-level old dates fail the date check.
A missing summary is acceptable for many candidates.
Nothing in the description concerns length.
Two checks fail.
questions.explain: Expert labels and month-level dates for older jobs fail two checks. The summary is optional.
questions.hint: Read each flaw against the seven questions.
questions.rule: Check section order, relevant technologies, your story, a tailored summary, detail on recent versus old work, date readability and length against your experience.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: Sort these audit findings.

items.t: Recent jobs have more detail than older ones
Old jobs have the same detail as recent ones
Technologies ordered by strength with no labels
Expertise level added to every technology
Titles show a promotion
Non-technical jobs fill half a page

questions.explain: The audit rewards focus on the recent and relevant.
questions.rule: Relevant, ordered, readable.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: True or false: According to the recap, adding an expertise level to each technology is helpful.
questions.explain: The recap says it is not helpful; if anything, use the listing order.
questions.rule: Check section order, relevant technologies, your story, a tailored summary, detail on recent versus old work, date readability and length against your experience.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: A director with 20 years of relevant experience has a five-page resume. What does the recap say about length?
options: Five pages is fine, as long as every line of the content is relevant to the role
It should be cut to one page
It should be sent as two separate resumes
It should not go above three pages, even with much relevant experience
optionExplain: The recap says no more than three.
One page is for starters.
That advice concerns different roles, not length.
The recap sets three pages as a ceiling.
questions.explain: The recap says that even with lots of relevant experience, length should not go above three pages.
questions.rule: Three pages is a ceiling.
questions.teaches: The recap says that even for leadership roles or over a decade of experience, length should not go above three pages.

questions.q: A hiring manager reads two bullets about the same project. Which one is more likely to stand out, according to the author?
options: The one that lists the most tasks you were responsible for, in detail
The one that uses the most senior-sounding job title for the role
The one that mentions the largest number of technologies in a row
The one that states what changed because of your work
optionExplain: A long task list feels thorough, but it describes duties, not results.
Titles help, but the author says the result and your part in it carry the weight.
Technology names matter, but the author puts impact ahead of them.
Right: results show your value and awareness of impact.
questions.explain: A guess is fine here. The card next shows the author's reason for writing about results.
questions.rule: Write each bullet around the result you produced, not only the task you were given.

questions.q: Focus on what you ____, as opposed to what you did.
questions.explain: The author's first advice for work and project entries is to focus on achievements rather than tasks.
questions.rule: Lead with what you achieved.

questions.q: A support engineer's bullet reads: Answered customer chat tickets. Which rewrite follows the author's advice best?
options: Answered chat tickets quickly and politely every day while working in a busy and demanding team of support staff
Responsible for the full ownership of customer chat tickets and for keeping the whole queue of chats in good order
Cut chat wait time from nine minutes to three by writing reply templates for the ten most common issues
Used the company chat tool to handle a large volume of chat tickets and to escalate hard cases to senior colleagues
optionExplain: It adds adjectives, but still describes the task and shows no result.
Responsibility language tells the reader the duty, which is what the author wants to move past.
Right: it states a result, a number and what the engineer did.
A tool and some volume are mentioned, but nobody can see what improved.
questions.explain: The rewrite names a measurable change and the action behind it. The others restate the job.
questions.rule: A good bullet shows what changed because of you.

questions.q: Sort each bullet: does it show an achievement, or only describe a duty?

items.t: Reduced build time from 40 minutes to 12 by caching dependencies
Led a team of four to launch a mobile checkout used by 80,000 customers
Cut monthly cloud costs by 22 percent after moving logs to cheaper storage
Responsible for maintaining the build system
Worked on the checkout feature with other developers
Took part in code reviews and sprint planning

questions.explain: The first three say what changed and by how much. The last three say only where the person worked or what the role included.
questions.rule: An achievement names a change, not a place or a duty.

questions.q: A mid-level engineer thinks results matter only for senior roles. What does the author say about this?
options: Results matter only for senior roles; juniors should list duties because they have no real impact yet
The expectation grows with seniority, but talking about impact helps you stand out at every level
Impact matters for every level equally, with no difference in what readers expect from each one
Results belong in the interview rather than on the resume, so the page can stay short and neutral
optionExplain: This reverses the author's view that impact language helps in all cases.
Right: seniors are expected to do it, and everyone benefits.
The author says the expectation does rise with seniority.
The author wants the results on the resume, where the first reader sees them.
questions.explain: The more senior you are, the more readers expect impact. Still, it makes you stand out in every case.
questions.rule: Impact language helps at every level, and is expected more as you grow senior.
questions.teaches: The more senior you are, the more of an expectation it is that your resume shows impact, but doing so makes you stand out in all cases.

questions.q: A developer's resume is all results and does not say what the job was. What does the author's cited advice suggest?
options: Add the responsibilities too, since effective resumes carry both what the job was and what the results were
Drop the results and keep only the job description, since the recruiter will ask about outcomes later
Keep as it is, since a result with no duty attached is stronger than a result with a duty attached
Move all of the results to a cover letter so the resume itself can stay as a clean list of duties
optionExplain: Right: responsibilities set the scene, accomplishments prove value.
That swaps one gap for another; most people already fail at the accomplishments part.
The cited developer says an effective resume needs both parts.
The advice is about the resume containing both parts, not splitting them across documents.
questions.explain: A developer cited by the author says effective resumes contain responsibilities and accomplishments, and that most people fail at the second.
questions.rule: Responsibilities tell the reader the job; accomplishments tell the results.
questions.teaches: A developer cited by the author says effective resumes need two things: responsibilities (what your job was) and accomplishments (what your results were), and most people fail at the accomplishments part.

questions.q: You want a bullet that proves your value. Which set of parts would you build it from?
options: Which team you were on, which tools it used, and who your manager was at the time
How long the project lasted, how hard it felt, and how often you worked late on it
Which words the job advert used, which verbs your friends like, and how short the line is
What improved, how much it improved by, and what you did to cause it
optionExplain: These add context, but none of them shows an outcome or your own part in it.
Effort is easy to describe, but it does not show what you achieved.
Wording matters elsewhere, but these parts say nothing about your results.
Right: result, measure and your action.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next gives the author's three-part formula.
questions.rule: Write bullets in the shape: accomplished impact, measured by a number, by doing a specific contribution.

questions.q: Put the parts of the author's formula in order, first to last.
questions.explain: The formula reads: accomplished impact, as measured by a number, by doing a specific contribution.
questions.rule: Impact first, then the number, then your action.

questions.q: A tester wrote: Tested the mobile app before releases. Which rewrite uses all three parts of the formula?
options: Tested the mobile app before every release using a careful process that all the other testers on the team followed
Reduced store complaints by half, an achievement that the whole team of testers and developers was proud of
Caught 35 crash bugs before launch, cutting store complaints by half, by building a test suite for the login flow
Built a test suite for the login flow in several stages with the help of many people from the team across the year
optionExplain: It repeats the task and gives no result or number.
It gives a result and a number, but no action of yours.
Right: result, number and action are all present.
It gives an action, but neither the result nor a number.
questions.explain: Only the first option names the impact, how much, and what the person did.
questions.rule: Check each bullet for impact, number and your action.

questions.q: Sort each bullet: does it contain all three parts of the formula, or is a part missing?

items.t: Cut page load from 3.2 s to 1.1 s by lazy-loading images
Raised test coverage from 40 to 85 percent by writing contract tests
Grew weekly signups by 18 percent by redesigning the onboarding emails
Improved performance a lot of the time
Cut deployment time from 30 to 5 minutes
Wrote tests by hand for the payments module

questions.explain: The first three have impact, number and action. The last three give only a vague result, a result without an action, and an action without a result.
questions.rule: A bullet is complete when result, measure and action all appear.

questions.q: The formula sounds stiff. What does the author say about using its exact wording?
options: You need not copy it, but the impact, your contribution and some specifics should still come through
You must copy it word for word, because screeners search for that exact phrase in every resume
You may drop the contribution part, because the number and the impact are enough to impress readers
You should avoid it, because it is similar to what recruiters see as a template used by many people
optionExplain: Right: the form is flexible, the content is not.
The author says no such thing and tells you the exact wording is optional.
The contribution is one of the three points the author wants clear.
The author calls it similar to a structure Google encourages for resumes, which is a point in its favour.
questions.explain: The author says you do not need the exact wording, but the impact, your contribution and specifics must be clear. The structure is also similar to one Google encourages.
questions.rule: Keep the three parts; the wording is yours.
questions.teaches: The formula is similar to the structure Google encourages for resumes, and you do not need to use its exact wording as long as impact, contribution and specifics are clear.

questions.q: You worked on a project with five others. The author's cited advice says what about describing it?
options: Skip it, because only solo projects can show a personal contribution to the person reading
You can still describe your own involvement, even though you were not the only person on the project
Describe the whole team's result as yours, because the recruiter cannot check who did which part
List only the team's name, since individual contributions can be discussed at the interview stage
optionExplain: The cited advice says the opposite for team work.
Right: shared work does not remove your part.
The author says do not claim untrue things.
The advice is to state your own involvement on the page.
questions.explain: Andy Lester's advice, quoted in the chapter, says that even if you were not the only person on a project you can still discuss your involvement.
questions.rule: Shared work still has a part that was yours.
questions.teaches: Even if you were not the only person working on a project, you can still discuss your involvement in it.

questions.q: A developer has no revenue figures for her project. What could she count instead?
options: Nothing, since numbers belong only to revenue and cost, so she should use strong adjectives
Users, installs, ratings, team size or tickets she resolved
Only lines of code, because other counts are too soft for a technical reader to accept
Only the hours she worked, since that is the one figure that nobody can dispute afterwards
optionExplain: Adjectives do not replace figures, and revenue is only one kind of number.
Right: many things count as numbers.
Lines of code is one option on the author's list, not the only one.
Hours say little about impact and are not what the author suggests.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next shows what the author says about numbers.
questions.rule: Quantify the impact of your work wherever you can.

questions.q: According to the author, most resumes do not contain ____, so adding them helps you stand out.
questions.explain: Adding numbers is one of the simplest ways to stand out.
questions.rule: Add numbers where you can.

questions.q: A backend engineer wrote: Improved the reliability of the order service. Which rewrite fits the author's advice on numbers?
options: Greatly improved the reliability of the order service so that customers rarely met an error again
Improved reliability across the order service and several related services with colleagues on the platform team
Raised order service uptime from 99.2 to 99.9 percent by adding retries and a circuit breaker
Worked on reliability for the order service during a long period in which many incidents were handled
optionExplain: It adds words like greatly and rarely, but no figure.
It widens the claim without making it measurable.
Right: a before-and-after figure plus the action.
Duration and incident count are hinted at, but nothing is quantified.
questions.explain: A before-and-after figure lets the reader see the size of the change.
questions.rule: Show the size of the change with a figure.

questions.q: Sort each bullet: does it carry a specific figure, or only vague wording?

items.t: Onboarded 12 new engineers to the deployment process
Cut weekly incident count from 14 to 5
Shipped a feature used by 40,000 monthly users
Made the app much faster for many users
Greatly reduced the number of customer complaints
Helped a large number of colleagues with their work

questions.explain: The first three carry counts or before-and-after figures. The last three say much, many or large without any measure.
questions.rule: Replace much, many and large with a figure.

questions.q: A developer cited by the author sets a goal for numbers per bullet. What is it?
options: One number per role, placed in the first bullet so the reader sees it before anything else
Two or three numbers in the top bullet of the resume, with none needed further down the page
A number in every sentence of the summary, because the summary is the part that gets read first
At least one number in each bullet, supporting the story the text tells
optionExplain: The goal is per bullet, not per role.
The advice spreads numbers across bullets.
The cited advice is about bullets in experience, not the summary.
Right: the goal is a number in each bullet.
questions.explain: The cited developer aims for at least one number in each bullet and says so few resumes have any statistics that this puts yours ahead of 90 percent of others.
questions.rule: Aim for one number in each bullet.
questions.teaches: A developer cited by the author sets the goal of at least one number in each bullet point, and says so few resumes have numbers that this puts you ahead of 90 percent of other applicants.

questions.q: A mobile developer wants figures for an app she built alone. Which ones does the author list as options?
options: Number of installs, number of five-star ratings, and customer tickets she resolved proactively
The app's colour palette, its icon design, and the name of the store where it was published
Her own salary at the time, the app's file size, and the year in which it was first built
The names of reviewers who liked the app, and the number of friends she told about it
optionExplain: Right: all three are on the author's list.
These describe the app but are not measures of impact.
These are details, not measures of the value created.
Names and informal word of mouth do not appear on the author's list.
questions.explain: The author's list of numbers includes people on the team, lines of code, code coverage before and after, SLA changes, revenue, users, installs, five-star ratings and tickets resolved proactively.
questions.rule: Many different measures count as numbers.
questions.teaches: Numbers can be team size, lines of code, code coverage before and after, SLA changes, revenue, users, installs, five-star ratings or customer support tickets you proactively resolved.

questions.q: Which opening makes a bullet sound most proactive?
options: Was part of a team that was rebuilding the search page for a while
Led a team of three to rebuild the search page
Search page rebuild, which was being done in a team across a few months
Responsible for the team that took part in rebuilding the search page
optionExplain: Being part of something sounds passive, as though it happened to you.
Right: an active verb names what you did.
It drops the actor, so the reader cannot tell who did the work.
Responsibility and taking part are both passive ways of saying it.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next gives the author's view on verbs.
questions.rule: Open each bullet with an active verb that shows what you did.

questions.q: Use active verbs like led, managed and drove over passive ones like improving or rolling ____.
questions.explain: The author's examples contrast led and rolled out with improving and rolling out.
questions.rule: Choose led over being responsible for.

questions.q: Which bullet opening follows the author's advice on language?
options: Rolled out a caching layer that cut API latency by a third
Rolling out a caching layer, which led to latency being reduced by a third
A caching layer was rolled out, and latency went down by a third
Involved in the rollout of a caching layer with positive effects on latency
optionExplain: Right: an active verb, a result and a number.
The participle form is the passive style the author advises against.
The passive voice hides who did the work.
Involved in and positive effects are both weak and vague.
questions.explain: The first option opens with an active verb and also states the result.
questions.rule: Open with who did what.

questions.q: Sort each opening: does it use active language, or passive and weak language?

items.t: Drove the migration of 60 services to the new platform
Improved checkout conversion by 6 percent
Managed a team of five engineers across two time zones
Was part of the migration of services to the new platform
Took part in discussions about checkout conversion
Team member in a group of five engineers

questions.explain: The first three say what the person did. The last three describe presence rather than action.
questions.rule: Say what you did, not where you were.

questions.q: A reader asks if a long list of action words, such as analyzed or devised, will fix a weak resume. What does the quoted advice say?
options: Yes, a long list of action words is the main thing that makes a bullet sound effective to readers
No, active verbs should be avoided, since they make bullets sound pushy to the person reading them
Only verbs from the job advert matter, so the rest can be ignored when you write your bullets
Active verbs are good, but the details of the work, including numbers, matter more than which verb you pick
optionExplain: The quoted advice calls such lists blah blah blah.
The advice still wants active verbs.
Mirroring is a separate point; this quoted advice is about specifics.
Right: use active verbs without fixating on them.
questions.explain: Andy Lester agrees you should use active verbs but warns against getting hung up on a snazzy word, and says to focus on the details instead.
questions.rule: Details beat a showy verb.
questions.teaches: The quoted advice says not to get hung up on which snazzy action word you use and to focus on getting as specific as possible about the work.

questions.q: A senior engineer's bullets all describe implementing tickets someone assigned. Which self-image does a developer cited by the author want a senior resume to convey?
options: An implementer who follows each ticket to the letter and finishes everything on time
A generalist who has touched many tools but owns none of the results of the work
A Solver or a Finder, rather than an implementer
A team player whose bullets avoid saying I and describe only what the group delivered
optionExplain: The cited developer says senior engineers are not implementers.
That is not one of the three types named.
Right: seniors are not implementers.
The author asks for first-person ownership of your part.
questions.explain: Itamar Turner-Trauring, cited by the author, argues that senior engineers are not implementers and that the resume should show a Solver or a Finder.
questions.rule: Active language shows you solve and find problems, not only implement.
questions.teaches: A developer cited by the author says senior engineers are not implementers, and a senior resume should convey that you are a Solver or a Finder.

questions.q: Where should the tools you used appear in a bullet about your work?
options: In the first words, so that a keyword scan finds them before anything else
In a separate line below each bullet, set apart in a smaller font from the main text
Toward the end, after the result and your part in it
Nowhere, since the skills section already lists every tool you have touched
optionExplain: Putting tools first pushes the result out of the spotlight.
The author describes mentioning them within the description.
Right: impact first, tools after.
The author says to repeat some of them, in the experience section too.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next gives the author's reason for the order.
questions.rule: Put the technologies near the end of the bullet, and keep them matching your Languages and Technologies section.

questions.q: Impact and your contribution matter more than technologies, so mention the tools toward the ____ of the description.
questions.explain: The author says to place technologies toward the end of a description.
questions.rule: Result first, tools after.

questions.q: Which bullet puts technologies in the right place?
options: Cut cold start time from 6 s to 2 s by trimming dependencies, using Kotlin and Gradle
Using Kotlin, Gradle, Room, Retrofit, Dagger and Coroutines, worked on app start time for the team
Kotlin and Gradle developer who worked on start time and other things throughout the year on the app
Improved cold start time with an approach that is fully described on the technologies list above
optionExplain: Right: the result and action lead, tools close.
A tool list leads the line and the result is missing.
The tools lead and the impact is missing.
It points to another section instead of giving any detail.
questions.explain: The tools are called out after the result and the contribution.
questions.rule: Impact, contribution, then tools.

questions.q: True or false: The technologies named in your bullets should differ from those in your Languages and Technologies section, so that nothing is repeated.
questions.explain: The author asks you to make sure the technologies in the descriptions overlap with those in your standalone Languages and Technologies section.
questions.rule: Keep the two places consistent.

questions.q: A candidate wants to repeat a technology in a bullet that is already in the skills list. What does the author think?
options: It hurts, because repeating a word counts as padding and annoys the recruiter at the first glance
It matters only for keyword search tools, and a human reader would ignore the repeats completely
It is acceptable only for the single newest technology that you have put on the resume this year
It helps, because it shows you used the technology, mostly for readers who read in detail
optionExplain: The author says repeating helps reinforce it.
The author says the repeat is powerful for hiring managers and interviewers who read in detail.
No such limit appears in the chapter.
Right: the repeat reinforces hands-on use.
questions.explain: The author says naming technologies in context is more powerful for detail readers, and that the names should overlap with your own technologies section.
questions.rule: Naming a tool in context backs up the skills list.
questions.teaches: Mentioning technologies in the description is more powerful for hiring managers and interviewers who read the resume in detail than only listing them in a separate section.

questions.q: A data analyst names a tool in every one of her twelve bullets. What does the chapter's recap say about this?
options: Do it in every bullet, since the more often a tool appears the more weight it carries with the reader
You need not do it for every part, but repeating tools from your skills list reinforces that you are hands-on
Do it only in the skills section, since repeating a tool in bullets counts as padding for readers
Replace the tools with the verbs that the job advert uses, so that the lines read as one voice
optionExplain: The recap says you do not need to do it for every part.
Right: some repeats help, every bullet is not required.
The recap says repeating tools reinforces hands-on use.
Mirroring verbs is a separate point from naming tools.
questions.explain: The recap asks whether you mention technologies in your examples, and says you need not do it for every part. Repeating tools from your Languages and Technologies section reinforces hands-on use.
questions.rule: Name tools where they back up a result, not in every line.
questions.teaches: You do not need to mention technologies in every part, but repeating those you also list in the Languages and Technologies section reinforces that you are hands-on with them.

questions.q: You are drafting bullets for a new resume. What is a good first step, according to the quoted advice?
options: Jot down everything you remember doing, without worrying about order or phrasing
Decide the exact wording of each bullet before writing anything about the project
Copy bullet phrasing from a list of action words you have found on a resume website
List only the three biggest achievements so the page is neat from the very first draft
optionExplain: Right: collect first, edit afterwards.
Wording comes later, once the material is on the page.
The quoted advice is sceptical about action-word lists.
Pruning is meant to happen later, not at the start.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next explains the quoted advice.
questions.rule: Write down everything you can recall doing, early, and cut it down later.

questions.q: It is far easier to get rid of extra information than to come up with one more ____ at the last minute.
questions.explain: That is the reason to collect widely first and prune later.
questions.rule: Collect widely, then prune.

questions.q: Order the steps of the quoted approach to getting bullets, first to last.
items: Start early and carry a sheet of paper
Scribble ideas, ignoring order and phrasing
Write down everything you remember doing
questions.explain: The quoted author says to start early, scribble ideas on paper without worrying about order or phrasing, write down everything you recall, and worry about pruning later.
questions.rule: Collect widely first; prune last.

questions.q: Which focus does the quoted advice recommend when you write bullets?
options: The buzzwords that recruiters search for, placed as often as possible
The longest list of action words you can find, which you then rotate through all the bullets
The story and the specific details of the work
The shortest possible bullets, even if no details of what happened remain in them at the end
optionExplain: The advice tells you to focus on the story, not buzzwords.
The advice says not to get hung up on snazzy words.
Right: the story, not buzzwords.
The advice asks for as many specifics as you can give.
questions.explain: The advice puts the story and the details of your work before buzzwords or showy verbs.
questions.rule: Story and details over buzzwords.

questions.q: A candidate plans to write her bullets on the night before the deadline, as it seems a quick job. What does the quoted author say?
options: That is a fine plan, since bullets are the easiest part and the layout is the slow step
Start early, because coming up with bullets is the toughest part of the whole resume process
That is fine if she copies the bullets from a friend with a similar job title and a similar background
She should write them the night before, because early drafts are usually thrown away in the end
optionExplain: The quoted author calls bullets the toughest part.
Right: the toughest part needs the most time.
Copying does not give you your own specifics.
The advice is to start early, and early notes get pruned, not discarded.
questions.explain: The quoted author calls writing bullets the toughest part of the entire resume process and recommends starting early.
questions.rule: Start the bullets early; they take the longest.
questions.teaches: The quoted author calls coming up with bullets the toughest part of the entire resume process and recommends starting early.

questions.q: An IT admin recalls a router upgrade. Based on the quoted examples, what is worth writing down alongside the upgrade?
options: Only the model name of the routers, since that is the specific fact a technical reader looks for
The names of colleagues who watched the installation, so the entry has more people in it
A general statement that the network felt faster, because a feeling is the real measure of success
What changed afterwards, such as the throughput gain and the share of help desk calls that disappeared
optionExplain: A model name is a detail, but it is not the result.
Colleagues are not what the quoted examples add.
The quoted examples use figures, not impressions.
Right: the result that followed the action.
questions.explain: One quoted example credits new routers with a 25 percent throughput increase that virtually eliminated the 20 percent of help desk calls about slow networks.
questions.rule: Write down the results that followed, not only the action.
questions.teaches: A quoted example credits new routers with raising throughput 25 percent, which virtually eliminated the 20 percent of help desk calls about network responsiveness: an impact that followed from the action.

questions.q: A bullet names an internal platform that only colleagues would know. What problem does this cause for a recruiter?
options: The reader will assume the platform is a competitor product and ignore the line
The reader will find the name too long and skip the line to the next one in the list
The reader will contact the platform team to check the facts before moving on
The reader cannot tell how big or hard the work was
optionExplain: Nothing suggests that readers assume this.
Length of the name is not the issue; understanding is.
Recruiters rarely have time for that kind of check.
Right: the outsider has no way to judge it.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next walks through the author's comments on this case.
questions.rule: Read your bullet as an outsider: if it needs company knowledge, has no figure or sounds assigned, rewrite it.

questions.q: Which problems does the author point out in the before version? Select all that apply.
options: It names a platform that only colleagues would understand
It has no numbers
It uses too many technologies
It ends the sentence with etc
It lists the wrong dates
optionExplain: Right: an outsider cannot judge the work.
Right: no figures are given.
The author does not say this; the after version adds technologies.
Right: the author calls this sloppy.
The author does not mention dates.
questions.explain: The author names the insider platform, the missing numbers, the passive feel and the etc.
questions.rule: Outsider-readable, numbered and active.

questions.q: A bullet reads: Worked on the Atlas pipeline and various tasks, etc. Which fix would the author make first?
options: Capitalise the word etc so that it looks deliberate rather than sloppy to the reader
Add the names of all colleagues who worked on the pipeline so the reader sees the group
Explain in outsider terms what Atlas does, add a figure and describe your own action
Replace the word worked with the word assisted to make the sentence sound slightly stronger
optionExplain: Keeping the etc keeps the sloppy ending.
The case calls for your own contribution.
Right: all three problems from the case.
That swaps one weak verb for another.
questions.explain: The case fixes insider names, missing numbers and unclear contribution, and drops the etc.
questions.rule: Make it understandable, measurable and yours.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a bullet that says a refactoring was assigned to you shows more initiative than one describing what you did.
questions.explain: The author says the assigned wording makes the role seem handed to the person, with the impact unclear. Describing what you did and what changed shows initiative.
questions.rule: Show what you did and what it changed.

questions.q: A candidate rewrites a vague bullet and the result is full of numbers and tools. Which outcome does the author attribute to the rewrite?
options: It conveys that the person moved the needle, gets things done and used specific technologies
It guarantees that the resume will pass every filter and that an interview will follow
It shows that the person works longer hours than the other candidates who applied
It proves that the person alone built the entire platform with no help from anyone
optionExplain: Right: the author lists these effects.
The author makes no guarantee.
Hours are not mentioned.
The case does not claim sole authorship.
questions.explain: The author says the after version conveys that the person moved the needle for the business, can get things done, and used specific technologies.
questions.rule: Specifics convey that you get things done.
questions.teaches: The author says the improved version shows someone who has moved the needle for the business, can get things done, and names the technologies used on the project.

questions.q: A candidate writes: We moved the billing job to a queue and we cut run time. What would the author change?
options: Add the full list of team members, so every colleague gets credit for the work
Make it about the person, describing their own part in the move and the run time
Add the word team in front of we so the contributors are named in the sentence
Leave it, since we shows modesty and teamwork, which hiring managers want to see most
optionExplain: The author wants the resume to be about you.
Right: the page should show what you did.
That moves the focus further from your own part.
The author advises against it.
questions.explain: A guess is fine here. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Write what you did in the first person, and leave we and the team's name out of your bullets.

questions.q: Avoid using we and use the ____ person instead.
questions.explain: The author asks for first-person writing, usually without the word I.
questions.rule: Write in the first person.

questions.q: Which rewrite of the following best fits the author's advice? We were responsible for moving the API to a new framework.
options: Moved the API to the new framework, with sole ownership of the auth module
Our team was responsible for the framework move, and I was glad to be in it from start to finish
The API was moved to the new framework by a group of developers, among whom was a person like me
We, as the team, completed the framework move with every member playing an important role in it
optionExplain: Right: first person, active and specific about your part.
It still leads with the team and is passive.
It hides the actor behind a passive sentence.
It keeps we and gives no individual detail.
questions.explain: The rewrite drops we, uses an active verb and states a personal contribution. The others keep the group.
questions.rule: Say what you did.

questions.q: Sort each line: does it centre you, or does it hide you behind the team?

items.t: Designed the retry logic for the order service
Led onboarding for three new hires on the payments team
Wrote the migration scripts that moved 2 TB of data
We delivered the new search page on time
Part of a team that rebuilt the search page
The team occasionally helped out on the data move

questions.explain: The first three name something the person did. The last three put the group, or a vague role, in the subject.
questions.rule: Put yourself in the subject of the sentence.

questions.q: A candidate who writes in a language where we is the norm for achievements asks what to do. What does the author say?
options: Keep we, since the recruiter will understand that it is normal in another language
Write we in the summary and I in the bullets, so both styles are visible on the page
Drop that habit; in an English resume, go with the first-person approach
Translate each we as the team name, so the reader knows which group is meant
optionExplain: The author tells you to drop it.
The author does not recommend mixing.
Right: the norm differs between languages.
That keeps the focus on the team, not on you.
questions.explain: The author notes that we is the norm for achievements in some languages, but says to drop it in an English resume.
questions.rule: In English, write about yourself.
questions.teaches: For non-native English speakers, talking about we is the norm when describing achievements in some languages, but the author says to drop it in an English resume.

questions.q: A candidate rewrites a bullet as: I led the move to the new database. What else does the author say about the word I?
options: Put I at the start of every bullet, so the reader notices that the work is yours
Replace I with the team name at least once per role to show how well you work with others
Use I only in the summary section, and leave the bullets in the third person for contrast
In most cases you can drop the I and start the bullet with the active verb
optionExplain: The author says in most cases you can drop it.
That works against the advice.
The advice is to use the first person throughout.
Right: leading with the verb already makes it first person.
questions.explain: Starting with a verb is already first person, so the author says that in most cases you can drop the I.
questions.rule: Start with the verb; I is implied.
questions.teaches: In most cases you can drop the word I and begin each bullet with the active verb.

questions.q: A candidate is unsure whether a result was big enough to include. According to the author, what is the better habit?
options: Leave it out, as a small result may look like boasting to a hiring manager
Include it and describe the result with confidence
Mention it in a footnote, so it does not distract from the bigger results above it
Describe it in softer words, so it cannot be challenged in an interview afterwards
optionExplain: The author advises against hiding achievements.
Right: the author prefers selling to hiding.
A footnote hides the result.
Soft words are what the author flags as undersell.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next gives the author's advice.
questions.rule: State your achievements plainly and fully; do not shrink them with soft wording.

questions.q: Be concise but not ____.
questions.explain: The author's line is: be concise but not humble.
questions.rule: Be concise but not humble.

questions.q: Sort each phrase: does it undersell the work, or state it plainly?

items.t: Occasionally helped with deployments
Sometimes took part in design reviews
Team member who assisted on several projects
Deployed 30 services to production
Designed the caching layer for the checkout
Ran design reviews for a team of eight

questions.explain: The author flags squinting modifiers such as sometimes and occasionally, and passive roles like team member. The plain statements say what was done.
questions.rule: Remove soft modifiers and passive roles.

questions.q: A candidate wants to stretch a borderline claim into a clear lie. Which advice from the same section applies?
options: Do not claim untrue things, while still aiming to paint a great picture of yourself
Stretch it anyway, because the author says inflating always hurts less than hiding
Remove the whole project, since any claim that could be questioned must be avoided
Add the claim to the cover letter only, since the resume itself cannot be checked there
optionExplain: Right: sell, but stay truthful.
The author's remark is about borderline cases and is not permission to lie.
The advice is to present true work in its best light.
Nothing in the chapter suggests this.
questions.explain: The section opens with: do not claim untrue things, but do paint a great picture of yourself.
questions.rule: Sell the truth; do not invent.

questions.q: When a claim sits on the borderline, what does the author say about inflating it versus hiding it?
options: Inflating hurts more than hiding, so the safest choice is to leave out anything uncertain
They hurt the same amount, so you should flip a coin if you are unsure about the claim
Neither is acceptable, so a borderline claim should be tested with a friend before using it
When in doubt, inflating on the borderline hurts less than hiding it
optionExplain: The author says the reverse.
The author gives a clear preference.
The author does not suggest a test, but a preference.
Right: this is the author's view for borderline cases.
questions.explain: According to the author, when in doubt, inflating achievements on the borderline will hurt less than hiding them.
questions.rule: On the borderline, lean toward credit, not silence.
questions.teaches: According to the author, when in doubt, inflating your achievements on the borderline will hurt less than hiding them.

questions.q: A candidate worked with four colleagues on a project and hesitates to claim credit. What does the chapter's recap advise?
options: Credit the whole team in equal shares, since stating your own part could look like boasting
Leave the project off, since shared work cannot be claimed by one person in a fair way
Err on the side of taking credit for the work you were involved in, without claiming anything untrue
Ask each colleague to approve the wording, so nobody feels left out of the resume lines
optionExplain: The recap says the resume is about your achievements.
Shared work still has your part in it.
Right: the recap tells you to take credit.
Nothing in the chapter asks for this.
questions.explain: The recap says your resume is about your achievements and not to be humble: err on the side of taking credit for work you were involved in.
questions.rule: Take credit for what you were involved in.
questions.teaches: The recap says to make sure the resume is about your achievements, and not to be humble: err on the side of taking credit for the work that you were involved in.

questions.q: A candidate lists a GitHub link under projects, with no description. What does the author expect to happen?
options: The reader will open every link, so the candidate gains time by writing less about each
The reader may not look at it in detail, because nothing tells them why it is worth a click
The reader will assume it is a large project because it has its own link on the page
The reader will contact the candidate to ask about it before the call is booked
optionExplain: The author warns that readers may not look.
Right: unsold work stays unopened.
A link alone does not signal size.
That is not how the author describes this.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Describe each side project by its goal, impact and your approach, not by a bare link.

questions.q: Follow the results-impact-contribution model for side projects, as opposed to only linking to your ____ profile.
questions.explain: The author warns against only linking to your GitHub profile with no explanation.
questions.rule: Explain the project; do not only link it.

questions.q: A candidate has a small CLI tool that formats config files. Which entry would the author prefer?
options: A personal CLI project to do config formatting that I find interesting and have kept up on weekends
Built a CLI that formats config files, saving 20 minutes per review for a 12-person team, in Rust
Config tool, https link to the repository, available for use under an open-source licence for everyone
A CLI that formats files and has several options, a short README and a few helper functions inside
optionExplain: It is casual and says nothing about impact.
Right: purpose, impact and tool.
Mostly a link and a licence, with no story.
It lists features without a goal or a result.
questions.explain: The strong entry says what the project does for people, with a figure and the tool.
questions.rule: Say why the project matters.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a generic description of a REST API project shows the complexity behind the work.
questions.explain: The author says a generic description could hide a Hello World-like simple project or a complex implementation, so it does not show the complexity.
questions.rule: Detail separates a complex build from a simple one.

questions.q: Which non-trivial elements did the author's improved REST API entry mention?
options: OAuth and rate limiting
Docker and Kubernetes
HATEOAS and content negotiation
Unit tests and continuous integration
optionExplain: These are real API topics, but they are not the ones the author names.
Common tools, but they are not in the case.
Right: the rewrite named these.
Standard practice, not named as the complex elements.
questions.explain: The improved entry listed HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State) and content negotiation, which the author says add detail on complexity.
questions.rule: Name the hard parts of the project.
questions.teaches: The improved REST API entry lists the not-so-trivial elements HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State) and content negotiation, which shows the complexity behind the project.

questions.q: A candidate contributes to an open-source library and wants a line on her resume. Which fits the author's approach?
options: Contributed a parser fix to a library used by 3,000 projects, cutting crash reports by a quarter, in Go
Active open-source contributor who enjoys giving back to the wider developer community in free time
Open-source work on GitHub: link to my profile with all contributions over the last several years
Submitted pull requests to many popular projects and received many comments from the maintainers
optionExplain: Right: impact, numbers and technology.
A claim about attitude, with no result or contribution.
A bare link, which the author warns against.
It lists activity but not what changed.
questions.explain: The author says the rewritten project entries mention impact, numbers and the technologies used.
questions.rule: Treat open-source work like any other result.
questions.teaches: The author's rewritten project entries mention specifics such as the impact, numbers and the technologies used, and the same approach applies to open-source contributions.

questions.q: Where in the resume should tech-adjacent activities such as running a meetup be placed?
options: At the very top, since they show more energy than any job entry on the page
In place of the work experience for candidates with less than two years of work
Inside the contact section, next to the phone number and the email address
Toward the end, after the main experience
optionExplain: The core experience comes first.
The activities do not replace experience.
Contact details have their own place.
Right: they add to the picture but do not lead.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next gives the author's placement and tips.
questions.rule: At the end of the resume, list tech-adjacent activities with their impact and a specific link.

questions.q: Many resumes are dry, so a standout extracurricular activity can make a good resume even ____.
questions.explain: The author says standout activities can lift a good resume.
questions.rule: Standout activities add value to a dry resume.

questions.q: A candidate ran a coding club for school students. Which line follows the author's advice?
options: Volunteered at a school coding club in my spare time, which was a great and rewarding experience
Member of the school coding club, and a supporter of the education charity that funds its work
Taught children about technology at a club, among a number of other volunteer jobs during the year
Ran a weekly coding club for 40 students over two years, with 12 learners now in computing degrees
optionExplain: It states feelings, not impact.
It names membership and a charity with no results.
It is vague and gives no numbers.
Right: it has an impact and numbers.
questions.explain: The strong line shows the scale and the effect. The others give attitude or titles.
questions.rule: Show the scale of the activity and its effect.

questions.q: True or false: The author says to link a blog's home page rather than one specific, high-quality article.
questions.explain: The author says to link a specific, high-quality article the reader can read, so the reader sees your best piece at once.
questions.rule: Link one strong piece, not a general page.

questions.q: A candidate applying for a job in Manchester plans to list her support for a Chelsea away-game supporters' group. What does the author warn?
options: It would be taken as a sign of long-term loyalty, which recruiters in the UK like to see
Listing it could trigger unconscious bias, so pick neutral activities
It is fine as long as the team is mentioned only in the cover letter and never in the CV
It would be ignored, since recruiters pay attention only to the technical parts of a resume
optionExplain: The author warns against it.
Right: the author uses a version of this example.
The warning is about bias in either document.
The author says it could trigger bias.

questions.rule: List neutral activities only.
questions.teaches: Be mindful of listing neutral extracurricular activities: for example, when applying in Manchester, UK, listing that you enjoy supporting Chelsea on their away games could trigger unconscious bias.

questions.q: A candidate organised a hackathon. Besides its impact, what else does the author ask you to say about an activity?
options: How many hours per week it took, so the reader sees how much free time you give
Which sponsors paid for it, so the reader sees the scale of the budget involved
How demanding it was, with a link to a high-quality resource you created
Which of your friends joined, to show that you can build a social network

Sponsors are not named.
Right: difficulty and quality links are on the author's list.
Friends are not named.
questions.explain: The author says to talk about an activity's impact, how demanding it was, and to link high-quality resources you have created.
questions.rule: Give impact, difficulty and a quality link.
questions.teaches: Talk about what an activity's impact was and how demanding it was, and link to high-quality resources that you have created.

questions.q: A resume says only: learned Scala. What would the author like to read in addition?
options: Why you learned it and what you did with it
The names of the courses you took and the dates you took them over the year
How much you enjoyed it compared with the languages you used before then
A long list of books about Scala that you have read or plan to read this year
optionExplain: Right: reasons and results add value.
Courses are details, not the reasons or results the author prefers.
Enjoyment is not the point.
Reading lists are not what the author asks for.

questions.rule: Add a short note on why you learned a skill, what it changed and what you want to do with it.

questions.q: Learning new and useful skills ____ is a positive trait that hiring managers will appreciate.
questions.explain: The word is proactively: the author values people who learn without being told.
questions.rule: Show that you learn on your own initiative.

questions.q: A candidate learned Rust to speed up a data job. Which line follows the author's advice?
options: Self-taught Rust, which I find to be an interesting language with a growing community
Learned Rust to speed up our nightly data job, cutting it from 3 hours to 40 minutes
Completed a Rust tutorial series and later read the language book from beginning to end
Familiar with Rust, among a range of other modern languages and tools for backend work
optionExplain: Interest is not the same as the reason and the effect.
Right: why, how it helped and a result.
It lists effort but not why or what changed.
A claim of familiarity with no story.
questions.explain: The author wants why the skill was picked up and how it affected the role.
questions.rule: State the reason and the effect.

questions.q: True or false: The author lists picking up a technology to speed up a project as a reason worth mentioning on a resume.
questions.explain: The author says to mention if you picked up a technology to speed up a project, to stretch yourself or for other reasons.
questions.rule: Name the reason you learned it.
questions.teaches: Do mention if you picked up a technology to speed up a project, to stretch yourself, or for other reasons.

questions.q: A candidate switched from Java to Go and doubts a learning note deserves a line. What does the author, as a hiring manager, say?
options: He skips them, since a hiring manager checks the skills list first and the story afterwards
He values them only for juniors, because senior engineers are assumed to learn on the job
He wishes he saw more learnings mentioned on resumes, because they make the resume more valuable
He values them only when the language is the one the company already uses in its stack
optionExplain: He says he wishes to see more of them.

Right: this is the author's own view.
No such condition is given.
questions.explain: The author writes that as a hiring manager he wishes he would see more of these learnings on resumes, and that they make the resume more valuable.
questions.rule: A learning note adds value that readers want.
questions.teaches: As a hiring manager, the author says he wishes he would see more learnings mentioned on resumes; it is information hands-on recruiters and hiring managers value.

questions.q: A candidate's last project was cancelled before launch. What does the author say about listing it?
options: You can leave it out, as you do not need to list what does not show you well
You must list every project, since an unlisted one looks like something you hide
You should list it but describe it as launched, to avoid questions in the first screen
You should list it with a note about the cancellation, to show you are honest
optionExplain: Right: omission is allowed.
The author says you do not have to.
That would be untrue.
The author says you do not need to highlight negatives.

questions.rule: Leave out failed projects, low grades and similar points; do not claim anything untrue.

questions.q: You do not need to highlight ____ from past experiences.
questions.explain: The author says not to highlight negatives, while also not claiming untrue things.
questions.rule: Do not highlight negatives.

questions.q: Sort each item: can the author's advice let you leave it out, or would leaving it out be dishonest?

items.t: A project that was cancelled before it shipped
A low grade average from university
A side project that never worked well
A degree you did not complete, listed as finished
A job title higher than the one you held
A technology you have never used, listed as known

questions.explain: The author lets you leave out things that do not show you well, but not claim untrue things.
questions.rule: Omit weak points, but do not invent strong ones.

questions.q: Two candidates have a low grade average. One omits it; the other writes a higher figure. Which matches the author's advice?
options: The second: a higher figure is a rounding of the truth that the author accepts
Both: the author treats leaving out and misstating as the same kind of selling
Neither: every resume must show its grade average, however low it may be
The first: leaving it out is allowed, while a false figure is not
optionExplain: The author says not to claim untrue things.
The author separates the two.
The author says low GPA can be left out.

questions.rule: Omit, but never falsify.

questions.q: A candidate's bootcamp project failed to launch. How should she treat it, by the author's advice?
options: Describe it as a success, since nobody can verify the outcome of a bootcamp project
Write a paragraph on why it failed, so the reader sees how honest she is about it
Leave it out and show the work that did succeed, without claiming that it launched
Move it to the top, because failures show that a candidate takes on difficult projects
optionExplain: That would be untrue.
The author says not to highlight negatives.
Right: omit, but be truthful.
The author gives no such advice.
questions.explain: The section opens by saying the resume should sell the professional you for the position, so a failed project that does not help that sale can be dropped.
questions.rule: Drop what hurts; do not invent what helps.
questions.teaches: The author says your resume should sell the professional you for the position you apply for, with the recruiter and the hiring manager as its audience.

questions.q: A volunteer entry has many details but no figures. What would the author most likely suggest?
options: Add more detail on the partnerships, because they show the scale of the work
Cut it down and focus on what you did and the results, with data
Keep the entry as it is, since volunteer work is not scored in the same way as paid work
Remove the entry, since volunteer work does not belong on a professional resume
optionExplain: The author removed partnerships because they added little.
Right: focused and measurable.
The author wants it improved.
The author keeps it, in a better form.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next walks through the case.
questions.rule: Replace team wording, passive roles and soft modifiers with your own actions, data and links.

questions.q: Which problems did the author find in the before version's work experience? Select all that apply.
options: References to the team over the person
Passive roles such as team member or took part
Missing contact details
Soft modifiers such as sometimes and occasionally
Too many numbers
optionExplain: Right: the team came first.
Right: passive wording.
The author does not mention contact details.
Right: they make the contribution seem small.
The author says the case lacked data, not that it had too much.
questions.explain: The work experience undersold the candidate through team wording, passive roles and soft modifiers.

questions.q: A volunteer entry says the candidate helped organise events. The author's rewrite pattern suggests which version?
options: Built a local group of 500 developers and organised 30+ events and hackathons
Helped in the organisation of several events for the group in my city across the year
Volunteer at a developer group, with partnerships with sponsors and a venue for the monthly meeting
Took part in a group of developers and sometimes occasionally led events in the area
optionExplain: Right: figures and ownership.
Passive and vague.
Partnerships added little, according to the author.
It uses the soft wording the author flagged.
questions.explain: The rewrite used data and active words, and left out partnerships.
questions.rule: Use figures and an active voice.

questions.q: True or false: In the rewritten volunteer entry, the author kept the partnerships and left out the press coverage.
questions.explain: It was the other way round: partnerships added little, so the rewrite left them out and pointed to press coverage for credibility.
questions.rule: Prefer proof over a list of names.
questions.teaches: In the rewritten volunteer entry the author left out partnerships that did not add much and instead pointed to press coverage, which gives further credibility to the activity.

questions.q: In the before version, what did the author say about the bareGo project description?
options: It was too technical for a recruiter, and it needed to be shortened to a single line
It listed the wrong language, and the person needed to correct the technology name
It was fine as written, and only the volunteer section needed editing in the end
It was casual, and did not say why the project was interesting or challenging
optionExplain: The author's complaint is that it is casual and generic.
No such mistake is reported.
The author lists it among the problems.
Right: it needed a goal and a challenge.
questions.explain: The author says the bareGo description was quite casual (this project is usually) and did not answer why it was interesting or challenging.
questions.rule: Say why the project is interesting.
questions.teaches: The before bareGo description was casual and did not say why the project was interesting or challenging; the rewrite states its goal and the complex problems it solves.

questions.q: A candidate's volunteer entry runs to six lines of detail and has no data. What did the author say about such an entry?
options: It is not bad, but it lacks data and is verbose, so it should be focused on what you did and the results
It is the strongest kind of entry, because detail is what separates volunteer work from paid work
It should be expanded further, with partnerships and sponsors, so that the scale of the group is clear
It should be moved to the cover letter, since volunteer work does not belong on the resume page
optionExplain: Right: the author's wording for the before entry.
The author calls it verbose and lacking in data.
Partnerships were left out in the rewrite.
The author keeps volunteer work on the resume.
questions.explain: The author says the before volunteer entry put in quite a few details, but lacked data and was verbose.
questions.rule: Focus on what you did and the results; cut the rest.
questions.teaches: The author calls the before volunteer entry verbose and lacking in data, though not bad, and says the rewrite focuses on what the candidate did and the results.

questions.section: Write a Resume for That Job
questions.q: An advert asks for Kotlin and Android. You have web, Android and Kotlin work. What should the resume do?
options: List the work in the order you did it, so the reader sees the whole timeline first
Show the Android and Kotlin work first and move the web work down
Show web work first, since it covers the widest range of skills of the three areas
Give all three areas equal space, so that no one reading can accuse you of leaving out any
optionExplain: Order of time helps a timeline, not a match.
Right: lead with what the advert asks for.
The job asks for Android and Kotlin.
Equal space hides the match.
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next gives the author's advice.
questions.rule: Re-edit your resume for each job so it echoes the job description and puts the matching experience first.

questions.section: Write a Resume for That Job
questions.q: To make your resume stand out, write it for that specific job ____.
questions.explain: The author says you need to write it for the specific job description.
questions.rule: Write for the job description.

questions.section: Write a Resume for That Job
questions.q: A backend job asks for Python and cloud experience. Your resume's first bullets cover mobile apps. What should you do?
options: Keep the order as it is, because the recruiter will look through all the bullets anyway
Add a line at the end saying the resume was written for another type of role than this one
Move the Python and cloud work to the top and reword it using the advert's language
Remove every bullet that does not mention Python, however good the results in it appear
optionExplain: Readers scan the top; the match must be there.
That signals a poor fit.
Right: reorder and echo the language.
The advice is to move or trim what does not help, not to delete good work blindly.
questions.explain: The tailored version leads with matching experience and uses the advert's words.
questions.rule: Lead with the match; echo the language.

questions.section: Write a Resume for That Job
questions.q: Sort each edit: does it tailor the resume to a Kotlin-focused Android role, or does it work against that aim?

items.t: Move the Android and Kotlin projects to the top
Reword a bullet to use the advert's phrase about mobile performance
Shorten the web experience and move it lower
Add three extra paragraphs about unrelated web projects
Remove the word Kotlin so the resume reads less specific
Use a generic bullet that matches no advert in particular

questions.explain: Tailoring puts the match first and echoes the advert. The others dilute the match or remove it.
questions.rule: Every edit should help the match.

questions.section: Write a Resume for That Job
questions.q: A candidate gets plenty of recruiter calls with one generic resume. Does the author say she needs to tailor?
options: Yes, always, because a generic resume works only by accident and will fail on the next application
No, because recruiters ignore tailoring and only notice years of experience and company names
Yes, but only for senior positions, because junior roles never have a job description to copy from
Not necessarily: it means her profile stands out or she has little competition for the roles she applies to
optionExplain: The author sets the tailoring advice for positions with many qualified applicants.
The author recommends tailoring where competition is high.
The author does not limit it to senior roles.
Right: it depends on competition.
questions.explain: The author says that if you have no problem getting recruiter calls, you either have a standout profile or little competition.
questions.rule: Tailoring matters most where competition is high.
questions.teaches: If you have no problem getting recruiter calls, it either means your profile is a standout one or that you have little competition for the roles you apply for.

questions.section: Write a Resume for That Job
questions.q: A candidate applies to ten similar roles in one afternoon and sends the same resume to each. What does the author's reasoning suggest?
options: She saves time, which the author calls the main advantage in a crowded field of applicants
She gains consistency, which recruiters reward more than any wording that matches an advert
She avoids errors, since changing a resume for each role risks mistakes that recruiters notice
She loses the chance to echo each advert, and for popular roles the extra work is what gets a reply
optionExplain: The author says more work is needed to stand out.

A veteran of older templates, which reviewers read as long experience
A weak eye for detail and poor skill at presenting yourself
optionExplain: Variety can look intentional in design work, but here it reads as an error.
The author does not describe such slips as forgiven; they colour how the rest is read.
Nothing in the chapter links uneven formatting to experience.
Inconsistent formatting suggests that you lack attention to detail and do not present yourself well.
questions.explain: The author reads uneven formatting as a signal about you, not just a cosmetic flaw. The card next explains the idea.
questions.rule: Keep font sizes, alignment and spacing consistent, and align elements with tabs rather than spaces.

questions.q: Align elements with tabs rather than spacing things to be approximately ____.
questions.explain: Spacing by eye leaves elements only approximately aligned; tabs make them line up the same way each time.
questions.rule: Keep font sizes, alignment and spacing consistent, and align elements with tabs rather than spaces.

questions.q: Your dates are lined up by typing spaces until they look level. What fix follows the author's advice?
options: Add more spaces until each date lines up in your word processor's preview
Set the dates with a tab stop so they line up the same way on every role and entry
Switch the dates to italics so that any misalignment is less noticeable
Make the dates bold so the eye is drawn away from where they sit
optionExplain: More spaces is the same approximate method and breaks when anything shifts.
A tab stop gives the same alignment every time, so it holds when the text changes.
Italics change the look of the dates but leave them misaligned.
Bold draws the eye to the dates and makes any misalignment easier to see.
questions.explain: The author contrasts aligning with tabs against spacing things to be approximately close.
questions.rule: Keep font sizes, alignment and spacing consistent, and align elements with tabs rather than spaces.

questions.q: Sort each formatting choice: consistent, or inconsistent?

items.t: Same font size for every company name
Dates aligned with a tab on each role
Section headings in one size throughout
A company name in 12 pt in one job and 10 pt in the next
Dates that wander a few characters between roles
Text pushed into place with the space bar

questions.explain: Consistency means that similar items look identical. Differences in size, drifting alignment and manual spacing make a resume look inconsistent.
questions.rule: Keep font sizes, alignment and spacing consistent, and align elements with tabs rather than spaces.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, uneven alignment matters because it suggests the candidate lacks attention to detail.
questions.explain: The author says inconsistent formatting conveys that you do not have much attention to detail.
questions.rule: Keep font sizes, alignment and spacing consistent, and align elements with tabs rather than spaces.

questions.q: A staff engineer's resume has uneven font sizes and slightly misaligned dates, but strong content. What does the author say follows?
options: Certain rejection, since senior candidates are held to a higher standard than juniors
No effect, since only junior candidates are ever judged on their layout
It reads as a deliberate design choice, which senior people are trusted to make
Not a rejection by itself, but it still suggests weak attention to detail
optionExplain: The author does not say that seniors are rejected on formatting alone.
The slip still sends a signal at every level, even if it is not fatal for seniors.
Uneven sizes and drifting dates look like errors, not decisions.
The author says that for more senior candidates this alone will not result in rejection, but it conveys weak attention to detail.
questions.explain: Seniority softens the penalty, but the impression remains.
questions.teaches: For more senior candidates inconsistent formatting alone will not lead to rejection, but it still conveys weak attention to detail.
questions.rule: Keep font sizes, alignment and spacing consistent, and align elements with tabs rather than spaces.

questions.q: A bullet ends with the words and so on. According to the author, what does a phrase like that signal?
options: A confident writer who trusts the reader to guess the rest of the list
Careless writing that makes the whole resume look unprofessional
A careful editor who saved space by not listing every single item
A flexible candidate who is open to many more kinds of work as needed
optionExplain: The reader cannot guess a list they were never given, so it reads as vague.
The author names etc. and and so on as sloppy phrases that hurt the impression the resume makes.
Saving space is a fair goal, but vagueness is not how the author wants it done.
Nothing in the chapter reads such phrases as openness; they read as careless.
questions.explain: The author treats such phrases as a mistake to fix. The card next shows what to write instead.
questions.rule: Replace etc., and so on and slang with specific items and clear, neat full sentences.

questions.q: Use clear and neat grammar, and ____ sentences.
questions.explain: The author asks for full sentences and neat grammar in place of etc., slang and fragments.
questions.rule: Replace etc., and so on and slang with specific items and clear, neat full sentences.

questions.q: Which rewrite of Fixed bugs, did some testing and stuff, etc. follows the author's advice?
options: Fixed loads of bugs, did a bunch of testing, plus other things as needed
Bug fixing, testing, stuff like that, among a range of other duties
Fixed 25 checkout bugs and wrote a regression test for each
Fixed bugs, tested and so on, as the team required from week to week
optionExplain: Loads and a bunch are slang, and plus other things is still vague.
The fragment keeps stuff like that and among other duties, both filler.
The rewrite names the work, uses a full sentence and carries no filler.
And so on is the exact phrase the author warns against.
questions.explain: The fix is to name the real items in a full, neat sentence.
questions.rule: Replace etc., and so on and slang with specific items and clear, neat full sentences.

questions.q: Sort each line: specific wording, or vague phrasing?

items.t: Built the billing service and its test suite
Led the migration of three databases
Wrote clear runbooks for on-call engineers
Worked with Java, Kotlin, etc.
Did loads of cool stuff for the team
Managed servers, deployments and so on

questions.explain: Specific lines name the work in full sentences. Vague lines rely on etc., and so on or slang.
questions.rule: Replace etc., and so on and slang with specific items and clear, neat full sentences.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, replacing and so on with full sentences means you should write longer, paragraph-style entries.
questions.explain: The same chapter asks you to avoid large blocks of text and long sentences, so neat means clear and concise, not long.
questions.rule: Replace etc., and so on and slang with specific items and clear, neat full sentences.

questions.q: A developer has strong, relevant experience but writes it up in slang and fragments. What does the author expect the reader to take away?
options: The content is overshadowed, as the page looks careless, rushed and hard to follow
The content speaks for itself, so the style is read as a casual personality
Only the first page suffers, since later pages are skimmed with less care
The style helps, since a relaxed tone makes the candidate seem approachable
optionExplain: The author says good and relevant experience can become hard to understand because of poor formatting and sloppy phrasing.
Slang does not read as personality to a recruiter scanning for seconds.
The chapter gives no reason to think that later pages are excused.
The author lists unprofessional language as a mistake, not as a strength.
questions.explain: Writing quality is part of the format. It can bury strong content.
questions.teaches: The author's example resume had decent content, yet its sloppy language and formatting gave the impression of poor attention to detail and made it harder to read and comprehend.
questions.rule: Replace etc., and so on and slang with specific items and clear, neat full sentences.

questions.q: Your resume says: Did QA for the Falcon and Osprey programs. A recruiter at another firm reads it. What will they likely understand?
options: Very little about the work, since the program names are internal ones
That you tested two flagship products, since the names sound important
That you worked on aircraft, since the names suggest flying machines
That you have strong QA skills, since you wrote the term out in full
optionExplain: Names that only your company uses carry no meaning outside it.
Importance is something the reader would have to know, not guess from a name.
A guess from the name is a guess; the recruiter has nothing solid to go on.
Writing QA does tell them the field, but not what you tested or achieved.
questions.explain: A recruiter outside the company has no way to decode these names. The card next shows what to write instead.
questions.rule: Do not rely on internal acronyms, project names or jargon; describe the work in terms an outsider can follow.

questions.q: Assume the reader of your resume knows ____ about you.
questions.explain: The author says to convey skills and tell a story assuming the reader knows nothing about you.
questions.rule: Do not rely on internal acronyms, project names or jargon; describe the work in terms an outsider can follow.

questions.q: A bullet reads: Migrated Atlas to Beacon before the Q3 freeze. Atlas and Beacon are internal systems. What follows the author's advice?
options: Keep the names, since the hiring manager can ask about them in an interview
Add a footnote listing every internal system you have ever worked on
Describe them by purpose, e.g. a billing database and a payment service, not by internal name
Replace them with the version numbers, which are shorter to write
optionExplain: The resume has to work before any interview happens, since it decides who gets invited.
A longer list of internal names adds more material the reader cannot decode.
Plain descriptions let a stranger see what you moved and why it mattered.
Numbers are as internal as names and tell the reader even less.
questions.explain: Replace the names with what the systems do.
questions.rule: Do not rely on internal acronyms, project names or jargon; describe the work in terms an outsider can follow.

questions.q: Sort each line: can an outsider follow it, or does it need inside knowledge?

items.t: Built the mobile checkout for an online grocery chain
Cut deployment time from 40 to 8 minutes
Wrote the test plan for a payments app used in 12 countries
Led QA on the Kestrel release train
Owned the TRX-9 migration
Supported the Q3 Nimbus programme

questions.explain: Plain descriptions, numbers and well-known product types travel. Code names and internal programme labels do not.
questions.rule: Do not rely on internal acronyms, project names or jargon; describe the work in terms an outsider can follow.
