questions.q: True or false: According to the author, internal acronyms are fine on a resume if your former colleagues would all understand them.
questions.explain: Your colleagues are not the audience. The author says the reader is an outside recruiter or hiring manager who does not know you or your company.
questions.rule: Do not rely on internal acronyms, project names or jargon; describe the work in terms an outsider can follow.

questions.q: A hardware engineer writes: QA for the N-series and E-series programs. According to the author, who would understand those labels?
options: Any recruiter, since manufacturing labels are common across the whole industry
Few outside the company, so a recruiter could not tell what was tested
Only recruiters who have worked for the same company in the past
Hiring managers, who are expected to learn each employer's naming style
optionExplain: Industry-wide naming is the exception; the labels in question are the company's own.
The author's own example makes the point that the recruiter will not know such labels, nor would most people outside the company.
Even then the first screener is rarely a former colleague, so the page is not read by insiders.
No part of the process asks a hiring manager to decode a candidate's private vocabulary.
questions.explain: Inside labels fail at the first read, before anyone can ask about them.
questions.teaches: In the author's example (QA for two named programs) the recruiter would not know what the first one was, and neither would most people outside the company.
questions.rule: Do not rely on internal acronyms, project names or jargon; describe the work in terms an outsider can follow.

questions.q: You have mobile and backend experience and apply for a backend job. Which of your examples should come first in each role?
options: The mobile ones, since they are the newest technology on your resume
The ones you enjoyed most, since enthusiasm shows in how you write
Whichever came first in time, since order of events is the safest order
The backend ones, since that is the position being recruited for
optionExplain: Newness is not the test; relevance to the job is.
Enjoyment matters to you but tells the recruiter nothing about fit.
Time order is neutral, yet it can bury what this reader cares about.
The reader is hiring for the backend role, so that is what they look for first.
questions.explain: The ordering should serve the job being applied for. The card next gives the author's reason.
questions.rule: Put the experience most relevant to the position you are applying for first.

questions.q: The audience of your resume is the recruiter hiring for that ____ position.
questions.explain: The author says the audience is the recruiter filling the specific position you are applying for.
questions.rule: Put the experience most relevant to the position you are applying for first.

questions.q: You are applying for a site reliability job and also have some app-development work. How should one role's bullets be arranged?
options: Keep a strict task order, whatever the job needs
Put the reliability work first, app development after it
Open with the most impressive project, even if it is unrelated
Put the app development first because it took most of your time
optionExplain: Strict order is easy for the writer, but it does not serve this reader.
Reliability work answers the recruiter's question first, and the rest follows as support.
Impressive work in another field is not what this reader is looking for.
Time spent does not match what the job asks for, and the first lines count most.
questions.explain: Order examples by what this job needs.
questions.rule: Put the experience most relevant to the position you are applying for first.

questions.q: You apply for a data engineering role and have web and data work. Sort each choice: tailored to the job, or ignoring it?

items.t: Pipeline work listed before web work
Warehouse design bullets first in each role
Spark jobs described near the top of the page
Web UI work first because it came first in time
The same ordering sent to a web agency
Data work buried below unrelated side projects

questions.explain: The first lines under each role should match the target role; the ordering of the page decides what a quick reader sees.
questions.rule: Put the experience most relevant to the position you are applying for first.

questions.q: Which reader should decide how you order your examples, according to the author?
options: The average recruiter, so one ordering suits every position
You, ranking your work from proudest to least proud
The hiring manager at the best-paying company you could reach
The recruiter filling the position you are applying for
optionExplain: One ordering for all positions is the untailored approach the author warns about.
Pride is a private measure; the reader's need is what counts.
The author never ties ordering to pay or prestige.
The author says the audience is the recruiter who is recruiting for that specific position.
questions.explain: The reader of a resume is a particular person with a particular job to fill.
questions.rule: Put the experience most relevant to the position you are applying for first.

questions.q: A candidate with frontend and backend experience applies for a frontend job. According to the author, which examples come first?
options: The frontend ones, even though your backend experience is also strong and relevant
The backend ones, since backend work is generally seen as harder
Equal numbers of each, so neither side seems favoured
The ones from the most recent job, regardless of which field they are in
optionExplain: The author's own illustration: with a frontend position in view, start with the frontend examples, not the backend ones.
Difficulty is not the standard; relevance to the position is.
Balance sounds fair, but it does not tailor the page to the reader.
Recency is secondary to relevance for the position being filled.
questions.explain: Even strong backend work waits when the job is frontend.
questions.teaches: The author's own example: a candidate with both frontend and backend experience applying for a frontend position should start with the frontend examples, not the backend ones.
questions.rule: Put the experience most relevant to the position you are applying for first.

questions.q: A resume says: I am a team player and a fast learner who can hit the ground running. What does the author say that tells a recruiter?
options: That you are a strong candidate, since the traits are the ones employers want
That you are confident, which is the main thing a recruiter looks for
Nothing useful, because it holds no facts, examples or specifics a reader can check
That you are self-aware, since you have named your own strengths
optionExplain: Wanted traits only count when something backs them up.
Confidence without evidence is easy to claim, so it tells the reader little.
The author calls it a cliche in its current form, because it gives the recruiter no information.
Self-description is exactly what the author wants replaced with evidence.
questions.explain: A claim without evidence is just a cliche. The card next shows what to use instead.
questions.rule: Replace trait claims such as team player with specific results from your experience entries.

questions.q: Demonstrate any trait through what you have ____.
questions.explain: The author wants traits shown through what you delivered, not stated.
questions.rule: Replace trait claims such as team player with specific results from your experience entries.

questions.q: Which line best replaces excellent communicator in a developer's experience entry, following the author?
options: Communicates effectively with colleagues in every situation and on all teams
Known by peers as a person who can explain hard ideas in plain language
Presented the migration plan to 40 engineers and wrote the onboarding guide for new hires
Strong communication skills developed over many years in tech roles
optionExplain: It restates the claim without a single fact to check.
It adds what others think, but still gives no example or specific.
It names what you did and for whom, so the reader can judge the trait themselves.
It adds years, but nothing the reader can verify or picture.
questions.explain: Specifics let the reader conclude the trait for themselves.
questions.rule: Replace trait claims such as team player with specific results from your experience entries.

questions.q: Sort each line: evidence of a trait, or a cliche?

items.t: Ran three onboarding sessions for new starters
Cut weekly reporting from six hours to one by automating it
Mentored two interns who both received full-time offers
Self-motivated go-getter who thrives under pressure
Passionate, hard-working team player
Fast learner who can hit the ground running

questions.explain: Evidence is something that happened, with detail. Cliches are claims about the person with nothing behind them.
questions.rule: Replace trait claims such as team player with specific results from your experience entries.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a trait stated as a claim persuades a recruiter more than the same trait shown by an achievement.
questions.explain: The author expects the achievement to persuade, since the claim gives the recruiter nothing to check.
questions.rule: Replace trait claims such as team player with specific results from your experience entries.

questions.q: You still want the recruiter to know you value teamwork, and your resume is full. According to the author, where could the claim go?
options: In a cover letter, but even there backed up by examples of the work
In the resume summary as a bold line, which is the safest place for a claim
In a skills section, rated out of five like your programming languages
Nowhere, because a trait you cannot show should be left out of everything
optionExplain: The author says that if it matters, save it for a cover letter, and even there back it up with examples.
A bold claim is still a claim, and bold inside the resume is also discouraged.
Self-ratings backfire, and a trait is not a skill that can be rated.
The author does allow it in a cover letter, with proof.
questions.explain: Claims can have a home in a cover letter, but only with examples.
questions.teaches: If you think traits like these are important, the author says to save them for a cover letter, and even there to back them up with examples.
questions.rule: Replace trait claims such as team player with specific results from your experience entries.

questions.q: A recruiter has a large pile of resumes. According to the author, how long will they glance at yours?
options: For several minutes, since a shortlist deserves a full careful read
For as long as the resume is, since each page gets equal attention
For about ten minutes, but only if the first page grabs them at once
For seconds, so large blocks of text mostly go unread
optionExplain: A careful read comes later, after the first scan has chosen who to read.
Attention is not spread evenly; the first glance decides.
Ten minutes is far beyond what the author describes.
The author says recruiters glance at a resume for seconds.
questions.explain: Seconds are all you can count on. The card next shows what that means for your wording.
questions.rule: Write short sentences, avoid large blocks of text and edit your descriptions ruthlessly.

questions.q: Avoid large blocks of text or long ____.
questions.explain: The author asks for short sentences and no large text blocks.
questions.rule: Write short sentences, avoid large blocks of text and edit your descriptions ruthlessly.

questions.q: A project bullet runs to five lines. Which rewrite best follows the author?
options: Responsible for redesigning the payments service across several phases and teams
Rewrote the payments service in Go, cutting failed charges by 30% in a year
Rewrote the payments service in Go. It was a big project. Failed charges dropped
Payments service redesign: a long project with much planning, coding and testing
optionExplain: It stays long and vague, with responsibility language instead of facts.
One short line holds the action, the tool and the result.
It splits into several sentences, adding length and padding without more facts.
It is shorter in form but still carries no concrete result.
questions.explain: Cut words that do not carry a fact.
questions.rule: Write short sentences, avoid large blocks of text and edit your descriptions ruthlessly.

questions.q: Sort each entry: easy to read at a glance, or hard?
groups: Easy to read at a glance
Hard to read at a glance

items.t: Three short bullets under a role
Sentences that hold one fact each
A trimmed description in which every word carries a fact
A seven-line paragraph describing the whole project
One sentence with five clauses joined by and
A job entry made of three long paragraphs

questions.explain: Short, single-fact lines support a glance. Long paragraphs and chained clauses do not.
questions.rule: Write short sentences, avoid large blocks of text and edit your descriptions ruthlessly.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, distilling years of experience into a few short sentences is easy, so editing can stay light.
questions.explain: The author says it is not easy and that you must edit ruthlessly anyway.
questions.rule: Write short sentences, avoid large blocks of text and edit your descriptions ruthlessly.

questions.q: A candidate's bullets each run to four lines. According to the author's recap, how long should a bullet rarely exceed?
options: Four lines, as long as the sentences are short
One line, with no exceptions at all
Six lines, if the project was a large one
Two lines, which keeps each bullet to a glance
optionExplain: Four lines is what the candidate already has; the recap sets a lower mark.
One line is stricter than the author, who says rarely more than two.
Project size is not a reason in the recap to allow more lines.
The recap asks for short sentences and bullet points that rarely run past two lines.
questions.explain: A two-line limit keeps each bullet a single glance.
questions.teaches: The chapter's recap suggests short sentences and bullet points that rarely run to more than two lines.
questions.rule: Write short sentences, avoid large blocks of text and edit your descriptions ruthlessly.

questions.q: A resume has a photo, phone, email, LinkedIn, GitHub, a website, Instagram and Medium. What would the author change?
options: Keep the photo but remove the contact details that are less formal
Remove the photo and keep no more than four contact details
Keep every contact detail but crop the photo to a smaller size
Move the contact details to the bottom, below the photo, in one list
optionExplain: Both parts of the header are the problem, not just the informal links.
The author recommends skipping the photo and choosing at most four contact details.
Size is not the issue with a photo; the bias it introduces is.
Moving them does not reduce the number or the bias.
questions.explain: Both the photo and the long contact list work against the resume. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Leave off your photo and list no more than four contact details or profile links, compact at the top.

questions.q: For contact details, do not share more than ____.
questions.explain: The author sets a cap of four contact details and social profile links.
questions.rule: Leave off your photo and list no more than four contact details or profile links, compact at the top.

questions.q: Your header lists email, phone, LinkedIn, GitHub, a personal site and Twitter, and you have a studio portrait. What follows the author?
options: Keep the portrait but cut Twitter, since six items is only slightly high
Keep all six and shrink the font so the header uses fewer lines
Drop the portrait and cut the header to four, keeping the most relevant
Drop the contact details and keep the portrait as a visual identity
optionExplain: Six is two over the cap, and the photo remains a source of bias.
Shrinking does not reduce what the reader must sort through.
That removes the bias risk and brings the header within the cap.
Without contact details the resume cannot be answered, and the photo adds bias.
questions.explain: Photo out, four contacts in.
questions.rule: Leave off your photo and list no more than four contact details or profile links, compact at the top.

questions.q: Sort each header choice: a good use of space, or wasted?

items.t: Email and phone in one compact line at the top
A link to a GitHub with recent projects
Only the four most relevant contacts
A photo beside your name
Seven profiles including Skype and Instagram
Upwork and Medium added to LinkedIn, GitHub and a website

questions.explain: A compact set of useful contacts is fine. Photos and a long profile list add bias or clutter.
questions.rule: Leave off your photo and list no more than four contact details or profile links, compact at the top.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, most recruiters will click through every social profile you list.
questions.explain: Most will not. The author says most recruiters and hiring managers will not even click through on these.
questions.rule: Leave off your photo and list no more than four contact details or profile links, compact at the top.

questions.q: You apply in a country where a photo is required. According to the author, what kind of photo should you use?
options: A professional, positive photo, not a grumpy passport-style shot taken in a booth
Any recent photo, since a required photo has no effect on how you are viewed
A relaxed holiday photo, which shows personality and approachability
A serious headshot with a neutral face, which is the safest style in a formal setting
optionExplain: The author says that in the rare countries where it is required, use a professional photo that makes you look good.
The author wants the photo to help you, not be treated as neutral.
A casual photo is not a professional one.
The author advises a smile or positive vibe, not a mugshot-like neutral face.
questions.explain: Where a photo is required, make it a good one.
questions.teaches: In the rare countries where a photo is required, the author says to use a professional one that makes you look good, smiling and avoiding grumpy, passport-like shots.
questions.rule: Leave off your photo and list no more than four contact details or profile links, compact at the top.

questions.q: Which reason does the author give for skipping the photo?
options: A photo introduces bias into how the reader sees you
Photos make the file too large for most recruiters to open
Photos are banned from resumes by hiring law in most countries
Photos make the page look less professional than plain text does
optionExplain: The author's strong recommendation to skip the photo is due to the biases it creates.
The author gives no argument about file size.
The author does not claim a legal ban; he notes only a few countries require photos.
Professionalism is not the reason given; bias is.
questions.explain: The reason is bias, which a photo can introduce before any content is read.
questions.rule: Leave off your photo and list no more than four contact details or profile links, compact at the top.

questions.q: A resume for an English-first tech company has a section: Languages: Portuguese (mother tongue), English (fluent). How much does it add?
options: A lot, since it shows you can work with colleagues from different countries
Enough to keep, since a short section costs almost nothing to read
Little: fluent English is assumed, and programming languages matter more to this role
It proves your English, which many companies check first at screening
optionExplain: The chapter does not say the section signals teamwork across countries.
Space on a one-page resume is not free, and the section adds nothing the reader needs.
The author says people assume you are fluent in English, and care about your programming languages.
Fluent English is assumed for an English-first company, so the section proves nothing new.
questions.explain: The reader assumes the English. The card next explains the rest.
questions.rule: Leave out the spoken-languages section and any self-rating, and list only the technologies you are proficient with.

questions.q: Remove all ratings, and list only things you have ____ with.
questions.explain: The author says to list what you have proficiency with and drop the ratings.
questions.rule: Leave out the spoken-languages section and any self-rating, and list only the technologies you are proficient with.

questions.q: Your skills block reads: Java four stars, SQL 80%, Docker 3 of 5. What follows the author's advice?
options: Raise every score to full marks so no tool looks like a weak point
List Java, SQL and Docker by name only, with no scores or stars
Keep the scores but explain what each number means in a footnote
Keep only the scores above 80% and drop the lower ones
optionExplain: Top marks look dubious, since no one knows everything about a language.
Plain names list your proficiency and leave nothing to doubt.
A footnote adds length and still invites doubt about the numbers.
Hiding low scores keeps the same flawed habit of rating yourself.
questions.explain: The author says to remove all ratings.
questions.rule: Leave out the spoken-languages section and any self-rating, and list only the technologies you are proficient with.

questions.q: Sort each item: keep it on a tech resume, or cut it?

items.t: Programming languages you work in
Tools and frameworks you are proficient in
Technologies listed by name, no scores
Portuguese (native), English (fluent)
Star ratings beside each language
Percentage bars for Python and Go

questions.explain: Technologies listed by name are useful. Spoken-language lines and self-rated scores are what the author removes.
questions.rule: Leave out the spoken-languages section and any self-rating, and list only the technologies you are proficient with.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a 5 out of 5 self-rating makes hiring managers more confident in you.
questions.explain: They will be dubious, because no one really knows everything about a programming language.
questions.rule: Leave out the spoken-languages section and any self-rating, and list only the technologies you are proficient with.

questions.q: You apply to a company that works mainly in Hungarian. What does the author say about listing the spoken languages you know?
options: It never makes sense, so always leave the languages out
It matters only for the languages you rate yourself highest in
It matters only if the languages are listed with their fluency scores
It can make sense there, since the language matters to that employer
optionExplain: The advice is a default for English-first employers, not an absolute.
Scores are what the author says to remove everywhere.
Fluency scores fall under the same self-rating the author warns against.
The author drops spoken languages unless you are interviewing for a company in that language, such as a Hungarian company.
questions.explain: The advice is tied to an English-first employer, so a different working language changes it.
questions.teaches: The author says a spoken-languages list can matter when the employer works in that language, for example when interviewing for a Hungarian company.
questions.rule: Leave out the spoken-languages section and any self-rating, and list only the technologies you are proficient with.

questions.q: A resume ends with the line: References available on request. According to the author, what does that line do?
options: It reassures recruiters, so it earns its place at the bottom of the page
It wastes space, since references matter only later in hiring and are expected anyway
It signals that you are open to checks, which employers value highly
It is required by large companies, so leaving it out risks rejection
optionExplain: Recruiters already assume you will provide them, so there is nothing to reassure.
The author calls both a list and the line a waste of space.
Openness is expected in tech, so the line adds nothing.
Large companies use background checks, not a line on the resume.
questions.explain: The line says what everyone assumes. The card next shows why the author wants it gone.
questions.rule: Leave out the references list, the line references available on request, and quotes from others praising you.

questions.q: Your developer resume is about you ____ yourself.
questions.explain: The author says the resume is about selling yourself, not adding quotes from others.
questions.rule: Leave out the references list, the line references available on request, and quotes from others praising you.

questions.q: A friend adds a list of three referees to fill a half-empty page. What does the author suggest instead?
options: Keep the list, but move it to its own second page for neatness
Replace the referees with a single praising quote from a manager
Pad the page with a skills table so that nothing looks empty
Cut the list and give the room to another result
optionExplain: A second page does not change that references are a waste of space.
Quotes from others also look out of place, according to the author.
A table adds filler; the author wants a concise, relevant resume.
The space is better spent on your own results.
questions.explain: Use the room to sell yourself.
questions.rule: Leave out the references list, the line references available on request, and quotes from others praising you.

questions.q: Sort each item: worth the space, or a waste?

items.t: A result with numbers from your latest job
A project you led, with its outcome
A new skill you applied, with what it achieved
Three referee names and phone numbers
A quote from a manager praising your standards
References available on request

questions.explain: Results are the content of a resume. Referees, praise from others and the on-request line are not.
questions.rule: Leave out the references list, the line references available on request, and quotes from others praising you.

questions.q: A bank candidate expects referees to be phoned before interviews. How does the author say large companies check references?
options: With background checks, while smaller ones follow up after asking you
By phoning every referee listed on the resume before the first interview
By asking recruiters to read the quotes printed on the resume
By waiting until a candidate offers the names unprompted at the first screen
optionExplain: The author says large companies use background checks and smaller ones follow up themselves, usually after asking you.
Checks come after the interviews, and not from names printed on the page.
Quotes on the resume are described as out of place, not as a check.
The author says smaller companies ask you first; they do not wait for you to volunteer.
questions.explain: References arrive late in the process, by request, so the resume has no need for them.
questions.teaches: Large companies use background checks, and smaller ones follow up themselves, usually after asking you, which is why the resume does not need references.
questions.rule: Leave out the references list, the line references available on request, and quotes from others praising you.

questions.q: A former manager wrote a glowing paragraph about you. According to the author, where does it fit best?
options: As an italic quote under your job title on the resume
As the first line of your cover letter, with the manager's name
In the recommendations section of your LinkedIn profile
Under a Praise heading at the bottom of the resume page
optionExplain: A quote on the resume looks out of place, in italics or not.
The author's pointer is LinkedIn, not the cover letter.
The author says to save any quotes for the recommendations section on LinkedIn.
A heading does not change that quotes from others do not belong on the resume.
questions.explain: Praise has a home: LinkedIn recommendations.
questions.teaches: The author says any quotes from others are best saved for the recommendations section on LinkedIn.
questions.rule: Leave out the references list, the line references available on request, and quotes from others praising you.

questions.q: A resume pastes a 90-character repository address as plain text. What does the author suggest?
options: Shorten the text to the first ten characters so that it takes less space
Keep the full address visible so that it can be typed in from a printout
Make it clickable, behind a name that describes what the link is for
Replace it with the word link in bold, so that the eye is drawn to it
optionExplain: A truncated address no longer works.
No one prints the resume and types in a long address, per the author.
A named, clickable link fits the space and is usable.
Bold draws attention to a detail, and link is not descriptive.
questions.explain: The reader should be able to click it and know what it leads to. The card next gives the reasons.
questions.rule: Make links clickable, show a descriptive name instead of the full address, and let them blend in with the text.

questions.q: A link that is not clickable fails because the recruiter will not copy-and-____ it.
questions.explain: The author says the recruiter will not copy and paste, so a link must be clickable.
questions.rule: Make links clickable, show a descriptive name instead of the full address, and let them blend in with the text.

questions.q: Your exported PDF has three links in default blue, each a full address. Which fix follows the author?
options: Name each by purpose, make it clickable, in body text colour and underlined
Keep the blue so the links are easy to find, but shorten the addresses a little
Move the three addresses into a footnote in a smaller font size
Make the links bold and larger so that recruiters notice them first
optionExplain: That covers the three problems: size, usability and colour.
Blue remains the one colour on the page and pulls the eye to details.
Footnotes remain full addresses, which the author warns against.
Bold and large make the links stand out even more, the opposite of the aim.
questions.explain: Make links useful but quiet.
questions.rule: Make links clickable, show a descriptive name instead of the full address, and let them blend in with the text.

questions.q: Sort each link choice: follows the author's advice, or breaks it?

items.t: Underlined text in the same colour as the body
A descriptive name such as Payments app source code
A clickable link in the PDF
A full repository path typed out
Default blue as the only colour on the page
A plain-text address nobody can click

questions.explain: Good links are clickable, named and quiet. Typed-out paths, loud blue and dead text are what the author warns about.
questions.rule: Make links clickable, show a descriptive name instead of the full address, and let them blend in with the text.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, recruiters usually click your links before they have read the rest of the resume.
questions.explain: They click only after finding the key information in their first scan.
questions.rule: Make links clickable, show a descriptive name instead of the full address, and let them blend in with the text.

questions.q: You like some colour in your resume. According to the author's improved example, where might colour go instead of on links?
options: On the links only, since they are the way to see your work and projects
On every section name and every bullet, for a consistent look throughout
On your contact details, so recruiters can reach you quickly and easily
On job titles, dates and project names, so important parts stand out
optionExplain: That recreates the original problem of colour on details.
Colour on every bullet is the loud style the author warns against.
Contact details are details too, not the first thing the reader should see.
In the improved example the highlight goes on titles, dates and project names, and links are underlined and quiet.
questions.explain: Spend colour on what you want the reader to see first.
questions.teaches: The author's improved example spends its highlight colour on job titles, dates and project names, and may also colour section names, while links stay underlined and quiet.
questions.rule: Make links clickable, show a descriptive name instead of the full address, and let them blend in with the text.

questions.q: Your GitHub shows no activity for four years, but you link it from your resume. What risk does the author describe?
options: No risk at all, since most recruiters never click through any links
A thorough recruiter who clicks through will be disappointed
The link will be flagged as broken by the applicant tracking system
The recruiter will assume that you now work on private repositories
optionExplain: Most do not click, but the ones who do shape the decision.
Most do not click, but the thorough ones do, and a stale profile disappoints them.
The risk described is the reader's reaction, not software flagging.
The author describes disappointment, not a charitable assumption.
questions.explain: Stale links can count against you. The card next shows the rule.
questions.rule: Link to GitHub, LinkedIn or a website only if it is up to date and shows good work; otherwise remove it.

questions.q: Link only if they are up to ____. Otherwise, save the space and remove it.
questions.explain: Up-to-date links are worth keeping; stale ones are better removed.
questions.rule: Link to GitHub, LinkedIn or a website only if it is up to date and shows good work; otherwise remove it.

questions.q: Your GitHub is active with READMEs, your LinkedIn matches your resume, and your personal site was last updated four years ago. What stays?
options: All three, because a missing link looks like you have nothing to show
Only the website, because it is the one you fully control
None of them, because recruiters rarely click through to any link
GitHub and LinkedIn stay; drop the website unless you refresh it
optionExplain: A stale site hurts more than a missing link does.
Control does not make a stale page useful.
Thorough recruiters do click, and current links can help.
Two current links help; one stale link hurts.
questions.explain: Keep what is current and drop what is not.
questions.rule: Link to GitHub, LinkedIn or a website only if it is up to date and shows good work; otherwise remove it.

questions.q: Sort each link: worth keeping, or better removed?

items.t: A GitHub with recent commits and README files on pinned repositories
A LinkedIn profile that matches your resume
A blog with well-written technical posts
A personal site last edited years ago
A GitHub profile with no visible contributions
A website that no longer loads

questions.explain: Current, professional pages support the application. Stale, empty or broken ones do not.
questions.rule: Link to GitHub, LinkedIn or a website only if it is up to date and shows good work; otherwise remove it.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, most recruiters will not click your links, so what the pages contain does not matter.
questions.explain: The thorough recruiters do click, so the contents matter.
questions.rule: Link to GitHub, LinkedIn or a website only if it is up to date and shows good work; otherwise remove it.

questions.q: A developer links her site from a one-page resume. What extras does the recruiter quoted in the book wish such sites had?
options: A video introduction, plus a list of all your referees
A more detailed resume, or a technical blog showing your work
A salary history and the contact details of your manager
A photo gallery of your workspace, to show your personality
optionExplain: The recruiter names neither a video nor referees.
The recruiter says a page could carry more helpful information for the application, such as a more detailed resume or a technical blog.
Salary history and manager contacts are not what the recruiter mentions.
Personality photos are not mentioned and would not help the application.
questions.explain: A link is worth including when what it leads to adds to the application.
questions.teaches: A senior technical recruiter quoted in the book says a site or GitHub page could add a more detailed resume or a technical blog, which would help the application.
questions.rule: Link to GitHub, LinkedIn or a website only if it is up to date and shows good work; otherwise remove it.

questions.q: Your resume says Senior Engineer at a company, but your LinkedIn headline still shows a previous job. What does the recruiter quoted in the book say?
options: Leave it, since LinkedIn and a resume serve different purposes
Delete the LinkedIn link so the mismatch cannot be seen
It should reflect your resume, so update it to match
Add a second resume to LinkedIn to explain the difference
optionExplain: Differences between them are what thorough readers notice.
Removing the link avoids the mismatch but misses the point of keeping it current.
The quoted recruiter says that a LinkedIn link should reflect the resume.
Adding material does not fix an outdated profile.
questions.explain: If a profile and a resume disagree, a thorough reader spots it.
questions.teaches: The recruiter quoted in the book says that your LinkedIn should reflect your resume.
questions.rule: Link to GitHub, LinkedIn or a website only if it is up to date and shows good work; otherwise remove it.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: You want a quick outside view on whether your resume is easy to scan. What does the author suggest?
options: Show a friend for five seconds, then ask for their immediate first impression of it
Ask a friend to proofread it line by line over an hour or more, with notes
Run it through an online scanner and trust the score it gives
Read it aloud to yourself and check that it sounds natural
optionExplain: The author's check is a five-second look followed by the friend's immediate impression.
A slow proofread tests accuracy, not what registers in a glance.
The chapter does not suggest a scanner; it suggests a human glance.
Reading aloud is useful for wording but not for first-glance scanning.
questions.explain: A first glance can only be tested with a glance. The card next lists all nine checks.
questions.rule: Before sending, run the chapter's nine checks: photo, contact count, working links, professional pages, scannability, simplicity, concision, bolding and consistency.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: To check your links, ____ through each of them.
questions.explain: The recap's check on links is to click through each one and see what a reader would see.
questions.rule: Before sending, run the chapter's nine checks: photo, contact count, working links, professional pages, scannability, simplicity, concision, bolding and consistency.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: Put the author's five-second friend test in order.
items: Give your resume to a friend
Ask them to look at it for five seconds
Check whether they saw the key details or found it crowded or thin
questions.explain: You hand over the resume, allow five seconds, ask what they felt, and then compare that to your aim.
questions.rule: Before sending, run the chapter's nine checks: photo, contact count, working links, professional pages, scannability, simplicity, concision, bolding and consistency.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: Match each finding to the fix the checklist points to.
pairs: Fix it or take it off
Keep bold for titles, companies, dates and headers
questions.explain: Each check in the recap pairs a finding with a plain action.
questions.rule: Before sending, run the chapter's nine checks: photo, contact count, working links, professional pages, scannability, simplicity, concision, bolding and consistency.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: A candidate says: I removed my photo, kept seven profile links and did not test the links. Which two checks did they miss?
options: Keep contact details and profile links to four or fewer
Click through each link to see that it works
Remove the photo from the page
Use tabs to align elements rather than spaces
optionExplain: Seven is over the cap of four.
Untested links can be dead or stale.
They did this one.
This is a real check, but nothing in the candidate's statement touches it.
questions.explain: The candidate passed the photo check but missed the contact cap and link testing.
questions.rule: Before sending, run the chapter's nine checks: photo, contact count, working links, professional pages, scannability, simplicity, concision, bolding and consistency.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: Your friend glances for five seconds and says the page feels crowded and she could not find your latest job. What does that suggest?
options: The page is too busy; simplify the layout and cut whatever hides the key details
The page is fine, since five seconds is too short for any fair verdict
The page needs more content, so add detail to fill the white space
The page needs bolder text, so that the latest job stands out in a glance
optionExplain: The test asks whether they saw the key details and found it crowded or too thin; this answer says crowded and missing key details.
Five seconds is the author's own test, not an unfair one.
The friend said crowded, not thin, so adding more goes the wrong way.
More bold is the habit the author warns against; simplifying is the aim.
questions.explain: A crowded impression after five seconds points to simplifying.
questions.teaches: After the five seconds the author wants to know whether your friend saw the key details, thought it was too crowded, or felt it had too little information.
questions.rule: Before sending, run the chapter's nine checks: photo, contact count, working links, professional pages, scannability, simplicity, concision, bolding and consistency.

questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Resume
questions.q: You worry that your resume's fancy design gets in the way of readability. Which of the nine checks suits that aim?
options: Click through each link to see what the reader would find there
Count the contact details and social links in the header
Ask whether any fancy design gets in the way of readability
Check that bullet points rarely run beyond two lines
optionExplain: That tests the destination of links, not the page design.
That checks the header cap, not the overall style.
That check is aimed at style that gets in the way of scanning.
That tests length, not design.
questions.explain: Choose the check that matches the worry.
questions.rule: Before sending, run the chapter's nine checks: photo, contact count, working links, professional pages, scannability, simplicity, concision, bolding and consistency.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A student wants one experience that most improves a future resume. Which does the author rate among the best?
options: Collecting several certificates from short online courses
Raising the grade average in every course by a few points
Working as an intern on real problems in an industry setting
Reading widely about how software companies are organised and run
optionExplain: Certificates show study, not work on real problems in industry.
Grades matter, but the author does not rank them as a top experience.
The author calls this one of the best experiences a student can have. The card says more.
Reading helps, but it is not hands-on industry work.
questions.explain: The author names internships as one of the best experiences. The card shows why and when to start.
questions.rule: Seek out internships well ahead of time and prepare for their interviews.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: As a student, seek out ____ to work on real-world problems in an industry setting.
questions.explain: The author names internships as the experience to seek, working on real problems in an industry setting.
questions.rule: Seek out internships well ahead of time and prepare for their interviews.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Jonas is in his second year and wants an internship next summer. According to the author's advice, which plan fits?
options: Apply months ahead and spend time preparing for the interviews first
Wait until final term, when his grades are strongest, and then apply to many firms at once
Apply a week before the summer to avoid committing to a firm too early
Skip interview practice, since an internship is meant to be where he learns the work
optionExplain: The author says to apply well ahead of time and to prepare for the interviews.
Waiting turns an advantage into a rush; applications usually close well ahead.
Late applications often miss the deadlines the author warns about.
Interviews still need preparation, which the author mentions directly.
questions.explain: Applications are usually due well ahead, and the interviews need preparation.
questions.rule: Seek out internships well ahead of time and prepare for their interviews.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Sort these replies to a student asking about internships by whether they follow the author's advice.

items.t: Look for placements early and rehearse interview questions
Class projects cover the same ground, so skip internships
Apply well before the term when companies start taking interns
Wait to see whether a job offer simply arrives at graduation
Treat an industry placement as a chance to work on real problems
Interviews for interns need no preparation

questions.explain: The author treats internships as real industry experience that needs early applications and interview preparation.
questions.rule: Seek out internships well ahead of time and prepare for their interviews.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A second-year student reads that the author urges internships and assumes the author did several during college. True or false: that assumption is correct.
questions.explain: The author says internships are something he did not do while at college and wishes he had. This is a personal note meant to persuade, not evidence.
questions.rule: A regret is persuasion; the rule stands on the reason given.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Aisha finished an internship in her last year. According to the author, what extra benefit could follow at graduation?
options: Every later employer would treat her resume as complete
Her degree classification would be raised by the company
The company would be obliged to hire her without interviews
She might receive a return offer from the company
optionExplain: An internship helps the resume, but the author does not claim it completes it.
An internship does not change a degree classification.
A return offer is possible, but nothing obliges a hire or removes interviews.
The author says internships can bring return offers when you graduate.
questions.explain: The author notes internships can be more than experience, because they may lead to return offers.
questions.teaches: An internship can lead to a return offer when you graduate.
questions.rule: Seek out internships well ahead of time and prepare for their interviews.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A student has plenty of time outside class. Which activity would the author count as good preparation for a job search?
options: Rewriting a finished class project privately for a better grade
Leading a lab practice for younger students
Watching recorded talks on how to lead a software team
Joining a study group whose members only revise for exams
optionExplain: Private rewrites give no visible proof; the author wants projects published.
Mentoring and leading groups are among the experiences the author recommends.
Watching is passive; the author points to hands-on experience.
Studying helps coursework but is not the initiative the author describes.
questions.explain: The author lists helping professors, leading practices and organising events. The card has the rest.
questions.rule: Step up for campus activities such as helping professors or running events, and publish your class projects online.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Consider ____ your class projects online so others can download or try them, especially final projects.
questions.explain: The author suggests publishing projects, final projects above all because they are more complex.
questions.rule: Step up for campus activities such as helping professors or running events, and publish your class projects online.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Dana built a chat app for a networking class. Following the author, what would she do to add value on a resume?
options: Keep the code on her laptop so classmates cannot copy it
Put the working app online with a way for others to download or try it
Delete the app and start a new one that is bigger than the class asked
Describe the app in a paragraph of the cover letter alone
optionExplain: A private project cannot be tried by anyone, which is the point the author makes.
Publishing a working class project is the author's advice.
Extra effort is welcome, but the advice is to publish what exists.
A description is weaker than something a reviewer can run.
questions.explain: The advice is to put a little extra effort into publishing the project so others can try it.
questions.rule: Step up for campus activities such as helping professors or running events, and publish your class projects online.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Match each student activity to the skill the author says it builds.
questions.explain: Campus activities build mentoring, leadership and initiative, while publishing lets others download or try the software.
questions.rule: Step up for campus activities such as helping professors or running events, and publish your class projects online.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, the extra effort of publishing is most worthwhile for a final project, which is usually more complex than other class projects.
questions.explain: The author says this is especially true for final projects.
questions.rule: Step up for campus activities such as helping professors or running events, and publish your class projects online.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Lena studies design, not software, but her course ends with a group final project. What does the book's approach suggest?
options: Leave leadership to others since only developers need leadership experience
Wait until she has a job offer before collecting any of this evidence
Submit the project for grading only and avoid putting it online
Put the project online and take a leading part in the group
optionExplain: The author presents leading groups as something every student can gain.
Evidence gathered while studying is what helps at the job search.
Publishing is the advice for class projects generally.
Our reading: the author's two habits, publishing and stepping up, carry over to any course.
questions.explain: The activities in this section build visible experience for any student.
questions.teaches: The author says these activities help you grow faster and help you stand out when you look for jobs as you graduate.
questions.rule: Step up for campus activities such as helping professors or running events, and publish your class projects online.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A bootcamp grad is publishing a project. Which README would the author most likely praise?
options: One with a summary, screenshots, and steps to run and test it
One that lists only the technologies and the date of completion
One that is a single sentence so the code speaks for itself
One that copies the bootcamp's standard template unchanged
optionExplain: These are the four parts the author asks for.
Technology names do not tell a reviewer what the project does or how to try it.
A short README leaves out what a reviewer needs to run the project.
A generic template looks like every other bootcamp project.
questions.explain: The author lists a summary, screenshots, how to run and how to test. The card has the detail.
questions.rule: Publish your projects on GitHub with a README that has a summary, screenshots, how to run and how to test.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Put these README parts in the order the author lists them.
questions.explain: The author lists a summary, screenshots, details on how to run, and how to test.
questions.rule: Summary, screenshots, run, test.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Omar's README for his weather app has a summary and screenshots only. What is the author's advice for the next edit?
options: Add a longer summary of the weather facts the app displays
Remove the screenshots so the page loads more quickly
Add how to run the project and how to test it
Add a list of all the other courses taken at the bootcamp
optionExplain: He already has a summary; the missing parts are practical steps.
Screenshots are on the author's list.
Run and test instructions are the two parts he is missing.
Course lists do not help a reviewer try the project.
questions.explain: The README should also tell a reader how to run and how to test the project.
questions.rule: Publish your projects on GitHub with a README that has a summary, screenshots, how to run and how to test.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Sort these README lines by whether they fit the author's advice for a good README.

items.t: Two-line summary of what the app does
Screenshots of the main screens
Steps to start the app locally
No mention of how anyone could verify the code works
Only the logo of the bootcamp
A link list with no explanation of the project

questions.explain: The author asks for a summary, screenshots, run steps and test steps.
questions.rule: Publish your projects on GitHub with a README that has a summary, screenshots, how to run and how to test.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, most bootcamp grads will have projects from their course listed, so those alone rarely differentiate you.
questions.explain: The author says most grads list course projects, so better examples are needed to stand out.
questions.rule: Publish your projects on GitHub with a README that has a summary, screenshots, how to run and how to test.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A career changer with a finished side project asks how to present it. Which fits the book's advice for bootcamp projects?
options: Replace it with a project from the bootcamp curriculum
Keep it unpublished and describe it only in the interview
Publish only the code with no explanation so reviewers dig into it
Publish it with a README showing what it does and how to run it
optionExplain: Course projects are what everyone else lists.
The author wants working projects linked, so reviewers can see them.
Reviewers skim; a README saves them the effort.
The advice for bootcamp projects applies to career changers too.
questions.explain: The book says career changers should follow the bootcamp advice to beef up projects.
questions.teaches: The author tells career changers to follow the bootcamp grad advice for strengthening their projects.
questions.rule: Publish your projects on GitHub with a README that has a summary, screenshots, how to run and how to test.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Why might a tested bootcamp project help a grad stand out?
options: Most projects from a bootcamp have no automated tests at all
Reviewers run the tests of every candidate before reading the resume
Tests make a project run faster than similar projects do
A tested project proves the author finished the bootcamp early
optionExplain: The author says this is the reason a tested project differs from the crowd.
The advice does not say reviewers run tests; it says to call tests out.
Tests check behaviour; they do not speed an app up.
Tests say nothing about timing or finishing a course.
questions.explain: The author says few bootcamp projects have tests. The card gives the full advice.
questions.rule: Give your project automated tests, add a Running tests section to the README, and state the code coverage percentage.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: In the project description, mention the code ____ percentage.
questions.explain: The author suggests mentioning the code coverage percentage in the project description, and then seeing if you can get it higher.
questions.rule: Give your project automated tests, add a Running tests section to the README, and state the code coverage percentage.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Mei has added tests to her budgeting app. What should she do next, following the author?
options: Tell reviewers about the tests only after they have asked about them
Delete the tests from the repository so the project looks simpler
Add a Running tests section to the README and call the tests out
Rename the project so it sounds more professional than a bootcamp app
optionExplain: The author says to call tests out on the project itself.
Hiding tests removes the proof the author wants shown.
This makes it clear how anyone can run the tests and calls them out.
A new name does not show anything about quality.
questions.explain: Tests are only helpful to a reviewer if they are called out and easy to run.
questions.rule: Give your project automated tests, add a Running tests section to the README, and state the code coverage percentage.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, many bootcamp grads have not heard of test-driven development.
questions.explain: The author says this and points to a resource for learning it.
questions.rule: Give your project automated tests, add a Running tests section to the README, and state the code coverage percentage.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Two projects have the same features. One has runnable tests and a README that says how to run them. What does the author predict?
options: Both look equal because reviewers only count features
The tested one stands out from the crowd
The untested one wins because it is simpler to read
The tested one is ignored because tests are outside a bootcamp's scope
optionExplain: Features are shared, but tests are the difference the author highlights.
The author says a tested project already helps you stand out.
The author does not treat simplicity as the goal here.
The author treats the gap in bootcamp projects as an opening.
questions.explain: With equal features, the tested project shows more of what the job needs.
questions.rule: A tested project stands out among bootcamp projects.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A grad wants a model for documenting how to run tests in a README. Which pointer does the author give?
options: The Leaflet open source map library, which shows how it is done
A bootcamp's internal wiki that explains its grading scale and rules
A résumé template site with sample README layouts for job seekers
A testing vendor's brochure listing its supported frameworks
optionExplain: The author names Leaflet as an example of documenting how to run tests.
The author points to a public open source project, not a course wiki.
The book's pointer is a real project, not a template site.
A brochure does not show a README in practice.
questions.explain: The author says to see how Leaflet documents running its tests, and points to a Learn Test Driven Development resource for the practice itself.
questions.teaches: The author points to the open source library Leaflet as an example of a README that documents running tests.
questions.rule: Give your project automated tests, add a Running tests section to the README, and state the code coverage percentage.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A grad wants a resume line from an open source project. What does the author say must happen first?
options: They write about the project in a long blog post series
They star the project on the hosting site and follow it
A pull request of theirs is merged into the project
They fork the project and publish it under their own name
optionExplain: A post is not a contribution to the code.
Starring is passive and is not a contribution.
Only a merged pull request lets you claim a contribution.
A fork is not accepted work in the original project.
questions.explain: The author says the claim follows a merged pull request. The card adds how to phrase it.
questions.rule: Get a pull request merged into a popular open source project and state how many developers use it.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Stars on the project are a metric you can use to say how many ____ rely on it.
questions.explain: The author uses the stars to say a project is used by more than a certain number of developers.
questions.rule: Get a pull request merged into a popular open source project and state how many developers use it.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Tom's pull request to a library with 12,000 stars was merged. Which resume line follows the author's example?
options: Familiar with many open source libraries on a popular code host
Fixed a bug in a library used by over 12,000 developers
Opened a pull request to a library that a few people liked
Maintains a library which received many stars in its first year
optionExplain: This claims familiarity, not a merged contribution.
It names the contribution and uses the stars as the size of the audience.
It leaves out the merge and the size of the user base.
Tom is a contributor, not the maintainer, so this overclaims.
questions.explain: Say what you contributed and how many developers use the project.
questions.rule: Get a pull request merged into a popular open source project and state how many developers use it.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Sort these resume lines by whether the claim fits what the author says an open source line needs.

items.t: Fix merged into a map library used by over 28,000 developers
Contributed to many popular projects, none yet accepted
Merged a pull request into a package manager used by over 20,000 developers
Opened an issue and starred a project that others use
Pull request still under review but described as a contribution
Merged bug fix in a widely used charting library

questions.explain: A claim needs a merged change and a sense of how many developers use the project.
questions.rule: Get a pull request merged into a popular open source project and state how many developers use it.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the guest voice in the book, a first pull request to a popular project will probably be accepted straight away.
questions.explain: The guest says it will probably be rejected at first, and the owners often leave comments that help you improve before they merge it.
questions.rule: A rejected pull request still gives feedback from senior engineers.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A grad's first pull request to a popular project gets many review comments. How does the book suggest viewing them?
options: As proof that the project owners dislike new contributors
As a sign that open source work is a poor choice for a newcomer
As a reason to remove the contribution from the resume and retry
As free coaching from senior engineers who own the project
optionExplain: The guest describes owners helping you improve the code.
The guest says the opposite: the comments are the education.
Nothing is on the resume until it is merged anyway.
The guest says rejection brings comments from senior engineers and calls it continuing your education.
questions.explain: Review comments such as add tests, fix this bug, or consider this algorithm are part of the learning.
questions.teaches: A rejected first pull request often brings review comments from senior engineers, which the guest sees as continued education.
questions.rule: Get a pull request merged into a popular open source project and state how many developers use it.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A candidate has submitted a takehome challenge. What does the author suggest as the next step?
options: Wait silently for the company's decision before doing anything else
Delete the solution so it cannot be copied by others
Keep improving it into a published, tested project
Start a different challenge from scratch to avoid repetition
optionExplain: Waiting wastes the effort already made.
Deleting wastes work; the author wants it published.
The author asks you not to stop at submitting.
Polishing the same work gives a stronger project.
questions.explain: The author suggests carrying on with the work. The card shows how.
questions.rule: Do not stop at submitting a coding challenge: keep working, publish a polished version, and put it on your resume.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Put the author's steps for a takehome in order.
items: Pass the resume screen and receive the challenge
Publish a more polished version with tests
Add the project to your resume
questions.explain: The author starts with the challenge and its submission, then publishing a polished version and adding it to the resume.
questions.rule: Submit, polish, publish, list it.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Nia was not invited to the next round after her takehome. According to the author, how could she use the experience?
options: Ask for feedback and build it into a published version
Remove the challenge from her records because it failed
Post the rejection online and tag the company in it
Wait for a follow-up from the company before touching the code
optionExplain: The author gives this exact advice.
A failed submission can still become a good project.
This helps neither the project nor her job search.
The author tells her not to wait.
questions.explain: Ask for feedback and use it to improve the project.
questions.rule: Do not stop at submitting a coding challenge: keep working, publish a polished version, and put it on your resume.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, once you send an improved version, you should expect the company to reconsider you.
questions.explain: The author says to send the follow-up but not to hold your breath.
questions.rule: Treat any reply as a bonus.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Which spending does the author regard as a good investment for the job search?
options: Nothing at all, since projects must stay on a local machine
A large amount on paid advertising for the project
A fee to a service that promises to rank the resume first
A small spend on a domain so anyone can reach the project
optionExplain: The author wants the project reachable by others.
The book mentions only a small spend on a domain and hosting.
The book names no such spending.
In the book's example, a grad paid fifteen dollars for a domain.
questions.explain: A modest cost can make the project accessible to anyone.
questions.rule: Spend a little on a domain so the project is reachable.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A grad has polished a takehome and bought a domain for it. In the book's example, how did the grad seek feedback?
options: By asking the company to approve the new version before it went online
By having friends try it and posting it to an online forum
By keeping it private until a recruiter requested a demonstration
By paying a consultant to review the code and rewrite the design
optionExplain: The example grad did not ask the company for permission.
The example grad tested with friends and submitted to a Reddit forum.
The example grad published and asked for opinions.
The example mentions friends and a forum, not a paid review.
questions.explain: Friends and an online forum gave the grad feedback on a finished, professional-looking project.
questions.teaches: In the book's example, the grad tested the project with friends and submitted the finished work and code to a Reddit forum for feedback.
questions.rule: Do not stop at submitting a coding challenge: keep working, publish a polished version, and put it on your resume.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A bootcamp grad has five months to improve their chances. Which approach does the book's example show?
options: Rewriting the same bullets in more impressive wording
Growing real experience through new and polished projects
Applying to every job until someone replies
Hiding the bootcamp so no one knows the training was short
optionExplain: The author says this example differs from phrasing changes.
The example shows change in experience, not just in phrasing.
The example shows effort building experience.
The example does not hide the training.
questions.explain: The example shows what changes when experience grows. The card lists the four activities.
questions.rule: While you search, build new experience: contribute to open source, finish a takehome, take a paid freelance project and publish what you learned.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Match each activity from the book's example to what the grad gained.
pairs: A production-ready product on its own domain
Real customers and a portfolio piece
A learning project with a tidy README
questions.explain: Each activity produced something to show: an accepted contribution, a polished product, client work or a public learning project.
questions.rule: While you search, build new experience: contribute to open source, finish a takehome, take a paid freelance project and publish what you learned.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A grad worries that a freelance client argues over price. According to the book's example, what did the grad decide?
options: To hide the project from the resume because it paid little
To refuse the project and look for a better-paying client
To deliver rushed work because the client paid so little
Not to care about profit, as experience was the goal
optionExplain: The grad published screenshots and snippets on a portfolio page.
The example grad took the project.
The example grad delivered high-quality work.
The grad delivered high-quality work and valued experience over money.
questions.explain: The grad accepted that experience was the goal.
questions.hint: Think about the grad's main goal.
questions.rule: While you search, build new experience: contribute to open source, finish a takehome, take a paid freelance project and publish what you learned.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Sort these statements about paid freelance projects in the book by whether the author says them.

items.t: Real customers use paid projects
You do not have to disclose how much you earned
A freelance project must pay a full market rate to count
The grad published screenshots and snippets on a portfolio page
A client's complaint about price is proof the project failed
Freelance work cannot go on a resume

questions.explain: The book says paid projects have real users and need not state the pay.
questions.rule: While you search, build new experience: contribute to open source, finish a takehome, take a paid freelance project and publish what you learned.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a coding challenge you struggled with can become a public project that also helps you learn.
questions.explain: In the example the grad implemented data structures with tests and a tidy README. The author did the same on an earlier job search.
questions.rule: While you search, build new experience: contribute to open source, finish a takehome, take a paid freelance project and publish what you learned.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A grad keeps failing interview questions on sorting algorithms. What does the book's example suggest?
options: Implement them with tests and publish them with a README
Avoid roles that ask for algorithms and apply only to others
Memorise answers without writing any code, to save time
Keep the practice code private so no one sees early mistakes
optionExplain: The example grad turned an interview weakness into a public project, as the author did.
The example faces the weakness instead.
The example learns by implementing.
The point is a project to show.
questions.explain: Public practice teaches the topic and leaves a project to show. The author notes that many examples of popular data structures and algorithms in a given language already exist on GitHub.
questions.teaches: GitHub already holds many public implementations of popular data structures and algorithms in a given language, which can serve as models.
questions.rule: While you search, build new experience: contribute to open source, finish a takehome, take a paid freelance project and publish what you learned.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A former teacher is moving into software. Which opening does the author think helps recruiters most?
options: A line about hobbies to show a well-rounded personality
A list of every school subject taught in the last decade
A summary stating the change of career and the reason
A list of the soft skills the teacher developed over time
optionExplain: Hobbies do not give the context of a career change.
Teaching details are not where the author puts the focus.
Recruiters want the context that this is a recent change into the field.
Soft skills belong in the brief past-experience entry, not the opening.
questions.explain: The author wants the change and its motivation stated at the start. The card shows what follows.
questions.rule: Open with a summary that says you changed careers and why, then show languages and linked working projects near the top.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Link to working projects and ____ code so the hiring manager can see you can build software.
questions.explain: The author asks you to link working projects and source code.
questions.rule: Open with a summary that says you changed careers and why, then show languages and linked working projects near the top.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Rob, a former chef, has two linked projects and a bootcamp certificate. Which top-of-page order fits the author?
options: Certificate first, then the projects, with no summary
Culinary experience first, since it lasted the longest, then projects
Education first, then a long list of kitchen achievements
Short summary, then languages and projects, then experience
optionExplain: The author recommends the summary so the reader has the context.
Long past experience in another field is not what the hiring manager looks for first.
The author puts projects and languages towards the top, not education.
The summary gives context and the projects give proof, ahead of the older career.
questions.explain: Context first, then the proof of hands-on skill, then the older work.
questions.rule: Open with a summary that says you changed careers and why, then show languages and linked working projects near the top.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: The advice in this card is aimed at people without professional software experience; a developer with five years of professional work should still open with a career-change summary.
questions.explain: The summary exists to give context for someone who has recently moved into the field. Our reading: it adds nothing for a developer with years of professional experience.
questions.rule: The summary and project emphasis are for people lacking professional software experience.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A career changer formats the languages-and-projects block. In the book's example resume, which details get the emphasis in bold?
options: The technologies, since recruiters care about these most
The names of the previous employers, since they show loyalty
The years of schooling, to make up for the missing degree
The soft skills, since they carry over from the old career
optionExplain: The book's example bolds technologies because that is what recruiters are most interested in.
The previous career is kept brief in the example.
Education comes last in the example.
Soft skills are kept to short bullets in the past-experience entry.
questions.explain: The example puts the emphasis and bold on technologies for a reader scanning for hands-on skill.
questions.teaches: In the book's career changer example, the emphasis and bolding is on the technologies, because recruiters will be most interested in them.
questions.rule: Open with a summary that says you changed careers and why, then show languages and linked working projects near the top.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A former retail manager has ten years of past roles. How should they treat that work on a career-change resume?
options: Remove the work entirely, so nothing distracts from the new field
Give it the most room, since it is the longest part of the career
Summarize it briefly and keep the skills that carry over
Describe every task in detail to show reliability over time
optionExplain: The author says to keep a brief summary, not to remove it.
The author says recruiters care much less about the past positions.
Short, relevant and focused on transferable skills is the author's advice.
Detail is the temptation the author warns against.
questions.explain: The author wants a short summary of the past job. The card gives the details.
