questions.rule: Summarize past work in one sentence, add bullets only for skills that transfer, and keep the resume to one page.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Keep the whole resume to one page, and do not go beyond one and a ____ pages.
questions.explain: The author says try for one page and no more than one and a half.
questions.rule: Summarize past work in one sentence, add bullets only for skills that transfer, and keep the resume to one page.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Carla taught music for years. Which bullet would the author prefer under that job on a software resume?
options: Prepared lesson plans for 30 hours of classes every week for years
Mentored new teachers and gave a conference workshop
Awarded teacher of the year by the school board in a second year
Organised the school library and maintained the loan records neatly
optionExplain: This is detail about the job, not a transferable skill.
Mentoring and public speaking are two of the author's examples of transferable skills.
An award may be a nice fact but the author asks for transferable skills.
Filing duties are tasks of the old job, not skills the new job asks for.
questions.explain: Choose bullets that show skills a software team values.
questions.rule: Summarize past work in one sentence, add bullets only for skills that transfer, and keep the resume to one page.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Sort these resume details by whether the author would keep them in a career-change resume.

items.t: One sentence describing the previous job
Bullet on proactively learning new things
Bullet on mentoring colleagues
Five bullets listing daily duties of the previous job
Page two with extra detail on old positions
Full paragraph on the old employer's history

questions.explain: Keep a one-sentence summary and transferable skills; cut duties and details that do not help.
questions.rule: Summarize past work in one sentence, add bullets only for skills that transfer, and keep the resume to one page.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A career changer's resume has a bachelor's degree in biology and a bootcamp. What does the book's example suggest for education?
options: List both, with more detail on the software-related education
List only the bootcamp, since the biology degree is unrelated
List only the degree, since universities outrank bootcamps
Skip education and rely on the projects alone
optionExplain: The book says degrees from other fields are usually worth listing, and the software-related one gets more detail.
The author calls listing unrelated degrees good practice.
The software education is the more relevant one and gets more detail.
The book's example closes with an education section.
questions.explain: Listing non-software degrees is good practice, and relevant courses or certifications would also be worth listing.
questions.teaches: The author says listing degrees from other fields is good practice, and related courses or certifications are worth listing too.
questions.rule: Summarize past work in one sentence, add bullets only for skills that transfer, and keep the resume to one page.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Eight years ago a developer took a year out and has worked steadily since. What does the author suggest for the resume?
options: Rewrite the dates so the gap does not appear anywhere
Add a paragraph explaining the reasons in full detail
Leave it unexplained, because it is too old to matter
Add a long cover note to every application about the year out
optionExplain: The author does not advise hiding dates.
The author says not to waste space on an old break.
Breaks more than four or five years old rarely concern readers.
A cover note is not needed for such an old break.
questions.explain: The author says old breaks seldom matter. The card has the exact threshold.
questions.rule: Explain a break only when it is recent: skip one from more than four or five years ago, and judge one that does not lead to the present.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Hiring managers rarely care about breaks that happened more than 4 or 5 ____ ago.
questions.explain: The author says breaks more than four or five years ago are rarely a concern.
questions.rule: Explain a break only when it is recent: skip one from more than four or five years ago, and judge one that does not lead to the present.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Sam had a nine-month break two years ago and has been employed since. According to the author, what is the right approach?
options: Always explain it in the summary so nobody wonders
Use judgment on whether to mention it, and how to tell it
Never mention it, because gaps are always read as warnings
Wait for the recruiter to ask before adding any dates at all
optionExplain: The author says to use judgment; an earlier gap might not be relevant.
A recent break that does not reach the present is a judgment call.
The author allows clarification if you decide to give it.
Dates belong on the resume, and the choice is about explaining.
questions.explain: It is a judgment call because he has been employed since.
questions.rule: Explain a break only when it is recent: skip one from more than four or five years ago, and judge one that does not lead to the present.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, if a hiring manager does care about an old career break, it will probably come up during a screening call.
questions.explain: The author says this, so the resume screen does not need the explanation.
questions.rule: Explain a break only when it is recent: skip one from more than four or five years ago, and judge one that does not lead to the present.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A teacher moving into software had a long break ten years ago. Does the book advise the same approach as for developers?
options: Yes, but only if the break lasted less than a month or two
No, a break needs an explanation for teachers whatever its age
No, only developers may leave old breaks unexplained, not others
Our reading: yes, since the break's age decides, not the field
optionExplain: The author gives no such limit.
No field-specific rule is given.
The author says career breaks are not unique to tech.
The advice about old breaks is general: it was not tied to tech roles, and the book says breaks are not unique to tech.
questions.explain: The author says breaks are not unique to tech, and gives general rules based on how long ago it happened.
questions.teaches: The author points out that career breaks are not unique to tech, so the advice on presenting them is not unique either.
questions.rule: Explain a break only when it is recent: skip one from more than four or five years ago, and judge one that does not lead to the present.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A candidate has been out of work for six months and is still searching. What does the author say about the resume?
options: It should list only the dates, with no reason attached
It should avoid the topic and let the interview bring it up
It should tell the story you would give a hiring manager
It should state that the market was bad and employers made mistakes
optionExplain: Dates alone leave the reader to guess.
The author asks you to take the lead, not to wait.
The author wants the resume to take the lead with the narrative.
The advice is to give a clear, positive story, not blame.
questions.explain: The author says to lead the narrative. The card gives the how.
questions.rule: For a recent break that runs up to now, take the lead and tell a short story, matching the answer you would give a hiring manager.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: For a recent career break leading up to the present, tell a ____.
questions.explain: The author says to tell a story that takes the lead on the narrative.
questions.rule: For a recent break that runs up to now, take the lead and tell a short story, matching the answer you would give a hiring manager.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Priya has been out of work for a year after caring for her father. What is the best draft line according to the author?
options: Took a year to care for my father, now back and building a project
Career break, reason confidential, available immediately for any role
Unemployed since last year, looking for an opportunity to grow
Self-employed consultant for the past year, many satisfied clients
optionExplain: It is brief, honest and matches what she would tell a hiring manager.
This invites more questions than it answers.
This states the gap without any story.
This invents work and would collapse in a screening call.
questions.explain: A short true story, in the same words you would use aloud.
questions.rule: For a recent break that runs up to now, take the lead and tell a short story, matching the answer you would give a hiring manager.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Sort these career break lines by whether they follow the author's advice for a recent break up to the present.

items.t: Travelled for six months, studied Spanish and met new cultures
Took time off to care for my brother, who has recovered
No mention, hoping nobody checks the dates
Invented a consulting role that did not exist
Time off to retrain, with a clear plan for what I learned
A vague line that avoids saying anything

questions.explain: A good line gives a true, short story that you would be happy to repeat in a screening call.
questions.rule: For a recent break that runs up to now, take the lead and tell a short story, matching the answer you would give a hiring manager.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A developer in Toronto left her job eight months ago to look after a parent and has not started a new one. How should her resume handle this break?
options: Say nothing, since a break that runs up to now does not deserve the space
Add one short line, such as time off to care for a relative who has recovered
Write a full paragraph on the family situation so the reader sees every single detail
Mention it only in the cover letter, and leave the resume out entirely
optionExplain: A recent break that leads up to the present is the case where the book says to tell a story.
Right: the book says to tell a short story that matches what you would tell a hiring manager, and the Monster UK article offers wording like this.
The book asks for a short, clear story, not a long account.
The book places the story on the resume, since recruiters will ask about the gap.
questions.explain: For a recent break that leads up to the present, the book says to take the lead with a narrative that says what you would tell a hiring manager. Its Monster UK sample for caring for someone is one short sentence.
questions.teaches: For a recent break leading up to the present, tell a short story that matches what you would say to a hiring manager; the Monster UK article gives sample wording for travelling, a fresh start, illness and caring for someone else.
questions.rule: For a recent break that runs up to now, take the lead and tell a short story, matching the answer you would give a hiring manager.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: During a study break a developer built a portfolio app used only by themselves. How strong is that evidence, according to the author?
options: Very strong, because it shows self-discipline and focus
Not a strong sign of what you can do on the job
Strong if the app uses the newest technology on the market
Decisive, because portfolio projects are rare in resumes
optionExplain: Discipline is good, but the author asks for proof of skill in use.
The author says a project used only by you is weak evidence.
Fashionable technology does not change that no one else uses it.
The author calls them very common.
questions.explain: Portfolio projects are very common and weak when only you use them. The card shows what stands out.
questions.rule: List a study break like a work experience, and prove your skills with something in production, teaching or open source, not only courses.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Match each way of proving a skill to why the author prizes it.
pairs: Shows it works for real users
Shows you understand it well enough to explain
Shows accepted code in the same technology
questions.explain: The author names shipping in production, teaching and open source as ways to prove mastery.
questions.rule: List a study break like a work experience, and prove your skills with something in production, teaching or open source, not only courses.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: After studying Rust for four months, Ali wants a line that stands out. Which fits the author's advice?
options: Completed a Rust course and built a to-do app for personal use
Shipped a Rust service for a clinic, halving report time
Studied Rust full-time and earned a perfect score on every exercise
Read three Rust books and practised daily on a puzzle site
optionExplain: A course and a personal app are the common, weaker evidence.
It is in production and states a result.
Scores on exercises are self-study results.
Reading and puzzles show study, not delivery.
questions.explain: Something in production with a result beats a course or self-study.
questions.rule: List a study break like a work experience, and prove your skills with something in production, teaching or open source, not only courses.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, recruiters usually value work experience above taking time to study full-time.
questions.explain: The author says so, which is why the next idea suggests turning the study into a freelance project.
questions.rule: List a study break like a work experience, and prove your skills with something in production, teaching or open source, not only courses.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: During a study break Ana finished a data pipeline project. How does the author suggest she describes it?
options: As a short sentence stating she completed a course project
As a list of the tools, libraries and versions she installed
As a count of the hours she spent each day on the project
With the results and impact framework, showing why it was hard
optionExplain: This gives the reader nothing to measure.
Tool lists show exposure, not the weight of the project.
Hours are effort, not results.
The author asks you to use the results and impact framework to quantify why a project was interesting or difficult.
questions.explain: Quantifying the results and the difficulty is how study work reads like work experience.
questions.teaches: The author says to use the results and impact framework to quantify why a study project was interesting or difficult.
questions.rule: List a study break like a work experience, and prove your skills with something in production, teaching or open source, not only courses.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A developer studied a new framework for a year and wants a stronger line than self-study. What does the author suggest?
options: Build a feature for a client or small business and list it as freelance work
Expand the course list with the hours spent on each module
Say the year was spent preparing and leave the rest unwritten
Wait until a full-time offer arrives before listing the framework
optionExplain: The author says freelancing shows production delivery and can replace the break entry.
Study hours remain self-study.
Preparation without delivery is the weaker story.
The author suggests creating the evidence now.
questions.explain: The author recommends freelance work. The card has the details.
questions.rule: Do a freelance project on your new stack, even for little or no pay, and present the time as freelancing instead of a break.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, freelancing is a stronger indication of working knowledge of a technology than self-study is.
questions.explain: The author says it speaks to a specialist who can deliver in production.
questions.rule: Do a freelance project on your new stack, even for little or no pay, and present the time as freelancing instead of a break.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Nora cannot find freelance work in her new stack. What does the author suggest she try?
options: Build a demo app and call it freelance work with a made-up client
Wait for paid clients before listing any freelance experience
Offer to build a feature for a friend or small business, free or at a steep discount
Apply only to companies that accept self-study as experience
optionExplain: The work has to be real; invented clients are not suggested.
The author says even unpaid work can be listed if it shipped.
The feature should ship in production.
The author gives a way to create the experience instead.
questions.explain: Real work for a friend or small business counts.
questions.rule: Do a freelance project on your new stack, even for little or no pay, and present the time as freelancing instead of a break.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Sort these ways of presenting study time by whether they follow the author's advice.

items.t: Freelance project that shipped for a small business
Unpaid feature for a friend, listed as freelance work
Offering to help a small business at a steep discount
A bare line saying studied for a year
A demo shown only to the developer's family
An invented client name

questions.explain: The work should be real and shipped; the client may stay unnamed.
questions.rule: Do a freelance project on your new stack, even for little or no pay, and present the time as freelancing instead of a break.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A freelancer under a confidentiality agreement cannot name the client. According to the author, what is acceptable?
options: Replacing the project with a personal side project
Leaving the project off the resume entirely
Naming a well-known company that is not the client
Describing the work and its results while leaving the client unnamed
optionExplain: A personal project is weaker proof.
The author does not ask you to drop it.
That would be a false claim.
The author notes you sometimes cannot or do not want to name the client.
questions.explain: The work can be shown without naming the client. This is the author's allowance for confidential work.
questions.teaches: The author says you can present freelance work without naming the client, because sometimes you cannot or do not want to name them.
questions.rule: Do a freelance project on your new stack, even for little or no pay, and present the time as freelancing instead of a break.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: An engineer with a decade of experience across many technologies applies for one role. What is the main challenge, according to the author?
options: Keeping the resume relevant to the position applied for
Finding enough experience to fill a page
Proving they know the newest tools released this year
Explaining why they have not changed employers more often
optionExplain: With many technologies behind you, relevance is the challenge.
A senior engineer usually has more than enough to fill a page.
The author does not make recency of tools the main issue.
Employer changes are not the challenge the author names.
questions.explain: The author says the challenge is relevance. The card gives the remedy.
questions.rule: Make promotions visible, state results and impact, and add a summary tailored to the position.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Add a ____ section tailored for the position to explain your motivation and how you can help the team.
questions.explain: A tailored summary tells recruiters and hiring managers about your motivation and how you can help.
questions.rule: Make promotions visible, state results and impact, and add a summary tailored to the position.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Kai was promoted from engineer to senior engineer after three years at one company. How should the resume show this?
options: List the latest title and rely on the interviewer to ask about the path
List only the latest title, since it says everything about level
Show both titles and dates, and state the results and impact delivered
Create a separate section that explains why he deserved it
optionExplain: The author wants the promotion visible on the page.
That hides the promotion.
The author says to make a promotion visible and to be clear about results and impact.
The author asks for results and impact, not a defence of the promotion.
questions.explain: A visible promotion plus clear results give context for the output delivered.
questions.rule: Make promotions visible, state results and impact, and add a summary tailored to the position.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a generic summary that could fit any candidate serves a senior engineer as well as a tailored one.
questions.explain: The summary is meant to be tailored for the position. Generic text does not show how you can help this team.
questions.rule: Tailor the summary to the position.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Two companies read the same resume of an engineer with a senior title and two years of experience. What might differ?
options: Both will treat the title as final, so no difference arises
One may weigh the years of experience more than the title
Neither will read the dates, so only the title matters
One will reject any resume that shows a promotion
optionExplain: The author says some companies look past the title.
The author says that with a senior title but few years of experience, some companies focus more on the years than on the title.
Years of experience are exactly what some will read.
The author says to make promotions visible.
questions.explain: Some employers look at years more than titles, so results and impact are needed to give context.
questions.teaches: Some companies focus on years of experience rather than on a senior title when the person has only a few years of work.
questions.rule: Make promotions visible, state results and impact, and add a summary tailored to the position.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A senior engineer lists only business results. What does the author say is missing?
options: Evidence of helping others and of influence on other teams
A longer list of programming languages used over the years
A statement of the salary expected for each role held
More detail on the first job held after graduation
optionExplain: Many companies look for a record of helping people and of influence.
Technologies are not the gap the author names.
Salary is not what the author asks for.
Early jobs should be shorter at this level.
questions.explain: Soft achievements and influence are on top of business results. The card has the details.
questions.rule: Add soft achievements and influence to your business results: mentoring, leading teams, and which teams you moved.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Sort these examples by the kind of evidence the author says they are.

items.t: Mentoring more junior developers
Leading a team
Helping others beyond your own tasks
Moving several teams toward a specific outcome
The impression your work made on the organisation
Shaping how another organisation works

questions.explain: Soft achievements are activities where you helped others. Influence is the effect on teams and organisations.
questions.rule: Add soft achievements and influence to your business results: mentoring, leading teams, and which teams you moved.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Dev wrote: Reduced build time by 40 percent. What should he add to follow the author's advice for a senior?
options: The name of the tool he used to cut the build time
That he works well under tight deadlines and enjoys hard problems
That he coached two juniors and got three teams to adopt the faster setup
A second business result, since results are all that matters
optionExplain: Naming the tool adds detail but not influence.
These are generic claims with no evidence of helping or influence.
Coaching is a soft achievement, and the adoption by other teams is influence.
The author says soft achievements and influence are expected on top of results.
questions.explain: Add evidence of helping others and of influencing teams.
questions.rule: Add soft achievements and influence to your business results: mentoring, leading teams, and which teams you moved.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, the more senior you are, the more you are expected to be able to influence.
questions.explain: The author says influence is expected to grow with seniority.
questions.rule: Add soft achievements and influence to your business results: mentoring, leading teams, and which teams you moved.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A staff-level engineer applies to a large technology company. What might its recruiters look for, according to the author?
options: A record of working in one team for many years without change
A track record of influencing multiple teams
A list of the largest projects completed alone
A personal statement about enjoying the company's products
optionExplain: The author points to influence beyond one team.
The author says staff-level engineers at the likes of Facebook and Google are expected to influence multiple teams.
Solo work does not show influence.
Enthusiasm is not the evidence recruiters look for.
questions.explain: At such companies the staff level is tied to influence over several teams, so evidence of it belongs on the resume.
questions.teaches: The author says staff-level engineers at companies like Facebook and Google are expected to influence multiple teams, so recruiters there may look for that track record.
questions.rule: Add soft achievements and influence to your business results: mentoring, leading teams, and which teams you moved.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Where should a senior engineer's education go, according to the author, and why?
options: In the summary, written as a sentence with the university name
At the very top, to prove the credentials behind the experience
Nowhere on the resume, to avoid revealing any dates
On the second page, which helps reduce age bias
optionExplain: The author wants it in a short entry, not folded into the summary.
At this level, education is less important, so it moves back.
The author keeps it in short form on page two.
The reader cannot do the maths on graduation dates on page one.
questions.explain: The author moves it back. The card gives the other details.
questions.rule: Put Education on the second page with only standout details, and give older jobs proportionally less space.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: The further in the past a work experience, the less ____ it is, so give it proportionally less space.
questions.explain: The author says older experience is less relevant and should take less space.
questions.rule: Put Education on the second page with only standout details, and give older jobs proportionally less space.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Elena has a degree with an average GPA, a long module list and a thesis. What does the author advise for her education entry?
options: The school and degree, adding the GPA since employers like numbers
The school, degree and date, plus the full list of modules studied
School, degree and date, with the rest left out
The thesis title and summary, to show depth of knowledge in the field
optionExplain: Only a standout detail is kept; an average GPA is not one.
Module lists are irrelevant to a hiring manager at this level.
A line or two with name, degree and date is enough unless something stands out.
A thesis summary takes space the author wants for current work.
questions.explain: Keep a line or two: school, degree and date.
questions.rule: Put Education on the second page with only standout details, and give older jobs proportionally less space.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: The author's advice to move education to the second page is meant for recent graduates with little work experience.
questions.explain: It is meant for seniors with plenty of experience to fill page one. Our reading: a graduate's education is a lead item and stays near the top.
questions.rule: Put Education on the second page with only standout details, and give older jobs proportionally less space.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Ravi has 15 years of experience, a perfect GPA, a relevant specialization, and a list of student clubs. Which would the author keep?
options: The perfect GPA and the relevant specialization
The student clubs, since they show he was an active member of a team
None of them, as education belongs only on page one at this stage
All of them, so no part of his background goes unmentioned
optionExplain: The author names such standouts as worth keeping, and treats other details as irrelevant by now.
Clubs are other details the author calls irrelevant at this stage.
The author keeps standouts in a line or two on page two.
The author wants only standout details.
questions.explain: Standouts include summa cum laude, a perfect GPA or a relevant specialization.
questions.teaches: The author lists summa cum laude, a perfect GPA and a relevant specialization as the standout education details worth keeping at a senior level.
questions.rule: Put Education on the second page with only standout details, and give older jobs proportionally less space.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A senior engineer is interested in a role at a company. What extra route does the author suggest?
options: Ask a former colleague to write a review of the company online
Send the resume to the company's general information address
Wait for a recruiter to find the profile and contact first
Message the recruiter and hiring manager directly on a professional network
optionExplain: That is not the route the author names.
A general mailbox is not the direct contact the author describes.
The author suggests taking the first step.
With plenty of experience, direct messages are worth trying.
questions.explain: The author recommends direct messages. The card says who is likely to reply.
questions.rule: Find the recruiter and hiring manager on LinkedIn and message them directly to ask about applying.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: The people doing the hiring are more likely to ____ to messages from experienced engineers.
questions.explain: The author says hiring people are more likely to respond to experienced engineers, which is why direct messages are suggested for them.
questions.rule: Find the recruiter and hiring manager on LinkedIn and message them directly to ask about applying.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Mara has 12 years of experience and has applied online. According to the author, what could she do next?
options: Apply again under a different name to reach another reviewer
Find the recruiter and hiring manager on LinkedIn and ask about her application
Send the same message to every employee at the company
Post about the application in public and tag the company
optionExplain: This is dishonest and not the author's advice.
A contact makes it easier to follow up.
The author names the recruiter and the hiring manager.
A public post is not the direct contact the author describes.
questions.explain: Direct contact helps in following the progress of the application.
questions.rule: Find the recruiter and hiring manager on LinkedIn and message them directly to ask about applying.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, the direct-message route is meant for people with plenty of relevant experience.
questions.explain: The author ties it to plenty of relevant experience, because hiring people are more likely to respond to such engineers.
questions.rule: Find the recruiter and hiring manager on LinkedIn and message them directly to ask about applying.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A recruiter replies to Mara's message. According to the author, what does having this contact let her do?
options: Skip the interviews that other candidates have to take
Follow up on the progress of her application more easily
Ask the recruiter to change the job description for her
Cancel the online application and avoid future screening
optionExplain: The author does not promise any skipped stages.
The author says a point of contact makes following up on your application progress easier.
The contact is for following up, not for changing the role.
The online application stays; the contact supports it.
questions.explain: A direct contact turns a silent application into one she can ask about.
questions.teaches: Once you have a point of contact, you can follow up on your application's progress more easily.
questions.rule: Find the recruiter and hiring manager on LinkedIn and message them directly to ask about applying.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A hiring manager says adding more engineers will not fix their team's late deliveries. Which resume evidence matches best?
options: A summary saying the candidate enjoys long hours and big goals
A longer list of programming languages known by the candidate
A record of writing more code than anyone else on the team
Examples of speeding up delivery on a past team
optionExplain: Enthusiasm is not evidence of improving a team.
Languages do not address a team problem.
This is what a senior engineer does, not a tech lead.
The author says tech lead posts arise when the problem is not solvable by adding people to deliver code.
questions.explain: The hiring problem is team delivery. The card lists the evidence to show.
questions.rule: Show on your resume how you made a team succeed beyond what a senior engineer does: faster delivery, better quality, mended relations.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Tech lead roles focus less on technical contribution and more on delivery and team ____ duties.
questions.explain: The author says these roles focus on delivery and team leadership.
questions.rule: Show on your resume how you made a team succeed beyond what a senior engineer does: faster delivery, better quality, mended relations.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A team has high turnover. Which line would best answer that problem on a tech lead's resume?
options: Cut attrition on a team of eight from five departures a year to one
Wrote 60 percent of the code in the largest project of the year
Attended all of the company's training days and workshops on leading
Worked on a team that had good morale and a pleasant office
optionExplain: It names a team problem and shows the outcome.
A coding record is a senior engineer's strength.
Attendance is an activity, not an outcome.
It says nothing about what the candidate did.
questions.explain: Show the effect you had on the team's problem.
questions.rule: Show on your resume how you made a team succeed beyond what a senior engineer does: faster delivery, better quality, mended relations.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Sort these resume lines by whether they show what a tech lead hiring manager asks for.

items.t: Sped up delivery by changing the release routine
Repaired the relationship with a key stakeholder
Improved quality on a team that shipped defects
Implemented the biggest feature of the quarter alone
Learned a new database engine
Fixed the most bugs on the team

questions.explain: A tech lead is expected to make teams better, not only to produce more code.
questions.rule: Show on your resume how you made a team succeed beyond what a senior engineer does: faster delivery, better quality, mended relations.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A developer in Poland sees a posting for a technical delivery lead on a single product team and wonders whether it is a senior engineer role or an engineering manager role. What does the author say?
options: A junior position below senior engineer at most companies
An engineering manager role, covering several teams at the same time
A tech lead role under another name, focused on one team
A senior engineer role with extra coding duties added on top
optionExplain: The lead roles focus on delivery and team leadership, which is a step beyond senior engineer.
A manager may be responsible for several teams; a tech lead focuses on just one.
Right: tech lead is often advertised as technical team lead, team lead or technical delivery lead.
The author says these roles focus less on technical contribution than a senior engineer does.
questions.explain: Tech lead is often advertised as technical team lead, team lead or technical delivery lead. It centres on delivery and leading one team, though a few companies advertise it as an engineering manager role.
questions.teaches: Tech lead roles are often advertised as technical team lead, team lead or technical delivery lead, focus less on technical contribution and more on delivery and team leadership, and cover one team; a few companies advertise the role as an engineering manager one.
questions.rule: Show on your resume how you made a team succeed beyond what a senior engineer does: faster delivery, better quality, mended relations.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A candidate writes: ran the daily scrums for a development team. What does the author say this lacks?
options: A longer description of how the scrums were held
The programming languages the team used
The name of the manager they reported to
The outcome: did the team deliver on time
optionExplain: More about the activity still leaves out what it achieved.
The author lists technical choices too, but the key gap here is the outcome.
The manager's name is not what recruiters seek.
The author wants outcomes as well as activities.
questions.explain: Activities need outcomes alongside them. The card lists the three kinds of proof.
questions.rule: State the team's size and make-up, the context it worked in and its main technical choices, and give outcomes as well as activities.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Match each kind of proof point to the author's sample wording.
pairs: Managed a team that delivered a project on time and on budget
Coached and mentored two graduates who became senior engineers
Worked with the architecture team to deliver an essential component
questions.explain: The author gives one sample for delivery, team leadership and technical leadership.
questions.rule: State the team's size and make-up, the context it worked in and its main technical choices, and give outcomes as well as activities.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Rhea led a team but wrote only: tech lead at a software company. Which rewrite follows the author?
options: Led two back-end and one front-end engineer in a 40-person programme; delivered the portal on time
Experienced tech lead with strong leadership and communication skills
Tech lead responsible for planning meetings, reviews and daily stand-ups
Led an excellent team that was always praised by management
optionExplain: It gives team size and make-up, context, and an outcome.
These are buzzwords with no specifics.
These are activities without outcomes.
Praise is vague and gives no size, context or outcome.
questions.explain: Size, make-up, context and outcome make the claim checkable.
questions.rule: State the team's size and make-up, the context it worked in and its main technical choices, and give outcomes as well as activities.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a tech lead who also applies for senior engineer or engineering manager roles should use a single resume for all of them.
questions.explain: The author recommends separate resumes for each track, highlighting the work experience relevant to it.
questions.rule: Make a separate resume per track.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A tech lead sees few tech lead postings and also applies to senior engineer and manager roles. What does the author recommend?
options: Apply only to tech lead roles to avoid mixed signals
Use one resume and rename the title for each posting
Create a separate senior engineer resume and a separate engineering manager resume
Put all three tracks in a single long resume of three pages
optionExplain: The author says you might apply to the others as well.
The author suggests separate versions with different highlights.
Each highlights the experience relevant to its track.
A long combined resume dilutes each track.
questions.explain: The author notes fewer tech lead roles are advertised, so the same person may apply to other tracks with tailored resumes.
questions.teaches: Because fewer tech lead roles are advertised, the author suggests creating a separate senior engineer resume and a separate engineering manager resume for those applications.
questions.rule: State the team's size and make-up, the context it worked in and its main technical choices, and give outcomes as well as activities.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: An engineering manager is drafting a summary. Which approach does the author favour?
options: Fill it with leadership buzzwords so keyword searches find it
Treat it as a cover letter, tailored and free of buzzwords
Leave it out, as managers are judged by their work history
Copy a peer's summary that earned an offer from a similar firm
optionExplain: The author warns against buzzwords and generic wording.
The author says the summary is your cover letter.
The author asks for a strong, relevant summary.
A copied summary will not represent you.
questions.explain: The summary is the cover letter. The card explains the rest.
questions.rule: Tell the story of how you made teams better, and write a specific, tailored summary that works as your cover letter.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: As an engineering manager, your ____ is your cover letter, so craft it carefully.
questions.explain: The author says the summary is your cover letter.
questions.rule: Tell the story of how you made teams better, and write a specific, tailored summary that works as your cover letter.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Which summary opening best follows the author's advice for a manager applying to a growth-stage fintech?
options: Led three payments teams through scale-up, cutting incidents and keeping attrition low
Dynamic leader and passionate people person with excellent skills
Manager with 12 years in the industry, looking for a new challenge
Hands-on engineer turned manager, open to any role in any sector
optionExplain: It is specific, relevant to the target, and tells a story of results with teams.
These are buzzwords that fit anyone.
This is generic and could apply to anyone.
Being open to anything signals no specific fit.
questions.explain: Specific, tailored and story-like.
questions.rule: Tell the story of how you made teams better, and write a specific, tailored summary that works as your cover letter.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to Neville Kuyt's advice quoted in the book, many summaries are full of buzzwords and so generic that they could apply to anyone.
questions.explain: He says to aim for the opposite and to position yourself for a niche.
questions.rule: Tell the story of how you made teams better, and write a specific, tailored summary that works as your cover letter.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: An engineering manager in Singapore has led two platform migrations and a hiring push, and her summary reads results-driven leader with a passion for teams. Following Neville Kuyt's advice, what should she change?
options: Keep the wording general so that it fits every employer she applies to
Add stronger buzzwords such as dynamic and visionary to help her stand out more
Name the challenge she solves best, and back it up in her work history
List every type of problem she has met, to show how wide her range is
optionExplain: He wants the opposite: a summary so generic that it could apply to anyone is the thing to avoid.
He warns that many summaries are full of buzzwords.
Right: capture the challenges that produced your best results, then give evidence in the work history.
He asks for a specific niche, not for everything.
questions.explain: Neville Kuyt asks managers to think about which problems led to their best results and to capture those challenges in the summary. The work history then provides the evidence.
questions.teaches: Neville Kuyt advises capturing in the summary the types of challenges you are best at solving, positioning yourself for a specific niche, then backing them up with evidence in the work history.
questions.rule: Tell the story of how you made teams better, and write a specific, tailored summary that works as your cover letter.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A manager wants an engineering manager role at a company whose culture is unknown. What does the author recommend first?
options: Rewrite the resume to match the posting's every phrase
Research what the culture and values are and reflect on which you share
Apply to as many roles as possible and learn the culture later
Wait until the interview to ask about values
optionExplain: The author warns against forcing the fit.
Managers are hired to keep teams thriving, so culture matters.
The author wants selective applications.
The advice is to research before and reflect it in the resume.
questions.explain: Culture research comes first. The card also covers fit.
questions.rule: Research the company's values, link them to your achievements, and only pursue roles where you can deliver your best results.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, role fit is a two-way street and you should not force it too much.
questions.explain: The author says to progress only at places where you can play to your strengths.
questions.rule: Research the company's values, link them to your achievements, and only pursue roles where you can deliver your best results.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Tomas could stretch his resume to look like the exact manager a startup wants, but doubts it suits him. What does the author advise?
options: Drop manager roles and apply only as a senior engineer from now on
Edit the resume until it matches the startup perfectly, then decide later
Apply anyway, since any manager role is a stepping stone
Think carefully and move forward only where his strengths apply
optionExplain: The advice is to know your environments, not abandon roles.
The author warns against editing to seem the fit.
Fit matters, and the author calls it a two-way street.
The goal is to reach conversations only where he can deliver his best.
questions.explain: Fit is two-way, so do not force it.
questions.rule: Research the company's values, link them to your achievements, and only pursue roles where you can deliver your best results.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Sort these preparations by whether they follow the author's advice for an engineering manager applicant.

items.t: Researching the organisation's culture before applying
Linking past achievements to the company's values
Knowing in which environments you deliver best
Editing the resume to look like the exact fit sought
Applying everywhere to improve the odds
Ignoring culture because skills transfer anywhere

questions.explain: Prepare by researching values and being honest about fit.
questions.rule: Research the company's values, link them to your achievements, and only pursue roles where you can deliver your best results.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: An engineering manager who has done well at a 30-person startup is deciding where to apply next. Which approach follows Neville Kuyt's advice?
options: Apply widely and argue the fit in interviews, since any manager opening is a good chance
Aim at early-stage companies like those where he did well, and skip other roles
Choose the largest companies, since they are safer and he can learn what is needed on the job
Pick by job title alone, since company type matters little to a hiring manager
optionExplain: The book says to progress only where you can play to your strengths.
Right: target the types of company where you do well, such as early-stage startups where being hands-on is a must.
He contrasts large organisations that need alignment with startups; the choice should follow where you do well.
He says role fit is a two-way street, so company type matters.
questions.explain: Kuyt asks whether you thrive driving alignment in a large organisation or being hands-on in an early-stage startup. The book adds that you should progress only where you can play to your strengths.
questions.teaches: Neville Kuyt advises targeting the types of companies where you would or have done well, such as large organisations needing alignment or early-stage startups needing hands-on work; the book says to progress only where you can play to your strengths.
questions.rule: Research the company's values, link them to your achievements, and only pursue roles where you can deliver your best results.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A manager lists projects shipped and OKRs met. What does the author say to add?
options: How they supported their people, such as promotions and low attrition
A second list of the same projects with different wording
A statement that results matter more than the team
The names of senior leaders who approved the projects
optionExplain: People are at the heart of engineering management.
Repetition adds no people-focused evidence.
The author says the opposite.
Approvers do not describe your support for people.
questions.explain: Team results complete the picture. The card lists examples.
questions.rule: Pair business results with results about your people, and look at other managers' profiles and feedback for ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: People are at the ____ of engineering management, so show how you supported them.
questions.explain: The author says people are at the heart of engineering management.
questions.rule: Pair business results with results about your people, and look at other managers' profiles and feedback for ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Lucia's resume says: Launched the billing platform on time. Which addition fits the author's advice?
options: The budget stayed within the original estimate
The platform handled a record volume on launch day
The launch was covered in the company newsletter
Two engineers on the team were promoted and attrition stayed low
optionExplain: This is another project result.
This is another business result.
Publicity is not about the team.
It adds people results beside the business result.
questions.explain: Business results plus team results make the full picture.
questions.rule: Pair business results with results about your people, and look at other managers' profiles and feedback for ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: Sort these lines by whether they give the people-focused picture the author asks for.

items.t: Helped three engineers get promoted
Kept attrition low through a reorganisation
Coached a manager in another department
Hit the quarterly OKRs
Launched a cross-team project on time
Cut cloud costs by a fifth

questions.explain: The author wants business results and team results.
questions.rule: Pair business results with results about your people, and look at other managers' profiles and feedback for ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, the book's advice for engineering managers includes browsing other managers' LinkedIn profiles to see how they describe their work and results.
questions.explain: The author says that, because there are few examples and resources for engineering resumes.
questions.rule: Pair business results with results about your people, and look at other managers' profiles and feedback for ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: A manager wants feedback on their resume. What do the book's final pointers for managers suggest?
options: Only ask friends who are not engineers for their opinion
Ask engineering manager peers and join a community where managers review each other's resumes
Skip feedback, since managers are expected to polish alone
Wait for the hiring manager to give feedback after rejection
optionExplain: The author says to ask engineering manager peers or friends.
The author names a channel in the Rands Leadership Slack for resume feedback.
The author says to look for more ways to get feedback.
The author suggests seeking input before applying.
questions.explain: The author points to peers and to the #vet-my-resume channel in the Rands Leadership Slack, after joining and reading its code of conduct.
questions.teaches: Managers can get resume feedback from peers, including the #vet-my-resume channel in Rands Leadership Slack, after joining and following its code of conduct.
questions.rule: Pair business results with results about your people, and look at other managers' profiles and feedback for ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer's resume feels stale after many small edits. Which move would you guess helps most?
options: Keep the same draft and polish each bullet point more carefully, one at a time
Start a new draft from scratch with a different look and content
Move the same bullet points into a fancier template and send it
Send the current draft to more employers and wait for replies
optionExplain: Careful rewriting is the tweaking habit the author says weaker resumes share.
Right: the book's exercise is a full restart, not another round of edits.
Changing only the look keeps the same achievements, so no new material appears.
Sending more applications tests the draft but does not improve it.
questions.explain: The author's exercise is a complete restart with different content. The card shows how it works.
questions.rule: Write a second resume from scratch on a different template, with new achievements, and do not copy the first.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: In the exercise, the second resume uses a completely different ____ from the first.
questions.explain: The second draft is written on a different template and with a different structure, so the two can be compared.
questions.rule: Change the template, not just the wording.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Dana writes her second resume on a new template but reuses her old bullet points. Which instruction of the exercise did she miss?
options: Choosing a template she is fond of rather than one she dislikes
Using a template that differs from the one on the first draft
Comparing the two drafts to pick out what works in each
Coming up with new achievements that were not used anywhere on the first resume
optionExplain: The book allows a template you are not in love with, so liking it is not required.
She did change the template, so this is not what she missed.
Comparing comes after both exist, so it is not yet due.
Right: the book says not to repeat the earlier achievements.
questions.explain: The exercise needs new achievements as well as a new look.
questions.rule: Write a second resume from scratch on a different template, with new achievements, and do not copy the first.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Sort each habit by whether it fits the second-resume exercise or breaks it.

items.t: Choose a template that looks very different from the first
Keep the old resume open to borrow its best lines
Write about projects not used in the first draft
Try bold colours and a new section order
Reuse the same bullets to save time
Peek at the first draft whenever the new one stalls

questions.explain: The exercise works because the second draft is independent. Borrowing from the first removes the new material.
questions.rule: Keep the two drafts independent.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Put the steps of the exercise in the order the book gives them.
items: Write a resume on your preferred template
Set it aside and start fresh on a very different template
Compare the two and note what is good in the second
Build a third resume from the best parts of both
questions.explain: The book has you write one, set it aside and write another, compare them and then build a third.
questions.rule: Two drafts first, then merge.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Every alternative template looks dull to Kai. Which choice does the exercise allow for the second draft?
options: A template he dislikes, as long as it differs from the first
Only a template he loves, since he must enjoy the whole exercise
The same template as the first, with new colours added
No new template, writing the second draft by hand instead
optionExplain: Right: the book says the template can be one you are not in love with, but it should be different.
The book does not require liking the template.
Colours on the same template do not give a different structure.
The exercise needs a different template, not a different medium.
questions.explain: The template only has to differ; liking it is not required.
questions.teaches: The second template can be one you are not in love with, as long as it is different from the first.
questions.rule: Write a second resume from scratch on a different template, with new achievements, and do not copy the first.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: You have two very different resumes for yourself. Which next step would you guess is best?
options: Pick the more colourful one and discard the other completely
Send the one you wrote first because you know it best
Build a third one by taking the best parts from each of the two drafts
Merge them by pasting both into one very long document
optionExplain: Discarding one wastes whatever it did better.
Familiarity is not a measure of quality; the exercise exists to break it.
Right: the book has you combine the strongest parts into a third resume.
Pasting both makes a long resume, not a better one.
questions.explain: The book's answer is a selective merge. The card next shows the step.
questions.rule: Compare the two drafts and build a third from the best parts of both.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: After writing two resumes you come up with a ____ one that takes what you like from both.
questions.explain: The exercise ends with a third resume built from the best parts of the first two.
questions.rule: Two drafts feed a third.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Sam likes the layout of his second draft but the project descriptions of his first. What does the exercise suggest?
options: Send the second draft since its look is what recruiters see first
Keep the first draft and ignore the layout as unimportant here
Build a third resume using that layout with those descriptions
Write a fourth from scratch because the drafts disagree on style
optionExplain: This drops the descriptions he judged better.
This throws away a layout he finds better.
Right: take what is good from each draft into the third.
Mixed strengths are the reason for a third, not a fourth restart.
questions.explain: The third resume is the merge of the strong parts.
questions.rule: Compare the two drafts and build a third from the best parts of both.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A friend says: I wrote two drafts and then sent only the one I liked more. What does she miss?
options: Combining the best parts of both drafts into a third, final resume
The need to write a third from scratch on a new template
The need to ask a recruiter which draft is stronger
The rule that the second draft must be sent as written
optionExplain: Right: the exercise does not stop at choosing one.
The third is a merge, not another restart.
The exercise asks you to judge the drafts yourself.
The book never says to send the second draft untouched.
questions.explain: Choosing a winner loses whatever the other draft did well.
questions.rule: Merge; do not just pick.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: True or false: If both drafts were written using the same achievements and template, the comparison would give the author's intended benefit.
questions.explain: The benefit comes from two very different drafts. Near-identical drafts leave nothing new to compare.
questions.rule: Difference between drafts is the point.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer finished the third resume. A job listing stresses mobile work. How does the exercise help with this listing?
options: She can attach both drafts and let the recruiter choose between them
The third resume now fits every listing without more changes
The bold colours will signal mobile skills to the recruiter reading it
The two drafts leave her many more details to pick from when tailoring
optionExplain: Nothing in the book suggests sending two resumes to one employer.
The author expects you to customise for specific listings later.
Colour is a style choice in the exercise and signals no skill.
Right: the extra material is a pool to draw on for each specific listing.
questions.explain: Writing two drafts yields more details than one, which pays off at tailoring time.
questions.teaches: Having two very different drafts gives you many more details to choose from when you customise the resume for a specific job listing.
questions.rule: Compare the two drafts and build a third from the best parts of both.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Find Out the Impact of Your Past Projects
questions.q: A resume says Built the billing dashboard. Where would you guess the missing impact numbers can come from?
options: The recruiter who will read the resume at the next stage
People who worked on or managed the project at the time it was built
The software that scans the resume for keywords later on
A template site that fills in typical figures by job title
optionExplain: Recruiters read the resume; they do not hold your project data.
Right: the team and managers can say what the project achieved.
Keyword scans match words and carry no project facts.
Template figures would be invented, not yours.
questions.explain: Colleagues and managers are the source. The card next gives the book's advice.
questions.rule: Ask your team, your manager or former colleagues what your projects achieved, then add the figures.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Find Out the Impact of Your Past Projects
questions.q: For a past position, the book says to reach out to your old team or previous ____ about the impact.
questions.explain: For old roles, the author suggests contacting the old team or previous managers.
questions.rule: Ask the people who saw the results.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Find Out the Impact of Your Past Projects
questions.q: Lena still works at her company and shipped a feature last month. According to the author, whom should she ask about its impact?
options: Only a recruiter at another company
Only the customers who used the feature
A resume tool that suggests numbers
Her team and her manager
optionExplain: Outside recruiters know nothing about her project.
Customers may help, but the book names the team and manager.
A tool cannot know what her feature achieved.
Right: for a current position, ask around on the team and through the manager.
questions.explain: For your current job, ask on the team and through your manager.
questions.rule: Ask your team, your manager or former colleagues what your projects achieved, then add the figures.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Find Out the Impact of Your Past Projects
questions.q: Sort each resume line by whether it states an impact or only a responsibility.

items.t: Cut page load time by about a third
Responsible for the checkout service
Shrank the codebase by roughly a quarter
Worked on the website rewrite
Helped raise signups from 2,000 to 3,500 a month
Maintained the mobile app

questions.explain: Impact lines say how much something changed or reached; responsibility lines only say what you were doing.
questions.rule: Show what changed, not just what you did.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Find Out the Impact of Your Past Projects
questions.q: Raj did not learn the impact of his rewrite and leaves it off his resume. What does the author expect?
options: The recruiter will assume the impact was large and credit him
The line stays a responsibility with nothing to set it apart
The line will rank higher because it is shorter and cleaner
The hiring manager will look the figures up for him
optionExplain: Readers do not credit what is not stated.
Right: without impact the line reads like many others.
The book gives no such ranking effect for short lines.
Nobody on the hiring side researches your projects for you.
questions.explain: The author says many resumes list tasks without impact, and so say little about the person.
questions.rule: Ask your team, your manager or former colleagues what your projects achieved, then add the figures.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Find Out the Impact of Your Past Projects
questions.q: A developer left a startup that has since closed. Her old manager is still reachable. What does the book suggest?
options: Skip impact since the company no longer exists
Invent figures that sound reasonable for such a project
Contact the old manager or former teammates
Ask the new employer's HR team about it
optionExplain: A closed company does not make the people unreachable.
Invented figures are not what the book means by an estimate.
Right: for past positions, the old team and managers may have better pointers.
The new HR team has no data on her earlier work.
questions.explain: The book points to former colleagues and managers, who may remember more than you do.
questions.teaches: Former colleagues and managers may have better pointers about a project's impact than you do, so asking them is worth the effort even for old jobs.
questions.rule: Ask your team, your manager or former colleagues what your projects achieved, then add the figures.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Find Out the Impact of Your Past Projects
questions.q: You cannot find exact numbers for a project you led. What would you guess is the best handling?
options: Give a rough, honest estimate of the change it made to the team's work
Leave numbers out because only exact numbers belong on a resume
Write a precise figure so the line looks convincing to readers
Replace the project with one that has exact numbers on record
optionExplain: Right: the author says a close-enough estimate beats nothing.
The author says you do not need to be exact.
A made-up precise figure is not an estimate and invites doubt.
Dropping a good project over missing data wastes it.
questions.explain: The author accepts rough figures. The card next shows how rough is fine.
questions.rule: If the exact impact is unknown, give a good approximate estimate.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Find Out the Impact of Your Past Projects
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, an impact figure on a resume has to be exact.
questions.explain: The author says you do not need to be exact: close enough is better than nothing.
questions.rule: Close enough beats nothing.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Find Out the Impact of Your Past Projects
questions.q: Mei's team halved a report's run time but nobody logged it. Which line follows the author's advice?
options: Cut report run time by roughly half
Improved reporting
Responsible for the reporting system
Cut report run time by exactly 51.3 percent
optionExplain: Right: a rough percentage gives specifics without claiming false precision.
This names no change, so it carries no impact.
This describes a duty, not a result.
Exact decimals she cannot support are not the estimate the book describes.
questions.explain: A rough but honest percentage is what the book asks for.
questions.rule: If the exact impact is unknown, give a good approximate estimate.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Find Out the Impact of Your Past Projects
questions.q: A candidate says: I could not prove the impact, so I wrote nothing about it. What does the author say against this?
options: A resume should never contain any numbers at all
Only the hiring manager is allowed to estimate impact
A close approximation beats giving no specifics at all about the impact
Any claim without proof is removed by the screening software
optionExplain: The book wants numbers where possible.
The book assigns no such role to the manager.
Right: the author prefers a rough estimate to silence.
The book says ATSes do not reject resumes on this basis.
questions.explain: Rough figures are acceptable; empty lines are the weaker choice.
questions.rule: Estimate rather than omit.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Find Out the Impact of Your Past Projects
questions.q: Put the author's order of attempts at finding impact, from first to last.
items: Ask your team and manager about the impact
For old jobs, reach out to the old team or managers
If still unknown, estimate a rough percentage
Add the figure to the resume line for that project
questions.explain: The book first says to find out, asking current and former colleagues, and only then to estimate.
questions.rule: Look it up first, estimate second.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Find Out the Impact of Your Past Projects
questions.q: A developer improved a build process and saw the nightly build go from about 40 minutes to about 25. How might she write it?
options: Made builds much quicker for everyone involved
Cut the nightly build from about 40 to about 25 minutes
Reduced build times by exactly 37.5 percent at all sites
Worked on the nightly build process
optionExplain: Vague words give no figure at all.
Right: a from-and-to estimate gives a reader something concrete.
Claiming exactness the numbers do not support is not what the book means.
This names the work but not the result.
questions.explain: From-and-to figures are one of the two forms the book mentions.
questions.teaches: The book names two forms of estimate: a rough percentage of improvement, or a rough from-number-to-number change.
questions.rule: If the exact impact is unknown, give a good approximate estimate.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Do a Grammar Check, Not Just a Spellcheck
questions.q: A resume passes a spellchecker. What would you guess is still worth checking before sending it?
options: Whether the font is the same as the employer's logo
Whether it contains the word resume near the top
Whether it is long enough to fill two full pages
Grammar and how easily each sentence reads
optionExplain: Matching a logo font is not a resume check in the book.
Labels such as the word resume add no value.
The book never asks you to fill pages.
Right: spelling alone misses grammar and readability faults.
questions.explain: Correct spelling does not guarantee readable sentences. The card next names the extra checks.
questions.rule: Use grammar and readability tools, but also re-read the resume yourself, more than once.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Do a Grammar Check, Not Just a Spellcheck
questions.q: The author suggests the free ____ Editor to make resume sentences easy to read.
questions.explain: The Hemingway Editor is the book's pick for easy-to-read text and sentences.
questions.rule: Tool for readability: Hemingway.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Do a Grammar Check, Not Just a Spellcheck
questions.q: Tom's resume has no typos but several 40-word sentences. Which step fits the book's advice?
options: Lengthen the sentences so they sound more senior
Shorten the sentences and run a readability tool over the draft
Run only a spellcheck and then send it
Replace plain words with rarer vocabulary throughout
optionExplain: Longer sentences go against the advice to keep them short.
Right: the book wants short sentences that are easy to read.
Spelling is not the fault here.
Rarer words make reading harder.
questions.explain: Short, readable sentences are the target.
questions.rule: Use grammar and readability tools, but also re-read the resume yourself, more than once.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Do a Grammar Check, Not Just a Spellcheck
questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it matches the book's advice on checking a resume.

items.t: Re-read the resume several times yourself
Trust the grammar tool and skip reading it again
Keep sentences short and easy to follow
Treat a spellcheck as a complete grammar check
Use a free readability editor as a help
Pay for a premium tool so no reading is needed

questions.explain: The tools help, and the author still asks you to re-read. A spellcheck covers only spelling.
questions.rule: Tools help; your own reading decides.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Do a Grammar Check, Not Just a Spellcheck
questions.q: A resume is clean in both tools but nobody has re-read it. What risk does the author's advice imply?
options: The tools will lock the file so it cannot be edited
Recruiters will assume the tools are the author
The ATS will reject the resume for being too clean
Mistakes the tools miss may stay in the text
optionExplain: Nothing in the book suggests this.
Readers do not ask who checked the text.
The book says ATSes do not reject resumes this way.
Right: the author says not to rely only on tools.
questions.explain: Tools cannot judge everything, so the author asks for repeated reading.
questions.rule: Use grammar and readability tools, but also re-read the resume yourself, more than once.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Do a Grammar Check, Not Just a Spellcheck
questions.q: A developer writes her LinkedIn summary and a cover letter. Which of the book's habits applies to those texts too?
options: Check grammar and readability, then re-read it
Stop at spelling because longer texts are forgiven
Skip reviewing because tools run when you post
Make sentences longer since there is more space
optionExplain: Right: the cover letter advice also says to spell check, and readability matters in any text.
The book never says longer texts need less care.
Posting does not run any review.
The book prizes short, readable sentences.
questions.explain: Good writing hygiene carries over from the resume to other application texts.
questions.teaches: The cover letter advice in the book also says not to forget the spell check, so the checking habit applies beyond the resume.
questions.rule: Use grammar and readability tools, but also re-read the resume yourself, more than once.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Ask for Friends or Family to Proofread
questions.q: You have read your own resume many times and find no mistakes. What would you guess is the best next step?
options: Read it a few more times late at night
Send it now since repeated reading found nothing
Have a trusted person read it carefully from start to finish before you send it
Make the font smaller to leave room for more text on the page
optionExplain: The same reader repeating the task keeps the same blind spots.
Many readings by one person do not prove the text is clean.
Right: a fresh reader sees what the author no longer can.
This changes the look, not the errors.
