questions.explain: Writers stop seeing their own mistakes. The card next explains the author's reason.
questions.rule: Have a friend or family member read your resume thoroughly before you send it.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Ask for Friends or Family to Proofread
questions.q: The author says that as you write a resume you develop tunnel ____ and ignore inconsistencies.
questions.explain: Tunnel vision is the author's reason for asking someone else to read it.
questions.rule: You stop seeing your own errors.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Ask for Friends or Family to Proofread
questions.q: Aisha finished her resume at midnight and plans to send it at once. Which step fits the book?
options: Ask a stranger online to rewrite the whole thing
Delete the sections she is unsure about
Ask a friend to read it thoroughly first
Run it through three keyword scanners and send
optionExplain: Rewriting by a stranger is not the book's proofreading step.
Deleting content is not proofreading.
Right: a friend or family member can catch typos and logic slips.
Keyword scanners do not catch typos or logic errors.
questions.explain: A fresh reader is the cheap fix for tunnel vision.
questions.rule: Have a friend or family member read your resume thoroughly before you send it.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Ask for Friends or Family to Proofread
questions.q: Which mistakes does the author say a fresh reader can catch? Pick two.
options: Grammatical issues and typos
Logical mistakes in the text
Which employer will answer first
Whether the recruiter likes your photo
optionExplain: Right: the book names grammatical issues and typos.
Right: the book also names logical mistakes.
A friend cannot predict who will reply.
The book does not link proofreading to photos.
questions.explain: The book lists grammar, typos and logic errors as what a proofreader finds.
questions.rule: Proofreaders catch errors, not employer replies.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Ask for Friends or Family to Proofread
questions.q: Two jobs on a resume have overlapping dates, and the writer has not noticed. What does the author's reasoning predict?
options: A fresh reader is likelier to notice the clash
The writer will see it on the fifteenth reading for certain
The applicant tracking system will fix the dates on upload
The recruiter will ignore the clash since resumes are skimmed
optionExplain: Right: tunnel vision hides this from the writer but not from a new reader.
The author says repeated reading is not enough.
The book does not say an ATS edits content.
Errors can make the reader doubt the resume, so they are not ignored.
questions.explain: A new pair of eyes spots what the writer overlooks.
questions.rule: Have a friend or family member read your resume thoroughly before you send it.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Ask for Friends or Family to Proofread
questions.q: A developer is nervous about showing her resume to family because they know nothing about tech. Is this a reason to skip it?
options: Yes, because only an expert in her field can proofread
Yes, because family would soften all their comments
No, because the family will read the job description for her
No, because they can still catch typos and logic slips
optionExplain: The book names friends and family, not experts, for this step.
The book gives no such reason to skip it.
The family's task is reading the resume, not the job description.
Right: the checks the book names need no technical knowledge.
questions.explain: Typos, grammar and logic need no field expertise, though technical advice comes from other sources.
questions.teaches: The book names friends and family for proofreading, since the errors listed (grammar, typos, logical mistakes) can be spotted without a recruiter's or developer's expertise.
questions.rule: Have a friend or family member read your resume thoroughly before you send it.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A free forum offers to review your resume. What attitude would you guess the author recommends?
options: Follow every comment because many people agree
Welcome the feedback but keep expectations modest
Avoid forums, since free advice is always wrong
Expect expert-level hiring judgments from every reviewer
optionExplain: Many comments can still be mistaken or conflicting.
Right: free reviews are favours, so take them with a grain of salt.
The author calls forums useful, just not perfect.
Members are doing a favour and may not be experts.
questions.explain: The author's tone is cautious optimism. The card next gives his advice.
questions.rule: Join feedback communities early, read other reviews, and take advice with a grain of salt.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: The author says to treat internet resume advice with a grain of ____.
questions.explain: A grain of salt means you weigh the advice rather than follow it blindly.
questions.rule: Weigh free advice.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Jin is an engineering manager seeking resume feedback. Which source does the book point to?
options: The Reddit thread meant for new grads
A thread aimed only at bootcamp graduates seeking jobs
A forum for hiring managers to rank all the candidates
A resume feedback channel in the Rands Slack
optionExplain: That thread is meant for new grads.
The book does not name a bootcamp-only thread.
No such ranking forum is mentioned.
Right: the book names the Rands Slack channel for engineering managers.
questions.explain: Match the community to your career stage.
questions.rule: Join feedback communities early, read other reviews, and take advice with a grain of salt.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Two reviewers on a forum give opposite advice on the same section. What fits the author's stance?
options: Follow the one with the longer reply, as it shows more care
Weigh both carefully, since each is only one volunteer's opinion
Follow the one who replied first, since speed shows confidence
Follow whichever advice is more flattering to you
optionExplain: Length is not quality.
Right: free feedback is advice to weigh, not orders to obey.
Speed does not measure quality either.
Flattery feels good but does not improve the resume.
questions.explain: With free advice, you decide.
questions.rule: You are the judge of advice.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: True or false: If you join a feedback community only on the day you need a review, you will have read many reviews first.
questions.explain: The author suggests joining well ahead of time, which is what gives you time to read feedback on other resumes.
questions.rule: Join early.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A new grad reads that a forum thread is meant for her group. What is the fit the book describes?
options: It is meant only for engineering managers and nobody else
It is a paid service for senior engineers
A Reddit thread on CS careers meant for new grads
It is a general review community for every level
optionExplain: Managers have the Slack channel.
The thread is free, like the others in the list.
Right: the book says that thread targets new grads, while a separate general sub exists.
The book describes a separate general review community.
questions.explain: Choose the forum that matches your level.
questions.teaches: The book says one Reddit forum on CS career questions is meant for new grads, while a separate Reddit community reviews CV and resume in general.
questions.rule: Join feedback communities early, read other reviews, and take advice with a grain of salt.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: You plan to post your resume on a public forum. Which preparation would you guess is wise?
options: Take out personal information such as contact details
Add your full address so reviewers can judge your location
Keep everything intact so the feedback is accurate
Add a photo so reviewers see who they are helping
optionExplain: Right: the resume may spread beyond your control.
Posting an address adds risk without helping the review.
Accurate feedback does not need your contact details.
A photo is personal data and adds a bias risk.
questions.explain: Once posted, you cannot control a resume's reach. The card shows the author's advice.
questions.rule: Strip personal information from a resume before posting it for public feedback.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Before posting to a forum, remove ____ information from the resume.
questions.explain: The author says to remove personal information because the resume might circulate beyond your control.
questions.rule: Anonymise before you post.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Noor is ready to post her resume for review. Which version follows the author's advice?
options: The one with her contact details replaced by placeholders
The one with a full address and phone number kept in place
The one with her employer's confidential figures added
The one with her passport details attached
optionExplain: Right: placeholders keep the content while hiding identifying details.
Contact details are the personal information to remove.
Extra confidential data adds risk.
Passport details are never needed for a review.
questions.explain: Keep the content, remove the identity.
questions.rule: Strip personal information from a resume before posting it for public feedback.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: True or false: Once a resume is posted on a public forum, the author says you decide who sees it.
questions.explain: The author warns the resume might be circulated well beyond your control.
questions.rule: Posting is a loss of control.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Sort each plan for sharing a resume online by whether it follows the author's advice.

items.t: Replace name and phone with placeholders
Post the resume with home address included
Delete personal details but keep the work history
Post it unchanged because forums are friendly
Remove contact information before sharing
Add an ID photo to look trustworthy

questions.explain: Personal details are removed, work content stays. Keeping them risks wide circulation.
questions.rule: Remove identity, keep content.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer wants a friend's feedback by emailing the resume to a private contact. Is the forum rule needed?
options: Yes, remove every detail from any resume sent to anyone at all
No, because friends do not forward emails to others
Not in the same way, since the rule concerns public posts
Yes, because friends need the details to stay anonymous
optionExplain: Sending to a recruiter needs the real contact details.
The book does not claim friends will not share a file.
Right: the book gives the risk of public circulation as the reason, which a private proofreader does not carry. This is our reading.
The proofreading step in the book comes with no such rule.
questions.explain: The rule targets forums, where reach is beyond your control. For a friend, the contact details usually stay.
questions.teaches: The anonymising rule is given for resumes submitted to forums, because they may be circulated beyond your control; the book places no such condition on the friend-and-family proofreading step.
questions.rule: Strip personal information from a resume before posting it for public feedback.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A posting asks for Go and Kubernetes experience, and you have used both. Which resume choice would you guess helps?
options: Leave them out since recruiters know what developers use
Mention both technologies in your experience
Mention only one so the resume looks less eager
List every technology you have ever touched in a long block
optionExplain: Readers should not have to guess your skills.
Right: matching the posting's key terms helps you stand out.
Dropping a match removes something that helps.
A long block is the keyword stuffing that other chapters warn about.
questions.explain: Mentioning the job's key terms helps when it is true. The card shows the author's check.
questions.rule: Compare the posting and your resume, and mention the job's key terms where they are true for you.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: For a Java backend position, mention Java and backend, assuming you have ____ with both.
questions.explain: The book adds the condition that you really have experience with both terms.
questions.rule: Match keywords only where true.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A posting wants React and TypeScript. Amir has used React but not TypeScript. What fits the book?
options: Add TypeScript anyway so the resume matches the posting
Leave React out so the resume looks balanced
Copy the posting text into the resume word for word
Mention React where true and leave TypeScript out
optionExplain: The book's condition is that you have the experience.
Dropping a real match hurts him.
Copying the posting is not a keyword check.
Right: keywords should reflect real experience.
questions.explain: Only truthful matches count.
questions.rule: Compare the posting and your resume, and mention the job's key terms where they are true for you.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Which describes the author's way to review a resume for one position?
options: Count how many pages the posting uses and match that length
Compare the posting with the resume for key terms, then adjust it
Ask a recruiter to rewrite the resume for you
Add the company's name as a keyword to every line
optionExplain: Page counts are not a keyword check.
Right: the book describes comparing the description and the resume.
The book does not suggest recruiters rewrite your resume.
Repeating the name is not a keyword match.
questions.explain: The review is a plain comparison of terms.
questions.rule: Compare the lists.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: True or false: If a posting names a tool you have used for years but your resume does not mention it, the keyword check would flag it.
questions.explain: The comparison would show the missing term, which you can then add if it is true.
questions.rule: Add true matches.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer applies to two posts, one for Python data work and one for Java services. How does the check apply?
options: Use one keyword list for both since they are both engineering
Use the posting titles only and ignore their text
Add every term from both postings to the same resume
Check the resume against each posting and adjust it
optionExplain: The book ties the check to the specific job.
Titles are only part of the key terms.
Including terms she lacks is not true and may confuse.
Right: the check is per position.
questions.explain: Each posting has its own key terms, and the check repeats for each.
questions.teaches: The book frames the keyword check as being for a specific position, so it is repeated whenever you submit the resume for a different job.
questions.rule: Compare the posting and your resume, and mention the job's key terms where they are true for you.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: An ATS scan site shows your resume at 72 percent match and offers a paid upgrade. What would you guess is wise?
options: Treat the score as a rough guess and skip the upgrade
Pay at once because a low score means you will be rejected
Rewrite the resume until the site reaches 100 percent
Assume the site speaks for the company you apply to
optionExplain: Right: the author calls such scores guesswork.
The author says ATSes will not reject your resume.
The site always shows below 100 to upsell, so 100 may never come.
The site is a third party, not the employer's system.
questions.explain: The author is sceptical of scores and upsells. The card gives his reasons.
questions.rule: Use a free scan only as a rough pointer, and do not pay for ATS optimisation for tech roles.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: The author says most ATS scores are ____, and an ATS will not reject your resume.
questions.explain: The author calls the scores guesswork and says ATSes will not reject resumes.
questions.rule: Scores are guesses.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Kofi wants a quick, free check of how his resume overlaps a posting. Which stance fits the book?
options: Trust the score completely and buy the premium plan
Avoid every tool because overlap never matters
Use it for pointers on overlap and skip the upsell
Run it daily until the match shows a perfect score
optionExplain: The author does not recommend premium for tech roles.
The author still sees value in checking overlap.
Right: the book allows a quick check for pointers, not the paid upgrade.
The match rate is designed never to hit 100.
questions.explain: A quick free check is fine; paying is not advised.
questions.rule: Use a free scan only as a rough pointer, and do not pay for ATS optimisation for tech roles.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Sort each belief about ATS scan sites by whether the author would agree.

items.t: Most scores are guesswork
A low score means the ATS will reject you
The sites aim to upsell paid advice
Premium upgrades are important for tech roles
A quick check can still give tailoring ideas
A perfect score is always reachable

questions.explain: The author is critical of scores and upsells, while allowing a quick check as a source of ideas.
questions.rule: Use, don't trust.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A site scores a candidate's resume lower than 100 percent after every edit. What does the author expect?
options: The candidate must have left out a required skill each time
The employer's ATS will reject the resume at that score
The sites keep scores below perfect to push paid advice
The score will reach 100 once the resume is long enough
optionExplain: The author says it is built into the tool, not a skill gap.
The author says the ATS will not reject.
Right: the author says you will always see less than 100 percent, which encourages paying.
Length does not move the score to 100.
questions.explain: The author says the sub-100 score is an incentive to buy.
questions.rule: Expect the upsell.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A friend says a scan site's report proves recruiters at tech firms auto-reject low-match resumes. What does the book say?
options: Most such claims rest on ATS myths that do not apply to tech
The claim holds for tech firms that use automated filters
The claim is true only for large companies with very many roles
The claim is true when the match rate is below 50 percent
optionExplain: Right: the book says to see the ATS Myths Busted section for why most of these claims do not apply to tech positions.
The author says ATSes will not reject resumes.
The book does not split the claim by company size.
The book gives no threshold at which rejection begins.
questions.explain: The author's reason for doubting scans is that their claims rest on ATS myths.
questions.teaches: The author's reason for hesitating over scan services is that most of their claims are based on ATS fallacies, which the book's ATS Myths Busted section explains do not apply to tech positions.
questions.rule: Use a free scan only as a rough pointer, and do not pay for ATS optimisation for tech roles.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A recruiter wants a developer with a certain skillset in a certain city. Where would you guess they look first?
options: In the pile of resumes sent in by applicants that morning
In the interview notes of earlier candidates for the role
In a list of employees at the hiring company
In a LinkedIn search view filtered by skills and place
optionExplain: Direct applications are a separate route, the one the resume serves.
Past notes do not help find new people.
Their own staff list does not find outside candidates.
Right: the author says recruiters mostly use the LinkedIn search view.
questions.explain: Recruiters search for skills and place. The card next shows what that means for your profile.
questions.rule: Treat LinkedIn as a search profile for recruiters and give it as much effort as the resume.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: The author compares a resume and a LinkedIn profile to yin and ____.
questions.explain: He says you apply with a resume, and opportunities find you through the profile.
questions.rule: Resume to apply, profile to be found.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Elif only updates her resume and leaves LinkedIn unchanged for years. What does the author's advice suggest she risks?
options: Losing the right to apply with her resume to open jobs
Missing recruiters who search profiles for her skills
Being rejected by every applicant tracking system
Having her resume rewritten by a recruiter without notice
optionExplain: Her resume still works for direct applications.
Right: opportunities find you through the profile, so a stale one is missed.
The book says ATSes do not reject on this ground.
Recruiters do not rewrite resumes.
questions.explain: A resume alone covers only the roles you apply to.
questions.rule: Treat LinkedIn as a search profile for recruiters and give it as much effort as the resume.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Which describes how a resume and a LinkedIn profile differ in use, according to the author?
options: A resume is read by recruiters only, and a profile only by friends
A resume is for startups, and a profile is for large companies
A resume is public, and a profile is private to you
A resume is how you apply, while a profile lets recruiters find you
optionExplain: Both are read by recruiters.
The book makes no such company split.
Both the resume and the profile are meant for others to read.
Right: the resume goes out, the profile waits to be found.
questions.explain: Use the resume to go out and the profile to be found.
questions.rule: Apply with one, be found with the other.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: True or false: If a recruiter filters by location, a profile with no useful location is less likely to appear for local searches.
questions.explain: Location is one of the filters recruiters use, so a profile that misses it falls out of local searches.
questions.rule: Filters decide who appears.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer has finished a polished resume. How can it help with her LinkedIn profile?
options: She must start the profile from nothing, since the two never overlap
She can reuse much of its content, with some differences
She should paste the resume file as the profile photo
She should leave the profile empty until a recruiter asks
optionExplain: The book says reuse is possible.
Right: the author says content can be reused with a few differences.
A file cannot serve as a photo.
The profile only works if it is in place before recruiters search.
questions.explain: Do the polishing once and adapt it.
questions.teaches: Once you have polished one of the resume and the LinkedIn profile, you can reuse much of the content for the other, with a few differences to keep in mind.
questions.rule: Treat LinkedIn as a search profile for recruiters and give it as much effort as the resume.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A recruiter sees one line under your name in search results. What would you guess it should do?
options: List every employer you have worked for in order
Repeat your full legal name one more time
Sum up what you want to be found for
Say only that you are a person who loves technology
optionExplain: A list of employers fills space without a message.
The name is already shown above it.
Right: the headline is the first thing a recruiter sees.
A vague tagline gives a recruiter no reason to click.
questions.explain: The line works as an advert for the profile. The card next gives the book's advice.
questions.rule: Make the headline and current title state the role you want recruiters to find you for.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: If you set no headline, LinkedIn shows your current ____ in its place.
questions.explain: Without a headline, the current position appears there.
questions.rule: An empty headline wastes the first line.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Marco leads a team of three frontend developers but his contract title is Software Developer. What does the author allow?
options: A title like Frontend team lead, since it fits his work
Only the exact contract title, since LinkedIn is not a resume
A senior director title to look more impressive
A blank title so recruiters guess his level
optionExplain: Right: the title may differ from the contract if it is accurate.
The author says LinkedIn is not your resume and the title can differ.
Inflating beyond what he does is not what the book allows.
A blank title gives recruiters nothing to match.
questions.explain: The title describes your role, not only the paperwork.
questions.rule: Make the headline and current title state the role you want recruiters to find you for.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Sort each LinkedIn title choice by whether it follows the author's advice.

items.t: Team lead title when you lead a team in practice
A title for a role you hope to have someday
Backend engineer specializing in Go, if true
Leaving the headline blank to keep it simple
A headline that names what you want to be found for
A title you invent that describes no part of your job

questions.explain: A title can differ from the contract if it is both what you do and how you want to be found. Invented roles break it.
questions.rule: Differ from the contract, not from the truth.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer's headline says only Employee at ExampleCorp. What does the author's reasoning predict about her profile?
options: It gives recruiters little reason to click or match
It will appear at the top of every search for developers
It will be hidden until she writes a summary
It will count as a strong title for recruiters
optionExplain: Right: the headline should summarise the message you want to convey.
Nothing makes a vague headline rank first.
The book does not say a headline is hidden.
A vague label conveys no skills.
questions.explain: A wasted headline wastes the first impression.
questions.rule: The first line should sell.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer wants to add key skills to the headline. What format does the book show?
options: One long sentence with no separators, written as a story
A single job title and nothing else, to stay clean
Several items separated by a vertical bar
A list of every course she has taken, in date order
optionExplain: The example uses separators to keep it scannable.
The book wants more detail, not a single title.
Right: the book uses the bar to pack in more information, and says a tailored headline ranks higher in keyword searches.
Courses do not say what she wants to be found for.
questions.explain: The bar separator lets you add skills and focus areas to the headline.
questions.teaches: Using a separator such as a vertical bar lets you add key skills and technologies to the headline, and the author says a tailored headline ranks higher in keyword searches.
questions.rule: Make the headline and current title state the role you want recruiters to find you for.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A recruiter types a short list of technologies into LinkedIn search. What decides whether your profile shows up?
options: Whether you recently posted a photo of your desk
Whether your profile contains those words
Whether your name is early in the alphabet
Whether your job title matches the company's own logo
optionExplain: Photos are unrelated to matching.
Right: the search matches phrases in the profile.
The book describes no alphabetical order.
Logos play no part in matching.
questions.explain: Search is word matching. The card next shows how recruiters combine words.
questions.rule: Put the terms recruiters would type into their searches into your headline, summary and job entries.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Recruiters use the technique called ____ search, with the operators AND, OR and NOT.
questions.explain: Boolean search uses AND, OR and NOT to filter profiles.
questions.rule: Recruiters search by Boolean rules.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Hana has used Vue and Go but her LinkedIn only says Passionate developer. Which edit fits the book?
options: Delete the summary so the profile is shorter
Add the word passionate in several more places
List technologies she has never used to appear in more searches
Name Vue and Go in the summary and job descriptions
optionExplain: An empty summary gives the search nothing to match.
Vague words are not search terms.
Words she cannot back up are not what the author means.
Right: name technologies recruiters can search.
questions.explain: Name the tools you use.
questions.rule: Put the terms recruiters would type into their searches into your headline, summary and job entries.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A recruiter writes software developer OR software engineer. What does the OR do?
options: It returns only profiles containing both phrases
It returns profiles containing either phrase
It removes profiles containing either phrase
It ranks profiles by how many years they list
optionExplain: That is AND.
Right: OR accepts either phrase.
That is NOT.
The operators filter, they do not rank by years.
questions.explain: OR widens a search, AND narrows it, and NOT excludes.
questions.rule: OR is either; AND is both.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: True or false: if two profiles contain the same keyword, the one with the closer match and closer network connection to the recruiter ranks higher.
questions.explain: The author says the closer the match, for example in the headline, and the closer you are in the recruiter's network, the higher you rank.
questions.rule: Closer match, closer network, higher rank.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A hiring manager hands a recruiter a job description. How might the recruiter use it in a search?
options: Turn its terms into searches
Search for the hiring manager's name only
Choose profiles at random from the first page
Read each profile in full before filtering anyone
optionExplain: Right: the book says recruiters often search for keywords from the job description.
A manager's name is not a skill.
Random choice is not how searches work.
Filters exist to avoid reading each profile.
questions.explain: Job descriptions are a source of search keywords.
questions.teaches: Recruiters will often run Boolean searches built from the keywords in the job description that the hiring manager gives them, so those words are the ones to include.
questions.rule: Put the terms recruiters would type into their searches into your headline, summary and job entries.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: On LinkedIn you have no one-page limit. How long would you guess the author wants the summary?
options: Exactly the same single sentence as on a resume
Several pages covering each job in great detail
Longer than on a resume, up to two paragraphs
Empty, since recruiters never read summaries online
optionExplain: He says it is fine to be more verbose than on a resume.
Several pages go beyond what he advises.
Right: the author prefers a longer summary of up to two paragraphs.
He says managers are likelier to read it on LinkedIn.
questions.explain: LinkedIn allows and rewards more text. The card shows what he wants in it.
questions.rule: On LinkedIn write a fuller summary and remove jobs that do not support your professional story.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: On LinkedIn the author recommends a summary of up to ____ paragraphs.
questions.explain: He recommends up to two paragraphs describing value and motivation.
questions.rule: Up to two paragraphs.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Cal has a years-old part-time job in a shop listed on his profile, unrelated to software. What does the book advise?
options: Keep it first, since variety makes a profile friendly
Move it into the headline so it is seen
Remove it, since it adds noise to his story
Keep it and add three paragraphs about it
optionExplain: The author says to omit work that does not support the story.
The headline is for what you want to be found for.
Right: positions that do not strengthen the story are noise.
More detail on an unrelated job adds more noise.
questions.explain: Cut what does not support the story.
questions.rule: On LinkedIn write a fuller summary and remove jobs that do not support your professional story.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Sort each choice for a LinkedIn profile by whether it follows the author's advice.

items.t: A summary describing value and motivation
A two-line summary copied from the resume
Dropping a job unrelated to your career path
Keeping every job ever held to look busy
Being more verbose than on the resume
Cutting the summary to fit one page

questions.explain: LinkedIn lets you write more, and the story should stay on your career.
questions.rule: More words, same story.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer adds a thoughtful two-paragraph summary to a bare profile. What does the author expect from recruiters?
options: Managers are likelier to read it than a resume summary
They will skip it as they skip all summaries
The profile will be removed for being too long
They will read only the headline and ignore everything else
optionExplain: Right: the author says managers are more likely to read it on LinkedIn.
On a resume the summary is barely looked at; on LinkedIn it is likelier to be read.
No such rule exists.
The author reads the summary and the last one or two job entries.
questions.explain: LinkedIn readers do look at the summary.
questions.rule: LinkedIn summaries get read.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer asks about the photo. According to the author, what is a sound approach?
options: Use a group photo so recruiters see that she is friendly
Use a photo where she looks stern, to seem serious
Use a poor photo, since any photo beats none
Use a clear, professional photo alone, or use none
optionExplain: The author says no one else should be in the picture.
He says a grumpy photo is worse than none.
He says no photo is better than a poor photo.
Right: the author says a photo is optional, and no photo beats a poor one.
questions.explain: A photo is optional, and a good one needs a clear face and nobody else.
questions.teaches: The author says to use a professional photo with your face clearly visible and nobody else in it, that you need not have a photo because photos can encourage biases, and that no photo is better than a poor one.
questions.rule: On LinkedIn write a fuller summary and remove jobs that do not support your professional story.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: You are starting a job search. Where would you guess is the best place to say so on LinkedIn?
options: At the start of your headline, written in capital letters for emphasis
In the dedicated setting that signals you are open to work
In the first line of your summary, in bold
In your profile photo, as a banner across it
optionExplain: The author says not to use the headline for this.
Right: the book says to use the Open to Job Opportunities feature.
This is a weaker use of your most valuable text.
The book mentions no banner.
questions.explain: A dedicated setting does the job without costing headline space.
questions.rule: Use the Open to Job Opportunities setting, not the headline, and always show a current position.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Even without a job, keep a ____ position listed, because LinkedIn ranks profiles without one lower.
questions.explain: A profile with no current position is ranked lower, so fill one in.
questions.rule: Always show a current position.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Lia was laid off last month and her profile shows her last job as ended. Which step follows the book?
options: Leave it empty so that the profile looks honest to readers
Write unemployed in the headline
Delete her profile until she finds work
Add a current position showing the skills she wants
optionExplain: An empty current position ranks lower.
The headline space is better used on skills.
A deleted profile cannot be found.
Right: a current position keeps the profile ranked and can showcase her skills.
questions.explain: List a current position, framed to your target role.
questions.rule: Use the Open to Job Opportunities setting, not the headline, and always show a current position.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Two developers both seek work. One writes Looking for opportunities in her headline; the other turns on the feature. Which does the book favour?
options: The first, since saying it loudly attracts recruiters
The second, since the headline stays free for the skills she wants to show
Neither, since a job search is best kept hidden from recruiters
Both are equal because they say the same thing
optionExplain: The author says this does not add much value.
Right: the author says the headline phrase takes space that sells you.
The book recommends the feature.
The cost of space makes them different.
questions.explain: Same message, better placement.
questions.rule: Use the setting, keep the headline for skills.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: True or false: Adding more contacts, including recruiters who reached out before, can help your profile rank higher for those recruiters.
questions.explain: The author says the closer you are connections-wise to the recruiter, the higher your profile ranks.
questions.rule: Network distance affects ranking.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer searches for frontend jobs but wants to exclude senior posts and one framework. What does the book suggest?
options: Search one word at a time and read every single result
Avoid job search filters to see more postings
Use Boolean operators
Ask a recruiter to run the search for her
optionExplain: Single words give too many results.
The author says narrowing helps you apply in a more focused way.
Right: Boolean search works for candidates too, to narrow results to better matches.
The book gives the job seeker the same tool.
questions.explain: The same operators recruiters use work for you on job sites.
questions.teaches: Candidates can use Boolean search on job sites like LinkedIn, with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses, to narrow results to fewer, better-matched opportunities.
questions.rule: Use the Open to Job Opportunities setting, not the headline, and always show a current position.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Your GitHub has two half-finished projects with messy code. What would you guess is the wise move for the resume?
options: Leave the link off until you have worthwhile work
Link it anyway because every developer includes GitHub
Link it and add a note that the code is messy
Link it twice so the manager is sure to see it
optionExplain: Right: the author says not to link an empty or poor profile.
The author says there is no expectation of a link.
Apologies call attention to the weakness.
Repeating a weak link adds nothing.
questions.explain: A link invites a look, so it should be worth looking at. The card gives the author's reasons.
questions.rule: Include a GitHub link only when the work visible there is worth showing, and clean it up first.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Only include a GitHub link if there is something you are ____ to show off on the site.
questions.explain: The most important rule is to link it only if there is something you are proud of.
questions.rule: Proud or leave it off.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Sora has one polished project with a good README and many abandoned forks. What fits the book?
options: Clean up the profile so the best project stands out
Link it as it is, because more repositories look busy
Delete the polished project to keep things uniform
Remove the link, since a single project is never enough here
optionExplain: Right: tidy the profile to describe what people will find, then link.
Clutter and poor code are what the author warns about.
Hiding the best work defeats the purpose.
The book does not set a minimum count.
questions.explain: Show your best, not your pile.
questions.rule: Include a GitHub link only when the work visible there is worth showing, and clean it up first.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Which describes how a hiring manager treats GitHub, according to the author?
options: He rejects any resume that lacks a GitHub link
He reads every repository in full before he does the first scan
He often clicks it after the first scan but does not seek it
He ignores the link in every case
optionExplain: The author says there is no expectation.
The click-through comes after the first scan.
Right: no expectation, but a frequent click-through.
He says he frequently clicks through.
questions.explain: A GitHub link is a bonus, not a requirement.
questions.rule: A bonus, not a requirement.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, developers on the onsite panel often click through and bring up a candidate's linked projects as talking points.
questions.explain: He says developers who interview you often click through and use the projects as talking points, so what you link may come up.
questions.rule: Be ready to discuss what you link.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A technical recruiter sees a GitHub link. How likely is a click, according to the author?
options: More likely than a hiring manager, as they screen every resume
Impossible, since recruiters cannot read code
Equal to a hiring manager's in every case
Somewhat less, though technical recruiters are more inclined
optionExplain: The author says recruiters are somewhat less likely.
The book says technical recruiters are more inclined.
The book says recruiters are less likely than managers.
Right: recruiters are somewhat less likely, but more technical ones are more inclined.
questions.explain: Technical depth of the reader changes the odds of a click.
questions.teaches: Recruiters are somewhat less likely than hiring managers to click through to GitHub, though the more technical the recruiter, the more inclined they are to look.
questions.rule: Include a GitHub link only when the work visible there is worth showing, and clean it up first.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A hiring manager opens a candidate's pinned project. Which would you guess matters most to them?
options: Whether the project has the most stars on the whole site
Whether the README explains it well and the code is clean and readable
Whether the candidate has a rare username
Whether the profile photo is of a pet
optionExplain: Stars matter little unless they come with a collaboration story.
Right: context and code quality are among the author's checks.
Usernames play no part.
Photos play no part.
questions.explain: Managers look at clarity and quality first. The card next lists his five checks.
questions.rule: Arrange your GitHub so a quick visit shows context, quality, tests, outside contributions and collaboration.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: One of the author's checks is whether a project has unit or integration ____, which shows awareness of them.
questions.explain: He says tests show the person is aware of testing and has at least played with it.
questions.rule: Tests signal care.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Ivo wants his pinned project to match what this manager checks. Which edit helps most?
options: Rename the repository to something shorter, catchier and trendier
Add a follower count badge at the top
Delete the tests so the code looks smaller
Add a README explaining what it does, how to run and test it
optionExplain: Names do not give context.
The author pays no attention to follower counts.
Tests are a plus.
Right: context and runnability are the first check.
questions.explain: Make the project understandable and runnable.
questions.rule: Arrange your GitHub so a quick visit shows context, quality, tests, outside contributions and collaboration.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Sort each GitHub trait by whether this manager looks for it.

items.t: A README with run and test instructions
Number of followers
Pull requests to larger projects
Number of repositories
Unit or integration tests
Contributions in the last year

questions.explain: He checks context, code, tests, outside contributions and standout repositories, and ignores vanity statistics.
questions.rule: Quality over counts.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A repository gets many stars and plenty of activity. What can the manager learn from how its owner handles issues?
options: How well she collaborates
How fast the developer types in a terminal
Which programming language she prefers at home
Whether she will accept a lower salary
optionExplain: Right: his reading of replies to issues and pull requests tells him about collaboration.
Nothing in the book links this to typing.
Language preference is shown by the code, not by replies.
Salary has no link to the repository.
questions.explain: How you respond to others shows how you work with them.
questions.rule: Replies show collaboration.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer's pull request to a large open source project is easy to find on her profile. How might a manager use it?
options: Count the lines she added and rank her by that number alone
Ignore it since it was not her own repository
Read the pull request and its comments for her teamwork
Reject her because the project is not hers
optionExplain: Line counts are not among his checks.
He values contributions to larger projects.
Right: the author sometimes looks at pull requests and their comments.
He treats such contributions as a positive.
questions.explain: Contributions to bigger projects are a signal.
questions.teaches: The author sometimes opens the pull requests a candidate made to larger projects, and reads the comments on them, if they are easy to find.
questions.rule: Arrange your GitHub so a quick visit shows context, quality, tests, outside contributions and collaboration.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A manager clicks into your profile. Which setup would you guess works best?
options: Every repository pinned, in the same order you created them
No pinned projects so nothing seems chosen
A few pinned, well-described projects showing your very best work
A long list of forks with the default descriptions
optionExplain: There is a limit and a manager only opens a few.
Pinning controls what shows first, so skipping it wastes the chance.
Right: the author says to pin the best repositories.
Defaults tell the reader nothing.
questions.explain: Curated beats complete. The card next shows the author's steps.
questions.rule: Build your profile page: a personal README, pinned best repositories, clear descriptions and strong READMEs.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: To create a personal profile README, make a repository with the same name as your ____.
questions.explain: The repository named like your username holds the profile README.
questions.rule: Repo named as you, then a README.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Ana has 40 repositories and none pinned. Which step fits the author's advice?
options: Pin her best projects
Pin all 40 so that nothing she built is missed
Delete all repositories except the oldest
Rename them all with one number each
optionExplain: Right: pinning guides the manager to the best.
The pinned list is limited, and a long list dilutes the best.
Deleting good work serves no purpose.
Numbers give no context.
questions.explain: Pin the few that count.
questions.rule: Build your profile page: a personal README, pinned best repositories, clear descriptions and strong READMEs.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: For a pinned project, which README does the author rank as better?
options: One that only shows the project name
One that is as short as possible
One that repeats the repository description word for word
One with examples, configuration and next steps
optionExplain: A name alone fails the minimum.
Shortness is not the aim.
Repeating adds nothing.
Right: at minimum the README says what the project does and how to use it; better ones add examples and more.
questions.explain: Aim above the minimum.
questions.rule: What it does and how to use it, plus more.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: True or false: If your pinned repositories have clear descriptions, a hiring manager is likelier to understand your projects at a glance.
questions.explain: The description says what the project does and why it is interesting, which is the aim.
questions.rule: Descriptions earn the click.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer wants feedback on how good her project READMEs are. What does the book mention?
options: A paid service that edits every README she writes
A README score tool that suggests improvements
A manager's inbox that rates all her projects
A button on GitHub that hides weak READMEs
optionExplain: No paid editing service is mentioned.
Right: the book names a README score tool, and also says to browse READMEs of popular projects.
No such inbox exists in the book.
The book does not mention such a button.
questions.explain: Compare your READMEs against popular projects and a scoring tool.
questions.teaches: The book suggests a README score tool for feedback on what to improve, and says to browse the READMEs of popular projects for ideas; it also says you can pin up to six repositories.
questions.rule: Build your profile page: a personal README, pinned best repositories, clear descriptions and strong READMEs.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: You write a developer blog and apply for a Python role. What would you guess is the best way to show it?
options: Link the blog's home page and hope they browse
Link every post in one long list
Leave the blog off because blogs distract recruiters
Link two Python articles with a line on each
optionExplain: The home page may show unrelated posts first.
A long list buries the best two.
The author sees a blog as a way to stand out.
Right: guide the reader to your most relevant work.
questions.explain: A chosen link beats a blind one. The card shows the author's before and after.
questions.rule: List one or two relevant articles with a short description rather than just linking the blog.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Instead of only listing your blog, link the most relevant one or ____ technical articles.
questions.explain: The author asks for the one or two most relevant articles.
questions.rule: One or two, not all.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Dev links her blog, where the newest posts are about travel and her good Kubernetes posts are many pages back. What should she change?
options: Delete the travel posts so that the blog looks fully technical
Link the Kubernetes articles directly with a description
Link the blog three times for emphasis
Remove the blog and link a social profile instead
optionExplain: Deleting is not the book's fix and loses her own content.
Right: direct links control what the reader sees first.
Repetition does not change what the reader sees.
The author discourages social profiles on resumes.
questions.explain: Make the click land on the proof.
questions.rule: List one or two relevant articles with a short description rather than just linking the blog.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Which resume line follows the author's advice for a frontend role that asks for Angular?
options: My blog: link to all my posts on any topic
Blogger and tech enthusiast with a large and loyal readership
Two Angular articles, each with a short description
Technical blog available on request
optionExplain: This is the plain blog link the author improves on.
This claims readership with no proof.
Right: relevant articles are named and described.
This hides the proof behind a request.
questions.explain: Name the proof, do not point at a pile.
questions.rule: Name articles, not archives.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: True or false: With the after version, a hiring manager can think this person has proven Angular knowledge without having to browse the blog.
questions.explain: The author says the manager need not look further to see the person has proved the skill by blogging.
questions.rule: Make the proof easy to find.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer has no technical blog but has written several detailed READMEs. What do the book's ideas suggest for linking?
options: Treat strong READMEs as writing to point to
Start a blog the night before applying and link it
Link random posts from a social site
Write nothing, since the resume needs no links
optionExplain: Right: our reading is that the same logic of pointing to your best proof applies to other writing.
A rushed blog adds nothing proven.
The author discourages social links.
The book encourages links to something you are proud of.
questions.explain: Point to proof, wherever it lives. This is our reading, not a rule from the book.
questions.teaches: The author says only a fraction of the resumes he has seen come from candidates who write technical blogs, so having one is a way to stand out, provided it is added to the resume.
questions.rule: List one or two relevant articles with a short description rather than just linking the blog.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: StackOverflow, Twitter, Instagram, Quora and Other Social Sites
questions.q: Your resume has room for one more link. Which would you guess a hiring manager finds most professional?
options: A StackOverflow profile with answers in your field
Your Twitter account, where you post often about tech news and trends
Your Instagram page, which shows your personality and creative side
Your Quora profile, with long opinion answers on career topics
optionExplain: Right: an active, on-topic profile supports your story.
An active tech feed looks relevant, but the author discourages linking Twitter: it conveys professional value poorly.
Personality can matter, but the author discourages linking Instagram on a resume.
Opinion answers can show thinking, but the author discourages linking Quora too.
questions.explain: A link should support your professional story. The card next shows the author's view.
questions.rule: Include StackOverflow only when active and on-story, and keep other social media off the resume.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: StackOverflow, Twitter, Instagram, Quora and Other Social Sites
questions.q: The author discourages linking to Twitter, Instagram and ____ on a resume.
questions.explain: He says these sites convey professional value poorly.
questions.rule: Keep the weak signals off.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: StackOverflow, Twitter, Instagram, Quora and Other Social Sites
questions.q: Vik has a StackOverflow account with one question from five years ago. What does the author's condition suggest?
options: Add it, since any account shows he exists
Add it above his GitHub for emphasis
Leave it off, as it is neither active nor connected to your story
Add it and delete older questions written by other people
optionExplain: Existence is not a reason to link.
Emphasis on a thin profile hurts.
Right: only link StackOverflow if you are active and the profile fits.
Deleting others' content is not possible or sensible.
questions.explain: Condition: active and on-story.
questions.rule: Include StackOverflow only when active and on-story, and keep other social media off the resume.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: StackOverflow, Twitter, Instagram, Quora and Other Social Sites
questions.q: Sort each link by whether the author would include it on a developer resume.

items.t: StackOverflow with many JavaScript badges for a JavaScript role
Instagram account of travel photos
Quora answers on career topics
Active StackOverflow that backs a stated skill
Twitter feed of daily opinions
StackOverflow profile with no activity

questions.explain: Only an active, supporting StackOverflow profile fits; the other sites do a poor job of conveying professional value.
questions.rule: Link only what supports the story.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: StackOverflow, Twitter, Instagram, Quora and Other Social Sites
questions.q: True or false: A StackOverflow profile helps most when its badges are in a technology that fits the story the candidate wants to tell.
questions.explain: The author's example is a JavaScript expert whose many JavaScript badges support credibility in that technology.
questions.rule: The profile must support the story.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: StackOverflow, Twitter, Instagram, Quora and Other Social Sites
questions.q: A developer has an active StackOverflow profile and a strong GitHub, but room for one extra link. What does this hiring manager's habit suggest?
options: StackOverflow, because it shows real answers to real questions
GitHub, which he opens far more often than StackOverflow links
Neither, because he never opens links on resumes
Both, as he opens each of them equally often
optionExplain: He says the opposite about how often he clicks.
Right: he says he clicks through far less to StackOverflow links than to GitHub.
He says he frequently clicks through to GitHub.
He says the rates differ.
questions.explain: Priority: GitHub ahead of StackOverflow.
questions.rule: GitHub ahead of StackOverflow.
questions.teaches: The author says that as a hiring manager he clicks through far less to StackOverflow links in a resume than he does to GitHub.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: You apply to a large tech company that asks only for a resume. What would you guess about a cover letter?
options: It is required, and without one you will be rejected
It will be read first, before the resume
It will replace the resume in the screening
It is unlikely to be read, so it adds little
optionExplain: The author says large firms rarely ask.
The resume is what they read.
The resume is not replaced.
Right: big tech rarely asks for them and only looks at the resume.
questions.explain: Large firms rely on the resume. The card next gives the author's rule of thumb.
questions.rule: Write cover letters mainly for small companies or direct contacts with the hiring manager.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Cover letters matter most at companies where the ____ manager does the resume screening.
questions.explain: Where the hiring manager screens, a cover letter can matter.
questions.rule: Letters matter where the manager screens.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Pia can email the hiring manager of a startup directly. What does the author suggest?
options: Skip the letter, since startups never read letters
Write a personal cover letter, since the manager can read it
Send only the resume, as the letter is banned there by the firm
Write a personal letter, since the manager can read it
optionExplain: He says smaller companies are where letters matter.
Right: direct reach to the manager is a case the author names.
Templates rarely help.
No such ban exists.
questions.explain: Write for a reader who exists.
questions.rule: Write cover letters mainly for small companies or direct contacts with the hiring manager.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Sort each situation by whether the author would write a cover letter.

items.t: A startup where the manager screens applications
A large firm that only reads the resume
A direct email to the hiring manager
A big firm with thousands of applicants
A small company that allows an attachment
A job board that asks only for a resume file

questions.explain: The author prioritises small companies and direct contact. Large firms rarely read letters.
questions.rule: Effort goes where it is read.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer's resume is tailored closely to the job. What does the author say about her cover letter?
options: It becomes less relevant, as the resume works like one
It becomes the only document recruiters read
It is forwarded to every interviewer by default
It becomes less relevant, since the resume already works like one
optionExplain: The author says the opposite.
The resume remains the central document.
He says you never know if a letter is read or forwarded.
Right: the tailored resume already serves as the cover letter.
questions.explain: A tailored resume carries part of the letter's job.
questions.rule: Tailoring reduces the need.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer asks which of her documents is certain to travel with her if she advances in hiring. What does the author say?
options: The resume always will, while a cover letter may never be read or forwarded
The cover letter will, since it is more personal and so is kept with the file
Both will, since recruiters forward every document an applicant sends
Neither, since recruiters keep only the LinkedIn profile
optionExplain: Right: you never know if the letter is read or forwarded, but the resume is always forwarded while you progress.
The author does not say personal letters travel further; he says the opposite.
The author warns that the letter might not be forwarded.
The book does not say recruiters keep only the profile.
questions.explain: The resume is the document that travels with you.
questions.teaches: The author says you never know if the cover letter will be read or forwarded, but as long as you progress in the hiring process the resume always will be.
questions.rule: Write cover letters mainly for small companies or direct contacts with the hiring manager.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: You write a cover letter for a developer job. Which content would you guess matters most to the reader?
options: A full history of every job you have held
A request for a higher salary than advertised
That you understand the role and the company
A long story about your childhood computer
optionExplain: A long history repeats the resume.
Salary demands do not help screening.
Right: understanding of the role and the company is what stands out.
Personal stories lengthen the letter without a link to the role.
questions.explain: A short, focused letter works best. The card next lists the elements.
questions.rule: Keep it short, name the company, show you understand the role and why you fit, and spell check.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A good developer cover letter should be short, and the writer should not forget to ____ check it.
questions.explain: The quoted advice says to spell check.
questions.rule: Check spelling.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Omar writes: I want a developer job. Which edit best follows the quoted advice?
options: Name the company and cite its website and the job ad
Replace the company name with Dear Sir or Madam
Name the company and say what he found in its website and the job ad
Remove every mention of the role so it can be reused later
optionExplain: Hobbies add length, not relevance.
Leaving out the company name goes against the list.
Right: the letter should show he read the ad and the site and mention the company.
A reusable letter shows no understanding of the role.
questions.explain: Specifics show you read the material.
questions.rule: Keep it short, name the company, show you understand the role and why you fit, and spell check.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Sort each cover letter feature by whether the quoted advice includes it.

items.t: Mention the company name
Show you read the company website
Explain briefly why you fit the role
Add your salary history
Write five pages to show effort
Demonstrate good communication skills

questions.explain: The list is about showing understanding and good communication, briefly.
questions.rule: Brief and specific.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A cover letter is two pages of text pasted from a template with the company name misspelled. What does the advice predict?
options: It will not make the company feel special and may lower your odds
It will impress readers through sheer length
It will be read first because it is long
It will not make the company feel special
optionExplain: Right: the advice asks for a short, coherent letter that shows you read their material.
The quoted recruiter says the letter should not be long.
Length does not earn attention.
A careless letter does not help.
questions.explain: Careless letters undermine the aim.
questions.rule: Care shows.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer submits the letter through a web form that accepts a file. Which format does the quoted advice suggest?
options: A scanned photo of a printed copy
A PDF, which is easier to read than typed text
A word-processor file with tracked changes on
A word-processor file with tracked changes left switched on
optionExplain: A photo is harder to read.
The advice favours PDF over typed text.
Tracked changes would clutter the document.
Right: attaching the letter as a PDF is among the listed elements.
questions.explain: Ease of reading drives the format.
questions.teaches: The quoted advice says to attach the letter as a PDF, since it is easier to read than pretty much any text format typed into a web interface.
questions.rule: Keep it short, name the company, show you understand the role and why you fit, and spell check.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A cover letter template lists your skills in nice phrases. What would you guess a hiring manager at a startup makes of it?
options: It shows great effort and is likely to impress
It adds little, since it repeats what the resume says
It is the best way to stand out
It adds little, since it repeats the resume
optionExplain: Effort in copying is not read as effort.
Right: templated letters are frequently ignored.
The author says they are ignored.
A template cannot show knowledge of the company.
questions.explain: Templates add little. The card next shows what works.
questions.rule: Write a sincere, personalised letter about the company first, and only where it will be read.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A strong letter talks about the company first and the ____ second.
questions.explain: The example letter shows the person understands and identifies with the company before listing what they offer.
questions.rule: Company first.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Zane wants to write to a startup he has followed for years. Which opening fits the author's view?
options: A list of every skill from his resume in the same order
Why he is excited about the mission and what he offers
A long paragraph on his previous employer's faults
Why he is excited about the company's mission and what he offers it
optionExplain: That repeats the resume.
Generic praise reads as copy-pasted.
Complaints about a former employer shift the focus away from the company.
Right: company first, then what he offers.
questions.explain: Start with the company, with sincerity.
questions.rule: Write a sincere, personalised letter about the company first, and only where it will be read.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Which pair marks the example letter the author praises, as opposed to a template?
options: Long and formal, versus short and plain-spoken in style
Sincere and energetic, versus generic and copy-pasted
Full of buzzwords, versus free of them
Sent to many firms, versus sent to one
optionExplain: Length is not the contrast the author draws.
Right: the praised letter was sincere and high-energy, not copy-pasted.
The praised letter's strength is sincerity.
Sending many is the template route.
questions.explain: Sincerity and energy are what the author notes.
questions.rule: Sincere, not templated.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: True or false: If you apply to a large firm that will not read the letter, spending hours on a highly personal one is a good use of time.
questions.explain: The author says to do this only where there is a chance the person would read it.
questions.rule: Match effort to readership.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer's letter describes herself with two short opposite descriptions, then states her case. What does the author call this approach?
options: Bold and concise, a good glance at fit in few words
Templated, since all letters use contrast
Bold and concise, giving a good glance at fit with few words
Off topic, since it is mostly not about the company itself
optionExplain: It is concise, not rambling.
The contrast is personal, not a template.
Right: the author lists bold and concise among what the example gets right.
The letter also covers the company; only this part is about herself.
questions.explain: Boldness and concision go together.
questions.teaches: The author counts it as bold and concise that the example letter shares only two opposite descriptions of the applicant, which still give an excellent glance at why they fit the team.
questions.rule: Write a sincere, personalised letter about the company first, and only where it will be read.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A very enthusiastic cover letter wins an interview in one country. What would you guess about its fit elsewhere?
options: It may not suit every country or company
It works everywhere because enthusiasm is universal
It always fails because letters should be formal
It works only if it is longer
optionExplain: Right: tone expectations differ by region and company.
The author says tone differs by region.
The author does not say it fails everywhere.
Length is not the point.
questions.explain: Tone depends on context. The card next shows the author's examples.
questions.rule: Weigh a letter's tone against the company's culture, the level you apply for and the country.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: The author warns that a bold letter may be too much for a more ____ company.
questions.explain: Some managers may find it too pushy, especially at a conservative firm.
questions.rule: Know the culture.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Beth applies to a long-established UK firm. Which letter style does the author's view favour?
options: A professional, reserved tone
A loud, joking tone like a startup pitch
A letter written in slang to seem friendly
A letter with bold claims about changing the world
optionExplain: Right: in the UK or Australia a professional tone is an unwritten expectation.
Startup style may go in the bin there.
Slang is too casual there.
Grand claims are too much for a traditional firm.
questions.explain: Reserved suits conservative firms.
questions.rule: Weigh a letter's tone against the company's culture, the level you apply for and the country.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: Two developers write equally enthusiastic letters. One applies to a young US startup, the other to a large UK bank. Which is likelier to succeed?
options: The bank applicant, since banks value enthusiasm most of all
The startup applicant, as the style fits the company
The startup applicant, since the style fits the company
Neither, since letters are always ignored
optionExplain: The bank is the more reserved case.
The author says tone matters.
Right: the author says the style suits a startup but may fail with a conservative firm.
Letters matter at smaller firms.
questions.explain: Fit of tone to audience decides.
questions.rule: Tone must fit the reader.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, a very eager, excited letter suits a staff or principal engineering application as well as a junior one.
questions.explain: He says an overly enthusiastic letter can portray a somewhat junior applicant, which would work poorly for a staff or principal role.
questions.rule: Tone signals level.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: A developer cannot tell how formal a company is. What does the book's advice suggest she do?
options: Pick the boldest style available to guarantee attention
Use judgment, tailoring style to company and country
Skip the cover letter without checking anything
Use judgment, tailoring the style to the company and country
optionExplain: Boldness can backfire.
Templates are frequently ignored.
Where a letter is read, style matters.
Right: tailor your style to the company and the country.
questions.explain: Research the company first.
questions.teaches: The book says a bold, enthusiastic style may suit a young startup in the US, while a large company in the UK or Australia may favour a more reserved approach.
questions.rule: Weigh a letter's tone against the company's culture, the level you apply for and the country.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Application Beyond the Resume
questions.q: You have two free hours to improve your application beyond the resume. Which would you guess is most valuable for a developer?
options: Opening an Instagram account to hold your portfolio
Improving LinkedIn, GitHub or technical blog links
Writing a cover letter for every large firm
Adding every social media link you own
optionExplain: Instagram conveys professional value poorly.
Right: the recap names LinkedIn, GitHub and technical blogs as usually most relevant.
Large firms rarely read letters.
Weak links dilute the strong ones.
questions.explain: The recap ranks the extras. The card shows the order.
questions.rule: Prioritise LinkedIn, GitHub and technical blogs, and add a tailored cover letter where it will be read.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Application Beyond the Resume
questions.q: Of the extras, LinkedIn, GitHub and technical ____ are usually the most relevant for software developers.
questions.explain: The recap names LinkedIn, GitHub and technical blogs.
questions.rule: Big three: LinkedIn, GitHub, blogs.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Application Beyond the Resume
questions.q: Leo's LinkedIn headline describes his current duties, but he wants a different kind of job. What does the recap tell him to do?
options: Update it for the work he wants
Add open to work in the headline
Delete the headline altogether
Update it for the work he wants to be found for
optionExplain: The recap says not necessarily what you work on now.
The book prefers the dedicated setting.
An empty headline wastes the first line.
Right: update based on what you want recruiters to find you for.
questions.explain: Aim the profile at the target role.
questions.rule: Prioritise LinkedIn, GitHub and technical blogs, and add a tailored cover letter where it will be read.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Application Beyond the Resume
questions.q: Match each extra to the action the recap gives for it.
pairs: Update the headline for what you want to be found for
Hand-pick high-quality projects with good READMEs
Call out specific articles rather than the blog
Tailor it and be brief about fit
questions.explain: Each extra has its own action, and they combine into one plan for the application beyond the resume.
questions.rule: One action per extra.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Application Beyond the Resume
questions.q: True or false: A developer who links an empty GitHub profile because the recap says GitHub matters is following the recap's advice.
