questions.explain: The recap asks for high-quality projects and good READMEs, and the earlier rule says not to link an empty profile.
questions.rule: Quality before links.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.section: Recap: Actions to Improve Your Application Beyond the Resume
questions.q: A developer's blog has forty posts and her resume has room to name a few. Which does the recap say to call out?
options: The most recent posts, since fresh writing shows she is still active
Ones relevant to the role, or that stand out for some reason
The longest posts, since length shows depth of knowledge
Any posts at all, as long as the blog link comes first
optionExplain: The author does not rank posts by date.
Right: the recap says to mention articles that are relevant to the position, or that stand out for some reason.
Length is not a criterion in the recap.
The recap says to call out specific articles instead of only linking the blog.
questions.explain: Pick articles by relevance or standout quality.
questions.teaches: The recap says to mention blog articles that are relevant for the position you are applying for, or that stand out for one reason or another.
questions.rule: Prioritise LinkedIn, GitHub and technical blogs, and add a tailored cover letter where it will be read.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: You are choosing a resume template for a developer role. Which template would a hiring manager most likely find easiest to work with?
options: One with bold graphics and a sidebar of eye-catching skill icons
One built around a unique, memorable colour scheme that stands out
A plain one that is easy to read and shows specifics
One with as many decorative touches as the page can hold
optionExplain: Eye-catching designs seem like a way to be remembered, but the card shows why they tend to backfire.
A memorable look is tempting; the author sees it as a distraction from your specifics.
Right: ease of reading and room for specifics is what the author favours. The card gives his reasons.
More decoration is the opposite of the advice; it makes reading harder.
questions.explain: A hiring manager reads many resumes, so ease of reading helps most. The card next gives the author's reasons.
questions.rule: Plain and readable beats flashy.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: According to the author, flashy standout templates encourage sharing fewer specifics and more ____.
questions.explain: The author says flashy templates, in his experience, incentivize fewer specifics and more buzzwords.
questions.rule: Flashy templates invite buzzwords.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: Dana applies for an engineering manager role and compares four builder sites. Which choice follows the author's advice?
options: The site with the boldest sample resumes shown on its front page
The site that offers the largest number of colourful, modern layouts
The site with plain, readable layouts and a record of success for developer resumes
The site whose tagline promises the most eye-catching designs on offer
optionExplain: Bold samples are the flashy style that the author finds harder to read.
A large choice of colourful layouts says nothing about readability or developer results.
Right: the author tells developers to look for sites that avoid flashy design and have a developer track record.
Standing out is the pitch the author warns against for engineers and managers.
questions.explain: The author advises sites that avoid flashy design and have a track record of success for software developers.
questions.rule: Pick the source by record, not by flash.
questions.hint: Look for the choice that avoids flash and has a developer record.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: Sort each choice by whether it follows the author's advice on templates.

items.t: A plain template from a site known for developer resumes
A template picked mainly for its striking layout
A template that leaves room for specific achievements
A template picked because it promises to make you stand out
A readable layout without much decoration
A design chosen to look unlike any other resume

questions.explain: Plain, readable templates that leave room for specifics follow the advice. Choices made for flash or standing out break it.
questions.rule: Choose for readability and specifics.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a flashy template tends to lead candidates to share more specifics about their work.
questions.explain: The author says the opposite: in his experience flashy templates incentivize fewer specifics and more buzzwords.
questions.rule: Flash costs you specifics.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: A friend finds a template labelled Software Engineer on a design-led site. What does the author's reasoning say to check first?
options: Who made the template, and whether it has a track record with developer resumes
Whether the template's label names a developer role in its title
Whether the preview image looks modern and professional enough
Whether the site has many users who have downloaded its templates before
optionExplain: Right: the author notes that even templates labelled for software engineers were likely put together by a designer, not a technical recruiter.
A label is easy to add; the author says even labelled templates are often designer-made.
A modern look is the flash the author warns about.
Popularity is not a record with developers; the author cites popular sites as examples of the problem.
questions.explain: The author says even sites with a software engineer template usually had it put together by a designer, not a technical recruiter, so check the maker and the record.
questions.rule: A developer label is not proof; check who made it.
questions.teaches: Even a template labelled for software engineers was more likely put together by a designer than by a technical recruiter, so the label alone proves little.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: In what order will a hiring manager most likely read your resume?
options: Starting with the last job and working up
Top to bottom, starting at the very first line
From the centre of the page outwards
In whatever order the page design suggests
optionExplain: Reading backwards is not the pattern the author reports.
Right: this is the direction the author reports. The card gives his reasons.
Nothing in the book describes readers starting from the middle; it reports a straight top-to-bottom read.
Designs differ, but readers bring their own habit with them.
questions.explain: Readers bring a habit of reading from the top. The card next shows where the author gets this.
questions.rule: Readers go top to bottom.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: Every hiring manager and tech recruiter the author talked with reads resumes from the ____ to the bottom.
questions.explain: The author reports that all of them, himself included, read resumes top to bottom.
questions.rule: Resumes are read from the top.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: Which layout fits the way the author says resumes are read?
options: Sections placed in a ring around a central photograph of the candidate
Sections in one flow from the page header to the last line
Sections arranged so the reader zigzags between page edges
Sections scattered as boxes of different sizes on the page
optionExplain: A ring has no clear start; the reader must work out an order.
Right: one flow down the page matches a top-to-bottom read.
A zigzag breaks the straight downward read that recruiters expect.
Scattered boxes give the reader no single path from top to bottom.
questions.explain: A single flow from header to last line follows top-to-bottom reading.
questions.rule: One flow down the page.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: Sort each layout into one that suits top-to-bottom reading and one that breaks it.

items.t: Name and summary at the top, then jobs, then education
A spiral of sections that begins in the page centre
Each section starts below the one before it
Boxes to be read in an order the reader must guess
A header, then a single run of dated roles
Sections scattered with no visible start

questions.explain: Layouts with a visible start and a downward run suit the habit. Spirals, guessed orders and scattered boxes make the reader choose a path.
questions.rule: Give the reader one path down.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, reading resumes from top to bottom is only a habit and not also a recommendation.
questions.explain: The book says it is not just a habit: it is also a recommendation, and cites a hiring guide that advises starting at the top.
questions.rule: It is a habit and a recommendation.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: An editor wants a newsletter to need no instructions on where to begin. Using the author's list of reading conventions, what should she rely on?
options: An unusual layout that readers will learn to follow after a few issues
A habit readers already bring from reading books and magazines
A colour code that assigns a reading order to each section
A numbered guide that tells readers which box to read first
optionExplain: Teaching readers a new path is the opposite of relying on conventions they already know.
Right: the author lists top-to-bottom reading as a convention people know from nonfiction such as books and magazines.
Colour can guide attention, but the first convention the author lists is top-to-bottom reading.
A guide could help, but the author's point is to rely on a habit people already have.
questions.explain: The author names top-to-bottom reading as a convention people know from books and magazines, so a layout that follows it needs no explanation.
questions.rule: Use a convention readers already know.
questions.teaches: Top-to-bottom reading is a convention readers already know from nonfiction such as books and magazines, so layouts that follow it need no explanation.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: Where on a resume should the details most relevant to the job go?
options: In the middle of the page, so they cannot be missed
Towards the top, ahead of the less relevant parts
Wherever they fit best on the page without leaving gaps
Towards the bottom, as a closing high point at the end
optionExplain: The middle is not where a top-to-bottom reader starts.
Right: the card explains why the top of the page matters most.
Placement is a choice with a reason behind it, not left to fit.
A strong finish suits a speech, but a resume is read from the top.
questions.explain: Readers start at the top, so the top should hold what matters most for the role. The card next gives the principle.
questions.rule: Relevant things go first.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: The recap says important things first, ____ important things towards the end.
questions.explain: The principle is important things first and less important things towards the end.
questions.rule: Important first, less important last.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: A data engineer's closest match is two years of pipeline work, and unrelated volunteering sits above it. Which fix follows the advice?
options: Move the pipeline work up and the volunteering further down the page
Delete the volunteering and put nothing in its place
Put every section in alphabetical order for neutrality
Keep the volunteering at the top because it shows character
optionExplain: Right: relevant items go towards the top and the less relevant ones later.
Removing is not the advice; the point is order. Less relevant items can go later.
Alphabetical order ignores relevance, which is the thing the advice asks you to rank by.
Character is a fair point, but the advice ranks sections by relevance to the position.
questions.explain: The pipeline work matches the role, so it belongs near the top, with the volunteering after it.
questions.rule: Rank by relevance to the role.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: For a mobile app job, sort each item by where it belongs on the resume.

items.t: Three years building an Android app
A mobile project shipped to a store
A summer job as a lifeguard ten years ago
A course in an unrelated field
Kotlin and Swift in the skills list
A hobby club membership

questions.explain: Items that match the position go near the top. Unrelated jobs, courses and hobbies belong later.
questions.rule: Match to the position, then order.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: The same developer now applies to a school that wants a coding teacher, and the volunteering was teaching kids to code. What follows from the advice?
options: Both sections should be hidden to avoid confusing the reader
Its position stays low, since the order was fixed already
It moves up, because relevance is judged against the position being filled
It moves to the very bottom of the resume, since volunteering is unpaid
optionExplain: Hiding both ignores that one is now relevant.
The advice has no fixed order; relevance is judged for each position.
Right: the same item can be minor for one role and central for another.
Pay does not decide relevance in the advice; the position does.
questions.explain: Relevance is measured against the position, so the volunteer teaching moves up for the school job.
questions.rule: Relevance depends on the job.
questions.hint: The order is not fixed; it follows the job.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: Sam applies to two jobs, one on mobile apps and one on cloud infrastructure, with one skills section. What does the recap imply for Sam?
options: List the skills in the order they were learned over time
Choose and order sections for each position
Put the skills the employer is likelier to know at the top
Send the same resume to both jobs so the content stays consistent
optionExplain: Chronology of learning does not match what the reader wants to see first.
Right: the recap says to put things relevant to the position towards the top and to choose sections accordingly.
Familiarity to the employer is not the criterion; relevance to the position is.
One resume for two different roles cannot put each role's relevant items first.
questions.explain: The recap says things relevant for the position should be towards the top, so choose sections accordingly for each position.
questions.rule: Choose sections for the position.
questions.teaches: The recap says to choose sections accordingly, so which sections you include and where you put them should change with the position.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: You want a reader to notice three details on a crowded page. What helps most?
options: Changing colours and fonts on every line for energy
Giving only those three details emphasis, such as bold or a colour
Using the same type for everything on the page to look neutral
Putting the three details in a footnote box
optionExplain: Constant change gives no hint of what matters most.
Right: emphasis works because it marks a few things. The card gives the author's view.
Uniform text gives the eye no signal about where to look.
A footnote is where readers look last, not first.
questions.explain: Emphasis guides the eye only when it marks a few things. The card next gives the author's advice.
questions.rule: Emphasis marks a few things.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: The author says bolding can draw attention, and ____ can also pull your attention.
questions.explain: The author names bolding and colours as the two tools that draw attention.
questions.rule: Bold and colour pull the eye.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: Which use of bold on a developer resume follows the author's advice?
options: Bold on job titles, companies and the technologies the role asks for most
Bold on every second sentence to keep the whole page lively and varied
A different colour for each bullet to add variety
Bold on the whole experience section for emphasis
optionExplain: Right: those are the details a reader scans for, so bolding them guides attention to what matters.
Bold at random marks nothing in particular.
Variety for its own sake is decoration, not guidance.
Bolding a whole section leaves nothing standing out within it.
questions.explain: Bold works as a guide when it marks the few details a reader scans for.
questions.rule: Bold what the reader scans for.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: Sort each formatting choice by whether it uses emphasis strategically.

items.t: Bolding years of experience and key technologies
Bolding every word in the summary
Colouring only the section headings
Colouring every line a different shade
Bolding job titles that match the role
Bolding random phrases for variety

questions.explain: Strategic emphasis marks a small set of details the reader needs. Emphasis on everything or at random guides nobody.
questions.rule: Mark a few things, with a reason.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: A candidate bolds all the text on page one. Using the book's idea that bold guides attention, what happens to its guiding job? (Our reading.)
options: It stays the same, because readers ignore formatting
It moves to the margins, where the eye then lands
It sharpens, because more bold on the page means more emphasis
It fades: bold on everything singles out nothing
optionExplain: The book says bold and colour do pull attention, so readers do notice them.
Nothing in the book suggests that bold travels to the margins.
More bold on everything raises the volume of the whole page, not of any detail.
Right: bold can only guide if it marks a few things, so bolding all removes the contrast.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book says to use bold strategically, and bold on everything has no contrast left to guide with.
questions.rule: Contrast is what lets bold guide.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: Mina colours company names blue on page one but colours dates green on page two. Which part of the recap's advice does this break?
options: Putting the important things first
Reading from top to bottom in one go
Keeping the layout to a single column
Using it consistently throughout
optionExplain: Order is not at stake; the problem is how emphasis is applied.
Her sections still run top to bottom; the problem is the colour code.
Columns are unrelated to the colour pattern here.
Right: the recap asks you to use bolding and colours to draw attention and to do this consistently.
questions.explain: The recap's fourth principle ends with doing this consistently, so a colour should mark the same kind of detail throughout.
questions.rule: Use the same emphasis for the same detail.
questions.teaches: The recap adds that bolding and colour should be used consistently, so the same style should mark the same kind of detail throughout.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: A manager reads your resume from the top. What does she most likely learn from what you put first?
options: How many words per minute you can type without errors
Which parts you think are your strongest points, shown in the order you chose
Whether you follow a fashionable design trend
How many words you could fit on a page
optionExplain: Typing speed is not what a resume's first lines show.
Right: the first lines show what you chose to lead with. The card gives the guide's view.
Fashion is not the point the guide makes.
Word count is not what the opening lines reveal.
questions.explain: What you lead with shows what you consider strong. The card next gives the guide's view.
questions.rule: What you lead with is a signal.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: A hiring-guide author the book quotes says the strong points a candidate puts first tell the reader a lot about the ____.
questions.explain: The quoted author says seeing what a candidate thinks are his or her strong points can tell you a lot about the candidate.
questions.rule: Your lead points describe you.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: Leo applies for an infrastructure role. Which opening gives a manager something to compare against the job's requirements?
options: A list of hobbies placed above all his jobs
An objective saying he will take any available role
A quotation from a former classmate praising his sense of humour
A summary of his cloud infrastructure experience and the tools he used
optionExplain: Hobbies tell the reader little about fit with the requirements.
A vague objective gives the manager no strong point to match.
A friendly quote does not give a manager anything to compare against requirements.
Right: it states strong points that relate to the role, ready to be compared with the requirements.
questions.explain: A summary of role-relevant experience and tools states strong points that can be compared with the requirements.
questions.rule: Lead with points the job can check.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: Put the steps of the guide author's way of reading a resume in order.
items: Start at the top of the resume
Work down towards the final line
Make mental notes on the resume's strong points
Compare the notes with the job's actual requirements
questions.explain: She starts at the top, works down to the last line and notes strong points as she goes. The comparison with the job's requirements comes after the notes.
questions.rule: Read down, note, then compare.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: Which areas does the guide's author make mental notes on while reading? Pick the three that apply.
options: Work experience
Hobbies and interests
Position objective
Professional training
Number of pages
optionExplain: Right: one of the five areas she names.
Not among the areas she names.
Right: she lists it among the five areas.
Right: she lists it among the five areas.
Page count is not among the areas she names.
questions.explain: She names work experience, position objective, strengths, education and professional training. Hobbies and page count are not on her list.
questions.rule: Five areas, each compared with the job.
questions.teaches: The guide's author notes five areas as she reads: work experience, position objective, strengths, education and professional training.

questions.section: Good Resume Template Layout and Principles
questions.q: A founder hiring her first engineer spots one weak area in a fitting resume. When does the quoted guide's author use an item to exclude?
options: Whenever any single item looks weaker than the job needs
Only when the item matches her elimination criteria
When the item is the first thing on the page
Only when the candidate has no work experience
optionExplain: Not so: a single weak item does not rule a candidate out by itself in her method.
Right: she uses items to include candidates and excludes only when an item matches her elimination criteria.
Position on the page is not her exclusion test.
The guide sets no such single test.
questions.explain: The guide's author uses items in the resume to include candidates, and uses them to exclude only when they match her elimination criteria.
questions.rule: Include by items; exclude only on set criteria.
questions.teaches: The guide's author uses resume items to include candidates and uses an item to exclude only when it matches her elimination criteria.

questions.q: Which layout are technical recruiters most used to reading every day?
options: A two-column infographic with icons
A free-form page that each candidate designs entirely alone
A poster-style page with large artwork
The profile format of a professional networking site
optionExplain: Infographic designs exist, but they are not the daily format of recruiters.
Unique designs mean each reading starts with fresh decoding.
Artwork pages are rare in daily recruiting work.
Right: recruiters read this format all the time. The card gives the book's example.
questions.explain: Recruiters read LinkedIn-style profiles all day. The card next gives the book's view.
questions.rule: Familiar format helps.

questions.q: Recruiters read the ____ profile format day in, day out, which makes it familiar.
questions.explain: The book names the LinkedIn profile as the format recruiters see most.
questions.rule: Recruiters know the LinkedIn format.

questions.q: Kofi copies a profile-style layout but his languages and tools appear only inside job descriptions. What should he change?
options: Give languages and technologies a visible place
Move his job descriptions to the last page of the resume
Drop the profile layout and switch to two columns
Remove tool names so the text reads more smoothly
optionExplain: Right: LinkedIn's generic format does not stress them, so the developer version should.
Moving the descriptions does not fix the missing emphasis.
Dropping the familiar layout loses its benefit; the fix is an adjustment.
Tool names are what the recruiter scans for.
questions.explain: The book adjusts the familiar layout so that languages and technologies, important for developers, get emphasis.
questions.rule: Keep the layout, add tech emphasis.

questions.q: Sort each tweak to a profile-style layout by whether it fits the book's advice.

items.t: Add an area that names languages and technologies
Keep the layout reading top to bottom
Replace the flow with a sidebar for skills
Hide technologies in the last bullet of old jobs
Keep a layout recruiters already know
Redesign it so that nobody has seen it before

questions.explain: Keeping the known layout and adding technology emphasis fits. Replacing the flow, hiding technologies or inventing a novel layout breaks it.
questions.rule: Familiar layout, emphasis on tech.

questions.q: True or false: LinkedIn's generic profile format puts special emphasis on programming languages and technologies, which is why developers can copy it unchanged.
questions.explain: The book says LinkedIn will not place emphasis on languages and technologies, so developers should add it.
questions.rule: Add what LinkedIn leaves out.

questions.q: Rosa wants a template that recruiters will not find odd. According to the author, which kind is a safe bet?
options: A template that follows the familiar LinkedIn profile layout
A template with an experimental, entirely new layout
A template that matches only her own personal taste
A template with the most columns possible
optionExplain: Right: the author says templates that follow this format in their layout are a safe bet.
A new layout is the opposite of a safe bet.
Taste is fine, but safety here comes from familiarity to recruiters.
More columns make reading harder, not safer.
questions.explain: The book calls resume templates that follow the LinkedIn profile format a safe bet.
questions.rule: Known formats are safe.
questions.teaches: The author describes resume templates that follow the LinkedIn profile layout as a safe bet.

questions.q: A resume has to run to two pages. Which layout would a recruiter likely find easiest to follow?
options: A layout that places the whole text in a small box
A layout that scatters sections across both pages
A layout that switches to columns on page two
One that reads down the page, as on page one
optionExplain: Small text blocks make long resumes harder to scan.
Scattering removes the straight path through the resume.
Switching layouts mid-resume makes the reader re-learn the page.
Right: continuing the same top-down flow keeps the page easy to read. The card gives the book's view.
questions.explain: A consistent downward flow works across pages. The card next gives the book's view.
questions.rule: One flow over many pages.

questions.q: The author says top-down layouts work well for ____ resumes as well.
questions.explain: The book states that top-down layouts work well for multi-page resumes as well.
questions.rule: Top-down scales to several pages.

questions.q: Ana has three roles with four bullets each. She is torn between squeezing onto one page and a top-down run onto page two. What does the author favour?
options: Run top-down onto page two so each role keeps all of its bullets
Cut two roles so a column layout fits on one page
Split the roles into columns that fit the page
Squeeze everything onto one page by shrinking the text size
optionExplain: Right: the format handles multiple pages well, and the downside is small.
Cutting roles loses the detail the book wants you to share.
Columns are the layout the author advises developers against.
Shrinking fits the page but not the reading ease the author values.
questions.explain: Because top-down works over several pages, Ana can keep each role's bullets without switching layouts.
questions.rule: Let the resume run down the page.

questions.q: A bank's recruiter must choose between top-down and multi-column templates for ten staff resumes. Which pairing matches the book's view?
options: Top-down is familiar and easy to read; multi-column seems to save space but costs reading ease
Both are equally hard for recruiters to read
Top-down is unfamiliar to recruiters; multi-column is what they read daily
Top-down is hard to read; multi-column is easy
optionExplain: Right: the book sets familiarity and ease of reading against the apparent space saving.
The book does not rate them equally.
The book says the opposite about familiarity.
The book says top-down is easy to read.
questions.explain: The book recommends top-down for familiarity and readability, granting that multi-column seems more space-efficient.
questions.rule: Weigh familiarity against space.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, the possible space downside of top-down layouts is a strong reason to avoid them.
questions.explain: The author says that given the format's familiarity and ease of reading, there is little reason not to use it.
questions.rule: The downside is small.

questions.q: Nadia is told top-down layouts waste page space. How does the author weigh that against the format's other traits?
options: He names it as the only downside and still favours top-down
He says space is irrelevant to resumes of any kind
He says top-down loses on both space and reading ease
He treats the lost space as decisive and so avoids the format entirely
optionExplain: Right: his only possible downside is that top-down seemingly uses space less efficiently than multi-column.
He names space as a possible downside, so he does not call it irrelevant.
He rates the format as easy to read.
He does not treat it as decisive; the format stays recommended.
questions.explain: The author names one possible downside, seemingly less efficient use of page space, and still finds little reason not to use top-down.
questions.rule: One small cost, many benefits.
questions.teaches: The author's only possible downside for top-down is that it seemingly does not use page space as efficiently as a multi-column layout.

questions.q: A recruiter opens a resume with two side-by-side columns. What is likely to slow the recruiter down?
options: Checking the page size before reading
Counting how many words the page holds across both columns
Deciding where to start and where each section is
Working out which font was used
optionExplain: Page size is not the issue.
Word count is not what slows the reader.
Right: the reader must work out the order of reading. The card gives the author's reasons.
Font identification does not slow the reading of the content.
questions.explain: Columns break the straight path down the page. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Columns make the reader choose a path.

questions.q: In a two-column layout the reader goes top to bottom, then starts again, going left to ____.
questions.explain: The book describes the reader going top to bottom, then starting again from left to right.
questions.rule: Down, then restart.

questions.q: A recruiter has 30 resumes: ten top-down and twenty two-column. Where will the extra effort most likely fall?
options: On all thirty equally, because format does not affect effort
On none, because recruiters read resumes by software only
On the ten top-down resumes, since they have more sections to read
On the twenty two-column resumes, where sections can sit anywhere on the page
optionExplain: The book says format does affect how quickly key information is found.
The book is about how recruiters read, not automated reading.
The book says key information is easy to spot in top-down resumes.
Right: the columns differ in order, so each resume must be decoded.
questions.explain: Two-column resumes have columns in different orders, so each one costs the recruiter more effort to decode.
questions.rule: Variable order costs effort.

questions.q: Sort each trait by the layout it describes, according to the book.

items.t: The reader must start again after the first column
Key sections such as education are easy to spot
Column order differs from one resume to the next
The recruiter reads from the first line to the last
The reader switches from going down to going left to right
A familiar route through the page

questions.explain: In a top-down layout the route is familiar and key sections are easy to spot. In two columns the reader restarts and column order varies.
questions.rule: Down the page, or down and restart.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, ten resumes with two-column layouts will mostly put their columns in the same order, so recruiters learn where to look.
questions.explain: The author says ten two-column resumes will have their columns in ten different orders.
questions.rule: Order varies between resumes.

questions.q: Tariq picks two columns to squeeze everything onto one page. Which trade does the author say he is making?
options: Familiarity in exchange for better colour
Readability in exchange for room for extra detail
Space on a one-page resume in exchange for readability
Nothing, because the layout costs the reader no extra effort
optionExplain: Colour is not part of this trade.
The book says two columns reduce room for detail.
Right: the layout's goal is to maximize space for one-page resumes, at the expense of readability.
The book says there is a readability cost.
questions.explain: The aim of the layout is to maximize space for one-page resumes, and the author says it does this at the expense of readability.
questions.rule: Space is bought with readability.
questions.teaches: The two-column layout's goal is to maximize space for one-page resumes, which the author says it does at the expense of readability.

questions.q: You have three results to report for one job. What layout feature do you need most?
options: A graphic that shows the job as an icon
A narrow sidebar that holds only the job title
A fixed box that holds a single short sentence
Room for several bullet points under that job
optionExplain: An icon does not carry results.
A sidebar title gives no room for the results.
One sentence is a squeeze for three results.
Right: bullets let you list each result. The card gives the author's view.
questions.explain: Several results need several lines. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Bullets carry results.

questions.q: Two-column designs do not cater for sharing several ____ points per position.
questions.explain: The author says none of the two-column designs cater for several bullet points per position.
questions.rule: Several bullets per position.

questions.q: An engineer has four projects, each with three measurable results. Which layout fits the author's advice?
options: A single paragraph that lists all four projects
A two-column page with a single line for each project
A page of skill icons in a sidebar
A top-down layout with bullets under each project
optionExplain: One paragraph blurs separate results together.
One line per project cannot hold three results.
Icons leave out the results the author wants shared.
Right: it leaves room to state each result.
questions.explain: Several bullets per project let the engineer state each result, which the two-column designs do not support.
questions.rule: Room for results.

questions.q: Jo says a two-column resume shows impact best because it looks compact. Which part of that is the weak link?
options: Compact pages are hard to print on ordinary paper
Compact looks leave no space for several bullets of impact
Recruiters skip bullets and read headings only
Impact belongs in a cover letter and not on the resume itself
optionExplain: The book does not raise printing; its objection is about detail.
Right: the author says two-column designs do not cater for several bullets.
The book says recruiters read the resume after a first scan.
The book wants impact described in the resume itself.
questions.explain: A compact page looks efficient, but the author says two-column designs leave little room for bullets that show impact.
questions.rule: Compact is not detailed.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a two-column resume is more likely to be full of buzzwords and cliches than to describe the impact of your work.
questions.explain: The book says this format is more likely to be filled with buzzwords and cliches than to describe impact.
questions.rule: Thin space breeds buzzwords.

questions.q: Ben has eight years of experience and uses a two-column template. Based on the author's remarks, what is likely to happen as he tries to add detail?
options: The template invites him to run onto a second page
The template gives him extra bullets per role automatically
The template turns buzzwords into measurable results
He is pushed to stay on one page and trim detail
optionExplain: Not so: the author says none of the layouts incentivize going beyond one page.
The author says none cater for several bullets.
Nothing in the book says a template does that.
Right: the layout does not encourage going past one page, so detail gets cut.
questions.explain: The author says none of the two-column layouts incentivize going beyond one page, so a long career gets squeezed.
questions.rule: A one-page push cuts detail.
questions.teaches: None of the two-column layouts incentivize going beyond one page, so a candidate with a long record is pushed to trim detail.

questions.q: Who is most likely to gain from a two-column resume layout?
options: Anyone whose resume is longer than one page
An engineering manager applying to a large firm
A backend developer applying to a platform team
A UX designer, whose layout shows craft
optionExplain: Longer resumes gain nothing from a layout built for one-page resumes.
The author's advice for software roles is against two columns.
Developers lose readability and room for detail, per the author.
Right: the card says why layout can be part of the application. It names the case.
questions.explain: Where the layout is part of the application, a distinctive layout can help. The card next names the case.
questions.rule: Layout matters where it is judged.

questions.q: For software developers, the author says a two-column layout has no ____ and only drawbacks.
questions.explain: The author says that for software developers there is no advantage to this layout.
questions.rule: No advantage for developers.

questions.q: Which candidate has the strongest case for a two-column layout, according to the author?
options: A UX designer applying for a product design role
A site reliability engineer applying to a cloud company
A mobile developer with a long project list
A data scientist with ten research papers
optionExplain: Right: design or UX positions are the author's example where layout is part of the application.
Software roles gain nothing from it, per the author.
A long project list needs room, which two columns do not give.
Not a design position; the drawbacks apply.
questions.explain: The author singles out design or UX positions, where the resume layout is part of the application.
questions.rule: Design and UX are the exceptions.

questions.q: Sort each applicant by the advice that fits them, according to the author.
groups: Two columns can be a good choice

items.t: A UX designer showing their layout skills
A backend developer
A design applicant whose layout is part of the application
An engineering manager
A mobile engineer with many projects
A UX candidate applying for a design role

questions.explain: Design and UX applicants, whose layout is on show, can use two columns. Software roles should use a single column.
questions.rule: Is the layout itself judged?

questions.q: A developer says a design friend did well with two columns, so it should work for him too. What does the author's reasoning predict?
options: It will help only if the resume exceeds two pages
It will work as well, because layouts are interchangeable between fields
It will give no advantage, because his layout is not judged the way a designer's is
It will help because recruiters like unusual layouts
optionExplain: Length does not decide this in the book.
The author separates cases where layout is part of the application from those where it is not.
Right: the advantage depends on layout being judged, and for developers it is not.
The author says it makes key information harder to find.
questions.explain: The friend's advantage came from layout being part of the application. For a developer it is not, so only the drawbacks remain.
questions.rule: The friend's case does not transfer.

questions.q: Mei applies for a job in an industry outside software. What does the author say about two columns there?
options: They are expected in every industry apart from software engineering
They might also work, though he stays tentative about it
They are as bad as in software, for the same reasons
They are ruled out in every field other than design
optionExplain: No such expectation appears in the book.
Right: he says that in industries outside software engineering they might also work.
He leaves room for them outside software.
The author does not say that.
questions.explain: The author says that in industries outside software engineering two-column layouts might also work.
questions.rule: Outside software, the answer may differ.
questions.teaches: The author allows that two-column layouts might also work in industries outside software engineering, but he stops short of saying they do.

questions.q: A recruiter says your resume is like an elevator pitch. What does that suggest it must do?
options: List every task you ever did
Tell a brief career story quickly
Wait for the reader to ask questions
Hide weaknesses behind decoration
optionExplain: A pitch is short, not exhaustive.
Right: a pitch is short and clear. The card gives the recruiter's view.
A pitch makes its point before questions come.
Pitching is about clarity, not hiding.
questions.explain: An elevator pitch makes the point quickly. The card next gives the recruiter's view.
questions.rule: Be quick and clear.

questions.q: The recruiter calls a resume a ____ story of your career.
questions.explain: He describes a resume as a brief story of your career, or a ten-second elevator pitch.
questions.rule: A resume is a brief story.

questions.q: A candidate asks the recruiter which format to use for a general software role. Which does he name as the most optimal?
options: A graphic infographic layout
A layout chosen at random
A top-down layout
A layout with three columns
optionExplain: He treats the two-column layout as infographic-like and risky.
He gives reasons for his choice.
Right: he calls the top-down format the most optimal.
He does not recommend more columns.
questions.explain: He considers top-down the most optimal format, as the most organized for readability and for flow of thought.
questions.rule: He names top-down.

questions.q: Which two reasons does the recruiter give for preferring the top-down format?
options: It is the most organized format for easy readability
It gets resumes past automated filters
It allows an easy flow of thought, starting with skills and relevant experience
It lets a candidate use less text
optionExplain: Right: his first reason.
He does not mention automated filters.
Right: his second reason.
He does not praise it for using less text.
questions.explain: He gives two reasons: it is the most organized for readability and it allows an easy flow of thought, starting with what the hiring team most wants.
questions.rule: Organized and easy to follow.

questions.q: True or false: According to the recruiter, the two-column format can hurt candidates who are not good at presenting relevant information briefly.
questions.explain: He says it saves reviewers time like an infographic, but can hurt candidates badly if they cannot present information succinctly.
questions.rule: It rewards brevity.

questions.q: A candidate with a wide, unfocused background picks a two-column layout. According to the recruiter, how is the result likely to go?
options: The reviewer will check page two for missing information
Rejection can be immediate if relevance does not show quickly enough to the reviewer
The candidate will be advanced because the format is currently trendy
The reviewer will take extra time to find the relevance
optionExplain: He describes a quick judgement, not a search of page two.
Right: he calls two columns a double-edged sword; if relevance does not show, the decision to reject is immediate.
He does not rate trendiness.
Not so: the format is quick to judge, in either direction.
questions.explain: The recruiter says that if you succeed in showing relevance you are an easy pick, and if not the decision to reject is immediate.
questions.rule: Two columns reward the brief and relevant.
questions.teaches: The recruiter calls two columns a double-edged sword: a candidate who shows relevance is an easy pick, but if relevance does not show, rejection is immediate.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: A recruiter glances at your resume for a few seconds. Which set of details do they most likely look for?
options: The names of your managers and teammates
Years of experience, technologies, titles and location
Your school grades and awards from long ago
Hobbies, referees, a photograph and a personal motto line
optionExplain: Names of colleagues are not what the first scan seeks.
Right: these answer the recruiter's first questions. The card gives the full list.
Old grades are not the first-scan list.
These are rarely what a first scan is for.
questions.explain: A first scan looks for fit with the role. The card next gives the book's list.
questions.rule: Scan for fit, fast.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: Besides years of experience, technologies, and titles and companies, recruiters check the ____ where you are based.
questions.explain: The fourth detail is your location, where you are based right now.
questions.rule: Location is the fourth detail.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: Sort each detail by whether it is on the book's first-scan list.

items.t: Dates of employment
Technologies relevant to the role
Your hobbies
A list of referees
Titles and companies
Where you are based now

questions.explain: The list is years and dates, relevant technologies, titles and companies, and location. Hobbies and referees are not on it.
questions.rule: Four details, not a long list.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: In the book's sample, the recruiter notes at least two years of experience that matches the manager's guidance. What happens next?
options: The recruiter stops and sets the resume aside for good
The recruiter reads page two in detail
The recruiter scans for technologies and titles
The recruiter writes to the candidate
optionExplain: Stopping would waste a match; the book continues scanning.
The book says page two comes only after further scans.
Right: the scan continues with a glance at technologies and titles.
Contact comes much later, if at all.
questions.explain: With the experience matching, the recruiter keeps scanning and next glances at the technologies listed and the titles.
questions.rule: A match keeps the scan going.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: A candidate hides their years of experience in the last bullet of their oldest job. Which problem does the first scan expose?
options: The recruiter expects the experience in the footer
The recruiter reads too much about the candidate's oldest job
The recruiter cannot spot a key detail
The recruiter sees too many technologies at once
optionExplain: The book gives no footer rule.
Reading too much is not the issue; the fault is what is hard to find.
Right: years and dates are on the first-scan list and need to be easy to find.
The problem here is the opposite: a key detail is not visible.
questions.explain: A first scan lasts a few seconds, so a key detail buried in a bullet is easily missed.
questions.rule: Do not bury key details.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: A company cannot sponsor visas. Why does the location on a resume matter to its recruiter?
options: It shows which accent the candidate is likely to have
It shows how long the candidate's commute was in their last job
Whether you are local or need a visa
It shows whether the candidate prefers remote work
optionExplain: The book gives no such reason.
Commute is not the book's reason.
Right: the book says location tells whether you are local, within an area that needs no visa, or would likely need a visa or relocation.
The book's reasons are about visas and relocation.
questions.explain: The book says location shows whether you are local, within an area that needs no visa, or somewhere you would likely need a visa or relocation.
questions.rule: Location answers a practical question.
questions.teaches: Location matters because it tells the recruiter whether you are local, in an area that needs no visa, or somewhere you would likely need a visa or relocation.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: When does a recruiter most likely look at the second page of your resume?
options: Only after the first page passes their quick scans
In the middle of the first scan
Never, because recruiters read one page only
First, to see how long the whole resume is before reading
optionExplain: Right: the second page comes late. The card gives the sequence.
The first scan covers the first page's key details, not page two.
The book says deeper reading follows a good first impression.
Page count is not where the read begins.
questions.explain: Deeper reading comes only after quick passes succeed. The card next gives the sequence.
questions.rule: Page two comes late.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: Put the recruiter's stages in order, from first to last.
items: Scan for key details such as experience, technologies and titles
Read top to bottom with a short scan for relevant or eye-catching items
Look at the second page or read in depth
questions.explain: The first scan collects key details. If most match, a short top-to-bottom scan follows. Only after that does the recruiter look at the second page or read in depth.
questions.rule: Scan, skim, then read deeper.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: Priya's strongest project is on page two, and page one lists only her older roles. How does the staged read affect her?
options: It may be reached only if page one passes the scans
The recruiter will read page two first as a summary of the rest
The project helps no matter where it sits
The recruiter will search page two for the project at once
optionExplain: Right: page two is reached late, so key items belong where the early stages see them.
The book does not describe reading page two first.
Position matters in a staged read.
The book says page two is looked at only after earlier scans succeed.
questions.explain: Only after earlier scans does a recruiter look at page two, so the strongest material belongs on page one.
questions.rule: Put the best where early stages reach.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: Lena says recruiters decide everything in the first scan and read nothing more. Which part of her claim conflicts with the book?
options: That recruiters read nothing more after the first scan
That the first scan collects key details
That the first scan comes before the longer read
That a recruiter glances at technologies in the first scan
optionExplain: Right: the book describes a short top-to-bottom read next, and deeper reading after that.
The book agrees with this part.
The order matches the book.
The book agrees they glance at technologies.
questions.explain: The first scan decides whether to continue. If most details match, the recruiter reads on, and later may look at page two.
questions.rule: The first scan opens the read.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: True or false: According to the book, a recruiter who finds a mismatch in every key detail will still start reading the resume top to bottom.
questions.explain: The book says that if most of the key details match, the recruiter will start to read top to bottom, so a mismatch stops the read.
questions.rule: Matches keep the read going.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: A candidate lacks one required technology but has a standout result in another area. What does the book say can happen?
options: The recruiter reads only the technology list
The recruiter rejects the resume at once, since a requirement is missing
The hiring manager changes the job requirements
Page two may get a look if standout information appears
optionExplain: The book describes a read of the whole resume if the scan goes well.
The book allows for standout information to earn more time.
The book does not say requirements change.
Right: the book says this can happen even when the candidate lacks some requirements.
questions.explain: The book says deeper reading can follow if the resume matches or if the recruiter has found enough standout information in other areas, even without every requirement.
questions.rule: Standout points can earn a deeper read.
questions.teaches: A recruiter may go on to the second page or read in depth even when the candidate lacks some requirements, if enough standout information appears in other areas.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: What should a good resume template do first for the recruiter?
options: Make the key details quick to find
Make the page look as distinctive as possible
Fit as many words as it can on a page
Hide the dates so the reader looks closer
optionExplain: Right: finding them fast saves time for reading. The card gives the book's view.
Distinctiveness is not the first job.
Cramming words works against quick finding.
Hiding dates makes the first scan harder.
questions.explain: A template's first job is to make key details easy to find. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Make facts easy to find.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: A good template lets the recruiter spend more time actually ____ the information you want to share.
questions.explain: The book says the recruiter gets the key information quicker and can spend more time reading what you share.
questions.rule: Saved time goes to reading.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: Two templates hold the same content. In one, years, technologies and titles stand out; in the other they are mixed into body text. Which does the book favour?
options: The one where they are mixed into body text, for a calm look
Neither, since the content is the same
The one where the key details stand out
Whichever one is easier to print
optionExplain: A calm look is not the book's test.
Same content does not make the templates equal; the book says the template changes how fast key details are found.
Right: it makes them easy to find so the recruiter can spend time reading.
Printing is not the book's test.
questions.explain: A good template makes key information easy to find, so the one where the details stand out is better.
questions.rule: Details that stand out save time.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: Which job does the template do, as opposed to the content, in the book's account?
options: It writes the bullets so they are specific
It decides which role you should apply for
It makes the key information easy to find at a glance
It supplies the achievements that the resume lists in its text
optionExplain: The bullets are the content's job.
The template does not choose the role.
Right: this is the template's job.
The content supplies the achievements.
questions.explain: The template makes information easy to find; the content makes it easy to digest and specific to the role.
questions.rule: Template finds, content persuades.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: True or false: According to the book, because a good template makes information quick to find, the recruiter has more time to read what you want to say.
questions.explain: The book says the recruiter gets the information much quicker and can spend more time actually reading what you want to share.
questions.rule: Speed to find, time to read.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: A candidate with an excellent template fills it with vague, generic text. What does the book say a good resume needs?
options: More pages, since length shows effort
A fancier template, since this fixes weak text
A readable template only, since the content matters much less
An easy-to-read template plus content specific to the role
optionExplain: Length is not the book's cure.
A fancier template does not fix vague text.
The book requires content as well as the template.
Right: the book says a good resume combines both.
questions.explain: The book says a good resume is a combination of an easy-to-read template and easy-to-digest content specific to the role.
questions.rule: Template and content work together.
questions.teaches: A good resume combines an easy-to-read template with easy-to-digest content that is specific to the role you apply for.

questions.section: The Results of Using a Good Resume Template
questions.q: A recruiter reads your resume late in a day, after many others. What helps you most?
options: A design that surprises the reader
A longer resume that proves how much effort you made
A dense page with small type
A format that is easy to read quickly
optionExplain: Surprise asks for effort a tired reader may not give.
Length costs a tired reader more effort.
Dense type is hard for a tired reader.
Right: tired readers rely on easy formats. The card gives the author's view.
questions.explain: A hurried reader needs ease. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Ease helps tired readers.

questions.section: The Results of Using a Good Resume Template
questions.q: With a hard-to-read format, the author says your chances will be down to ____.
questions.explain: The author says a harder format makes the recruiter work hard, and your chances come down to luck.
questions.rule: Hard formats leave it to luck.

questions.section: The Results of Using a Good Resume Template
questions.q: Which resume does the author expect to get its information across to a tired recruiter?
options: A flashy template with strong content
A readable template with well-written, specific content
A readable template with vague, generic text
A long resume with the best content saved for the very end
optionExplain: A hard-to-read format makes the recruiter work, as the book says.
Right: even tired or hurried recruiters get what they need from it.
The book pairs the template with good content.
A tired reader may never reach the end.
questions.explain: The book says that with a well-written resume even recruiters who are tired or in a hurry get the information they need.
questions.rule: Both parts together.

questions.section: The Results of Using a Good Resume Template
questions.q: Two equally good resumes use a hard-to-read format. One is read early in a pile of 100 and the other late. What does the author's reasoning suggest?
options: The later one gets more attention because it is fresh
The later one is more likely to be set aside by a tired recruiter
The earlier one is certain to be rejected
Both get the same treatment, because format does not matter at all
optionExplain: A tired recruiter gives less, not more.
Right: the author says later in the pile the recruiter may set a hard-to-read resume aside.
Nothing is certain in the book's account.
The author says format shapes the outcome.
questions.explain: Late in a big pile, recruiters are tired and under time pressure and may set aside a resume that is hard to read.
questions.rule: Pile position matters if reading is hard.

questions.section: The Results of Using a Good Resume Template
questions.q: True or false: Because recruiters need no effort to find information in a good template, content quality no longer affects the recruiter's experience.
questions.explain: The book says content that is well written makes reading an easier task as well, so content still matters.
questions.rule: Content still matters.

questions.section: The Results of Using a Good Resume Template
questions.q: Omar's resume arrives first among 100 applications with a hard-to-read format. According to the author, what is likely?
options: The recruiter will probably take more time with it
The format will be fixed by the recruiter before reading
The recruiter will skip it, since early resumes are ignored
The recruiter will rank it above better-formatted ones
optionExplain: Right: the author says a recruiter who reads it early in 100+ applications will probably take more time.
The recruiter does not reformat resumes.
The book does not say early resumes are ignored.
Nothing in the book supports this.
questions.explain: The author says that if the recruiter reads it as one of the first of 100+ applications, they will probably take more time.
questions.rule: Luck can favour a hard format early in the pile.
questions.teaches: A recruiter who reads a hard-to-read resume among the first of 100+ applications will probably take more time over it, so luck can work either way.

questions.q: You must pick one resume template from a shortlist. What is the most useful test to run on each?
options: Which one uses the fewest words
Which one has the most sections, columns and decorative elements on the page
Whether it reads top to bottom, in one column, with relevant items first
Which one looks the most unusual
optionExplain: Fewer words is not a stated principle.
More sections do not mean a better template.
Right: this checks the book's principles. The card lists them.
Unusual looks are not the book's test.
questions.explain: A checklist of reading ease and order beats looks. The card next gives the four principles.
questions.rule: Test the template against principles.

questions.q: The recap says easy-to-read templates can be scanned in one go, from top to ____.
questions.explain: The first principle is top-to-bottom reading, scanned in one go.
questions.rule: Scan in one go.

questions.q: Which template description satisfies all four principles?
options: One column, chronological sections with no emphasis at all
Two columns, sections in order of relevance, bold used on key technologies and titles
One column, relevant sections first, bold on key technologies and titles
One column, sections in random order, bold used on whole paragraphs
optionExplain: Without emphasis the fourth principle is unmet.
Two columns breaks the single-column principle.
Right: top to bottom, single column, important first, strategic bold.
Random order and bold on paragraphs break two principles.
questions.explain: Only the first meets all four: a single column that reads top to bottom, relevant items first and purposeful emphasis.
questions.rule: Check all four.

questions.q: Match each principle to what it gives the recruiter.
pairs: A template scanned in one go
Room to share enough about your work
Strategic use of colour and bold
Attention guided consistently to key details
questions.explain: Each principle supports a different benefit: one-go scanning, room for detail, relevant items first, and guided attention.
questions.rule: Each principle has a purpose.

questions.q: A template reads top to bottom and uses one column, but lists the weakest section first. Which principle does it still fail?
options: Important things first
None of them
Single column
Top-to-bottom reading of the page
optionExplain: Right: relevant things should be towards the top.
It breaks the ordering principle.
It uses one column.
It still reads top to bottom.
questions.explain: Order is a separate principle: relevant things belong towards the top, so the template fails important things first.
questions.rule: Order is its own test.

questions.q: Someone argues a two-column design looks neat and is fine for a developer. How does the recap answer?
options: Neatness is irrelevant to recruiters, so the recap sees nothing to answer in the argument
Two columns are fine if the colour scheme is strategic
Two columns are fine whenever the resume fits one page
Two columns can look neat, but they are harder to read and leave less room for detail
optionExplain: The recap does not call neatness irrelevant; it grants it.
Colour does not fix the column problem.
The recap does not make an exception for one page.
Right: the recap grants that they can look neat, then names the readability and detail costs.
questions.explain: The recap says two-column and multi-column layouts can look neat but are more difficult to read and make it harder to share enough about your experience and projects.
questions.rule: Neat is not the same as readable.
questions.teaches: Two-column and multi-column layouts can look neat, but the recap says they are more difficult to read and make it harder to share enough about work and projects.

questions.q: A resume site offers hundreds of templates and says they are proven to win interviews. What is the author's concern for developers?
options: It charges more than developers can afford, so most of them skip it
Its templates are designed by developers, who write too densely
Its templates serve every profession, so few suit a developer
It limits each user to a single download, which blocks edits for each job
optionExplain: Price is a separate matter; the author's main complaint is fit, not cost.
The author's complaint is the reverse: they are not written with developers in mind.
The author says the sites are optimised for resumes for everyone, so only a small share fits tech.
Download limits are not part of his argument; the issue is who the templates are made for.
questions.explain: The pitch of being proven does not mean proven for developers. The card next shows what the author found.
questions.rule: Prefer a generator or template made with developers in mind over one optimised for all professions.

questions.q: The author says most resume generators work poorly for developers because they are optimised for resumes for ____.
questions.explain: A generator that aims at everyone does not tune its layout or sample content to what tech hiring managers look for.
questions.rule: Prefer a generator or template made with developers in mind over one optimised for all professions.

questions.q: A generator lists 400 templates, 6 of them aimed at software roles. The site claims its resumes work for everyone. What is the best next step?
options: Review the few tech templates and their sample text with a developer's eye
Pick the most popular template, since popularity shows it works for tech
Assume all 400 are suitable, because the site tests every layout widely
Skip templates and paste your work history into the site's default form
optionExplain: Only a few templates target your field, so you check those for fit instead of trusting the claim.
Popularity across all professions says little about developer hiring managers.
Testing for everyone does not mean testing for tech; this is the gap the author describes.
The default form is built for everyone too, so the same fit problem remains.
questions.explain: The author's own test was to look closely at the tech templates, not to accept the site's general promise.
questions.rule: Prefer a generator or template made with developers in mind over one optimised for all professions.

questions.q: Sort each statement: is it the author's view of generator sites, or not?

items.t: Most sites cater to many professions, not to developers
Their tech templates tend to use hard-to-read two-column layouts
Looking nice from afar does not make a template good for developers
A site with many templates is likely to have the best developer one
Every generator has templates written by hiring managers in tech
Paying for a template proves it works for software roles

questions.explain: The author warns that range of choice and a price tag do not show that a template fits developers.
questions.rule: Prefer a generator or template made with developers in mind over one optimised for all professions.

questions.q: A student with no budget wants to try the five generator sites the author names first: resume.io, EnhanCV, VisualCV, Resume Now and Europass. All of them promise professional, proven resumes. What should the student expect about price?
questions.explain: The author names Europass as the one site that is not a paid solution. Free does not make it a good pick: he gives the Europass format one star.
questions.teaches: Of the named generator sites, only Europass is free to use; the others charge for what they promise.
questions.rule: Prefer a generator or template made with developers in mind over one optimised for all professions.
options: All five are free, since the sites earn their income from the employers who hire them
All five charge, because each one sells a professional and proven result
Most are free, and a few charge for extras such as additional templates
Four charge and one is free, so the promise alone does not say which
optionExplain: The book says the opposite: apart from one, these sites are paid solutions.
Close, but one of the five is the exception to paying.
The book does not describe a free base with paid extras; it names a single exception.
Right: Europass is the one that is not paid. The others charge in return for their promise.

questions.q: A teammate says a site's tech templates look great on screen, so they must suit developers. How does the author's judgment answer this?
options: He agrees, since polished layouts are what hiring managers prize most
He disagrees only because the templates cost money, whatever their layout
He accepts the claim once a site offers more than ten tech templates
Looks are not the test; he found them nice from afar but not great for developers
optionExplain: Polish is not what the author rewards; he looks at readability and fit.
Price is a separate matter; he faults the layouts and their content.
Template count did not settle it: he reviewed the tech ones and still did not recommend them.
The author judged the templates by developer fit, noting they look nice from afar yet resemble nothing in the real world.
questions.explain: Looking good is a weak test. The author says these templates look nice from afar but are poor choices for developers.
questions.teaches: The author says the tech templates look nice from afar but are not great choices for developers, partly because their content does not resemble anything in the real world.
questions.rule: Prefer a generator or template made with developers in mind over one optimised for all professions.

questions.q: A template for programmers lists spoken languages but no programming languages. What does this most likely tell you?
options: It was designed to help recruiters screen applicants more quickly
Its author probably did not know what tech readers look for
It shows the template was reviewed by engineering managers
It reflects what developers most want to highlight on a resume
optionExplain: Screening speed is not served when the key information is absent from the template.
Missing the languages that matter for the job points to a writer outside the field.
Review by engineering managers would likely have caught the gap, as the author points out.
The skills a developer wants to show are programming languages, which the template omits.
questions.explain: A gap like that points to a writer who did not check with tech readers. The card next shows how the author sees it.
questions.rule: Judge a template by its sample content: it should look like something a developer would really write.

questions.q: Most generator sites use content ____ to write developer resumes, and the results are not checked with tech recruiters.
questions.explain: Writers who are not engineers produce content that misses what engineering managers look for.
questions.rule: Judge a template by its sample content: it should look like something a developer would really write.

questions.q: You preview a template whose sample developer has Skills: Teamwork, Passion, Fluent French. What should you conclude?
options: Its skills section is a good model, since soft skills decide most hiring in tech
It is fine, because sample content gets replaced and so does not matter
Its authors probably have not worked in tech hiring, so look elsewhere for a template
It is ideal for developers, since spoken languages are essential on their resumes
optionExplain: The author does not treat soft-skill labels as what matters for developers.
Sample content is replaceable, but its quality reveals who made the template and how well it fits.
The sample does not name the technologies readers want, which suggests a lack of tech input.
Spoken languages are not what the author says tech readers look for.
questions.explain: The author used the sample content of the Programmer example as evidence the template was not made with tech in mind.
questions.rule: Judge a template by its sample content: it should look like something a developer would really write.

questions.q: Sort each sample-content detail: does it suggest the template fits developers, or not?

items.t: Lists programming languages and tools by name
Describes work in terms hiring managers recognise
Written with input from engineering managers
Lists spoken languages but no programming languages
A skills section full of buzzwords
Content written by someone outside software

questions.explain: A fit shows in real technical content; buzzwords and missing languages show an outside writer.
questions.rule: Judge a template by its sample content: it should look like something a developer would really write.

questions.q: Two templates look equally polished. One has realistic developer sample text; the other has generic text. What does the author's reasoning favour?
options: The generic one, since blank content leaves more room for your own details
Neither, since polish is the only thing that makes a template good enough
Both equally, since sample text never says anything about who made the template
The realistic one, since it suggests the maker knew what developer resumes need
optionExplain: Generic text does not leave room; it just signals that nobody tailored the template.
Polish is not the only quality; the author also checks content and audience fit.
Sample content tells you who made the template, so the two are not equal.
Realistic content suggests knowledge of the field.
questions.explain: Content is evidence of audience awareness, which polish alone does not show.
questions.rule: Judge a template by its sample content: it should look like something a developer would really write.

questions.q: You are choosing a template from a site that shows only blank layouts. According to the author, which check should you add before trusting it?
options: Count how many colours the layouts use across the gallery
Check how many people have downloaded the blank layouts
Look for real, even anonymised, resumes of developers who were hired
Read the biography of the site's founder to see how long they have traded
optionExplain: Colour count says nothing about developer fit.
Download counts reflect popularity, not tech fit.
Real examples that led to jobs are one of the author's tests of a decent site.
A founder's biography is not among the author's criteria.
questions.explain: Real developer examples (even anonymised) are one of the author's five criteria for a decent generator.
questions.teaches: One of the author's criteria is that a site shows real, even anonymised, resume examples that got people hired.
questions.rule: Judge a template by its sample content: it should look like something a developer would really write.

questions.q: A paid resume site says its customers get more callbacks. What would the author want to see before believing it?
options: A long list of five-star reviews from the site's own customers
A statement that the templates were designed by a branding agency
Testimonials from real hiring managers or recruiters in tech
An offer of a money-back guarantee on any plan you choose
optionExplain: Customer reviews show satisfaction, not that recruiters in tech approve of the result.
A branding agency may make a template pretty, but pretty is not the same as proven.
A claim about callbacks is best backed by the people who hire in the industry.
A refund promise limits your risk but offers no proof of hiring results.
questions.explain: A paid solution should back its claims with real hiring managers. The card next sets out the author's three tests.
questions.rule: Ask a paid generator to show hiring-manager testimonials and real, successful resumes, not only claims.

questions.q: A decent generator shows testimonials from real hiring managers or ____ in its industry.
questions.explain: The author expects hiring managers or recruiters in tech to vouch for any paid solution that promises more callbacks.
questions.rule: Ask a paid generator to show hiring-manager testimonials and real, successful resumes, not only claims.

questions.q: A site shows glowing quotes signed only with first names and has no resume examples of people hired. Which author test does it fail?
options: Testimonials from real hiring managers and real, successful resume examples
Having at least one template with a single-column layout that is easy to read and scan
Offering a web link that tracks who has viewed your resume after you share it
