Listing the price of each plan in a table on the front page of its website
optionExplain: Nameless quotes are not hiring-manager testimonials, and with no examples of hired people there is no evidence.
Layout is a separate test and is not what the quotes or examples are about.
View tracking is a feature the author likes, but it is not one of the evidence tests.
Price clarity is another of the author's tests, and it is not the one failing here.
questions.explain: The author wants named industry voices and real examples, even anonymised ones, that got people hired.
questions.rule: Ask a paid generator to show hiring-manager testimonials and real, successful resumes, not only claims.

questions.q: Match each author criterion to the question it asks of a resume site.
pairs: Was it designed with the real audience and easy reading in mind?
Do real hiring managers or recruiters in tech back its claims?
Does it show real, even anonymised, resumes that got people hired?
questions.explain: Each criterion asks for a different kind of proof: audience fit, expert backing and real results.
questions.rule: Ask a paid generator to show hiring-manager testimonials and real, successful resumes, not only claims.

questions.q: A resume site for data analysts blurs the names on all its sample resumes, which it says led to job offers. True or false: by the author's test, blurred names are a reason to distrust the site.
questions.explain: He accepts anonymised examples as long as they are real and got people hired. What should make you wary is a site that shows no real resumes of that kind at all.
questions.teaches: Anonymised examples are acceptable evidence to the author, but a site that shows no real resumes that got people hired should make you wary.
questions.rule: Ask a paid generator to show hiring-manager testimonials and real, successful resumes, not only claims.

questions.q: A paid coaching service, not a template site, promises more callbacks. How would the author's testimonial test apply?
options: Skip it, because his test was written only for template websites, not services
Relax it, because personal coaching needs no outside backing from recruiters
Reverse it, because coaching clients judge results better than recruiters do
Apply it too, since any paid solution should back such a claim with tech hiring voices
optionExplain: The text names both generators and services, so the test is not limited to template sites.
Personal coaching is a paid solution, and his test covers any such solution.
Recruiters in the industry are the experts he names, not the clients.
The author words the test for resume generators and resume services alike.
questions.explain: He expects any paid solution to back its callback claims with real hiring managers or recruiters in its industry.
questions.teaches: The author applies the testimonial test to resume services as well as generators: any paid solution should back its claims with hiring managers or recruiters in its industry.
questions.rule: Ask a paid generator to show hiring-manager testimonials and real, successful resumes, not only claims.

questions.q: A site warns that 75% of resumes go unseen by any human, then offers a paid fix. What is the author's view?
options: It is a trustworthy statistic, which explains why the paid fix costs money
It is a typical ATS myth used to upsell, which signals weak industry expertise
It holds true for big companies only, so the upsell is fair for them
It shows the site has strong insight into how recruiters really work
optionExplain: The author names this exact figure as a myth rather than a reliable statistic.
Quoting this kind of myth to sell a service is how the author says you can spot sites lacking industry expertise.
The author does not limit the myth to small firms; it is a false fact used to upsell.
Repeating it suggests the opposite: little knowledge of how hiring works.
questions.explain: The author treats such claims as a red flag. The card next explains the criterion.
questions.rule: Choose a service with clear pricing and a clear value beyond a PDF, and walk away from pitches built on ATS myths.

questions.q: Some sites advertise as free, then use dark ____ to charge you.
questions.explain: The author calls this bait pricing: an apparently free service that charges through manipulative design.
questions.rule: Choose a service with clear pricing and a clear value beyond a PDF, and walk away from pitches built on ATS myths.

questions.q: A site's signup says Free, but the download button asks for a card, and the paid tiers have no list of what each includes. What does this match?
options: A fair free trial, which the author treats as proof of quality
Bait pricing with unclear tiers, which the author asks you to avoid
A normal premium upgrade, which needs no explanation
A sign the site is run by software engineers, who prefer terse pages
optionExplain: A trial is clear about when it ends; the author's concern is hidden charges.
Free that turns into a charge, plus tiers that are not spelled out, are the two pricing problems the author names.
The author wants the value of any upgrade stated, so it does need explaining.
Nothing in the author's view links terse pages to engineer-run sites.
questions.explain: The author wants the value of any paid plan to be spelled out.
questions.rule: Choose a service with clear pricing and a clear value beyond a PDF, and walk away from pitches built on ATS myths.

questions.q: Sort each site behaviour: is it a warning sign under the author's criteria, or not?

items.t: Advertises free, then charges through confusing screens
Quotes the 75% never-seen figure to sell a plan
Lists tiers without saying what each one gives you
States its price up front and what the subscription includes
Says nothing about ATS and shows hired resumes
Shows plain monthly pricing with a clear value

questions.explain: Hidden charges, vague tiers and myth-based urgency are warnings. Clear prices and honest claims are the opposite.
questions.rule: Choose a service with clear pricing and a clear value beyond a PDF, and walk away from pitches built on ATS myths.

questions.q: A site advertises a free resume builder, then asks for a subscription at the download step and does not say what each plan includes. True or false: the author would count this against the site even if the finished PDF looks good.
questions.explain: He warns about bait pricing: advertising as free, then using dark patterns to charge, or leaving pricing tiers unclear. If you pay, he wants the value proposition to be clear, meaning what you get beyond the PDF.
questions.teaches: The author warns about bait pricing, where a site advertises as free and then uses dark patterns to charge, or leaves tiers unclear; if you pay, the value proposition should be clear.
questions.rule: Choose a service with clear pricing and a clear value beyond a PDF, and walk away from pitches built on ATS myths.

questions.q: A resume-review newsletter says its ATS secrets decide whether you are seen, then sells a course. Using the author's test, what is the best response?
options: Buy at once, since a secret that decides whether you are seen is worth any price
Treat the fear-based pitch as a warning sign and look for real evidence from tech hiring
Trust it, because a newsletter that gives free tips cannot also be selling
Ignore all resume advice from now on, because no source can be trusted
optionExplain: Urgency about a hidden system is the tactic the author warns about.
The pitch matches the pattern: ATS fear, then an upsell. The author asks for evidence from real hiring.
A newsletter that sells a course has a selling interest, like a generator.
The author does not say to distrust everyone; he sets criteria to judge sources.
questions.explain: The same two checks (clear value, no ATS myths) work on any seller of resume advice, not only generators.
questions.teaches: The author treats unclear value and ATS myths as warning signs when sites sell resume templates and services alike, so the same check fits any paid resume advice.
questions.rule: Choose a service with clear pricing and a clear value beyond a PDF, and walk away from pitches built on ATS myths.

questions.section: Standard Resume: By Developers, for Developers
questions.q: You are messaging a hiring manager on a platform that does not let you attach files. What could still let you share your resume?
options: Pasting the full resume text into one very long message
Attaching a screenshot of the PDF in place of the real file
Waiting until you can email a PDF to the company
A link to a web version that matches the PDF layout
optionExplain: A wall of pasted text loses the layout and reads poorly in a chat.
Screenshots are often blocked and cannot be searched, so this does not solve the problem.
Waiting delays the contact, while a link lets you reach out before formally applying.
A web link is the author's answer when sending a PDF is a hassle.
questions.explain: Sending a PDF over a chat is awkward, and a web version avoids it. The card next lists the author's four benefits.
questions.rule: Pay for a generator only for concrete benefits, such as uncramped layouts, a shareable web version, view tracking and real examples.

questions.section: Standard Resume: By Developers, for Developers
questions.q: With Standard Resume you can send a web ____ that renders your resume in the same layout as the PDF.
questions.explain: The link replaces a PDF where a PDF is hard to send.
questions.rule: Pay for a generator only for concrete benefits, such as uncramped layouts, a shareable web version, view tracking and real examples.

questions.section: Standard Resume: By Developers, for Developers
questions.q: You sent your web resume link to a recruiter and want to know if it was opened. Which benefit helps?
options: The designer-set spacing, which stops fonts being squeezed to fit more text
Web view tracking, which shows whether anyone has visited the link you sent
The library of real developer examples, which shows what hired engineers wrote
The paid subscription itself, which the site says unlocks quicker replies
optionExplain: Spacing helps readability, but it says nothing about whether the link was opened.
Tracking visits to the link is how you tell if someone has read it.
Examples inspire your content but cannot report on your own link.
The author does not claim a subscription speeds up replies.
questions.explain: Tracking turns a link into a signal that someone looked at your resume.
questions.rule: Pay for a generator only for concrete benefits, such as uncramped layouts, a shareable web version, view tracking and real examples.

questions.section: Standard Resume: By Developers, for Developers
questions.q: Match each benefit the author names to the problem it addresses.
pairs: Fonts and margins get squeezed to fit more
A PDF cannot be sent in a LinkedIn message
You cannot tell whether anyone read the resume
You do not know what a hired engineer's resume looks like
questions.explain: Each benefit solves a separate problem: crowding, sending, feedback and not having a model to follow.
questions.rule: Pay for a generator only for concrete benefits, such as uncramped layouts, a shareable web version, view tracking and real examples.

questions.section: Standard Resume: By Developers, for Developers
questions.q: A developer using Standard Resume wants more room on the page and plans to shrink the fonts and squeeze the spacing, as she would in a document template. True or false: the platform's design stops her from cramming the page that way.
questions.explain: UX professionals set the spacing, so you cannot cram the fonts; the author notes it is harder to fit everything on one page, by design. Almost all its templates are single-column.
questions.teaches: Standard Resume's spacing and typography are set by designers, so you cannot cram the fonts; almost all its templates are single-column and all but one follow the top-down layout.
questions.rule: Pay for a generator only for concrete benefits, such as uncramped layouts, a shareable web version, view tracking and real examples.

questions.section: Standard Resume: By Developers, for Developers
questions.q: A friend has a full LinkedIn profile and dreads retyping it into a new resume. Which Standard Resume feature was built for that?
options: Tracking views, so the friend can see who read the old resume sent last month
Letting the friend crop a profile photo so it fits inside the chosen template
Scoring each skill on a five-star scale before the resume is exported
Importing details from LinkedIn to make building the resume quicker
optionExplain: Tracking shows readers of a shared link, not saved typing.
The author advises against profile photos in resumes.
The author argues against star ratings of skills on a resume.
The founders built an import so the CV can be built quicker from LinkedIn data.
questions.explain: The founders wanted to solve three gaps: web plus PDF, view tracking and a LinkedIn import.
questions.teaches: Besides the web version and view tracking, the founders added an import from LinkedIn to make building the resume quicker.
questions.rule: Pay for a generator only for concrete benefits, such as uncramped layouts, a shareable web version, view tracking and real examples.

questions.section: Standard Resume: By Developers, for Developers
questions.q: A resume is ten lines too long for one page. A founder of a resume tool would advise which fix?
options: Shrink the font a little and trim the space between sections
Narrow the margins and keep the text at the same size
Cut to the critical parts, or accept a second page
Merge sections so the headings take up less room
optionExplain: Tiny fonts and tight gaps are named as what makes resumes hard to scan.
Narrower margins squeeze the same cramped text and hurt scanning too.
Whitespace and readable type matter more than a single page.
Merging sections removes the structure a recruiter uses to scan.
questions.explain: Fitting everything is the temptation the cofounder warns about. The card next gives the advice.
questions.rule: When the content does not fit, cut to the critical parts or use two pages; do not shrink fonts and spacing.

questions.section: Standard Resume: By Developers, for Developers
questions.q: The cofounder says removing the ____ between paragraphs and sections makes a resume harder to scan.
questions.explain: Whitespace gives the eye places to rest and helps the reader find where each section begins.
questions.rule: When the content does not fit, cut to the critical parts or use two pages; do not shrink fonts and spacing.

questions.section: Standard Resume: By Developers, for Developers
questions.q: A designer friend shows you a resume with eight-point type and no gaps between jobs, all fitting one page. What do you advise?
options: Raise the type size, restore the gaps and cut the least relevant lines from the page
Keep it as it is, since one dense page shows seriousness and discipline
Shrink the font further and add one more role so no job is left out
Turn it into two narrow columns to claim back room for the extra lines
optionExplain: Readability comes first; the content can be cut to the critical parts.
Density is not a virtue here: a hard-to-read page can be skipped.
More cramming makes the main issue worse.
Columns are another way to cram and are hard to scan.
questions.explain: The cofounder says to focus on the critical parts or make it two pages.
questions.rule: When the content does not fit, cut to the critical parts or use two pages; do not shrink fonts and spacing.

questions.section: Standard Resume: By Developers, for Developers
questions.q: Sort each fix for a too-long resume: does it follow the cofounder's advice, or does it cram?

items.t: Cut older, less relevant bullet points
Let the resume run to two pages
Keep the gaps between sections
Shrink the type until it fits
Delete the blank lines between sections
Reduce margins to squeeze in more lines

questions.explain: The advice is to cut or use a second page. Anything that removes space or shrinks type makes the page harder to scan.
questions.rule: When the content does not fit, cut to the critical parts or use two pages; do not shrink fonts and spacing.

questions.section: Standard Resume: By Developers, for Developers
questions.q: A candidate's resume runs eight lines over one page. The cofounder of Standard Resume says he sees this all the time. Which fix fits his advice?
questions.explain: He calls cramming content onto one page the number one issue he sees. His fix is to focus on the critical parts or accept two pages, and to get line length, font sizes and line heights right, or leave them to professionals.
questions.teaches: Cramming content into a single page is the number one issue the cofounder sees; his fix is to focus on the critical parts or make it two pages, and to get line length, font sizes and line heights right or leave them to professionals.
questions.rule: When the content does not fit, cut to the critical parts or use two pages; do not shrink fonts and spacing.
options: Cut to the critical parts or make it two pages, and keep the whitespace
Shrink the font a little and remove the space between sections until it fits
Narrow the margins to the edge of the page and switch to a condensed typeface
Merge the last two sections into a single dense paragraph to save a few lines
optionExplain: Right: he says to either focus on the critical parts or make it two pages.
He names removing whitespace and tiny fonts as what makes a resume harder to scan.
This is another way of cramming, which is the issue he describes.
Dense blocks make the resume harder to scan, the opposite of his aim.

questions.section: Standard Resume: By Developers, for Developers
questions.q: A developer applying to a design-led studio wonders whether an evening spent on line length, font sizes and spacing is worth it. According to the cofounder, how much does typography weigh?
options: Very little, since design companies look only at portfolios, not resumes
Only a little, since type matters mostly for printed resumes, not screens
A great deal: resumes are mostly text, so type sets the first impression
None at all, since every employer judges the content and not the look
optionExplain: The cofounder says typography is particularly important for those companies.
Resumes are mostly text, so type matters on screen and in PDF alike.
Typography carries much of the first impression, especially for design-heavy companies.
He says the first impression is formed largely by typography, not content alone.
questions.explain: He singles out design-heavy companies as places where typography is particularly important.
questions.teaches: Typography is particularly important when applying to design-heavy tech companies, since resumes are mostly text and typography forms much of the first impression.
questions.rule: When the content does not fit, cut to the critical parts or use two pages; do not shrink fonts and spacing.

questions.q: A friend has spent weeks comparing resume templates and has not yet written any bullet points. What is the author's likely advice?
options: Keep comparing until one template is perfect for the job, then start on the content
Hire a designer to build a custom layout from scratch, then write the content afterwards
Use whichever template looks most unusual, so the resume stands out from the others
Pick a proven template and put the effort into the content
optionExplain: The author says there is no such thing as a perfect template.
A custom layout is not what he recommends; he suggests customising a proven one.
Standing out through layout is not his priority; readable content is.
A proven template is enough to start; the content is what takes work.
questions.explain: More hours on layout rarely helps. The card next shows the author's priorities.
questions.rule: Pick a proven template early, customise it lightly and put your effort into writing strong content.

questions.q: It is good practice to start with a tried and proven template and then ____ it to your own style.
questions.explain: Start from something that works and adjust it, instead of designing from nothing.
questions.rule: Pick a proven template early, customise it lightly and put your effort into writing strong content.

questions.q: Two candidates have the same experience. One has a popular template and sharp, specific bullets; the other has a custom design and vague bullets. Who is better placed?
options: The second, because a custom design always catches the eye first
The first, because content counts for more than the template
Neither, because template choice alone decides the outcome
The second, because vague bullets leave room for the layout to impress
optionExplain: Eye-catching layouts are not what the author rewards.
A proven template with strong content beats a distinctive layout with weak content.
He argues the opposite: the template matters less than the content.
Vague content wastes the one thing the resume is for.
questions.explain: The content is the part the author says you must write yourself.
questions.rule: Pick a proven template early, customise it lightly and put your effort into writing strong content.

questions.q: A candidate adopts a recommended template and then reads that its review lists a drawback, such as a dated style. True or false: that is normal in the author's reviews, where even good templates come with a list of weak points and ways to improve.
questions.explain: The author says there is no such thing as a perfect template, which is why each review has a bad list and ways to improve beside the good. A known flaw is a reason to customise, not to keep searching.
questions.teaches: The author says there is no such thing as a perfect template; every review lists drawbacks and ways to improve it, so a known flaw is a reason to customise, not to keep searching.
questions.rule: Pick a proven template early, customise it lightly and put your effort into writing strong content.

questions.q: Sort each use of your time: does it match the author's priorities, or not?

items.t: Customise a proven template in an afternoon
Rewrite bullets to show your results and impact
Start from a template that others have used successfully
Compare thirty templates before writing a word
Wait to apply until the layout is perfect
Redesign a template from scratch for a single application

questions.explain: A proven template plus effort on content matches the author. Endless layout hunting does not.
questions.rule: Pick a proven template early, customise it lightly and put your effort into writing strong content.

questions.q: A bootcamp graduate has a free tool that produces a polished layout in seconds. What does the author's intro say the tool cannot supply?
options: The content itself, which you still have to write for yourself
The font choices, which only a professional designer can make
The page margins, which no software is able to set for a document
The file format, which the hiring manager has to choose each time
optionExplain: The intro says content is what you must write; a template alone is not worth much.
Fonts are part of any template and can be customised.
Margins are part of a template's layout.
Format is not raised in the intro.
questions.explain: The tool gives you structure, not substance.
questions.teaches: The author says a template is not worth much without great content, and that this content is something you must write yourself.
questions.rule: Pick a proven template early, customise it lightly and put your effort into writing strong content.

questions.q: A template review gives a rating for software developers. What does that rating most likely show?
options: How many developers downloaded the template over the previous year
How attractive the template looks to the person who owns the resume
How well the template follows principles for good developer templates
How cheaply the template can be bought compared with other templates
optionExplain: Popularity is a different measure from fit with developer principles.
Looks to the owner can be high even when recruiters find a page hard to scan.
The rating is an assessment against principles for developer templates.
Cost is not the basis of the rating.
questions.explain: The rating is an assessment against principles. The card next explains the rest of the format.
questions.rule: Use a review's rating to compare, its bad points to find risks and its ways to improve to customise.

questions.q: Match each part of a review to what it contains.
pairs: Where to find the template or site
How well it fits developer template principles
Features that could be a disadvantage
Ideas for customising or improving the template
questions.explain: Each part has its own job, which makes it possible to compare templates on the same terms.
questions.rule: Use a review's rating to compare, its bad points to find risks and its ways to improve to customise.

questions.q: A review says a template has no space for personal details. Where would you look for how to deal with that?
options: In its link, which shows the template's price and tiers
In its rating, which lists the changes you can make
In its ways to improve it, which suggests how to customise it
In its good section, which lists features worth copying instead
optionExplain: The link only shows where to find the template.
The rating is a score, not a list of changes.
Fixes and customisations belong to ways to improve it.
The good section lists positives that could inspire you.
questions.explain: Read the bad points for risks and the improvement section for what to change.
questions.rule: Use a review's rating to compare, its bad points to find risks and its ways to improve to customise.

questions.q: Sort each statement about the reviews: does it match the author's description, or not?

items.t: Every review includes the good, the bad and ways to improve
You can borrow ideas from a template you do not use
The rating is for software developers
A review lists only the strengths of a template
A high rating guarantees a job offer
Ratings measure how popular a template is

questions.explain: Reviews are balanced and developer-specific. They assess fit, not popularity or outcomes.
questions.rule: Use a review's rating to compare, its bad points to find risks and its ways to improve to customise.

questions.q: A reader claims that every template in these reviews was made by the author for the book, so the stars are self-praise. What does the review format show?
questions.explain: The chapter reviews templates made for the book and popular templates from elsewhere, using the same format. Ratings run from five stars down to one, so they are not all praise.
questions.teaches: The reviews cover templates the author created for the book as well as popular templates from elsewhere, and the outside ones range down to one star.
questions.rule: Use a review's rating to compare, its bad points to find risks and its ways to improve to customise.
options: The reader is right, because the reviews cover only templates made for the book
The reader is right about the top picks, while the others get no review at all
The reader is wrong: outside templates are reviewed too, some with one star
The reader is wrong, because only paid templates are ever reviewed and rated
optionExplain: The author says the reviews cover templates created for the book and popular ones.
Other templates are reviewed, including ones he advises against.
Right: popular templates from elsewhere are reviewed as well, and the lowest earns one star.
The reviewed templates include free ones, such as the Google Docs layouts.

questions.q: A colleague points out that a template rated two stars here helped a friend get hired. How does this fit the author's framework?
options: It shows the review is wrong, because a rating ought to predict getting hired
Ratings assess fit with principles; success also depends on content and the match
It shows the friend's content must have been weak, or the template would have failed
It shows the template was misrated, so its number of stars should be raised
optionExplain: A rating is an assessment of the template, not a forecast of a single job result.
The rating measures adherence to principles, and the author says popular templates likely worked with the right content.
Nothing in the text implies poor content; strong content can carry a weaker template.
The author expects some success with all of them without changing the stars.
questions.explain: A single success does not overturn a principle-based rating.
questions.teaches: Ratings assess how well a template follows developer principles; the author expects people to have had success with popular templates when the content fits the role.
questions.rule: Use a review's rating to compare, its bad points to find risks and its ways to improve to customise.

questions.q: Why might a recruiter at a US tech company scan a resume faster when it resembles a format they often see?
options: They already know where to find the dates, titles and companies
They spend longer reading unfamiliar layouts, so those get more attention
They assume a familiar layout means the person worked at a famous firm
They are required to favour templates that appear on a company list
optionExplain: A familiar layout lets the reader find the information without searching.
Unfamiliar layouts tend to slow scanning instead of earning care.
Layout does not tell a recruiter about the employer; it just helps them read.
No such requirement appears in the text.
questions.explain: Familiarity is a real asset for a scanner. The card next shows the template the author rates highly.
questions.rule: Choose this template for a clean, scannable layout that US tech recruiters recognise.

questions.q: The Pragmatic Engineer's template is similar to the ____ template, so US tech recruiters find it familiar.
questions.explain: The similarity to a template US recruiters often see is one of the review's first good points.
questions.rule: Choose this template for a clean, scannable layout that US tech recruiters recognise.

questions.q: You are applying to a US software company and want a layout that recruiters recognise. How well does this template fit?
options: It fits poorly, since the review says US recruiters dislike one-column resumes
It fits only for UK jobs, as the layout is geared to non-US firms
It fits well, since it resembles a template US tech recruiters know
It fits only when the resume is extended to three pages
optionExplain: Nothing in the review criticises one-column layouts.
Familiarity with US recruiters is what the review praises.
The review cites familiarity for US tech recruiters as a strength.
The review praises it for one and two pages, not three.
questions.explain: Pick the template for the audience it suits.
questions.rule: Choose this template for a clean, scannable layout that US tech recruiters recognise.

questions.q: Sort each point: is it a strength the author lists for this template, or not?

items.t: Consistent formatting and good use of bold
Dates and titles are easy to read
Familiar to US tech recruiters
Built-in tracking of who views the resume
Skill ratings out of five stars
A sidebar for contact details and photo

questions.explain: The strengths are scanning and familiarity. Tracking belongs to Standard Resume, and ratings and photos are things the author advises against.
questions.rule: Choose this template for a clean, scannable layout that US tech recruiters recognise.

questions.q: A reader assumes that a template with five stars has no drawbacks listed in its review. True or false: the Pragmatic template's review lists at least one.
questions.explain: Even this five-star review notes that the template does not cater to people who want to add more personal information, though it can be customised. Good templates still have a weak point.
questions.teaches: Even the five-star Pragmatic review lists a drawback: the template does not cater to people who want more personal information, which can be customised.
questions.rule: Choose this template for a clean, scannable layout that US tech recruiters recognise.

questions.q: A candidate likes the layout but finds the plain look too bland to feel personal. What does the review suggest?
options: Customise the highlight colour and the fonts to suit personal preference
Drop the template altogether, since it cannot be changed without breaking it
Add a profile photo to the header, which gives the page some personality
Place the content in two columns, which adds interest to a plain page
optionExplain: The review's own suggestion for improving the template is to change colour and fonts.
The review expects customisation, not abandonment.
The author advises against photos because they invite bias.
Two columns are the layout he warns against.
questions.explain: Small personal touches in colour and font are the suggested way to make it your own.
questions.teaches: The review suggests customising the highlight colour and the fonts to your preferences.
questions.rule: Choose this template for a clean, scannable layout that US tech recruiters recognise.

questions.q: You hold senior titles at small companies that recruiters will not recognise. Which part of the resume deserves more visual weight?
options: The job titles, which show your level where company names say little
The company names, since a recruiter will research each one carefully
The graduation year, since it shows how long ago you studied
The location of each office, since it shows where you worked
optionExplain: Where employers are unknown, the title carries the signal.
Unknown companies add little weight, and the reader may not look them up.
Education dates are not what shows seniority here.
Office location is not the signal that shows your level.
questions.explain: The author makes this exact point about unrecognised companies. The card next shows which template does it.
questions.rule: Pick the variant that emphasises the signal that is strongest for you: standout companies or, if they are unknown, your titles.

questions.q: The Mono Engineer's template is a slight modification of The ____ Engineer's template.
questions.explain: It keeps most of that template's strengths and changes the emphasis.
questions.rule: Pick the variant that emphasises the signal that is strongest for you: standout companies or, if they are unknown, your titles.

questions.q: A candidate has worked at a famous employer and wonders if the Mono template fits. How does the author see it?
options: It cannot fit, because the template is meant only for small firms
It fits only if the candidate hides the employer names to look humble
It fits only for people with no work experience yet
It can fit, as it suits people with standout companies on the resume
optionExplain: The author names standout employers as a fit, not a misfit.
Hiding the names would remove the very signal the template stresses.
The template is a variation for people with experience, not for beginners.
The author says standout companies are a good fit for this emphasis.
questions.explain: Mono suits both standout profiles and profiles where titles carry more meaning than employers.
questions.rule: Pick the variant that emphasises the signal that is strongest for you: standout companies or, if they are unknown, your titles.

questions.q: Sort each profile: does the Mono template's emphasis suit it according to the author, or is it not mentioned?

items.t: Worked at standout companies
Has a standout education
Employers are unknown, so titles carry the meaning
Wants to list a long hobbies section
Needs a layout with two narrow columns
Wants skill ratings next to each language

questions.explain: The author ties Mono to company, education and title emphasis, not to extra sections or columns.
questions.rule: Pick the variant that emphasises the signal that is strongest for you: standout companies or, if they are unknown, your titles.

questions.q: A developer has worked at three small companies that recruiters are unlikely to recognise. True or false: the Mono template, which can draw attention to the job title instead of the company, could suit this person.
questions.explain: The review says Mono can draw attention to either company or title. It fits standout companies and education, or employers that recruiters will not recognise, where focusing on titles makes more sense.
questions.teaches: The Mono template can draw more attention to either the company or the job title, which suits standout companies or education, and also people whose employers recruiters will not recognise.
questions.rule: Pick the variant that emphasises the signal that is strongest for you: standout companies or, if they are unknown, your titles.

questions.q: A recent graduate from a well-known university has one short internship. Could the Mono template's emphasis suit them?
options: It could not, since the template was made for senior engineers only
It could not, since education never belongs anywhere near a job title
It could, but only if the graduate removes the university name
It could, since the author counts a standout education as a fit too
optionExplain: The review does not restrict the template to seniors.
The review links the template to standout education as well as companies.
Hiding the name would defeat the signal.
The author lists people with standout companies and education as a good fit.
questions.explain: Standing out can come from the school as well as the employer.
questions.teaches: The author says the Mono template can also fit people with a standout education, not only standout companies.
questions.rule: Pick the variant that emphasises the signal that is strongest for you: standout companies or, if they are unknown, your titles.

questions.q: A developer keeps ten tailored resumes and wants to track changes to each. Which approach fits a developer's habits?
options: Save ten word-processor files named final, final2 and final-new
Use one resume and edit it for each application without keeping copies
Keep each as a text file in a repository and build the PDF from it
Ask a recruiter to keep copies of every version for you
optionExplain: File names are a weak form of version control with no history.
Overwriting loses earlier versions and makes comparison impossible.
Plain text under version control gives a history for every version.
A recruiter has no reason to hold your versions.
questions.explain: Developers often handle text this way already. The card next shows the template built for it.
questions.rule: Use Markdown as the source of your resume when you want versions in a repository and a build from the command line.

questions.q: The Markdown to PDF template lets you build your resume from the command ____.
questions.explain: A command-line build suits people who live in a terminal.
questions.rule: Use Markdown as the source of your resume when you want versions in a repository and a build from the command line.

questions.q: You want a backend version and a frontend version of your resume, each with a change history. According to the review, what helps?
options: Pasting both versions into one long document, with a heading for each role
Storing the Markdown versions in GitHub or another source with history
Printing each version and filing the paper copies with the date on them
Sending both versions to yourself in a chat message in date order
optionExplain: A merged document loses separate versions.
The review's good points include storing different versions in GitHub.
Paper has no searchable history.
Chat messages do not give a clean version history.
questions.explain: Version control is the benefit that comes with the Markdown source.
questions.rule: Use Markdown as the source of your resume when you want versions in a repository and a build from the command line.

questions.q: Sort each item: is it listed among this template's good points, or not?

items.t: A clean template
Markdown as the data source
Versions stored in GitHub
Real-time tracking of recruiter views
A web link to share the resume
A drag-and-drop layout editor

questions.explain: The good points are clean design, Markdown and versions. Tracking and web links belong to Standard Resume.
questions.rule: Use Markdown as the source of your resume when you want versions in a repository and a build from the command line.

questions.q: A developer wants to keep four versions of her resume, one per type of role, and track every change in version control. True or false: the Markdown to PDF approach fits that need.
questions.explain: The review praises Markdown as the source of truth and the option to store different versions on GitHub or another source. The resume is built from the command line.
questions.teaches: The Markdown to PDF template uses Markdown as the source of truth, lets you store different versions in GitHub or another source, and builds the resume from the command line.
questions.rule: Use Markdown as the source of your resume when you want versions in a repository and a build from the command line.

questions.q: A teammate wants to try the Markdown template but worries it will look bare. What does the review say about its default style?
options: It copies the Google Docs Serif layout, with two columns and a sidebar
It is a blank page with no style until you write your own style sheet
It resembles the Mono template and can be customised through its CSS
It is a colourful design with a placeholder for a profile photo
optionExplain: Nothing links it to a two-column layout.
It ships with a clean default style, not a blank page.
The default style is similar to the Mono template's, and CSS lets you change it.
The author advises against photos and does not mention one here.
questions.explain: A plain, clean starting point with room to tune the look.
questions.teaches: The default style of the Markdown to PDF resume template is similar to the Mono Engineer's template.
questions.rule: Use Markdown as the source of your resume when you want versions in a repository and a build from the command line.

questions.q: A template deliberately leaves the left side empty and pushes the technologies list to page two. Who is it likely built for?
options: Beginners who want to hide how little experience they have by spreading out
Candidates who prefer to keep their resume to a single page with skills on top
Candidates whose employers and titles are strong enough to carry the page
Anyone who wants the languages they know shown first and in large type
optionExplain: A beginner has little to show in those places, so the design hurts them.
The template is for two pages.
Space is spent on names and titles, which only helps if those are impressive.
The technologies come later in this layout, not first.
questions.explain: Deliberate trade-offs reflect a target audience. The card next shows which.
questions.rule: Match the template to your profile: a two-page layout that stresses names and titles pays off only if you have standout names and titles.

questions.q: The Experienced Engineer's template is a ____-page template for developers with standout experience.
questions.explain: It is designed for a longer career history.
questions.rule: Match the template to your profile: a two-page layout that stresses names and titles pays off only if you have standout names and titles.

questions.q: A principal engineer has built a well-known open source project. The author's review rates this template how for them?
options: Three stars, since open source experience does not count toward the rating
Five stars, because standout contributions such as open source suit it
One star, since principal engineers should use a single page
Four stars, since the template has no dedicated section for open source
optionExplain: Three stars is the rating for people without standout experience.
Standout contributions such as open source are named as a good fit.
The template is for two pages and for senior levels.
The review does not say a dedicated section is missing.
questions.explain: The rating depends on the profile: standout experience gets full marks.
questions.rule: Match the template to your profile: a two-page layout that stresses names and titles pays off only if you have standout names and titles.

questions.q: Sort each profile: does the author see this template as a fit, or a poor fit?

items.t: Staff engineer at a well-known company
Distinguished engineer with open source work
Principal engineer with strong titles
Junior developer with one internship
Candidate with few standout areas
Bootcamp graduate with a first job

questions.explain: It rewards standout experience; with less experience or few standout areas, the emphasis has little to work with.
questions.rule: Match the template to your profile: a two-page layout that stresses names and titles pays off only if you have standout names and titles.

questions.q: A principal engineer opens the Experienced Engineer's template and finds blank space on the left and the technologies list on page two. True or false: these are layout mistakes she should fix before using it.
questions.explain: The review calls both deliberate. The space gives more focus to company names and titles, and technologies on page two suit standout profiles, where recruiters scan the second page as well.
questions.teaches: The Experienced template deliberately leaves space on the left and puts technologies and languages on page two; it is meant for standout profiles whose recruiters scan the second page too.
questions.rule: Match the template to your profile: a two-page layout that stresses names and titles pays off only if you have standout names and titles.

questions.q: A candidate with a plain career and no standout projects likes this layout's look. What does the review advise?
options: Expect weaker results, since it works poorly with few standout areas
Use it anyway, since the rating is five stars for every kind of candidate
Use it but add a photo to make up for the plain career and few projects
Use it and move the technologies section to the bottom of page two
optionExplain: Without standout experience the review's rating falls to three stars.
Five stars is for standout experience only.
Photos invite bias, which the author warns against.
The technologies already sit on page two; moving them would not help.
questions.explain: A look you like is not the same as a profile the layout supports.
questions.teaches: Without standout experience the author's rating for this template falls from five stars to three, because it does not work well for less experienced people or few standout areas.
questions.rule: Match the template to your profile: a two-page layout that stresses names and titles pays off only if you have standout names and titles.

questions.q: A resume tool gives you a layout that you cannot break by editing fonts and tables. What is the likely trade-off?
options: You gain freedom to restyle every part of the page, fonts and margins included
You lose the ability to export the finished resume as a PDF file
You give up all control over the content, which the tool writes for you
You cannot cram the page, and some details may not fit its fixed fields
optionExplain: A fixed structure restricts freedom rather than adding it.
The text shows PDF and web versions both available.
You still write all the content.
A fixed structure protects the layout but limits what you can change.
questions.explain: A guard-rail layout limits mistakes and options alike. The card next shows the example in the book.
questions.rule: Prefer a port when you value its spacing and web features more than the freedom to edit the layout.

questions.q: Parker is the Standard Resume port of The ____ Engineer's template.
questions.explain: Parker ports the Pragmatic template and Venables ports the Experienced one.
questions.rule: Prefer a port when you value its spacing and web features more than the freedom to edit the layout.

questions.q: You have a role in three cities and want each location shown per position in Parker. What did the author do?
options: Added the location to the company name field for that position
Switched to Venables, which has a separate field for each location
Dropped locations, since recruiters seldom read them on a resume
Used a second column beside each position for the location text
optionExplain: The tool has no per-position location field, so he put it in the company name.
Venables shares the same limitation, so this does not solve it.
The author does not say locations are unimportant; he worked around the gap.
Second columns are the layout the author avoids.
questions.explain: A workaround within a field lets you keep the information.
questions.rule: Prefer a port when you value its spacing and web features more than the freedom to edit the layout.

questions.q: True or false: The author says Venables is a port of the Pragmatic Engineer's template.
questions.explain: Venables ports the Experienced Engineer's template; Parker is the port of the Pragmatic one.
questions.rule: Prefer a port when you value its spacing and web features more than the freedom to edit the layout.

questions.q: Why does the author say it is harder to cram everything on one page with Parker than with a plain template?
options: The tool limits you to a single section per page by accident of design
The templates lack any space for work experience on the page
The design makes cramming hard on purpose; the author calls this by design
The tool automatically deletes older jobs from the page to save space
optionExplain: It is a deliberate choice, not an accident.
Work experience is the main content and has room.
He notes it is harder to cram everything on one page, and calls that 'by design'.
Nothing in the review says it removes jobs.
questions.explain: Resistance to cramming is a feature, though it can feel like a limit.
questions.teaches: The author says it is harder to cram everything onto one page in Parker, and that this is by design.
questions.rule: Prefer a port when you value its spacing and web features more than the freedom to edit the layout.

questions.q: A developer in Berlin reads the author's five-star praise of the Parker and Venables themes and treats it as a neutral review. Which fact should she keep in mind when judging it?
options: The author rates both of them lower than the templates that they were ported from
The author collaborated with the Standard Resume team on both
Standard Resume stopped selling its templates a year ago, so the praise is out of date
Both were made entirely by hiring managers at large tech companies with no designers
optionExplain: The ratings match the originals, not lower.
He says he collaborated on both, which is a relevant interest to weigh.
The text says nothing of the sort.
The text names the author, with designers, as contributors.
questions.explain: Knowing that the reviewer helped build a product is part of reading a recommendation fairly.
questions.teaches: The author collaborated with the Standard Resume team to build the Parker and Venables themes from his own templates, so his praise comes from a participant.
questions.rule: Prefer a port when you value its spacing and web features more than the freedom to edit the layout.

questions.q: A template was made in 2014 for US tech firms, when printing resumes was common. What drawback should a modern non-US applicant expect?
options: Slower loading because of the large colour images that the layout uses
A dated black-and-white look and a US-centred focus that needs adjusting
No place on the page for dates or titles, which the layout leaves out
