questions.q: You love how a template looks on screen, but a hiring manager would find it hard to scan. Whose view should decide?
options: Yours, since you are the one who will present the resume later
Neither, since how a page looks has no effect on how fast it scans
A friend's, since friends judge looks fairly and are not close to it
The hiring manager's, since they are the one who reads the resume
optionExplain: Your pleasure in the look is not the purpose.
Layout does affect scanning.
A friend is not the reader who decides.
The resume exists for the reader.
questions.explain: The reader's seat is the right one. The card next shows the author's cautionary example.
questions.rule: Choose the template your reader can scan fastest, even if another looks more striking to you.

questions.q: The author uses EnhanCV as a cautionary example of sites that make resumes that job seekers find ____.
questions.explain: Looks to the owner can hide scanning problems.
questions.rule: Choose the template your reader can scan fastest, even if another looks more striking to you.

questions.q: A friend shows a stunning two-column design and asks for approval. What question should you ask first?
options: Can a busy recruiter scan it quickly from the top to the bottom?
Does it use as many different colours as possible?
Does it look like a design that has won an award?
Does it make the friend happy every time they look at it?
optionExplain: Scannability for the reader is the test.
More colours do not help scanning.
Design awards are not hiring criteria.
The friend's pleasure is not the reader's.
questions.explain: Ask first whether the reader can find what they need.
questions.rule: Choose the template your reader can scan fastest, even if another looks more striking to you.

questions.q: Sort each point from the EnhanCV review: is it listed as a problem, or not?

items.t: Hard for recruiters to scan
Encourages adding a photo, which leads to bias
Sections such as Life Philosophy add little
The design lacks any colour
It cannot be exported to PDF
It is not available in English

questions.explain: His problems are readability, bias and low-value sections.
questions.rule: Choose the template your reader can scan fastest, even if another looks more striking to you.

questions.q: A candidate fills the empty right column of a template with a section called Power Skills, listing words like team player. True or false: the author advises leaving that section out of a developer resume.
questions.explain: He says Power Skills are something you probably do not want on your CV, because they are empty buzzwords. He suggests Languages and Technologies sections in that space.
questions.teaches: The author says Power Skills are empty buzzwords you probably do not want on your CV, and suggests separate Languages and Technologies sections instead.
questions.rule: Choose the template your reader can scan fastest, even if another looks more striking to you.

questions.q: You must fix an EnhanCV-style resume with a Toolbox section. What does the author suggest?
options: Keep Toolbox as it is and add a short Life Philosophy paragraph
Add more columns for visual balance, so Toolbox sits beside experience
Rename Toolbox to Skills and add separate Languages and Technologies sections
Add a photo to improve engagement, since the page is otherwise all text
optionExplain: He would remove Life Philosophy.
More columns add the scanning problem.
Those are his suggested improvements.
The photo leads to bias.
questions.explain: Use plain, standard section names that readers expect.
questions.teaches: The author would remove Life Philosophy, rename Toolbox to Skills and add separate Languages and Technologies sections.
questions.rule: Choose the template your reader can scan fastest, even if another looks more striking to you.

questions.q: A format asks you to add your photo, birth date and gender. What risk does the author see?
options: They make the resume too short to read
These details lead to bias against candidates
They are rejected by every system automatically
They help recruiters by adding relevant facts
optionExplain: They add length, not shortness.
Such details can trigger bias.
Systems do not reject them automatically in the text.
They are not relevant to job performance.
questions.explain: Some formats push bias-inviting details. The card next names one.
questions.rule: Skip Europass for tech applications.

questions.q: The author says the Europass format is ____ required to apply to jobs in Europe.
questions.explain: Some people wrongly assume it is required.
questions.rule: Skip Europass for tech applications.

questions.q: A friend in Berlin thinks they must use Europass to apply to a tech job. What does the author say?
options: It is required by law in Europe, so every applicant must use it
It is required, but only for large companies with an HR team
It is optional and a strong choice, since recruiters in Europe prefer it
It is not required to apply in Europe, and tech recruiters advise against it
optionExplain: He says it is a misconception.
Size of company does not change this.
Tech recruiters advised not to use it.
The format is not required, contrary to the assumption.
questions.explain: Do not assume local rules require a format.
questions.rule: Skip Europass for tech applications.

questions.q: Sort each point from the Europass review: does the author list it as a problem, or not?

items.t: Encourages photos, birth dates and gender
Dated format that uses tables
Unnecessarily wastes space
Too many bright colours
A required subscription
Limited to one page

questions.explain: His list: bias details, tables, wasted space, noise, poor representation of tech.
questions.rule: Skip Europass for tech applications.

questions.q: A developer in Spain hears that Europass was designed with recruiters and job seekers, and concludes that it must read well to tech hiring managers. True or false: the author supports that conclusion.
questions.explain: The format came from a working group within the European Commission, and recruiters told him it had no recruiter, HR specialist or job seeker on it, though he could not confirm this. Every tech recruiter he spoke to advised against it.
questions.teaches: The format came from a working group within the European Commission; recruiters told the author it had no recruiter, HR specialist or job seeker, though he could not confirm this.
questions.rule: Skip Europass for tech applications.

questions.q: A form from a public body asks for driving licence and spoken languages on a developer resume. What does the author's review imply?
options: Such details are noise that wastes space on a tech resume
They are the most important facts to show for a tech job
They must be included by law in every country that has such a form
They signal seniority to tech recruiters who read the resume
optionExplain: Driving licences and spoken languages count as noise.
Tech recruiters do not rank them important.
No such rule is stated.
They do not signal seniority.
questions.explain: Leave out fields that add noise.
questions.teaches: The author lists details like spoken languages and driving licences as noise that the Europass format adds.
questions.rule: Skip Europass for tech applications.

questions.q: Two templates are equally readable. One has a photo slot and a birth-date field. Which should a developer choose?
options: The one with them, since more details help recruiters
Either one, since details play no role in decisions
The one without them, since those fields invite bias
The one with them, since photos make resumes memorable
optionExplain: More details are not more help; they can lead to bias.
The author says they lead to bias.
Fields for personal details invite bias.
Memorability by photo is the thing he warns about.
questions.explain: The choice is simple. The card next shows where the author flags it.
questions.rule: Pick templates without a photo slot or personal-detail fields.

questions.q: The author says templates that encourage photos, birth dates and gender lead to ____.
questions.explain: These details invite judgments unrelated to skills.
questions.rule: Pick templates without a photo slot or personal-detail fields.

questions.q: A Canva template you like includes a circular portrait frame. What should you do?
options: Choose another single-column template that has no photo frame at all
Add your best portrait so the resume stands out from those that have none
Keep the frame empty and hope nobody notices the blank circle
Move the frame to the second page, where it does less harm to the page
optionExplain: Photos are something to avoid.
Standing out through a photo invites bias.
An empty frame is odd and still signals the template.
Moving it keeps the problem.
questions.explain: Pick a template without the frame.
questions.rule: Pick templates without a photo slot or personal-detail fields.

questions.q: Sort each review remark: does it flag bias risk, or not?

items.t: Many Canva templates come with photos
EnhanCV encourages adding a photo
Europass encourages birth dates and gender
Serif has a clean one-page format
VisualCV highlights job titles
CareerCup dates are easy to read

questions.explain: Only the photo and personal-detail remarks concern bias.
questions.rule: Pick templates without a photo slot or personal-detail fields.

questions.q: A friend thinks a smiling headshot will make their resume memorable. What does the author's comparison with star ratings suggest?
options: A photo helps if it is smiling, since it shows warmth that the rest of the page cannot
A photo helps if the template has room for it, since the space would be wasted otherwise
A photo will not help, so leave it off
A photo helps recruiters remember the candidate, so it should be placed at the top
optionExplain: The author finds that photos do not help and can lead to bias.
Spare room is not a reason; the template with a slot is the problem.
He says a profile photo won't help your resume and that bias risk comes with it.
Memorability by looks is exactly the bias risk.
questions.explain: A photo adds risk without adding value.
questions.teaches: The author says a profile photo will not help your resume, just as star ratings can only work against it.
questions.rule: Pick templates without a photo slot or personal-detail fields.

questions.q: Your template has sections for Awards, Spoken Languages and References. Which approach fits a tech resume best?
options: Keep them all in place, since a full page looks more professional
Cut them and give the freed space to technologies and experience
Move them above the experience, since they show range and character
Merge them into one section called Personal to take up less space
optionExplain: Space is better used on what recruiters want.
Those sections are noise for tech.
Putting noise first makes it worse.
Merging keeps the noise.
questions.explain: Think of the reader. The card next lists the sections the author flags.
questions.rule: Keep sections a tech reader looks for, and cut the rest.

questions.q: The author says Awards are rarely ____ for tech resumes.
questions.explain: A section should earn its space.
questions.rule: Keep sections a tech reader looks for, and cut the rest.

questions.q: A template section is titled Skills, but you want recruiters to see languages and tools. What does the author suggest?
options: Rename it Technologies, or split it into Languages and Technologies
Keep the Skills heading and add a star rating beside each item in it
Rename it Power Skills so that it sounds more impressive to readers
Put it at the very end of the second page, where it clutters nothing
optionExplain: Plain names that match what readers look for.
Stars hurt.
Power Skills is a buzzword.
It should be easy to find.
questions.explain: Name sections after what the reader seeks.
questions.rule: Keep sections a tech reader looks for, and cut the rest.

questions.q: Sort each section: does the author want it removed, or kept?

items.t: Life Philosophy
Power Skills
References
Languages and Technologies
Work experience
Technologies on the first page

questions.explain: He wants sections that match what tech readers need.
questions.rule: Keep sections a tech reader looks for, and cut the rest.

questions.q: On the VisualCV template the author suggests dropping the title Software Engineer. What is his reason?
options: It reveals the candidate's seniority too early in the page
It clashes with the summary, which states the same words directly below
It is a section name that most developer templates leave out
It is obvious for the role and takes up space on the page
optionExplain: The reason is not seniority.
He wants a short summary, not a title that repeats it.
Nothing suggests that other templates leave it out.
The title is obvious for a software engineer resume and takes up space.
questions.explain: Cut words that tell the reader nothing new.
questions.teaches: For the VisualCV template the author suggests dropping the title Software Engineer, because it is obvious and takes up space.
questions.rule: Keep sections a tech reader looks for, and cut the rest.

questions.q: A template has a Skills heading with a decorative coloured line under it, listing soft-skill words. What does the author say about such a section?
options: The line helps the eye find the skills, so the section is one of the strongest parts
The line adds noise for no reason, and the skills are not what tech looks for
The line is fine, but the skills should be shown as star ratings beside the words
The line should be thicker so the section stands out, while the words can stay
optionExplain: He calls the line noise, not guidance.
He says the skills heading and the blue line add noise for no reason.
He argues against star ratings.
Making it thicker adds more noise.
questions.explain: Decoration around the wrong content makes the page worse.
questions.teaches: On the resume.io software engineer template the author says the Skills heading and the blue line beneath it add noise for no reason.
questions.rule: Keep sections a tech reader looks for, and cut the rest.

questions.q: A posting asks for C++, Java, PHP and JavaScript. You work daily in PHP and JavaScript and barely touched C++. What leads your skills line?
options: Every language in the posting, in the posting's order, so it mirrors the ad exactly
All languages you have touched, in alphabetical order, so no skill is favoured
PHP and JavaScript first, because they match the posting and you use them
Each language with a 1 to 5 score, so the reader sees your level in every one
optionExplain: It looks tailored, but it puts a language you barely know ahead of those you use daily.
Neutral, but it hides your strongest match among the rest and does no tailoring.
Right: it matches the ad and is true to your experience.
Scores look informative, but the book argues self-ratings work against you.
questions.explain: The skills line is a place to tailor: the match with the posting should be the first thing seen. The card shows how.
questions.rule: Match the posting with what you really use.

questions.q: The author says your resume should be about your experience and tailored for the ____ you are applying for.
questions.explain: Tailoring means shaping the same real experience for one specific position.
questions.rule: Tailor to the position.

questions.q: A backend developer is going after mostly Java-based roles and has one long line of every tool used. What is the best fix?
options: Put languages first, then the technologies those roles need
Delete every tool that is not Java, so the whole line is short and focused
Keep the line as it is and make the Java items bold so they stand out more
Sort the whole line by years of use, longest first, so that experience shows up
optionExplain: Right: this is the order the refactored backend resume used.
Shorter is not the aim; the author says it is good to list all technologies you are proficient in.
Bolding was itself one of the problems on that resume: it drew attention to the wrong places.
Years of use ignore what the target roles ask for.
questions.explain: The fix was strategic order and format, not removal: languages first, then the job-relevant technologies the person knew.
questions.rule: Order skills for the job.

questions.q: Sort each way of building a skills section: does it tailor to the position, or not?

items.t: Names PHP and JavaScript first for a posting that lists them and that the candidate uses
Puts the languages first, then the tools the target Java roles ask for
Keeps a second version that leads with different tools for a different kind of job
Sends one unchanged master resume to every position
Dumps every technology one after another in the order they were learned
Lists skills in alphabetical order for every application, whatever the job

questions.explain: Tailoring is a choice of what comes first for this position. One-size-fits-all copies and unordered dumps leave that choice to the reader.
questions.rule: Choose the order for the position.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, listing every technology you are proficient in is itself the mistake, and the fix is a much shorter list.
questions.explain: The author calls listing all of them good; the weakness was the order and format, and not focusing on what the position needs or what you want to call out.
questions.rule: Order and focus, not deletion.

questions.q: A nurse who retrained as a data analyst applies to a posting that welcomes career changers. What would the author consider adding?
options: Nothing, because a summary only repeats the experience section below it
A line copying the posting's sentence about career changers, word for word
A larger skills table, because career changers need to prove tools first
A short summary that reflects on the posting's welcome, where it applies to her
optionExplain: The author suggests a summary where there is something to reflect from the posting.
Copying the posting says nothing about her own path; the aim is to reflect on how it applies to her.
Tools matter, but this is the posting's invitation, and it is answered in words, not in a table.
Right: the author would consider a short summary that speaks to what the posting asks, if it applies.
questions.explain: In the 2-year example the author would consider a short summary reflecting on the posting's call for non-traditional paths, if some of it applied to the candidate. Resumes should also be tailored per position, not used as one-size-fits-all.
questions.rule: Answer what the posting invites, if it fits you.
questions.teaches: The author would consider adding a short summary when the posting invites something that applies to the candidate, such as non-traditional career paths or self-taught developers.

questions.q: A resume has generous side margins and different heading sizes in each section. What impression is it most likely to give?
options: Confidence, since plenty of white space shows the writer has nothing to hide
Sloppiness, and less room for content than the page could hold
Creativity, because varied headings keep the reader interested in each part
Nothing much, since recruiters only read the words and ignore the layout
optionExplain: White space can help, but unusually large margins were criticised for wasting space.
Right: both points are in the author's review.
Different sizes in different sections read as inconsistency, not style.
The author says formatting differences bring a sloppy feel.
questions.explain: Layout is read before the words are. The card says what to do about it.
questions.rule: Consistent and compact.

questions.q: Different font sizes and alignment in different sections give a resume a ____ feel.
questions.explain: The author's word is sloppy.
questions.rule: Inconsistency looks careless.

questions.q: You are about to send a two-page resume. Which check follows the author's advice from these examples?
options: Widen the margins so the page looks airy and calm to anyone who opens it
Use a different font for each section so that every section stands out well
Shrink every font until all of the text fits on a single page, whatever size
Check that sizes and alignment match and the header is not repeated on page two
optionExplain: The author counted wide margins as wasted space.
That is the inconsistency the author criticised.
The examples do not recommend shrinking text; the problem was waste and inconsistency.
Right: consistency, and not wasting page-two space on a repeated header, are both in the examples.
questions.explain: Check consistency and reclaim wasted space. A repeated header on page two was listed as space wasted.
questions.rule: Match everything, waste nothing.

questions.q: Which of these were flagged as layout problems in the author's examples? Select all that apply.
options: Font sizes and alignment differing between sections
A header repeated at the top of the second page
Bullet points used for each achievement
Very large margins at the top and sides
optionExplain: Yes: flagged as inconsistency.
Yes: flagged as wasting space.
No: bullet points were praised as easy to read.
Yes: flagged as reducing what fits on each page.
questions.explain: Inconsistency and wasted space were problems; bullets were praised.
questions.rule: Bullets help; waste and inconsistency hurt.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, very large margins on a resume are acceptable as long as the spacing is the same on every page.
questions.explain: The author says good spacing can help, but very large margins at top and sides are no good reason to lose space.
questions.rule: Spacing is not the aim.

questions.q: A candidate trims margins and aligns every heading but still has a strange look to bullets and spacing. What does the author suggest?
options: Add more bold text to hold the layout together and make the page feel solid
Consider a better template or a template service such as Standard Resume
Leave it as it is, since formatting matters far less than wording by now
Convert to a word-processor file so the layout stays easy to edit later on
optionExplain: Too much bolding was a separate problem in another example.
Right: the 8-year remote example had a DIY layout and the author recommends that route.
The author still flags it among the improvements.
The author prefers PDFs over docx files.
questions.explain: When customised layout still feels DIY, the author suggests a better template or a service like Standard Resume.
questions.rule: Let a template carry the layout.
questions.teaches: The author suggests a better template or a template service such as Standard Resume when a self-customised layout still feels DIY.

questions.q: Every company on your resume links to its website, in blue. What is the main risk?
options: The reader's eye goes to company names instead of your title and dates
The links may break if a company changes its website later on
The reader may leave your resume to browse those sites for far too long
Links make the file larger, so upload forms may reject the resume outright
optionExplain: Right: that is the author's main complaint.
Possible, but the author's complaint is about attention, not link rot.
Not the author's concern; the sites add little and a reader can search the name.
Nothing in the examples mentions file size.
questions.explain: Links are loud. The card says what to steer toward.
questions.rule: Choose where the eye lands.

questions.q: The author says attention should go to the engineer's title and the ____, not to company names.
questions.explain: Title and date are what a glance should catch.
questions.rule: Title and date first.

questions.q: Your technical blogging section is a link to your whole blog page. What does the author's refactor suggest?
options: Link the blog's home page twice so that it is easier to click on
Remove the blogging section entirely, because links only distract readers
Call out two articles you would like the hiring manager to glance at
Link to every article you have written, newest first, with a short note on each
optionExplain: Repeating a general link adds nothing.
The refactor kept the section and focused it.
Right: a focused approach instead of one general link.
That scatters attention; the point was a few chosen items.
questions.explain: Pick the one or two pieces you want read and point to them directly.
questions.rule: Point, do not scatter.

questions.q: Sort each emphasis choice: does it guide the reader well, or pull attention to the wrong place?

items.t: Dates placed where the eye can scan them
Two chosen articles named under a blog heading
Link colours toned down so titles stand out
Every technical skill in bold
A past employer's website linked on each job
W4 forms in bold in a payroll role

questions.explain: The good choices point to dates, titles and chosen work; the bad ones decorate things that bring little value.
questions.rule: Emphasis is a limited resource.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a recruiter who wants to learn about a past employer needs the link on your resume to do so.
questions.explain: The author says they can simply search the company name, and a company landing page rarely says anything relevant.
questions.rule: Links earn their place.

questions.q: Links on a resume draw the eye in bright blue. Besides cutting links, what else did the author say could help?
options: Making every link bold so that all of them look equally important
A different template that puts the title and date in focus
Moving all links to the last page where nobody sees them at all
Replacing each company name with its logo, which readers find faster
optionExplain: That adds more emphasis, which is the problem.
Right: a different template could help, as would toning down link colours.
The author asks for steering the eye, not hiding information.
Logos would draw more attention to companies.
questions.explain: The author said a different template could help draw attention to title and date, as could toning down link colours.
questions.rule: Template and colour steer too.
questions.teaches: A different template can steer the eye to title and date, and so can toning down link colours.

questions.q: Your bullet says you built a mobile app. A hiring manager reads it. What does the bullet still not tell them?
options: Which programming language the app used, which every bullet must state
Whether the app was built for iOS or Android, the most important detail
How long it took, which is the only measure of effort that counts
What was impactful, challenging or interesting about the app
optionExplain: The author does want specifics, but the author's named gap is the work's importance.
Platform detail may help, but it is not the gap the author names.
Time is not the focus; the author asks about impact and challenge.
Right: that is the gap the author names.
questions.explain: Task-only bullets leave out the reason the work mattered. The card names the fix.
questions.rule: Say what it achieved.

questions.q: The refactored resume used ____ language and showed specific examples of impact.
questions.explain: Active language puts what you did and what resulted in the foreground.
questions.rule: Active voice, impact first.

questions.q: A bullet says only that you maintained the billing service. Which rewrite best follows the author's advice, assuming the facts are true?
options: Responsible for the billing service, including all of the maintenance duties
Maintained the billing service reliably and with excellent communication skills
Cut invoice errors by moving billing to a retry queue
Maintained the billing service, which is important to any business at all
optionExplain: Passive and duty-based: it says what you were told to do.
Adds clichés but no result or specific.
Right: it opens with the result and shows what the person did.
Vague importance; no outcome shown.
questions.explain: Impact, specifics and active verbs make the contrast with a duty list.
questions.rule: Result first, verbs active.

questions.q: Sort each bullet: does it show impact, or only a task?

items.t: Cut page load time and raised sign-ups by shipping a rewrite
Reduced support tickets by building self-service tools
Led a migration that let the team deploy daily
Built a mobile app
Was told to maintain the reporting scripts
Worked on the API and on the database

questions.explain: A bullet with a result shows the reason the work mattered; a bullet with only a task leaves the reader to guess.
questions.rule: Result, not duty.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, the improved version of the first resume described a different, larger body of work than the original did.
questions.explain: The author stresses it is exactly the same person and the same work; it was expressed better.
questions.rule: Better words, same facts.

questions.q: A QA engineer in Nairobi opens each role with Responsible for regression suites, and puts the result, fewer escaped defects, at the end of the entry. What would the author's backend refactor suggest?
options: Keep the order, since the reader will get to the end of every entry
Move the technology list into the first line of each role
Open each role with the impact, so the result is not buried
Delete the task wording and keep only the result in every entry
optionExplain: Skimming readers may stop before the result; the refactor moved it up.
The refactor led with the impact of the work, not the technologies.
Right: the refactor began each role with its impact instead of burying it deeper.
The refactor changed the order of what was said; it did not strip out the work details.
questions.explain: A scanning reader meets the first words of an entry, so the result belongs there. The backend refactor began each role with the impact of the work.
questions.rule: Lead each entry with the result.
questions.teaches: In the backend refactor, the writer began each role with the impact of the work instead of burying it deeper in the entry.

questions.section: Machine Learning Engineer with 5 Years Experience
questions.q: A bullet says you created a full-stack web app for internal stakeholders. What would make it stronger?
options: A longer description of the company that owned the app and its history
A line saying the app was excellent and very well received by users
The tools you used and numbers about what you built
Moving the bullet into a separate section named Projects further down
optionExplain: The author asks to talk about yourself, not the company.
Praise without specifics adds a cliche.
Right: the author suggests technologies and numbers.
Where it sits does not add the missing details.
questions.explain: The bullet is general. The card lists three kinds of detail to add.
questions.rule: Tools, numbers, role.

questions.section: Machine Learning Engineer with 5 Years Experience
questions.q: The author's example of a number is 4 microservices serving ____ RPS.
questions.explain: The suggested line was: designed, implemented and deployed 4 microservices serving 100 RPS.
questions.rule: Numbers show scale.

questions.section: Machine Learning Engineer with 5 Years Experience
questions.q: 'Created troubleshooting tools that improved support efficiency by more than 30%.' Which questions does the author ask of it?
options: Which tools, whose idea, who led, and how many used them
Did your manager sign off on the percentage in writing before you used it?
Why does the figure say more than instead of giving an exact number?
Could you add a hobby that relates to tooling to show your passion?
optionExplain: Right: those are the questions the author lists.
Not asked; the questions are about tools, idea, team and users.
Not asked by the author.
Personal detail was not the point.
questions.explain: The questions probe language and frameworks, who came up with the idea, leadership, and reach.
questions.rule: Ask what the reader would ask.

questions.section: Machine Learning Engineer with 5 Years Experience
questions.q: Which additions would the author consider useful for a bullet about a deployed service? Select all that apply.
options: The frameworks and cloud platform used
A rating of how well you know each framework
The number of services built or requests served
A long paragraph about the employer
optionExplain: Yes: technologies were suggested.
No: self-ratings work against you.
Yes: numbers were suggested.
No: talk about yourself, not the company.
questions.explain: Tools and numbers were suggested; ratings and company descriptions were criticised in the same example.
questions.rule: Add facts, not ratings or backdrops.

questions.section: Machine Learning Engineer with 5 Years Experience
questions.q: True or false: A resume that already has some results and percentages cannot be improved further with more specifics.
questions.explain: The backend resume had percentages, yet the author said other bullets needed more detail, and the refactor added a small team lead that was left off.
questions.rule: More detail still helps.

questions.section: Machine Learning Engineer with 5 Years Experience
questions.q: An engineer left out that they led a team of four on a project. What does the author's backend refactor suggest?
options: Leave it out so the focus stays on technical skill alone
List leadership as a skill in the skills section of the resume
Mention it only in the cover letter and not on the resume itself
State that you led a small team
optionExplain: The refactor did the opposite.
Leadership as a listed skill was criticised as irrelevant in another example.
The refactor placed it in the resume.
Right: the refactored resume added the leadership detail.
questions.explain: Leading a team is the kind of specific the original left off and the refactor included.

A resume that can still feel dated, so a rebuild in a current template pays
optionExplain: The look comes from the template and structure, and these stay unchanged.
The example shows the downside: the old look and older, less relevant positions stay.
The author rebuilt the SRE resume rather than extending the old one.
Right: the original only added ten years to the 2010 resume, and the refactor used an easier, more modern template.
questions.explain: The SRE original just added the last ten years to the resume used in 2010, and it felt dated. The refactor rebuilt it in an easier-to-read template that feels more modern.
questions.rule: Rebuild, do not just append.
questions.teaches: The SRE candidate's original resume was the one used when applying in 2010, with the last ten years of employment added, and the refactor swapped it for an easier-to-read template that feels more modern.

questions.q: You finished your resume in a word processor. What should you send to employers?
options: A PDF export of it
The editable docx so recruiters can add notes
Both files in the same email to cover all cases
A screenshot pasted into the email body
optionExplain: Right: the author prefers PDFs.
The author advised against docx.
Not what the author advises; one clean PDF is the choice.
Not suggested in the examples.
questions.explain: Format is a last, small decision. The card has the rule.
questions.rule: Send PDF.

questions.q: The author says using a ____ checker would have surfaced sentences that did not flow well.
questions.explain: A spellcheck is not enough; grammar needs its own check.
questions.rule: Grammar, not just spelling.

questions.q: Which wording of a past job follows the author's tense advice?
options: Creating backend microservices for payments
Responsible for the creating of backend microservices
Created backend microservices for payments
Creation of backend microservices for payments
optionExplain: This is the form the author said to change.
Passive and wordy.
Right: active past tense.
A noun form; not active.
questions.explain: Active past tense reads as something you did.
questions.rule: Verb in the past.

questions.q: Sort each item: does it polish the resume, or leave a flaw?

items.t: Exports the final file as PDF
Runs a grammar checker on every bullet
Writes 'Created' instead of 'Creating' for a past role
Sends the docx file
Leaves sentences that read awkwardly
Uses 'Creating' for a job held years ago

questions.explain: The first three follow the author's tips; the others are named flaws.
questions.rule: Small flaws add up.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, running a grammar checker would have caught the unnatural wording in the troubleshooting-tools bullet.
questions.explain: Yes: the author says a grammar checker would have surfaced such sentences.
questions.rule: Tools help.

questions.q: A bullet is grammatically perfect but says only that you worked on the backend. Does a grammar check fix it?
options: Yes, since a grammatically correct sentence is a strong sentence too
No: a grammar check adds no results
Yes, as long as the file is also exported to PDF format
No, because grammar checkers only check spelling and nothing else
optionExplain: The examples ask for results and specifics as separate steps.
Right: the bullet lacks content, which a checker cannot supply.
Format does not add content.
The author says a grammar check is more than a spellcheck.
questions.explain: Our reading: the author lists grammar among small fixes, and results and specifics as separate improvements.
questions.rule: Polish is not content.
questions.teaches: Our reading: the author treats grammar and file type as separate fixes from missing results and specifics, which must be added by the writer.

questions.q: You find an improved resume for a role like yours. What is the best use of it?
options: Copy its bullets and change only the company names
Send it unchanged since it already worked for its author
Ignore it, because every career is too different to learn from
Check your own resume for the same kinds of weakness
optionExplain: It is someone else's experience, which the author warns against copying.
The facts are another person's, and the details were altered.
The author offers the examples to show typical areas to address.
Right: use it as inspiration.
questions.explain: The examples show typical areas you could address in your own resume.
questions.rule: Compare, do not copy.

questions.q: The author says to resist copying anything ____-for-one from these examples.
questions.explain: The warning is about copying one-for-one.
questions.rule: Do not copy.

questions.q: Your friend likes a bullet in an example and wants to paste it into their resume. What is the author's advice?
options: Paste it if the friend does similar work, which makes it true
Paste it but change the numbers, so that nobody can tell
Use it as inspiration and write about their own work
Paste it only in the summary section where copying is common
optionExplain: Similar work is not the same work.
Changing numbers makes the claim false.
Right: the resume should be about your experience.
The author does not say that.
questions.explain: The experience belongs to someone else, so it must be your own words.
questions.rule: Your experience, your words.

questions.q: Which statements about the chapter's examples are true? Select all that apply.
options: They are real resumes
Names of people and companies were altered
Each improved resume was the author's own invention
They often came from people with a low response rate
optionExplain: Yes: real resumes the author received.
Yes: anonymised.
No: the improved version was the one the person used.
Yes: often from people not getting the response they hoped.
questions.explain: Real, anonymised and often from people with low response rates; the improved versions were what the people ended up using.
questions.rule: Real people, real results.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, the improved versions were what each person ended up using as their master resume.
questions.explain: Yes: the improved version is the one the author of each resume ended up using.
questions.rule: Master resume.

questions.q: An engineering manager in Lagos wants to see how real engineering manager resumes are laid out before she edits her own. Where does the book point her, and with what warning?
options: To public job boards, where applicants' resumes can be searched and copied
To company career pages that publish the resumes of their past hires
To Standard Resume's real resumes, as inspiration, not to copy one-for-one
To the chapter's examples only, since the book names no other source
optionExplain: The chapter names no job board as a source of resumes.
Career pages are not mentioned.
Right: the book points to Standard Resume, and the chapter says to resist copying anything one-for-one.
Section 12.6 names Standard Resume as a source of more real resumes.
questions.explain: Section 12.6 points to Standard Resume, which shares real engineering manager resumes to browse. The chapter intro adds that these are someone else's experience, so use them as inspiration.
questions.rule: Browse for inspiration.
questions.teaches: Standard Resume shares real software engineer, web developer, iOS, frontend, data scientist and engineering manager resumes to browse for inspiration, but the book says to resist copying anything one-for-one because they are someone else's experience.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: Your team receives 300 resumes for one role. Which view of the resume screen is most defensible?
options: Once the criteria are written down, it will catch every strong candidate who applies to the team
It shrinks the pile, but it will also turn away some strong people with weak resumes
It tells you so little about anyone that a team cannot gain anything useful from running it at all
It is accurate about strong candidates and unreliable only for the weak ones, who write poor resumes
optionExplain: Written criteria feel objective, but a poor resume can still hide a strong person.
Right: it has a real use, shrinking the pool, and a real cost, missing some strong people.
The signal is weak, but the author says the filter still helps by reducing applicants.
This reverses the problem: the risk is a strong person with a poor resume.
questions.explain: A resume screen is useful for reducing numbers and unreliable at the edges. The card next shows the author's view.
questions.rule: Know the screen's cost as well as its use.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: As long as you screen resumes, you will reject good people with poor ____.
questions.explain: The author says this is a fact you will not change unless you relax or drop the resume screen.
questions.rule: Screening has a built-in error.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: A director says: our checklist is strict, so no strong applicant is lost at the resume stage. What fits the author's view?
options: A checklist cannot fix this, because a strong person with a weak resume still fails it
The director is right, since strict criteria make a screen close to objective and lossless
A stricter checklist keeps strong applicants, because it rewards clear written evidence of skill
The director is right as long as two recruiters apply the same checklist to every resume
optionExplain: Right: the loss comes from the resume as a signal, not from how strict the checklist is.
Objective is not the same as accurate: the checklist still reads only what the resume shows.
Clear evidence helps a strong writer, but the strong person with a poor resume is the one lost.
Two readers improve consistency, but both still see only a weak signal.
questions.explain: Rigour in applying criteria does not make the resume a stronger signal of a person's ability.
questions.rule: A better checklist does not remove the loss.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, the only way to stop rejecting good people with poor resumes is to relax or drop resume screening.
questions.explain: The author says the loss is a fact of resume screening unless you relax or drop the requirement.
questions.rule: Remove the loss only by changing the screen itself.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: A manager at a 40-person software firm has 300 resumes for one opening and doubts that resumes say much about people. Which pair of views does the author hold together here?
options: Resumes are a strong way to judge people, so rejecting a poor one is a safe and low-cost decision
Resumes are a weak way to judge people, so every team should stop reading them from this week
Resumes are a weak way to judge people, yet the screen still shrinks the applicant pool
Resumes are a weak way to judge people, so the screen only adds delay and gives the team no benefit
optionExplain: This contradicts the quoted view that a resume gives only a faint clue.
The author does not call for dropping screening; he asks managers to know its cost.
Right: the author sees both the weakness of the signal and the usefulness of the filter.
Filtering does have a benefit: it reduces applicants and removes likely non-fits.
questions.explain: The author's position is balanced: a weak signal, kept for a good reason, used with care.
questions.rule: Weak signal, real purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: A school panel reads CVs to pick one teaching assistant from 200 applicants. According to Spolsky, what can a CV tell the panel most safely?
options: Pretty strong negative clues about a poor fit, with little else of value beyond that
Which applicants will teach best, since a CV lists qualifications that predict classroom skill closely
How well each applicant relates to children, because a careful CV shows personality quite directly
Which applicants will stay the longest, because the length of past jobs predicts loyalty in the role
optionExplain: Right: Spolsky says a resume can sometimes give pretty strong negative clues, but is otherwise hard to read much from.
A CV is not a close predictor of teaching skill; Spolsky says it gives only the faintest clue.
Personality is the sort of thing a CV hardly shows; this overstates the signal.
Job length is not what Spolsky says a resume reveals; he points to negative clues.
questions.explain: In the setting of a school panel the same reading holds: the CV is better at warning than at selecting.
questions.rule: Use a resume to spot red flags more than to rank strengths.
questions.teaches: Joel Spolsky, quoted by the author, says a resume can sometimes give pretty strong negative clues about an applicant's quality, but otherwise it is extremely hard to tell much from one.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: You screen 40 resumes and several are borderline. What is a sound way to handle them?
options: Hold them in a middle pile and re-read it if your first choices do not fill the role
Reject them to keep the process quick, since any doubt about a resume is a good reason to say no
Pass all of them on to the interview stage so that nobody is turned away early in the process
Ask the team to vote, and drop any resume that receives even a single no vote from a reader
optionExplain: Right: a middle pile keeps doubtful people alive without committing interview time to all of them.
Quick, but this is exactly how promising people are rejected too early.
Kind, but it removes the filter's purpose and floods the interview stage.
Voting adds a bias toward the safest profiles and drops anyone a single reader doubts.
questions.explain: A middle pile gives doubtful resumes a second look. The card next names the three piles.
questions.rule: Doubt belongs in Maybe, not in No.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: Rothman reads resumes with an eye to giving each person the benefit of the ____, which leads to the Maybe pile.
questions.explain: Giving the benefit of the doubt is what produces the Maybe pile.
questions.rule: Maybe is where doubt goes.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: A manager has phone-screened every Yes candidate for a data-analyst role, and the post is still open. What does the author's approach suggest?
options: Widen the Yes pile by relaxing the checklist for the remaining open weeks
Close the role and restart the search with a freshly written job advert
Re-read the Maybe pile to check whether a diamond in the rough was missed
Go back to the No pile first, since the Maybe pile was already judged once
optionExplain: Relaxing criteria blindly drops the care the three piles were meant to give.
Restarting loses the candidates already in hand, including the Maybe pile.
Right: Rothman re-reads Maybe after screening the Yes candidates when the opening is not filled.
The Maybe pile is the planned next step; the No pile was a firmer decision.
questions.explain: The Maybe pile is the planned fallback when the Yes pile does not fill the role.
questions.rule: Re-read Maybe before you start over.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: A manager sorts resumes only into Yes and No, putting every doubtful one in No. What is the likely cost, in the author's terms?
options: More interviews wasted on weak people, because the No pile stays too small
Early rejection of people who might be strong, with no second look
A longer screen overall, because every resume ends up read twice
A rise in bias, because a second reviewer has more resumes to compare
optionExplain: Putting doubt in No shrinks the interview list, so it does not waste interviews.
Right: with no middle pile, doubtful but promising people are lost at once.
Reading twice is the feature of Maybe; two piles means less rereading.
Bias is not the cost the three-pile method addresses here.
questions.explain: Without a Maybe pile, doubt turns directly into rejection, which is the early rejection the author warns about.
questions.rule: No Maybe pile, more early rejections.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: Sort each screening step: does it follow the three-pile approach, or break it?

items.t: Places a resume with an unusual career path in Maybe
Re-reads Maybe after phone-screening the Yes candidates, with the role still open
Chooses a pile on purpose for every resume it reads
Discards the Maybe pile while the role is still open after the Yes screens
Rejects a resume on a first glance without choosing any pile
Re-reads the Maybe pile first, before any Yes candidate is screened

questions.explain: The approach asks for a conscious pile for each resume, a Maybe pile for doubt, and a re-read of it after the Yes screens if the role is unfilled.
questions.rule: Choose consciously; re-read Maybe later.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: A lab manager hires technicians, most of whom write few resumes. Why does the author's reasoning favour a Maybe pile here?
options: Technicians are rarely strong, so the Maybe pile is where the best of the group will be found
Labs have fewer applicants, so every resume can be moved to Yes to save the manager time
A Maybe pile removes the need for any phone screen, since the lab can rely on the resumes alone
Capable people in such a field may present themselves poorly, so doubt deserves a second look
optionExplain: This runs the reasoning backwards and insults the group; the issue is presentation, not ability.
Fewer applicants does not make weak resumes safe to advance without a look.
The Maybe pile is read after phone screens, not instead of them.
Right: Rothman gives benefit of the doubt because technical people may not know how best to present themselves on paper.
questions.explain: The reason for the Maybe pile is that the people being judged may write badly about good work.
questions.rule: Poor presentation can hide a good fit.
questions.teaches: Rothman reads resumes with benefit of the doubt because she mostly hires technical people who may not know how best to present themselves in a resume.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: For a backend role, which resume belongs in the Maybe pile?
options: A resume that meets every requirement and shows measured results, which belongs in Yes
A resume with no related skills or work for the role, which belongs in No
A poorly worded resume that links to a project that looks solid
A resume identical in content to ten others, which belongs in No by default
optionExplain: That resume is a clear Yes and needs no second look.
That resume gives no reason for doubt, so it belongs in No.
Right: the weak wording raises doubt, the link offers a reason to look again.
Being similar to others is not a reason in this method; the piles rest on evidence and doubt.
questions.explain: Maybe is for resumes where doubt and promise sit together, such as weak presentation next to strong work.
questions.rule: Maybe means doubt plus promise.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: Your company rejects most resumes, and you suspect some rejected people would do well. What could you try?
options: Rescreen their resumes a second time against the same list of criteria
Give rejected applicants a short hands-on exercise before closing their file
Send them a longer written form about their motivation before rejecting them
Ask each rejected applicant for three references before closing the application
optionExplain: A second pass over the same weak signal is likely to repeat the same result.
Right: a hands-on exercise gathers new evidence about what they can do.
More writing tests how they present themselves, not what they can do.
References come late and tell you about past colleagues' opinions, not current skills.
questions.explain: Fresh evidence is what the rejected resume cannot give. The card next shows how the author sees it.
questions.rule: Add evidence, not another read of the resume.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: Woven takes your rejected resume screens and assesses them with an hour-long, hands-on ____.
questions.explain: That is the author's description of Woven's hybrid approach.
questions.rule: Hybrid: resumes first, an exercise for the rejected.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: A 12-person startup is hiring a mobile developer and cannot tell the 150 resumes apart. Which plan follows the book's hybrid idea?
options: Reject all resumes and choose by a short chat about the applicants' favourite tools
Hire the first five applicants and let a probation period sort the strong from the weak
Keep only resumes from known companies and skip any exercise to save team time
Advance strong resumes as usual, and run a hands-on exercise on the rejected ones
optionExplain: A chat about tools is another weak signal, and it discards all the resume information.
Probation puts the whole cost of a wrong choice on the team after hiring.
Known employers are a narrow filter; it repeats the problem of rejecting hidden gems.
Right: strong resumes move on, and the rejected ones are re-checked with hands-on work.
questions.explain: The hybrid keeps the cheap first pass and adds effort only where the first pass is likely to be wrong.
questions.rule: Re-check the rejected with real work.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, Woven claims that a third of the hires made through its approach would otherwise have been rejected.
questions.explain: The author reports that Woven claims to find a third of hires made this way who would otherwise have been rejected.
questions.rule: These are the hidden gems.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: Match each company with how the author describes its approach.
pairs: Runs an hour-long hands-on exercise for people your resume screen rejected
Lets developers who pass its assessment go directly to onsites
Offers coding challenges you can set as your main first screen
questions.explain: Woven re-checks rejections, Triplebyte replaces the resume with its own assessment, and Hackerrank challenges can replace the resume screen.
questions.rule: Three different roles for assessments.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: A hospital IT team picks a coding-challenge tool to screen sysadmins. Which setup follows the author's advice?
options: Exercises close to the daily work, built and marked with engineers' time
The hardest algorithm puzzles the platform offers, scored automatically by the tool
A stock challenge scored automatically, so recruiters can filter applicants quickly
A broad quiz on many unrelated topics, in case the role needs one of them later
optionExplain: Right: the author asks for exercises that mimic day-to-day skills and for engineering time to build and evaluate them.
The author warns against going overboard with algorithms people will never use.
Relying on the automated score alone can miss people who wrote good code but missed one small edge case.
Breadth for its own sake does not match the skills the role actually uses.
questions.explain: The same care applies to any skills platform: tests should mirror the job, and a person should read the results.
questions.rule: Mirror the job; spend human time on the marking.
questions.teaches: For a coding-challenge platform, the author advises exercises that mimic daily skills, engineering time to build and evaluate them, and not relying only on the automated score, which can miss good code with one small edge-case miss.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: You and a colleague each screen the same 50 resumes alone. What is the use of comparing your Yes piles?
options: It halves the work, since each of you then reads only the other person's Yes pile
It proves which of you has the better eye for strong candidates over the long run
It shows where your expectations differ and helps reduce bias
It lets one reader overrule the other on every borderline resume to save time
optionExplain: Both read the full set, so the work is not halved; the aim is calibration.
Comparing piles does not rank readers; it exposes differing expectations.
Right: overlap and difference show how consistent the two of you are.
Overruling would cancel the benefit of having two views.
questions.explain: Two independent readings surface differences a single reader cannot see. The card next states the advice.
questions.rule: Compare independent readings.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: Involve at least one other person in screening, and screen the same set of resumes ____.
questions.explain: Screening the same resumes independently makes the overlap of Yes piles meaningful.
questions.rule: Independence makes the comparison honest.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: A lead has booked no hours for hiring, and resumes are piling up. What does the author advise?
options: Skim a few resumes in spare minutes between meetings and fix gaps at the onsite
Budget dedicated hours, or hand the process to someone who has them
Wait for the recruiter to forward only the five best resumes and decide from those
Screen at speed on Friday afternoons, since rushing keeps the criteria simple
optionExplain: Spare minutes lead to the rushed, poor results the author describes.
Right: hiring needs protected time, or a delegate who has it.
This leaves the screen to one filter and gives up the manager's role in it.
Rushing is what the author warns against.
questions.explain: Without dedicated time, the work is rushed and the results are poor.
questions.rule: Time first, or delegate.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, you will most likely favour people who resemble you, and you should aim to select profiles that do not resemble your background.
questions.explain: The author calls this a self-selection bias that works subconsciously, and asks you to acknowledge it.
questions.rule: Name the bias, then choose against it.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: A lead plans resume screening. Which plans fit the author's advice? Select all that apply.
options: Ask a peer to screen the same 60 resumes alone, then compare Yes piles
Give one junior opening the same hiring time as a plan to double the team
Hand hiring to a teammate who has time, when the lead has none
Pick people who look like past top hires, as the safest fit
Let the peer read my notes first so that we agree more quickly
optionExplain: Right: independent screening of the same set calibrates and reduces bias.
Fails: time should scale with the number and importance of roles.
Right: delegation is the author's answer to lacking time.
Fails: this feeds the self-selection bias the author warns about.
Fails: reading notes first removes the independence of the second view.
questions.explain: The two good plans are independent comparison and delegating when you lack time. The others weaken calibration or feed bias.
questions.rule: Independent, scaled and aware.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Know that your screening process is broken
questions.q: A head teacher is hiring one teaching assistant, and later 30 teachers for a new campus. How should hiring time differ?
options: Far more hiring time for the 30-teacher campus than for the single assistant
The same time for both, so every applicant gets an equal chance at a fair screen
More time for the single assistant, since one hire must be perfect on the first try
Time only at the offer stage in both cases, since screening can be left to the system
optionExplain: Right: the author scales hiring time with the number and importance of open roles.
Equal time ignores the very different stakes of the two jobs.
One hire matters, but the author asks for far more time when the team is about to double.
Time at the offer stage alone leaves the screen rushed.
questions.explain: The author puts it this way: spend far more time when you are about to double the team than when hiring one junior.
questions.rule: Scale time with the stakes.
questions.teaches: The author says to adjust hiring time to the number and importance of open roles: far more when about to double the team than when hiring one junior developer.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: You have headcount for three engineers and have not yet worked with your recruiter. What would you do first?
options: Send over a finished job description and wait for the recruiter to return a shortlist
Meet the recruiter early, explain what makes people succeed, and ask how they screen
Ask for weekly candidate counts and avoid further contact until the onsite stage
Replace the recruiter if the first shortlist misses what you had in mind
optionExplain: Handing over a document leaves the recruiter to guess your traits and signals.
Right: understanding comes from early contact in both directions.
Counts show activity but not whether the candidates fit; and silence is read as disinterest.
Changing recruiters before explaining what you want solves nothing.
questions.explain: Early two-way contact lets the recruiter learn what you want. The card next states the author's advice.
questions.rule: Meet early, in both directions.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: Whenever hiring managers and HR or recruitment work in ____, it is a huge missed opportunity.
questions.explain: The author says working in silos misses a chance to improve recruitment.
questions.rule: Silos waste a chance.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: A manager has not spoken to the recruiters for two months, and they send her no questions. What does the author's view suggest?
options: Keep waiting, since recruiters will ask when they need something from the manager
Add a weekly report from recruiters, which keeps the manager informed without a meeting
Reach out first, since silence from a manager can be read as lack of interest
Treat the silence as a sign that recruitment is going well and the process is working
optionExplain: Waiting is how the assumption of disinterest forms.
A report is one-way; the author asks for conversation where both share details.
Right: the author says that without outreach, recruitment may assume the manager is not interested.
Silence alone says nothing about results.
questions.explain: Proactive contact from the manager closes the gap that silence opens.
questions.rule: The manager moves first.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, a hiring manager who stays away from recruiters risks being seen as uninterested in their work.
questions.explain: The author says HR or recruitment may assume the manager is not interested if the manager does not reach out.
questions.rule: Silence is read as disinterest.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: Sort each habit: does it show a partnership with recruiters, or a silo?

items.t: Sits with recruiters to learn how they move candidates between stages
Explains the traits that make people successful on the team
Holds regular check-ins where both sides share details
Hands over the job and waits for a shortlist
Assumes managers are not welcome to help with recruiting
Contacts recruiters only when the pipeline has stalled

questions.explain: Partnership means sitting together, sharing traits and holding regular check-ins; a silo means contact only when something breaks.
questions.rule: Regular, shared, two-way.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: A hospital ward manager is learning to work with HR on nurse hiring. Which question shows the curiosity the author asks for?
options: How soon can you fill all three posts, so that I can plan the rota for next month?
Can you rank the candidates so that I meet only your top two for each post?
Which job boards cost least per applicant, so I can cut our advertising budget?
Which signals do you look for first, and how do you find such people?
optionExplain: Speed matters, but this asks about results, not how HR works.
Asking for a ranked top two hands the judgment to HR instead of sharing it.
Cost is a fair concern, but it does not build shared understanding of signals.
Right: asking about signals and sourcing is the curiosity the author recommends.
questions.explain: The author asks managers to be curious about sourcing strategies, the key signals the recruitment team looks for, and the diversity of traits on their team.
questions.rule: Be curious about how they work.
questions.teaches: The author asks managers to be curious: talk about sourcing strategies, the key signals the recruitment team looks for, and the diversity of traits people on the team have.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: A recruiter finds a promising candidate with 3 years of Kotlin when the job asks for 5. What helps most?
options: Remind the recruiter that every requirement is fixed and no exception is allowed
Tell the recruiter they may champion people who stand out, within sensible guidelines
Ask the recruiter to wait until a candidate with the full 5 years turns up
Ask the recruiter to drop the requirement from the advert, so it is never an issue again
optionExplain: This is the strict stance the author asks managers to avoid.
Right: sensible guidelines plus room to champion standouts keeps exceptions possible.
Waiting may leave a strong candidate unconsidered, and wastes the recruiter's judgment.
Dropping the requirement entirely removes the guideline the author still wants.
questions.explain: Recruiters need both a guideline and permission to make a case. The card next sets this out.
questions.rule: Guidelines plus permission.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: Encourage your recruitment team to take the ____ and champion people they feel stand out for one reason or another.
questions.explain: The author asks hiring managers to encourage recruiters to take the initiative.
questions.rule: Give recruiters the initiative.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: A manager's rule is 5 years of Java and 2 of JavaScript, no negotiation. Which change follows the author's advice?
options: Keep sensible guidelines, and let recruiters put forward standouts who fall short
Remove every requirement so that recruiters can send anyone they like to the engineers
Raise the bar to 7 years so that recruiters send only people who are strong
Keep the rule and ask recruiters to explain each rejection in writing every week
optionExplain: Right: guidelines stay, and the recruiters get the room to champion someone who stands out.
No guidelines would waste engineering time, which recruiters try to protect.
Raising the bar narrows the pool and removes more promising people.
Written explanations of rejections add paperwork without giving recruiters any room.
questions.explain: The author's point is flexibility inside a framework, not the removal of a framework.
questions.rule: Sensible guidelines, room for exceptions.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, recruiters tend to send engineers candidates who miss some of the manager's stated requirements.
questions.explain: The author says recruiters try not to waste engineering resources on candidates who do not meet all requirements, unless the manager gives them room.
questions.rule: Recruiters follow the rules you set.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: A hiring manager at a logistics firm insists that recruiters pass on only candidates with five years of Java and two of JavaScript. Which stance on requirements does the author recommend instead?
options: Keep the requirements strict so that no engineering time is wasted on near misses
Let recruiters decide alone, and do not review any resume yourself to save time
Set sensible guidelines and also encourage recruiters to champion standout people
Remove all requirements so that everybody is passed on for the engineers to judge
optionExplain: This is the rigid stance that closes off hidden gems.
The author asks managers to review resumes together with recruiters.
Right: guidelines plus initiative, plus the manager reading some resumes too.
No guidelines at all would flood the engineers with unfit candidates.
questions.explain: The author wants both sides of the balance: some structure and some room.
questions.rule: Structure and room.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: A design-studio manager is looking through rejected applications. Which one deserves a second look, on the author's view?
options: A polished CV that makes general claims and links to no samples of work
A CV that copies the wording of the job advert almost line by line
A CV with a long skills list laid out in a very tidy table
A plainly written CV that links to a challenging, well-made project
optionExplain: Polish is not evidence of skill, and there is nothing to examine.
Copying the advert shows effort at matching, not ability.
Tidy skills lists are claims, not proof of work.
Right: the author says managers can read more into weaker resumes that link good work or challenging projects.
questions.explain: A manager's own review can find value where the screen saw only poor writing.
questions.rule: Look at the linked work.
questions.teaches: The author notes that hiring managers can often read more into weakly written resumes that link good code or challenging projects, so they should look through some rejected resumes personally.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: Two managers share the same recruiters. One delegates hiring and rarely checks in; the other meets weekly. What result does the author expect?
options: The weekly-meeting manager will hire faster and better, as recruiters know the brief
The delegating manager will hire faster, because recruiters are free of constant interruptions
Both will hire equally well, since the recruiters and the headcount are the same for each
The weekly manager will hire slowly, because meetings take time away from the actual hiring
optionExplain: Right: shared understanding is what the author credits for the difference.
Interruptions were welcome in the successful case; freedom from them did not help.
The author's story is about a gap in results despite identical recruiters.
Meetings were the way MakeTimeManager hired quickly.
questions.explain: Same recruiters, different managers, different results. The card next gives the story.
questions.rule: Hiring results depend on the manager too.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: BusyManager and MakeTimeManager worked with the exact same set of ____.
questions.explain: The author stresses that both managers had the same recruiters, to point at the manager's behaviour.
questions.rule: Same recruiters, different results.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: A team lead gets new headcount while swamped with shipping. Which action follows MakeTimeManager?
options: Give recruiters a short job description and ask for results as fast as they can manage
Set a weekly meeting with the recruiters and tell them that hiring comes first
Keep the calendar clear and let recruiters decide when a candidate is ready for the onsite
Switch to a different recruiter if the first two shortlists are not accepted
optionExplain: This repeats what BusyManager did.
Right: weekly contact and a clear priority are what MakeTimeManager did.
Leaving recruiters alone is the delegating behaviour of BusyManager.
BusyManager changed recruiters several times, and the results did not improve.
questions.explain: The lead has to make the time and tell recruiters it is a priority.
questions.rule: Make time and say so.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: BusyManager rejected almost every onsite candidate. What does the author give as the cause?
options: The recruiters were too inexperienced to find strong candidates in the market
The headcount grant was too large for the team to fill with good people
Recruiters found it hard to understand what BusyManager wanted to hire for
The onsite process was unfair to candidates and scared them away
optionExplain: The same recruiters worked well for MakeTimeManager.
The grant was large, but size was not the cause the author names.
Right: the author blames a lack of mutual understanding.
The author does not describe candidates as being scared away.
questions.explain: Same recruiters, a vague brief, a poor outcome: the gap was in understanding.
questions.rule: A vague brief gives poor candidates.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: True or false: in the author's story, replacing BusyManager's recruiters improved the results.
questions.explain: BusyManager changed recruiters a few times, and the results did not come.
questions.rule: The recruiters were not the cause.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.section: Treat recruitment as a partner function
questions.q: A restaurant owner works with an agency to hire chefs, and wants to copy MakeTimeManager beyond meetings. Which step matches?
options: Let the kitchen team skip the interviews so that service is never disturbed
Share the headcount only with the agency, to keep the kitchen from being distracted
Limit the agency's interruptions to Friday afternoons, so that cooking is not disturbed
Ask the kitchen team to prepare for interviews and put candidate experience above other tasks
