optionExplain: Skipping interviews is the reverse of the story.
MakeTimeManager involved the team, not just the recruiters.
He told recruiters they were always free to interrupt.
Right: MakeTimeManager asked the whole team to put recruitment first.
questions.explain: In the story, the manager also asked the whole team to put recruitment first, make time for interviews, prepare for them, and put candidate experience above other tasks.
questions.rule: The whole team shares the priority.
questions.teaches: MakeTimeManager also asked all team members to put recruitment first, always make time for interviews, prepare for them, and put candidate experience above other tasks.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: You must hire a customer-support lead, and last year's advert exists. What is the best start?
options: Reuse last year's advert with the dates changed, since it already worked once
List every tool and skill the team has, so that the advert is complete
Sit with the recruiters and decide what the person will do in month one and year one
Ask the previous lead which skills were most important to them before they left
optionExplain: Reuse is the copy-paste habit that produces a poor experience for everybody.
A complete list mixes must-haves with things a person can learn.
Right: the work the person will do defines what the advert should ask for.
The previous lead's view is useful, but it does not replace an analysis of the role now.
questions.explain: The role should drive the advert. The card next gives the author's questions.
questions.rule: Start from the work, not the old advert.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: Ask which skills and experience are absolutely ____, and what the person can pick up on the job.
questions.explain: The author asks which skills are non-negotiable and which can be learned on the job.
questions.rule: Separate must-have from learnable.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: A manager hires a team lead for a logistics software team that uses Go. Which reading of requirements fits the author's advice?
options: Leading people is likely a must, logistics experience is not, and Go may be negotiable
Logistics experience is a must-have, while leading people can be learned in the first month
All three are must-haves, so the advert should list them as required and nothing else
None is a must-have, since a motivated person can learn the whole job after joining
optionExplain: Right: it mirrors the author's ads and Node.js reasoning.
This swaps the must-have and the learnable, against the author's example.
Listing everything as required shrinks the pool and ignores learnable skills.
Not everything can be learned on the job; some skills are truly needed.
questions.explain: Applying the same sorting to a new role gives the same pattern: people experience is core, domain and stack are often negotiable.
questions.rule: Sort must-have from learnable.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: True or false: removing a constraint such as a specific language gives you a larger pool of qualified candidates to work with.
questions.explain: The author says that removing such a constraint widens the pool.
questions.rule: Fewer constraints, a larger pool.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: Sort each habit: does it follow the author's advice on job descriptions, or break it?

items.t: Writes the advert after a talk with recruiters about month one and year one
Separates must-haves from skills a person can learn on the job
Treats a language as negotiable for a fast learner with backend experience
Copies last year's advert with the dates changed
Lists every tool the team has used as a requirement
Writes the advert alone and sends it to recruiters at the last minute

questions.explain: The advice is to be involved, to challenge each requirement, and to talk to recruiters before writing.
questions.rule: Challenge the list with recruiters.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: A manager at a regional bank is drafting an advert for a team lead and wants to list five years in banking as required. Which question best helps decide whether any requirement is a must-have?
options: Did the last person in this role happen to have it when they were hired?
Could a motivated person pick this up on the job after joining?
Does a competitor's advert for a similar role also list it as required?
Is it easy to check on a resume by reading it for a few seconds?
optionExplain: The past hire's profile is one data point and may include extras.
Right: it asks whether the skill must exist before the first day.
Competitors may be copying each other.
Ease of checking is about screening, not about what the job needs.
questions.explain: The author's test is need versus learnable, not habit or ease.
questions.rule: Ask what can be learned.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: A bank advert for a backend role lists one language as required. A candidate did similar work on another stack. What is the author's reasoning?
options: Similar work on a different stack can work as well as deep domain expertise
Language knowledge is the only reliable way to tell whether a person can do the work
Big companies drop the language only because they have too many applicants to read
A different stack shows the person lacks focus, so the bank should be cautious
optionExplain: Right: the author notes that most big tech companies do not specify a language for this reason.
This is the assumption the author asks you to challenge.
The author gives the quality of hires, not volume, as the reason.
The author does not read other stack experience as a lack of focus.
questions.explain: Big tech companies do not specify a language, because someone with similar work elsewhere can do as well as a domain expert.
questions.rule: Similar work can transfer.
questions.teaches: Most of the big tech companies do not specify a specific language, because hiring someone who has done similar work on a different stack can work as well as hiring someone with deep domain expertise.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: An advert uses very competitive, masculine-sounding wording. What is a likely effect, on the author's view?
options: More strong applicants apply overall, because the wording signals a demanding team
Fewer women apply, as some turn away because of the language alone
The same people apply as before, since candidates ignore wording and read only the pay
Fewer applicants of every gender apply, since vivid wording makes adverts hard to read
optionExplain: Demanding tone may attract some, but the author says it narrows who applies.
Right: the author says masculine wording means fewer female applicants.
The author says wording does change who applies.
The effect the author reports is on women in particular.
questions.explain: Wording works as a filter before any resume is read. The card next gives the author's example.
questions.rule: Wording filters applicants.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: Accenture in the UK saw the share of female applicants rise from 34% to ____%.
questions.explain: The author cites the HR Magazine figure of a rise from 34% to 50%.
questions.rule: Wording changes who applies.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: A nursing agency has two draft sentences for an advert. Which one follows the author's rule?
options: We want a hard-charging individual who will dominate the ward and beat every target
We need a strong man who can handle the toughest shifts without any complaint
We are only interested in ambitious candidates who see other staff as rivals to beat
We welcome people who enjoy learning and working in a team
optionExplain: Competitive, forceful wording is the kind that can turn people away.
This is openly gendered phrasing.
Rivalry language is narrow in who it invites and is not welcoming.
Right: it uses welcoming, inclusive wording.
questions.explain: Plain, welcoming wording invites more people to apply.
questions.rule: Welcome people in.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, masculine wording in a job advert has no effect on who applies.
questions.explain: The author says that masculine wording leads to fewer female applicants.
questions.rule: Wording matters.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: An HR lead at a consultancy reads that Accenture UK reworded its job adverts and tells her board that the change raised the share of women hired. What does the figure the author cites actually show?
options: That after the change in wording, the share of female applicants rose
That the new wording raised the quality of the people hired by the firm
That half of everyone hired at the firm afterwards was a woman
That wording matters little once an advert states its salary openly
optionExplain: Right: it reports applicants, not hires or quality.
Quality of hires is not what the figure reports.
The figure is about applicants, not hires.
The author does not link the figure to salary.
questions.explain: Read the figure for what it measures: a rise in female applicants.
questions.rule: Match claim to what was measured.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: A small clinic wants to check its advert for biased wording. Which action matches the resources the author names?
options: Ask the current team which words they like and keep those words in the advert
Add a line saying all applicants are welcome and leave the rest unchanged
Run the draft through a gender-decoder tool and compare it with a well-written advert
Translate the advert into a more formal register so that it reads as neutral
optionExplain: The current team's tastes may reflect the same bias.
A welcome line leaves the biased wording in place.
Right: the author points to the Gender decoder for job ads and a well-written advert as a model.
Formality is not the same as neutral wording.
questions.explain: The author names a Gender decoder tool for job ads and the Honeycomb.io engineering manager opening as an example of a well-written advert.
questions.rule: Use a checker and a model.
questions.teaches: The author points to the Gender decoder for job ads, and to the Honeycomb.io engineering manager opening as a well-written advertisement.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: Your team's offer rate fell over two quarters. What first step suits a good feedback loop?
options: Look at pass rates per stage over time, and talk with recruiters
Replace the recruiter who handles the final stage, since the fall shows up there
Tighten the job requirements until the pass rate rises back to where it was
Wait one more quarter to see whether the fall is random variation only
optionExplain: Right: numbers plus conversation show where and why people drop.
Changing a person before locating the cause may fix nothing.
Tightening shrinks the pool and may worsen things.
Waiting loses time and the chance to spot a problem early.
questions.explain: Numbers show where; talking shows why. The card next sets out the loop.
questions.rule: Numbers plus conversation.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: Don't rely fully on the numbers alone; keep your ears on the ____ to see how hiring is progressing case by case.
questions.explain: The author asks managers to keep an ear on the ground alongside the figures.
questions.rule: Numbers need stories.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: A manager has no data on who applies or who passes the resume screen by background. What does the author say?
options: Rely on instinct, since people with experience can sense where gaps in the pipeline lie
Without data you cannot act on it, so get involved in collecting it with recruitment
Leave the topic to HR, because diversity data is not a hiring manager's concern
Assume the pipeline is diverse, until a candidate complains about it directly
optionExplain: Instinct cannot show where applicants drop.
Right: no data, no ability to act; so pair with the recruitment team to get it.
The author says the manager should get involved.
Waiting for a complaint is far too late.
questions.explain: Data on who applies and who progresses is the starting point.
questions.rule: No data, no action.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, if you have no data on diversity in your pipeline, you will not be able to act on it.
questions.explain: The author says this directly and asks managers to pair with the recruitment team to get the data.
questions.rule: Measure to act.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: A dashboard shows steady pass rates, but a recruiter says strong candidates withdraw after the phone screen. What follows?
options: Trust the dashboard, since figures are more reliable than one recruiter's impressions
Trust the recruiter and drop the dashboard, since stories show more than numbers do
Look into the recruiter's report too, since the numbers alone may hide case-by-case problems
Wait for the figures to change before talking to anyone about the withdrawals
optionExplain: Steady figures can hide a problem the numbers do not capture.
The author asks for both.
Right: numbers and stories complement each other.
Waiting delays a problem that can be found now.
questions.explain: The author wants both the percentages and the case-by-case view.
questions.rule: Use both signals.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: A sales team's final-round candidate was rejected for missing an unwritten requirement. What would the author have the manager ask?
options: Should the next advert hide the requirement, so as to widen the pool?
Should the final round be shortened next time, in case it tires candidates?
Should the person be asked to apply again next week, to be fair?
Should that unwritten requirement be added to the job description?
optionExplain: Hiding a requirement does not make it go away.
Nothing here suggests the final round was the problem.
Re-applying is a policy matter, and next week is not after a given time.
Right: retrospectives ask whether the loss could have been predicted earlier.
questions.explain: After a rejection, ask whether anything predicted it earlier, such as an unwritten requirement that belongs in the job description, and after a close call, look for more such profiles.
questions.rule: Learn from every outcome.
questions.teaches: After a failed onsite, ask whether anything could have predicted it earlier, such as an unwritten requirement for the job description; after a close call, encourage looking for more similar profiles.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: A candidate rejected at the resume stage asks for detailed feedback. Which approach best matches the author?
options: Reply with honest details on every resume, whatever the effort it costs the team
Send no reply at all to rejected applicants, to avoid any legal risk to the firm
Follow an agreed policy, set with recruiting, that fits legal and company limits
Let each interviewer decide case by case what to say to each rejected person
optionExplain: Honest and kind, but the author says this is not feasible for many reasons.
Silence avoids risk but gives candidates a poor and inconsistent experience.
Right: an agreed, sensible policy beats both extremes.
Case-by-case choices give an inconsistent experience.
questions.explain: A shared policy gives consistency within limits. The card next names it.
questions.rule: Policy, not improvisation.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: Be clear when you encourage certain people to ____ after a given time.
questions.explain: The author asks managers to be clear when they encourage certain people to re-apply after a given time.
questions.rule: Say when people may come back.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: One recruiter writes long feedback after phone screens and another writes none. What should the manager do?
options: Ask the first recruiter to write less, so that the two are at the same level
Agree one policy with recruiters, so candidates have a consistent experience
Let each recruiter decide, since their styles reflect real differences in how they work
Offer candidates the choice of which recruiter handles their case by default
optionExplain: Equalising by shrinking feedback may break the policy the firm wants.
Right: consistency across candidates is the author's goal.
Style differences should not decide what a candidate gets.
Candidates cannot choose a recruiter, and it does not create consistency.
questions.explain: The aim is a consistent experience, set by policy rather than by who happens to handle the case.
questions.rule: One policy for all.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, hiring managers should give honest feedback on every single resume.
questions.explain: The author says that would be amazing but is not feasible for many reasons.
questions.rule: Aim for a sensible policy, not total feedback.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: Sort each policy statement: does it follow the author's advice, or break it?

items.t: Confirms the feedback process with the recruitment team
Takes legal and company constraints into account
Says what happens at the resume stage and after the phone screen
Promises full written feedback to every applicant
Lets each recruiter improvise at every stage
Never states whether anyone may apply again

questions.explain: A good policy is agreed, bounded by real limits and clear at each stage.
questions.rule: Agreed, bounded, clear.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: A community college in Ontario wants to promise a personal written explanation to every rejected applicant. How does the author's guidance bear on this?
options: Promise it, since candidates value any reply and the cost is small
Agree a policy with HR by stage; notes for every resume are not feasible
Leave each manager to decide, as a written policy would only slow hiring
Offer it only to those who ask twice, so the workload stays low
optionExplain: The author says honest feedback on every single resume is not feasible for many reasons.
Right: he asks for a clear policy by stage that fits legal and company limits, with a consistent candidate experience.
He asks for a policy confirmed with the recruitment team, not ad hoc choices.
He does not suggest rationing by persistence; he asks for consistency.
questions.explain: The author says honest feedback on every single resume is not feasible, with legal limits and the resources needed among the reasons. He still wants a policy per stage and a consistent candidate experience.
questions.rule: Know the real constraints.
questions.teaches: The author names legal limits and the resources needed as reasons that honest feedback on every single resume is not feasible, yet asks for a clear policy per stage and a consistent candidate experience.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: You are hiring for the first time and have no organised strategy. What does the author suggest?
options: Read a book on hiring developers; a resume guide does not cover it in depth
Rely on this resume book, since it covers every stage of hiring in enough detail
Copy the process of the biggest company you know, and adjust it as problems arise
Skip planning, since an organised strategy slows down teams that need to hire fast
optionExplain: Right: the author says this book is not about hiring well.
The author says it is not about hiring developers well.
Copying may not fit your setting, and it replaces learning with imitation.
Planning is what the recommended book teaches.
questions.explain: The author points elsewhere for hiring strategy. The card next names the books.
questions.rule: Learn hiring from hiring books.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: Hiring Geeks That Fit is a must-read if you are hiring for the ____ time.
questions.explain: The author calls it a must-read for first-time hiring, or for no organised strategy yet.
questions.rule: A starter for new hirers.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: A lead wants a concise, opinionated guide on hiring good developers. Which book does the author point to?
options: Chapter 13 of this resume book, which lays out a complete plan for the hiring process
Smart and Gets Things Done by Spolsky
Hiring Geeks That Fit, which the author calls concise and opinionated and a quick read
A resume template, which already shows how a manager reads applicants
optionExplain: The author says this book is not about how to hire well.
Right: that is how the author describes Spolsky's book.
The author describes Rothman's book as a guide through a full process, not as concise and opinionated.
Templates are for candidates, not for hiring strategy.
questions.explain: Spolsky's book is the concise, opinionated guide.
questions.rule: Match the book to the need.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: Match each book with how the author describes it.
pairs: Concise, opinionated and written in 2007, with little that is dated
Guides you from hiring strategy to the new person's first day
Not about how to hire developers well
questions.explain: The two recommended books cover hiring; this resume book does not.
questions.rule: Know what each book is for.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: A founder hiring a first developer sees that a recommended hiring guide dates from 2007 and decides to skip it as out of date. True or false: the author would agree with skipping it.
questions.explain: The author notes it was written in 2007 but says there are not many things dated about its contents. Age alone did not make the guide outdated.
questions.rule: Age does not mean outdated.

questions.unitTitle: Advice for hiring managers on running a good screening process
questions.q: A founder has interviews sorted but nothing planned for after them. Which part of the book Hiring Geeks That Fit would help?
options: Its closing chapters on reference checks, making an offer and a great first day
Its opening chapters on defining a strategy, since interviews come before that step
Its chapters on writing a resume, since new hires need a strong profile on arrival
Its chapter on sourcing, because the founder has no candidates in the pipeline yet
optionExplain: Right: the book ends with reference checks, the offer and a great first day.
Strategy comes at the start of the process, before interviews.
Resumes are the candidate's task, not the founder's.
The founder already has interviews, so sourcing is behind them.
questions.explain: The book runs from strategy and job analysis to executing every part, ending with reference checks, an offer and a first day.
questions.rule: Cover the whole process.
questions.teaches: Hiring Geeks That Fit guides you through defining a strategy, analysing the job and planning and executing all parts of the process, ending with reference checks, an offer and a great first day.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A friend asks what a resume is for. Which answer comes closest to the author's view?
options: To record your whole work history as accurately as possible, so that the reader can check every role you held
To win you an interview for one specific position by selling you to a reader within seconds of the first scan
To pass the company's automatic filter, which decides whether any person will ever look at your file at all
To tell the full story of your career, so that the reader understands who you are as a person and as a worker
optionExplain: Completeness feels honest, but the author says sharing your complete history is not the goal.
Right: the author says the goal is the interview for that position, reached by selling you in under ten seconds of reading.
A common worry, but the author argues that people, not a filter, decide which resumes advance.
A story helps in places, but the author names the interview for that position as the goal.
questions.explain: A resume is a tool with one job. The card next shows how that job shapes every rule.
questions.rule: Judge each resume choice by whether it helps a hurried reader see that you fit this job and call you in.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The author says the goal of a resume is to get you an ____ for that specific position.
questions.explain: The goal is the interview, not the job offer and not a full record of your career.
questions.rule: The goal is the interview.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A developer with 12 years of experience wants to list all 14 past jobs in full, for completeness. Which test applies?
options: Keep every job in full, since a fair resume is one that represents all of your work as accurately as it can
Keep every job in full but shrink the font, so that the reader still sees your complete history within the page limit
Keep only the current employer, since a hurried reader cares about nothing that happened before your latest job
Keep what helps this job's reader see your fit, and cut the rest, because the aim is the interview and not completeness
optionExplain: Accuracy sounds fair, but the author says the aim is not to represent everything you did.
Shrinking type squeezes more in but makes the page harder to scan, which defeats the end.
Over-cutting also fails: older roles can still show fit, they just get less space.
Right: the test is fit for this job, so material that does not help the reader see it goes.
questions.explain: Completeness is not the goal; fit is. Anything that does not help the reader see fit costs attention.
questions.rule: Cut what does not show fit for this job.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which summary of the book's approach overstates what the author claims?
options: Follow every rule and the call is certain, because the rules remove luck from the screening
Rules help you avoid misrepresenting yourself, but the author says there is no magic formula for the call
Competition and plain luck can still sink a good resume, though referrals can reduce the part luck plays
A good resume will not win over every recruiter, since a mismatch of profile or stronger rivals can decide
optionExplain: Right: this claims certainty, and the author says there is no magic formula.
This is the author's own caution, so it does not overstate.
The author names luck as a factor and names referrals as the way to cut it down.
The author lists profile mismatch and stronger candidates as reasons a good resume can still fail.
questions.explain: The author promises a fair, well-aimed resume, not a guaranteed interview.
questions.rule: Better odds are not certainty.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each choice by whether it serves the goal of a quick, clear fit for one job.
groups: Helps a hurried reader see fit

items.t: Putting the technologies the job names near the top of page one
Keeping a project you are proud of that is unrelated to the job
Giving a number for the effect of a bullet
Shrinking the font so that every old role fits on two pages
Bolding only dates, titles and companies
Adding older roles for completeness, with no link to this job

questions.explain: Each helpful item makes a scanned fact easier to find or more convincing; each other item adds length without showing fit.
questions.rule: Ask what the item does for the scan.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, deciding what to leave out gives you licence to claim things that are not true.
questions.explain: The author says you need not list things that do not show you well, such as failed projects, but you should not claim anything untrue.
questions.rule: Select; do not invent.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Same goal, new condition: a former colleague at the company will refer you. What does the author say about how your resume is read?
options: It skips human reading altogether and goes straight to the hiring manager for a decision on an offer
It is read as quickly as any other resume, because a referral only adds a name to the application form
It almost always gets an in-depth review, and a strong referral may bring a recruiter call straight away
It waits until every non-referred resume has been read, since referrals carry the lowest priority of all
optionExplain: The resume is still read by people; a referral does not skip the screen to an offer.
The author says referrals change how closely the resume is read, so it is not treated like the rest.
Right: the author says referrals almost always guarantee an in-depth review, and strong ones can speed the recruiter call.
It is the other way round: referrals are placed first in the priority order.
questions.explain: A referral changes the route but not the end: your resume still has to show fit for that job once someone opens it.
questions.rule: A referral earns a closer read, not a free pass.
questions.teaches: The author says a referral almost always guarantees an in-depth resume review, and a strong referral may get you a recruiter call set up straight away.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A service charges $300 to make your resume pass an ATS. What is the author's likely view of the offer?
options: Pay it, because parsing decides whether any person ever sees your file, and only an optimised file reaches a reader
Pay it only if you send a Word file, because an ATS rejects PDFs that it cannot break into its separate fields
Doubt it: people, not the ATS, decide which resumes advance, so the fee buys little for most tech roles
Doubt it only at small firms, because large companies run an ATS that rejects resumes by a keyword score
optionExplain: This is the claim the service makes; the author says the tracker does not reject on content.
The author says PDF and Word files are both parsed well enough, and recruiters often prefer PDF.
Right: the author calls ATS optimisation a myth that sellers profit from, since people make the calls.
The author does not draw a size line here; his point is that the tracker does not make the choice.
questions.explain: The claim that software rejects you is what a seller needs you to believe. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Write for the hurried person who reads your resume, and answer form questions carefully because only they can trigger an automatic rejection.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: In the author's account, an applicant tracking system is a status ____ that people operate.
questions.explain: The author describes the ATS as a status tracker, not a decision maker.
questions.rule: People decide; the tracker records.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A candidate strips all structure from a resume to make a plain text blob that a program could read. What does the author's reasoning say?
options: It hurts: a person must scan the file in seconds, and parsing already handles normal PDF and Word files
It helps: a program ranks resumes by their content, so plain text gives the cleanest parse and the highest rank
It makes no difference, because neither a person nor a program looks at layout during the first pass
It helps at large companies only, where the ATS filters on formatting before any recruiter opens the file
optionExplain: Right: the reader is a person who needs structure to scan, and the tracker does not need the blob.
The author says trackers do not rank by content, so there is no rank to win.
Layout matters a good deal to the person doing the first scan.
The author does not describe any format-based filter at large companies.
questions.explain: Writing for software costs you in readability and gains nothing, because software is not the one deciding.
questions.rule: Format for the scanning human.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: An application form asks about work authorisation and rejects a No answer instantly. What does the author call this?
options: Resume parsing, where the ATS reads your dates and drops anyone who seems to lack authorisation
A ranking score, where the ATS compares your keywords with the advert and drops the lowest scorers
A formatting check, where the ATS drops files whose layout it cannot read into its own fields
A knockout question, which uses your form answer and nothing read from your resume
optionExplain: Parsing fills in details and indexes keywords; it does not reject on dates.
The author says trackers do not score or filter on resume content.
Parsing is not used to drop files for layout; the file is parsed well enough.
Right: knockout questions are set by recruiters and read form answers, never the resume.
questions.explain: The one real automatic rejection comes from the form, so answer it accurately and read it carefully.
questions.rule: Forms can knock you out; resumes cannot.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A non-technical screener at a small firm drops resumes without the word distributed. Yours says microservices and message queues. What follows?
options: Nothing, since a screener who drops resumes by term would still read microservices as the same thing
Use the screener's term where it is true, in readable sentences, since such screeners look for the term itself
Repeat the word in a long block of unrelated tools, because the screener only counts how often it appears
Skip the firm, since all screening of this kind is done by software that you cannot influence in any way
optionExplain: The author's example is that the screener looks for the term, not the idea behind it.
Right: the readers differ, and the author advises using the job's own words where your experience supports them.
The author warns that stuffing makes a resume look unprofessional.
The screener in the example is a person, so wording can influence the result.
questions.explain: The principle of writing for the person holds even when that person is a checklist reader: give them their words, honestly.
questions.rule: Know your reader, then use their words.
questions.teaches: The author says less hands-on tech recruiters may discard a resume that lacks a term such as distributed, even if it describes the same work in other words, though this is less common at large companies with technical recruiters.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, an ATS scores each resume against the advert and rejects the lowest scorers, so keyword density gets you through.
questions.explain: This is the myth the author rejects: trackers parse and index keywords, but people decide which resumes advance.
questions.rule: Keywords help a reader; they do not feed a ranking.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A resume has strong content, but the languages the job asks for sit on page two. What is the likely result at a first glance?
options: The reader turns to page two at once, because a strong first page makes them want every further detail
The reader may not find the technologies in the first seconds and may move to the next resume
Nothing changes, because recruiters read the whole resume from top to bottom before any decision is made
The reader treats page two as the more important page, since the best material is usually saved for last
optionExplain: Interest in page two comes only after the first scan has matched.
Right: the first glance looks for key details, and missing ones can end the read.
The author says the first read is a short scan, not a full read.
Readers expect key facts early; the author says to put the relevant parts first.
questions.explain: Placement decides whether a fact is seen at all. The card next lays out the stages.
questions.rule: Put each fact where the stage of reading that needs it will reach it, and emphasise only what that stage needs.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Put the author's stages of reading in order, first to last.
items: Glance for years, key technologies, titles, companies and location
Skim top to bottom for anything relevant or eye-catching
Look at page two or read in depth
questions.explain: The glance comes first and decides whether the skim happens; the deeper read comes only if the earlier stages match.
questions.rule: Glance, skim, then read.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A resume opens with a decade-old degree; current work and languages sit on page two. Which edit follows the combined rules?
options: Bold the whole degree entry, so that the glance lands on it before it reaches anything else on the page
Switch to two columns, so that education and work can both appear on page one beside each other
Keep the order and add a long summary, so the reader meets the key facts in sentences before the lists
Move current work and relevant languages to page one, and move education lower down the resume
optionExplain: More bold on a low-value item draws the eye to the wrong place.
Two columns scramble the order the reader expects and hide where key sections are.
A long summary adds reading before the facts and is usually skipped.
Right: the glance needs work and technologies at the top, and older education matters least.
questions.explain: Order by what the reader needs first, and let age and relevance push items down.
questions.rule: Most relevant first, oldest and least relevant last.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: One rule says use bold to guide attention; another says use little bold. How do the two fit together?
options: Bold only the few details the scan needs, such as dates, titles and companies, and do it the same way throughout
The first rule covers page one and the second covers page two, so bold freely at the top and sparingly below
The second rule wins everywhere, so use no emphasis at all and let the content speak for itself
Bold every technology and verb, since more emphasis means the scan has more to find on each line
optionExplain: Right: guiding the eye needs a few consistent anchors; too much bold removes the guidance.
The author does not split the rule by page.
The author endorses strategic emphasis, so none at all loses the guidance.
If everything stands out, nothing does.
questions.explain: The two rules are one rule: emphasis works only when it is scarce and consistent.
questions.rule: Scarce, consistent emphasis guides; heavy emphasis hides.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, a resume read early in a pile of 100 or more is likely to get more reading time than one that comes late.
questions.explain: The author says a recruiter reading early will probably take more time, while a tired, pressed one later may set a resume aside.
questions.rule: A scannable page protects you when the reader is tired.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A UX designer is told the layout of the resume will itself be judged. How does the single-column advice apply?
options: It applies in full: a designer's resume must be a plain single column or it will be dropped at once
It applies the same way, because the author says two columns have no use outside of software jobs
It need not apply in full: two columns can suit design or UX roles where layout is part of the application
It lapses for every role, since the author says that layout never matters to a hurried reader at all
optionExplain: The author's own exception is for design and UX positions.
The author says two columns might work in industries outside software.
Right: the author makes an exception for roles where layout is part of what is judged.
He still treats layout as vital for developers; the exception is narrow.
questions.explain: A rule serves an end; when the end changes, as when layout itself is on show, the rule can change.
questions.rule: Check what the layout is for before you copy a rule.
questions.teaches: The author says two-column layouts can be a great choice for design or UX positions, where the layout is part of the application, but offer software developers no advantage.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which line gives a hurried reader the most to go on?
options: Responsible for improving the performance of the checkout service as part of a highly motivated team
Passionate full-stack engineer with excellent communication skills and a strong work ethic in every team
Worked on the checkout service, taking part in a number of performance improvements over some time
Cut checkout latency from 900 ms to 300 ms by caching price lookups, a design I led
optionExplain: It names a task and a team, but no result or number.
These are trait claims with nothing a reader can check.
It describes participation with no measure of what changed.
Right: it has a result, a number and a personal contribution that a reader can compare.
questions.explain: A claim can be copied by anyone. A result with a number is harder to fake and easier to compare. The card next names the pattern.
questions.rule: Wherever you are about to claim a quality, replace the claim with a result, a number or a named technology a reader can see.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The author's bullet shape is: accomplished impact, measured by a ____, by doing a specific contribution.
questions.explain: The measure is the part that makes the claim checkable.
questions.rule: Impact, measured by a number, by your contribution.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A skills list reads Python 5 stars, Go 3 stars. What do the book's rules suggest?
options: Keep the stars, because they let a hurried reader compare your strengths at a single glance on the page
Drop the stars; list technologies you are proficient with, and show them in use inside your bullets as evidence
Replace the stars with years-of-use numbers beside every tool, including the ones you touched only briefly
Move the list to the end of the resume, so the stars do not take attention away from your work history
optionExplain: The author advises against self-ratings, which a reader cannot verify.
Right: ratings are a claim with no proof; use of the tool in a bullet is the proof.
Listing tools you used briefly weakens the list; the rule is to list those you are proficient with.
The technologies belong near the top of page one, where the glance looks.
questions.explain: The rating replaces proof with a self-score. Show the technology working instead.
questions.rule: Show the tool in use; skip the score.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each line by whether it shows proof or only claims a quality.

items.t: Cut page load time from 4.1 s to 1.8 s by caching the product API
Strong team player with excellent communication skills
Python: expert level, 9 out of 10
Raised test coverage from 40% to 78% by adding integration tests
Hard-working and passionate about technology
Wrote the billing export used by 1,200 customers; I owned the rollout

questions.explain: Lines with a result, a number and a personal role can be checked; the other three are labels the reader must take on trust.
questions.rule: If the reader cannot check it, it is a claim.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, if you cannot find the exact impact of a past project, you should leave impact out.
questions.explain: The author says to ask your team or former colleagues first, and if the exact figure is unknown, to estimate it to a good approximation.
questions.rule: Estimate honestly before you drop the number.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader does not know your former employer's product. According to the author, which description travels best?
options: One with a measured figure, such as requests per second, daily visitors or a percentage improvement
One that explains the product's business model in a long sentence, so the reader grasps what it was
One that praises the quality of your work and the strength of the team you belonged to on the project
One that names the project's code name and lists the internal tools the team used to build it each week
optionExplain: Right: a figure carries over to a reader who knows nothing of your company.
Explanation costs the reader time and does not show what you achieved.
Praise is a claim and not a measure.
Internal names mean nothing outside the firm; the author warns against jargon.
questions.explain: Proof has to be portable. A measure carries across employers when a story of the product does not.
questions.rule: Use figures a stranger can read.
questions.teaches: The author says numbers such as daily visitors, requests per second or an improvement percentage are easier to translate across employers than a qualitative description of the project.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: You hold a detailed three-page resume. A posting wants Android and Kotlin; you also have web experience. What is a sound step?
options: Send the three-page version unchanged, so that the reader can see everything and decide what is relevant
Delete the web experience entirely, because any item the posting does not mention counts against you
Add every Android, Kotlin and web term to a skills block, so each possible search will find a match
Make a copy, put the Android and Kotlin work first with the posting's wording, and trim or lower the web work
optionExplain: The reader will not search a long file for the fit; you must show it.
Cutting is right, but removing relevant support entirely goes further than the author asks.
A block of every term reads as stuffing.
Right: tailoring echoes the job and reorders without deleting the master.
questions.explain: You adapt a copy to the reader instead of expecting the reader to adapt. The card next names the routine.
questions.rule: Keep one full master, then build each application by echoing the job's own words in true experience and cutting the rest.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The author says to keep a ____ resume that may run past two pages, then trim it for each job.
questions.explain: The master holds all the material, and each application takes the part that fits.
questions.rule: One master, many trimmed copies.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A backend posting asks for distributed systems; your bullets say microservices and message queues. Which edit fits the routine?
options: Add a line saying distributed systems expert to the top, without changing the bullets that follow it
Describe the same work with the posting's term where it truly applies, and keep the sentences readable
Replace the bullets with a list of all the distributed-systems terms you have heard of in the field
Leave the wording as it is, since a reader who knows the field will translate the terms for you
optionExplain: A label without support is a claim, and it may not be true.
Right: the tailoring uses the job's words only for experience you really have.
That is stuffing, and it lists things you may not have done.
Some screeners look for the exact term, so leaving the wording as is can cost you.
questions.explain: Echoing is a change of words for the same true work, not a change in what you did.
questions.rule: Same work, the job's words.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each choice into sensible tailoring or something the author warns against.

items.t: Moving the Kotlin and Android projects above web work for an Android posting
Listing 40 tools, many never used, so every search term matches
Keeping a short Technologies section and naming the same tools in the bullets that used them
Claiming a framework you have only read about because the posting names it
Removing old bullets that the posting does not need
Writing filler sentences just to repeat the posting's keywords

questions.explain: Sensible tailoring reorders and selects true material; the other three add terms the work does not support or sentences that exist only for the words.
questions.rule: Select and reword; do not pad or invent.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: according to the headhunter the author quotes, removing bullets that do not help costs you little, since the interview gives room to discuss them.
questions.explain: She says you lose very little by cutting, and that the resume exists to win the interview, where you can talk about the rest.
questions.rule: The resume wins the interview; the interview tells the rest.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: An applicant moves from a product company to a consultancy that contracts developers to clients. What change does the author suggest to the technologies list?
options: Keep to the few technologies the posting names, since an agency rewards a narrow focus above everything else
List only fundamentals and drop certifications, because agencies assume you can pick up any tool quickly
List all the technologies you are proficient with and all your certifications, since the agency may place you anywhere
Remove the technologies list altogether, because an agency reads the work experience section only
optionExplain: That is the advice for a role with one set stack, not for an agency.
That is closer to the advice for big generalist tech companies.
Right: agencies can contract people for many clients, so a broad list and certifications make you more attractive.
The author's agency advice is about what to list, not to drop it.
questions.explain: The same end, a fast view of fit, calls for a different list when the employer's need differs: breadth for an agency.
questions.rule: Let the employer type set how broad the list is.
questions.teaches: The author says that for an agency you should consider mentioning all technologies you are proficient with, not only those in the job description, and list all certifications, since agencies can contract people with proven skills more easily.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A developer applies to a large generalist tech company and to a consultancy. How should the technologies lists differ?
options: Keep a short, fundamentals-led list for the large company and a broad one for the consultancy
Use the same long list for both, because a longer list improves the odds with every kind of employer
List more tools for the large company, since its hiring managers expect you to know each tool in depth
Use the same short list for both, since consultancies reward focus and pay no attention to certifications
optionExplain: Right: generalist firms assume you can pick up tools, while agencies place you across many client stacks.
A long list is a risk at generalist firms, where stuffing counts against you.
Generalist firms assume you can pick tools up quickly, so a long tool list does not help.
Agencies value breadth and certifications, so this advice is wrong for them.
questions.explain: One end, different readers. The card next shows how stage and employer set the variant.
questions.rule: Fix the reader, the scan and the proof first, then pick the variant that matches your stage and the type of employer.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each applicant to the layout of advice the book gives.
pairs: One page, with work, internships and projects at the top
A short summary of the switch, then projects with working links
Promotions, results and influence, with a summary tailored to the job
Two separate resumes, each with its own story
questions.explain: Each pair is a stage-specific variant on the same fixed core of a fast, visible, proven fit.
questions.rule: Same core, different emphasis.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A teacher is moving into software. Which opening follows the book's advice for a career changer?
options: Twelve years of teaching duties in full, then a projects section tucked at the end of page two
A resume that presents the teaching years as if they had been software jobs, to hide the change of field
A short summary of the switch and why, then languages and linked working projects, with teaching in one sentence
A long summary of every course taken, with the projects left out so that the page stays short
optionExplain: This buries the new skills and spends the page on the old career.
This misleads the reader, and the author asks you to be open about the change.
Right: the switch is explained up front and the proof of new skill is near the top.
Courses without projects are weaker proof than working code.
questions.explain: The changer's job is to make the new fit visible fast and keep the old career short.
questions.rule: Explain the switch, show the proof, keep the past brief.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Advice for a generalist firm says list few tools; advice for a one-stack firm says list the advert's tools. What settles which applies?
options: Your seniority: juniors list many tools and seniors list few, at every kind of firm and in every country
The type of employer: generalists expect you to pick up tools, while stack-specific firms screen for the stack
The length of the advert: a long advert means you should list many tools, wherever the job is based
The country: the author ties each rule to the place where the company has its head office
optionExplain: The author does not tie tool lists to seniority in this way.
Right: the employer's way of hiring decides which list serves the scan.
Advert length is not the author's test; what matters is whether the stack is fixed.
The author does not base this on the company's country.
questions.explain: When two rules conflict, look at what each one serves, then see which end your situation calls for.
questions.rule: Let the employer's needs pick the rule.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, a short summary that states your years with the main language is worth having when you apply to a technology-specific company.
questions.explain: He says it is worth having a short summary listing this, since less technical recruiters may screen for specific technologies.
questions.rule: Make the number of years easy to find.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which advice misapplies the book?
options: A new grad fits the resume on one page, with the most relevant parts placed first
A senior engineer makes promotions visible and adds a summary tailored to the job
A career changer summarises the old career in a sentence and adds bullets for transferable skills
A manager open to both paths sends one hybrid resume that mixes management and coding equally
optionExplain: This matches the advice for new grads.
This matches the advice for senior engineers.
This matches the advice for career changers.
Right: the author advises two separate resumes, each telling its own story.
questions.explain: A hybrid story is weak for both readers; each target role needs its own clear story.
questions.rule: One story per target.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A developer spent a year studying a new stack and wants to present it. Which proof does the author rank higher?
options: Something shipped in production, taught to others, or contributed to open source with that technology
A list of completed courses with certificates, which the author calls the strongest evidence of skill
A portfolio project that only the candidate uses, because it shows initiative on the page to the reader
A paragraph on how many hours a day were spent studying, since effort is what hiring managers value most
optionExplain: Right: work in production speaks louder than a course, and shipping, teaching or open source prove mastery.
The author says work in production beats completing a course.
A project used only by you is not a strong sign of what you can do on the job.
Effort without a result is a claim, not proof.
questions.explain: The claims-versus-proof rule applies to study breaks too: present them like work, with evidence.
questions.rule: Present study time like work, with proof.
questions.teaches: The author says work in production speaks more than finishing a course or self-study, and a portfolio project used only by you is not a strong sign of what you can do on the job.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: You found a role at a large firm where a former colleague works, and you have not applied yet. What should come first?
options: Apply on the company site now, then ask the colleague to refer you once you are in the system
Ask the colleague for a referral first, then apply with a resume tailored to the job at hand
Send the resume to the careers inbox, then ask the colleague to mention it if anyone replies
Post on a forum for feedback, then apply once your colleague is back from any planned leave
optionExplain: After you apply, you often count as an active candidate and cannot be referred.
Right: many firms only accept a referral from someone not already in the pipeline.
A cold send adds nothing a referral would add, and it can block the referral.
Feedback is useful, but it does not put you ahead in the queue.
questions.explain: Sequence matters: the referral has to come before the application. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Spend effort where it moves you up the queue or puts proof in the reader's path: a referral first, a tailored resume, then LinkedIn and GitHub.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Put the author's typical priority order of resumes in order, first read to last.
items: Candidates who need a visa and relocation
questions.explain: The more costly a candidate is to hire in time and money, the later the resume tends to be read.
questions.rule: The costlier the hire, the later the read.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: An applicant abroad targets entry-level jobs at large firms and hears nothing back. What does the author's reasoning suggest?
options: Send the same resume to more large firms, since volume beats the priority order for people abroad
Leave the visa status off the resume, so that the reader cannot put it in the lower-priority pile
Wait for senior-level openings only, because large firms hire entry-level staff abroad in the first year
Lean on referrals and on listings from smaller firms that struggle to find local talent for the role
optionExplain: More of the same applications keep landing at the bottom of the order.
The author says to state work authorisation clearly, not hide it.
Large firms usually sponsor only for senior or hard-to-fill roles, not within a year.
Right: large firms mostly hire entry level locally, so the routes that skip or soften that order matter.
questions.explain: When the default queue works against you, change the route, not just the document.
questions.rule: If you are low in the queue, change the route.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which application is the best place for a tailored cover letter, according to the author?
options: A small company where you can email the hiring manager directly
A large firm's online form with no named contact and no field for a letter at all
A one-click application on a job board for a firm that rarely reads attachments
Any role, since a letter is the surest way to be read before the resume is opened
optionExplain: Right: letters matter where the hiring manager screens, typically at smaller firms.
Big companies rarely ask for letters and recruiters seldom read them.
A one-click route offers no sign that anyone will read an attachment.
The author says your tailored resume should already work as the cover letter.
questions.explain: Effort follows the chance of being read, and a letter is read only in particular situations.
questions.rule: Write letters only where someone will read them.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, if you apply on the company site first and then ask for a referral, you can usually still be referred.
questions.explain: Most referral systems accept only candidates not yet in the pipeline, so applying first often rules the referral out.
questions.rule: Refer first, apply second.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A friend says a referral will carry him through to an offer. What does the Microsoft engineer the author quotes say?
options: A referral all but guarantees an offer, because the employee who refers you must stand behind you
A referral makes no difference, because recruiters read every resume in the same order and depth
A referral can get you an interview faster, but it does not help you get an offer
A referral matters only before the onsite, where it replaces the technical interviews for the role
optionExplain: That is more than any quoted engineer claims.
Several quoted engineers say referrals change the speed and depth of review.
Right: the quoted view is that a referral speeds the interview and does not decide the offer.
No quoted engineer says a referral replaces interviews.
questions.explain: Even the best route to a read leaves the resume and interviews to do their jobs, so do not let one route stand in for the rest.
questions.rule: Routes get you read; content and interviews win the job.
questions.teaches: A Microsoft engineer quoted by the author says a referral can get you an interview faster, but it does not help you get an offer, though the author notes these quotes are not representative of the companies.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: You have two days before a deadline and only a rough resume. Which plan is most sensible?
options: Spend the first day choosing a template, then fill in details in whatever time remains before the deadline
Gather your results, tailor one copy to the job, then have someone proofread that copy before sending it
Proofread the rough resume first, then write the tailored version in the last hour without a second check
Send the rough resume now, and revise it only if a recruiter replies to ask for something more specific
optionExplain: The author says to pick a proven template early and move on to the content.
Right: content and tailoring come before polish, and the check belongs on the version you send.
Checks done before tailoring will not cover the text that actually goes out.
A weak first read is hard to recover from, as most inbound applications fail at the screen.
questions.explain: Order protects effort: do the work that changes what the reader sees before the work that polishes it. The card next gives the sequence.
questions.rule: Work in order: choose targets, write one strong master, tailor it per job, check it with outside eyes, and ask for the referral before you send.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Put these steps in the order the book's logic suggests, first to last.
items: Ask others what your past projects achieved
Write the long master resume with results and impact
Tailor a copy to one job description
Run grammar checks and have a friend proofread
Send a PDF named with your own name
questions.explain: Evidence comes first, then the master, then the tailored copy; checks and the send come last.
questions.rule: Gather, write, tailor, check, send.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A candidate has chosen between 20 templates for a week and has written three bullets. What does the book's approach say?
options: Keep comparing, since a flawless template makes up for thin content in the first seconds of the scan
Switch to a two-column design, so that the page looks full even when there are few bullets to show
Stop writing bullets until the template is final, so you do not have to reformat the text again later
Pick a proven template now, customise it lightly, and put the effort into strong content
optionExplain: The author says content beats template.
Two columns hide thin content but also make the page harder to read.
Settling the template early is fine; stalling the content is the problem.
Right: a template is not worth much without content, and a proven one is enough.
questions.explain: Effort should go where it changes the reader's view: the content.
questions.rule: Proven template early, effort on content.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which plan conflicts with the book's advice?
options: Ask former colleagues what a project achieved, then write the bullets with those figures
Apply on the company site today, then ask a friend there for a referral next week
Write a second resume from scratch on a different template, then merge the best parts
Tailor a copy to the job, then have a friend proofread that copy before it is sent
optionExplain: This matches the advice to find out the impact.
Right: asking for a referral after applying often fails, since you are already in the pipeline.
This matches the author's exercise of writing two resumes and building a third.
This matches the advice to get fresh eyes on the resume.
questions.explain: A plan can contain only good steps and still fail if two are in the wrong order.
questions.rule: Check the order as well as the steps.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, a well-chosen template can make up for thin content.
questions.explain: He says a template is not worth much without great content, and that a good resume combines an easy-to-read template with content specific to the role.
questions.rule: Template and content both matter; content leads.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A hiring manager with no extra budget wants to lose fewer good people at the resume screen. Which step does the author give?
options: Have a second person screen the same resumes independently, then compare the two Yes piles together
Move to only reading resumes from referrals, since those are certain to be the strongest in the whole pool
Make the screen stricter by adding more required keywords, so that only the best-matching resumes pass
Read the resumes faster and in larger batches, so that no single resume is judged for very long
optionExplain: Right: a second reader helps calibrate and reduce bias, at low cost.
The author does not say referred resumes are certain to be the strongest.
More required keywords would reject more good people with poor resumes.
Faster reading is the rush the author warns against; he advises budgeting dedicated time.
questions.explain: The hiring chapter shows the other side of the book's order: readers are fallible, so a candidate should make the resume easy to read.
questions.rule: Reader fallibility is why the writer's work matters.
questions.teaches: The author tells hiring managers without extra budget to involve at least one other person who screens the same resumes independently, and to compare the overlap of the two Yes piles, which calibrates expectations and reduces bias.

questions.q: In the status flowchart, which steps can end with the application marked Rejected? Select all that apply.
options: The recruiter's review of the application
The hiring manager's review of the application
The step where the candidate is extended an offer
The technical screens and onsite interviews
questions.explain: Rejected is reachable from the recruiter review, the hiring manager review and the technical and onsite stage. Once an offer is extended, the candidate either accepts or declines, so that step does not lead to Rejected.
optionExplain: Yes: a recruiter can reject on the resume or on knockout questions.
Yes: the hiring manager can reject after reviewing the application.
No: this step leads only to Accepted or Declined, which are the candidate's choices.
Yes: failing the interview process sends the application to Rejected.
questions.rule: In the ATS workflow people move statuses; rejection can happen at each review, while the offer ends in the candidate's choice.

media.alt: Flowchart of statuses in an applicant tracking system. A grey Unviewed Applicant moves through four decision diamonds: recruiter review, hiring manager review, technical screens with onsite interviews, and offer extended. Passing leads to In Review, Interview and Offer boxes. Three of the first diamonds have arrows to a red Rejected box; the offer diamond leads to Accepted or Declined.

questions.q: In the diagram, 190 ordinary resumes lead to 20 recruiter screens, while 10 referrals lead to 8. What does this suggest?
options: Referrals convert at a similar rate, and the gap appears only because fewer referrals were submitted
Inbound resumes are the better route, because they produced more recruiter screens in absolute terms
A referral is far likelier to reach the recruiter screen: about four in five against about one in ten
Referrals help only when strong, since ordinary referrals were screened out as often as inbound resumes
questions.explain: Eight of ten referrals reach the recruiter screen, while about one in ten ordinary resumes does. That is the sense in which the author says referrals get priority.
optionExplain: Tempting if you compare counts, but the rates are about 80 percent against about 10 percent.
Absolute numbers favour inbound only because far more of them were submitted.
Right: the rate per candidate is far higher for referrals.
Wrong: 8 of the 10 referrals reach the recruiter screen while only about 1 in 10 ordinary resumes does, so referrals help far beyond a few strong ones.
questions.rule: Compare rates, not counts, when judging a route into the pipeline.

media.alt: Funnel diagram like the large-company pipeline, now with referrals. Of 250 submitted resumes, the resume screen holds 190 inbound resumes plus 10 referrals entering by a side arrow. The recruiter screen holds 20 from screened resumes, 8 from screened referrals and 2 strong referrals entering by a second arrow. Technical screen, onsite and offer follow.

questions.q: Suppose the recruiter clears the disqualify checkbox in this form. What changes for an applicant who answers no?
options: The ATS starts reading the resume for work authorization wording instead of the form answer
The question is ignored, because this information is always taken from the resume anyway
Every applicant is rejected, because a yes or no question type removes everyone who answers
A no answer no longer triggers automatic rejection by this question
questions.explain: The rejection comes from the rule the recruiter set up with the checkbox, applied to the answer on the form. Without the checkbox the question only gathers information.
optionExplain: Wrong: the ATS does not use resume contents for this, and the data comes from the form.
Wrong: the answer is explicitly given on the application form, never taken from the resume.
Wrong: the question type does not reject anyone; the checkbox rule does.
Right: the automatic rejection depends on the recruiter's checkbox.
questions.rule: A knockout question rejects only because a recruiter configured it to, using the form answer.

media.alt: Screenshot of a recruiter's form editor in an applicant tracking system. A yes or no question asks whether the applicant is legally eligible to work in the country. A ticked checkbox beneath the question text says to disqualify the candidate if the answer is no.

questions.q: True or false: In the small-company funnel, the resume screen removes no one, because the hiring manager reads all ten resumes.
questions.explain: The diagram shows ten resumes reaching the resume screen but only five reaching the hiring manager call, so the screen removes about half. The hiring manager does that screening in a small company.
questions.rule: At a small company the hiring manager reads the resumes, and the resume screen is still where many applicants drop out.

media.alt: Funnel diagram for a small company: ten resumes submitted, ten in the tracking queue, ten at the resume screen, then five at a hiring manager call, four at a technical screen, two onsite and one offer. Side callouts say even small firms use a tracking system and the hiring manager reads all resumes.

questions.q: In the highlighted skills list, which kinds of entries are marked as problems? Select all that apply.
options: Self-rated levels such as expert and proficient
Everyday tools that anyone can learn in hours
Core languages the person works in daily
Older languages the person no longer uses actively
questions.explain: The author marks level labels, trivial or overly specific tools and older languages the person has not used in years. The person's current languages stay as they are.
optionExplain: Yes: the labels are double-edged and imply the person is not an expert elsewhere.
Yes: they add clutter and little signal.
No: the main languages are not highlighted; only their labels are.
Yes: old languages can add age bias and are not relevant to the job.
questions.rule: Keep a skills list to current, relevant technologies and drop level labels.

media.alt: The same skills section as an annotated critique, with pink highlights on the self-rating labels, two older languages near the start of the language line, and a run of generic tools in the final bullet. A note says those tools are either trivial or overly specific. Core language names are unhighlighted.

questions.q: In the career listing, two consecutive entries share one employer, with different titles and adjacent date ranges. This layout shows a ____.
questions.explain: Entries with the same employer, a higher title and the next date range make the promotion visible. The author says reviewers should see it because promotion is an important signal.
questions.rule: Show each promotion as its own titled entry so progression is visible at a glance.

media.alt: Plain bullet listing of career history, newest first, with three columns: title, employer and years. A senior role is at the top, followed by two consecutive entries at one employer with different titles and adjacent date ranges. Two summer internships and a mathematics degree complete the list.

questions.q: Suppose a Java backend posting asks for Java, Spring and SQL. In the dense skills block, which entries would the author's advice trim?
options: Spring Boot and Spring MVC in the back-end line
Office applications such as a word processor and spreadsheet
The SQL entry and the relational databases line
Front-end libraries and the frameworks still being learned
The Java entry at the start of the programming line
questions.explain: The author says to drop unrelated or trivial technologies and keep those relevant to the job. Office tools and front-end frameworks do not serve a Java backend posting.
optionExplain: Spring is named in the posting, so cutting it would remove a keyword the recruiter screens for.
Office applications are trivial for this role, so they are the first to go.
SQL is named in the posting, so cutting it would hide a required skill.
Front-end and learning frameworks are unrelated to this posting, so they are clutter.
Java is the posting's main language and must stay.
questions.rule: Keep technologies relevant to the posting and remove unrelated or trivial ones.

media.alt: A dense technical skills block written as one run-on paragraph. Many underlined bold categories are separated by double bars, covering languages, databases, back-end and front-end technologies, frameworks still being learned, build tools, testing, editors, CI, API styles, infrastructure, queues and a final other-tools category containing task trackers and office applications.
