questions.q: True or false: In the advert shown, a candidate who codes only in Python still meets the stated requirement for coding experience.
questions.explain: The advert accepts any one of three named languages, which fits the author's point that generalist employers care less about the specific language than about engineering skill.
questions.rule: Generalist employers ask for one strong language, not a particular one.

media.alt: A job advert for a generalist engineer. Minimum qualifications have four bullets: a degree or equivalent, coding in any one of three named languages, web markup and scripting, and full-stack features. Three preferred front-end items follow, then paragraphs about wide-ranging fields, versatility, switching teams and owning delivery.

questions.q: In the annotated resume, match each red label to the flaw it points at.
pairs: A whole skills paragraph and many phrases inside bullets are bold
Contact details and dates are placed and styled differently from job to job
Bullets trail off with open-ended filler words
questions.explain: The author names three issues: far too much bold, uneven formatting such as sizes and alignment, and sloppy wording. Together they suggest poor attention to detail.
questions.rule: Uneven formatting and filler wording signal carelessness.

media.alt: The resume with hand-drawn red annotations and arrows. Label one, too much bolding, points at the skills paragraph and bold bullet phrases. Label two, inconsistent formatting, boxes the contact block and the differing date styles. Label three, sloppy phrasing, underlines filler endings in bullets.

questions.q: In the resume shown, some bold phrases concern tax processing, yet the job is at a tech company. What is wrong with that bolding?
options: Tax terms are too long to bold, so bold should cover single words only
It draws the eye to details that matter little for the role, and what is bold is inconsistent
Bold should be reserved for numbers, so these phrases need figures added
Bold phrases belong at the end of a bullet, and these sit in the middle
questions.explain: The author asks why a tax term is bold for a tech application: the emphasis lands on details irrelevant to the job and is applied unevenly. Bold is best kept for labels like titles, dates and companies.
optionExplain: Length is not the issue; the problem is what gets emphasised, not how many words.
Right: bold pulls attention to something unimportant for this job, and it is inconsistent.
Numbers may be worth stressing, but the author's advice is to bold labels, not to bold figures inside sentences.
The author gives no position rule; mid-sentence bold is the wider problem.
questions.rule: Bold only key labels such as titles, dates and companies.

media.alt: Top of a resume with name and role at left and phone, email and profile link at right. A bold skills paragraph follows. Two jobs list six and four bullets. Many phrases inside bullets are bold, including tax and payroll terms, and date styles differ between jobs.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: In the career changer resume shown, put the main sections in order from the top.
items: A short summary about the earlier career and the change
Brief past work experience from the old field
questions.explain: The author starts with a short summary, then languages and projects because the person has no full-time software work, then a brief experience section, and closes with education.
questions.rule: A career changer leads with summary, technologies and projects, then past work and education.

media.alt: One-page career changer resume. A centred name and contact line lead to a one-sentence summary mentioning the earlier finance career. Purple headings follow: languages and technologies, projects with bold stacks, two finance experience entries with two bullets each, education with a bootcamp and a degree, and an interests line.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: In the resume shown, what makes it stronger than a version that has only a self-study entry?
options: The self-study entry is dropped entirely so that no study time appears anywhere
Freelance work is listed first with a longer date range and no mention of studying
The self-study entry gets extra bullets so the study period looks like a full job
A freelance entry with production results leads, and a short self-study entry sits below it
questions.explain: The author says freelancing is a stronger sign of working knowledge than self-study. The picture puts the freelance entry on top with delivered results and keeps a shorter study entry for the earlier months.
optionExplain: The picture still shows self-study; it is kept, not removed.
The picture still shows a self-study entry, so saying there is no mention of studying is wrong.
The study entry has fewer bullets than the freelance entry, so this is wrong.
Right: freelance proof of shipped work leads and the study entry is demoted.
questions.rule: Show freelance delivery ahead of study time.

media.alt: A resume with a freelancer entry running from March 2020 to the present, with five bullets: a reporting tool with measured speed-up, a shipped API with monitoring, an open-source contribution, posts and mentoring. Below it a shorter self-study entry covers only the earlier months, with three bullets.

questions.section: Write a Resume for That Job
questions.q: Suppose the advert stresses reliability and distributed systems. Which edit to this snippet follows the author's tailoring advice?
options: Reword the skills line and bullets with the advert's terms where they truly match the work
Add a new job entry that covers reliability and distributed systems work
Replace the skills block with a paragraph claiming deep distributed systems expertise
Keep the wording as it is and let the recruiter infer how the work matches the advert
questions.explain: The author's tailored version keeps the same experience but uses the advert's language, so a recruiter scanning for those phrases finds them.
optionExplain: Right: same experience, advert wording.
This invents experience; the case changes wording, not facts.
A bold claim with no evidence replaces specifics, which the author warns against.
A non-technical screener looks for the phrases and will not infer them.
questions.rule: Echo the advert's language in your real experience.

media.alt: A generic resume snippet: a skills summary with four bold-labelled lines (languages, databases, tools, other) and a job entry with four short bullets about back-end work, a dashboard generator, a testing proxy and a beta environment. No wording echoes a particular advert.

questions.unitTitle: Different experience levels, different career paths
questions.q: In the projects list shown, what do the five months of growth in the book add that the entries lack?
options: A longer technology list in the brackets after each project name
A bootcamp certificate and graduation date beside each project
Evidence of quality or real use, such as tests, users or merged contributions
A different file format, since underlined project names do not open in a PDF
questions.explain: The entries only describe small apps. The book's improved version adds open-source contributions, tests and a paid project with real users.
optionExplain: Stacks are already listed; adding more does not prove quality.
Credentials are not the gap the book addresses; the issue is proof of work.
Right: the entries give no sign of use, testing or contributions.
Format is not the problem; the content lacks evidence.
questions.rule: Grow projects with tests, real users and open-source contributions.

media.alt: Two project bullets under a projects heading. Each has an underlined project name, the technology stack in brackets and a one-sentence description of a small web app.

questions.q: In the diagram of the adjusted top-down template, put the blocks in reading order from the top.
questions.explain: The adjusted layout keeps the LinkedIn-style top-down flow but adds a languages and technologies block between the summary and the work experience, so the details a developer's reader wants come early.
questions.rule: Keep the familiar top-down order and give languages and technologies their own block near the top.

media.alt: Wireframe of an adjusted top-down resume template: one column of white boxes on blue, with a long arrow down the side meaning read top to bottom. From the top: name and details, Summary, Languages and Technologies, Work Experience with three entries, Education, Projects, then Interests or Honors and Awards. It adds a dedicated technologies block to the LinkedIn-style order.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: In the first-scan diagram, how does the recruiter work out the candidate's years of experience?
options: By adding up the length of every position listed anywhere on the page
By reading a years-of-experience figure the candidate states in a summary line
By quick date maths from the first work date or the education end date
By counting how many technologies appear in the tech stack section
questions.explain: The diagram shows the recruiter doing quick date maths from the earliest work date or the graduation date, which here gives two to three years. Clear dates make that step instant.
optionExplain: Adding every role would need careful reading, but the diagram shows only a glance at a few dates.
The sample resume has no such stated figure; the recruiter infers the years from dates.
Right: a few dates are enough for a quick estimate of experience.
Technologies are checked in a separate step for relevance, not used to count years.
questions.rule: Make dates easy to find so the recruiter can work out your years of experience at a glance.

media.alt: The sample resume blurred, with callouts. One arrow points at the city in the header, labelled as location, with a note on whether a visa or relocation might be needed. Arrows to the latest job's date range, an earlier job's start and the graduation year show quick date maths for years of experience, concluding with two to three years.

questions.section: How Recruiters and Hiring Managers Scan Resumes
questions.q: In the first-scan diagram of the revised resume, what makes the four key details quicker to find than in the original?
options: Each detail sits in a predictable, distinct spot: location up top, technologies under the header, dates and titles aligned
A summary paragraph at the top states the location, years, technologies and titles in one sentence
A boxed sidebar next to the main column repeats the four details in a short list for the reader
Skill-level bars next to each technology show proficiency, so the reader does not need to read the dates
questions.explain: The revised template is a plain single column with the details in fixed, easy-to-spot places, so the recruiter does not need to hunt for them and has more time to read the content.
optionExplain: Right: placement and alignment make the same four details stand out at a glance.
The revised resume as described has no summary block; the details are found where they sit.
The revised layout is a single column with no sidebar, so nothing is repeated beside it.
The revised resume lists technologies as plain text with no bars, and dates are read separately.
questions.rule: A good template puts the key details in fixed, visible places.

media.alt: The revised resume, blurred, with four boxed regions and callouts: the city line at the top, the technologies block under the header, the date column at the right of each job, and the aligned titles, companies and school name on the left. Notes say location is immediately clear, dates stand out, relevant technologies are listed upfront, and titles and companies stand out.

questions.section: The Results of Using a Good Resume Template
questions.q: In the diagram of the revised resume's body, which two features do the notes credit for its easy top-to-bottom read?
options: Every bullet starts with the full list of tools used
Impact is clear from the first few words of each bullet
Each project is one dense paragraph with no breaks
Figures and numbers draw the reader's attention
A narrow sidebar holds the most important results
questions.explain: The notes on the diagram say impact shows in the first words and that numbers draw attention, which together make a quick scan down the page productive.
optionExplain: The boxed phrases show tools appearing inside bullets, not leading every bullet.
Right: opening with the result lets a tired reader see the impact at once.
The revised resume uses separate bullets, not dense paragraphs.
Right: figures such as percentages and team sizes catch the eye during a scan.
The revised resume is a single column with no sidebar.
questions.rule: Open bullets with impact and use numbers so a scan down the page finds results.

media.alt: The revised resume with the body blurred and short phrases boxed down the page: figures such as a conversion gain, team size, number of apps served and scholarship selectivity; action words like re-architected and built; tool names; and project results with audience numbers. A note says impact is clear from the first words, numbers draw attention, and the resume reads easily top to bottom.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: In the report, the recruiter-findings bar is full but the skills bar is almost empty. What mainly pulls the match rate down?
options: Section headings and the education block are missing from the resume
Most of the skills and keywords in the posting are absent from the resume
The resume file is in a type that the scan tool cannot read at all
The job title in the posting appears too many times in the resume
questions.explain: The report ticks the education and section checks, and the nearly empty skills bar reflects posting keywords missing from the resume. The author still calls most such scores guesswork, useful only as a rough pointer.
optionExplain: The report marks education and section headings with green ticks, so they are found.
Right: the empty skills bar shows posting skills that the resume does not mention.
A file the tool could not read would produce no findings at all, yet several checks show results.
The report flags missing items, not repeated ones, so too many mentions is not the issue.
questions.rule: Read a scan score as a rough pointer to word overlap, not as proof.

media.alt: Screenshot of a scan service's report comparing a resume with a job posting. A large ring shows a low overall match rate under twenty percent. Beside it, horizontal bars rate several check groups: the recruiter-findings bar is full while the skills-match bar is almost empty. Below, a findings table marks missing skills and job title with red crosses, and education and section headings with green ticks.

questions.unitTitle: Polishing the resume and going beyond it
questions.q: In the template letter, each bullet pairs a requirement with proof. According to the author, why do such letters get ignored in tech?
options: Backing every requirement with specifics is a risk that belongs only in interviews
Almost everything in them is already in the resume, so they add little
A letter this short looks like low effort, and only long letters are read
Naming the position and the website makes the letter too targeted to read
questions.explain: The author says templated letters add little beyond the resume, since nearly everything listed is probably already in the CV. A personalised letter for that position and company is the alternative.
optionExplain: The author's own advice is to be specific, so specifics are not the problem.
Right: repeating the resume gives the reader nothing new.
The advice for letters is to keep them short, so shortness is not the fault.
Naming the company and position is part of the advice for good letters.
questions.rule: A templated letter that restates the resume adds nothing; write a personal one for that company.

media.alt: Plain-text cover letter template full of curly-brace placeholders: a greeting with a name slot, an opening line with slots for position, site, skills, years and a problem to solve, then three bullets each pairing a job requirement with proof of having done it, a polite closing request and a name slot.

questions.q: In the picture, every skill has all five dots filled. According to the author, what do those top scores add to the resume?
options: Nothing useful, because a technology listed on a resume is already assumed to be one you are proficient with
Evidence of strong skills, because a top score tells recruiters you rate yourself above the usual level for your role
Extra trust, because a recruiter reads identical top ratings across the list as a sign of consistent, calibrated skill
A warning only when the dots differ, because uneven scores show the candidate is unsure about some listed skills
questions.explain: The author says anything shown at four or five stars is a given, since recruiters assume you are proficient with whatever you list. Self-ratings are also often off, so he advises dropping them.
optionExplain: Right: listing a skill already signals proficiency, so a top score repeats what the reader assumes.
Tempting, but the author says high ratings add nothing the listing does not already say.
Tempting, but he says people rate themselves poorly and recruiters know it, so uniform scores earn no trust.
Tempting, but his advice is to drop ratings altogether; low scores belong off the resume and high ones are a given.
questions.rule: Drop star, point and bar ratings: list only technologies you are proficient with.

media.alt: Close-up of a resume skills section: spaced-capital heading with a rule, then seven skill lines, each with a row of five dots beneath it. Every dot in every row is filled, so all skills show the top score, one entry appearing twice.

questions.q: True or false: According to the author, in the picture the blue employer links pull a glancing eye to company names before titles and dates.
questions.explain: The author says a recruiter glancing at this resume is drawn straight to the linked company names, when the engineer's title and the dates should get that attention.
questions.rule: Make links and colour point to titles, dates and results, not to employer names.

media.alt: Page one of a plain single-column resume on white. Centred name and contact lines with a website link, then a short bulleted tech stacks section, then work experience. Every job heading begins with the employer name as a blue underlined link, followed by the job title and a date range at the right margin, with bullet points beneath.

questions.section: Machine Learning Engineer with 5 Years Experience
questions.q: In the picture, each job opens with a paragraph about the employer before the work. What does the author expect a scanning reader to do?
options: Read every paragraph in full, because employer context frames the achievements that follow it
Skip to the next paragraph after the company sentence, assuming the whole paragraph is about the company
Jump to the stack line of each job, because tools matter more to a scanner than any prose
Stop reading at once, because a resume with employer descriptions is rejected without a second look
questions.explain: The author says a scanner reads the first sentence, sees it is about the company, and moves on to the next paragraph, assuming it covers the same topic. Achievements placed after it go unread.
optionExplain: Readers scan rather than read, so full reading is not what the author expects.
Correct: the opening company sentence signals the topic, so the scanner skips ahead.
The author does not say scanners go to the stack line; his concern is results being skipped.
The author says such resumes lose attention, not that they are rejected outright for this alone.
questions.rule: Spend each entry's words on your own results, in bullets, not on the employer.

media.alt: Page two of the same resume, under a black bar headed detailed experience. Each job has title, employer, place and dates, then a paragraph describing the employer and its business, then a dashed list of responsibilities, then a stack line of technologies. The page is dense grey text with no emphasis on results.

questions.section: Remote Software Engineer With 8 Years Experience
questions.q: In the picture's experience column, jobs run from the earliest year at the top to 2020 at the bottom. How does the author judge this order?
options: It is sound, because a reader follows the career growing in the order it actually happened
It is acceptable when dates are aligned at the right and each job has a clear title
It is confusing and suggests the writer does not know basic resume conventions
It is correct only on page one, as long as page two lists the newest jobs first
questions.explain: The author criticises listing the oldest experience first on the first page: it is confusing and shows the writer is unaware of resume basics. Newest-first puts the strongest proof where a scanner looks.
optionExplain: Many people assume chronological means oldest first, but the author wants newest first.
Right-aligned dates help scanning but do not fix the order; the author still faults it.
Correct: the author calls this order confusing and a sign of ignorance of resume basics.
Mixing orders across pages is exactly the confusion the author points out, not a fix.
questions.rule: List work experience in reverse chronological order, newest first.

media.alt: Full-page template in blue and pale cyan with a round portrait photo at top left, name, contact lines and a banner offering remote work. Two columns: left holds education, profile links and an other skills list with leadership and a driving licence; right lists five employers from earliest year at the top to 2020 at the bottom, then a skills block of dot rows. Icons sit beside headings.

questions.q: Which parts of this first page does the author flag as weak for an SRE application? Relevant current technologies count as a strength.
options: A long personal profile with few specifics
A training course design skill in the key skills area
A technologies column naming current infrastructure tools
Generic phrases about interpersonal skills instead of specifics
questions.explain: The author flags the long intro with too few specifics, the training skill that does not help SRE roles, and the cliches. The up-to-date technologies were listed as a strength.
optionExplain: Flagged: the author says to trim the introduction and talk about results.
Flagged: course design is not relevant to the positions this person was applying for.
Not flagged: the author counts these technologies as a strength of the resume.
Flagged: the author says to remove such cliches or replace them with specifics.
questions.rule: Leave out intros, skills and phrases that do not help the job you want.

media.alt: Page one of an original two-page CV with a grey running header, shaded section bars and a name followed by degree letters. Below the address block is a personal profile of several prose paragraphs. Key skills sit in two columns: operating systems, training and support, programming languages and technologies. The career summary opens with the current senior role and a long list of square bullets. Dense and dated.

questions.q: In the picture, the page after the work history holds linked projects, teaching and training, and conference talks. How does the author treat them?
options: As filler like the old roles, and he would cut them to keep the resume short
As material that should move above the work history because readers prefer side projects
As useful only to a candidate with fewer than five years of professional experience
As additions that strengthen the resume, with the repositories linked and the talks closing it well
questions.explain: The author says the projects, teaching and conference talks add to the resume, with the repositories linked, and close it off strongly. Cutting targets items that do not help the job, not all extras.
optionExplain: The old roles were cut for being off-target; these items were kept because they add value.
The author does not say to reorder them above experience; they close the resume.
The author gives no such experience threshold; the section was praised for this senior candidate.
Correct: the author says projects, teaching and training add to the resume and the talks close it off.
questions.rule: Cut by relevance to the target job, keep what adds proof.

media.alt: Second page of the refactored CV. It starts with an earlier, lower-titled role at the same employer, with an earlier date range. Then education as three bold degree lines with years, a projects and community section whose open-source tools link to repositories, a teaching and training section with course topics, and a short interests list.
